  notification content is hidden when locked is an Android setting ("hide sensitive notification
  content"), off by default, and not something an app should quietly decide for you. What this does
  add is a proper redacted version for people who have turned that on: they are told a file arrived,
  without its name, instead of the blank system placeholder.
  The notification never previews the picture itself. Note this is tidiness rather than secrecy — a
  received image is added to your gallery by Android the moment it is written, whatever the
  notification does.
  (`FileHostHandler.kt`, `FileTransferNotificationManager.kt`, `FileOpener.kt`; RemEx-pwkc.)

### Fixed

- **The Wake PC quick-settings tile could only work when the PC was already awake.** It asked the PC
  to send the wake signal — which of course needs a PC that is switched on and connected, the one
  situation where nothing needs waking. And what it asked for was the PC to wake *itself*, so even
  then it did nothing. The tile offered itself as available whenever you had saved a MAC address,
  connected or not, so there was nothing to suggest it would not work.
  It now sends the wake signal from your phone, the same way the Dashboard and Remote Control buttons
  always have, and uses the broadcast address you configured rather than a fixed one. If you never
  set one, that is the same address it used before.
  (`RemexWakeOnLanTileService.kt`, `TileCommand.kt`; RemEx-wgpm.)

- **Accepting a file and then getting nothing now tells you why.** When you agreed to receive a file
  from the PC and it could not be saved, your phone said nothing at all — the reason went into a log
  on the PC, which you were never going to read. That is indistinguishable from the app being broken,
  and for a while it *was* broken in exactly that way, which is why nobody could tell the two apart.
  You now get a notification — including for the worst case, where the whole file transfers and then
  cannot be saved, which is the point you have waited longest. The one that matters most says what to
  do: if no folder on your phone is shared for writing, there is nowhere to put an incoming file, and
  it tells you to share one.
  An offer refused under a ticket your phone never issued stays silent, deliberately — nothing on your
  phone agreed to it, so there is nothing to explain, and announcing it would let a paired PC post
  notifications at you at will. Repeats of the same reason are shown once.
  (`FileHostHandler.kt`, `AndroidFileTransferHost.kt`; RemEx-gipu.)

### Changed

- **When several files are offered at once, the prompt now names all of them.** It used to list five
  and trail off with "…", while what you were agreeing to covered every file in the offer — so a
  ten-file offer asked you to approve five you could read and five you could not. How many are listed
  now depends on how long their names are rather than on an arbitrary count of five: a share of eight
  or ten camera photos is listed in full, while files with long names — screenshots, say — still run
  out of room sooner. Whenever any are left out they are now **counted** (`+3`) instead of hidden
  behind an ellipsis, so you can see how much you are not being shown.
  The prompt also scrolls now, which it did not before: a longer list used to push the "remember this"
  checkbox and the countdown off the bottom with no indication they were there.
  Both the phone and the PC word this identically, since they are describing the same offer to two
  people.
  (`FileTransferHandler.cs`, `PushConsentRegistry.kt`, `AndroidFileTransferHost.kt`; RemEx-7iub.)

### Security

- **Agreeing to receive one file no longer lets the PC send a different one.** When the PC offers your
  phone a file, your phone asks you by name and — if you accept — hands back a one-time ticket per
  file. Your phone only ever checked that the ticket was real, not that it was being used for the file
  you were shown. A PC could take the ticket you approved for a photo and use it to send something
  else entirely, and your phone would accept it without asking again.
  Each ticket is now tied to the exact file name it was issued for, and a mismatch is refused. This
  needs a PC you have already paired with to exploit, which is the same attacker the ticket check
  itself was added to stop.
  **The size you were shown is tied to the ticket as well.** Otherwise a PC could offer
  `holiday.jpg (1.0 KB)`, take the ticket you approved, and then send five gigabytes under the very
  same name — your phone had nothing to compare the claim against, because the only size it knew was
  the one the PC supplied at the last moment. It now compares against the figure you were shown, and
  a file arriving without a believable size is refused rather than being allowed to write without
  limit.
  Separately, and on the PC rather than as a defence against one: the number sent is now taken from
  the moment you were asked, so a file that changes size in between is not sent at all instead of
  arriving as something other than what you agreed to.
  One related gap is deliberately **not** closed and is tracked separately: the prompt still lists
  only the first five names when more files than that are offered, and shows one combined size rather
  than a size for each.
  (`PushConsentRegistry.kt`, `FileHostHandler.kt`, `TransferSessionManager.cs`, `PingPongHandler.cs`;
  RemEx-ccqb.)
  (`PushConsentRegistry.kt`, `AndroidFileTransferHost.kt`, `FileHostHandler.kt`; RemEx-tutz.)

### Fixed

- **A file the PC offered your phone was always refused, so nothing the PC sent ever arrived.** You
  would see the prompt asking whether to accept the file, tap Allow — and nothing happened. Every file
  was turned down immediately afterwards, silently, because the PC never said *where* on your phone to
  put it and your phone insisted on being told.
  Your phone now decides that for itself, which is the right way round: the PC has no business
  choosing folders on your phone. A pushed file goes into the first folder you shared for writing, and
  a file already there with the same name is **left alone** — the incoming one is saved beside it
  under a new name. That matters because nobody picked this folder, so a file the PC happens to name
  the same as one of yours must not be allowed to replace it.
  If you have not shared any folder that can be written to, the transfer is declined. Be aware the
  reason currently only reaches the PC's log — your phone still shows nothing either way, which is
  tracked separately.
  This is what was refusing every screenshot the PC tried to send. Whether one now arrives end to end
  has not been confirmed on a real phone yet.
  (`FileHostHandler.kt`; RemEx-h1p5.)

- **Wake-on-LAN said the wake signal was sent even when your phone could not send it.** The signal is
  a broadcast aimed at a machine that is switched off, so nothing can ever confirm the PC woke up —
  but whether the signal left your phone at all is knowable, and that was being thrown away. A saved
  MAC address in the wrong format, or a phone with no usable network connection, reported success just
  the same. The Dashboard and Remote Control screens had both been written to show a failure when one
  was reported; neither could ever show one, because a failure was never reported.
  They now do. The wording says the signal was **sent**, not that the PC woke — that part still cannot
  be known, and is not claimed.
  One thing to expect: a phone whose only network connection refuses the send has never actually been
  waking anything, and will now say so instead of claiming success. That will look like Wake-on-LAN
  breaking; it is Wake-on-LAN admitting.
  (`AndroidNativeExports.cs`, `RemexCoreClient.kt`, `WidgetCommand.kt`, `RemoteControlWidget.kt`,
  `DashboardViewModel.kt`; RemEx-52n0.)

- **Commands sent from your phone told you they worked whether or not they did.** Every command — lock,
  sleep, shut down, end a task, launch an app, take a screenshot — reported success the moment your
  phone handed it off, without waiting to hear back from the PC. A PC that had dropped off the network,
  a PC too old to understand the command, and a command the PC tried and failed to carry out all looked
  exactly like success. Ending a task was the clearest case: if the PC refused, the error was
  unreachable and you were told it had worked.
  Your phone now waits for the PC's actual answer and tells you what really happened. If the PC does
  not reply within ten seconds, that is reported as a failure rather than a success.
  The screenshot confirmation, which had to hedge and say the PC was only *asked*, now says plainly
  that the screenshot was taken — because that can finally be known.
  (`AndroidNativeExports.cs`, `RemexCoreClient.kt`, `TaskManagerViewModel.kt`; RemEx-66rf.)

- **The Quick Settings tiles could have frozen your phone once commands started waiting for a reply.**
  Seven of the eight tiles fired their command straight from the tap, on the thread that draws the
  screen — harmless while nothing waited for an answer, an "app isn't responding" freeze the moment
  something did. They now run off that thread.
  The eighth, Wake-on-LAN, was already off that thread but had a different problem: its wake was
  cancelled when the tile went away. That was a narrow window before and a wide one now that a command
  waits for the PC — tapping Wake and immediately closing the Quick Settings panel could have thrown
  the wake away. All eight now run somewhere that outlives the tile, which is what Wake-on-LAN's own
  notes had always said should happen.
  The two home-screen widgets are on the same footing: they hand the command over and tell you it was
  sent, rather than holding up the tap for a reply they have nowhere to show. When a command does fail
  from a widget or a tile, that now at least reaches the device log, which it never could before.
  (`TileCommand.kt`, `WidgetCommand.kt`, the eight tile services and both widgets; RemEx-66rf.)

### Added

- **There is now a Screenshot button on your phone, so you can actually ask for one.** The PC has been
  able to take a screenshot on request for two releases, but nothing on the phone asked it to. The
  button is on the Remote Control screen's quick-actions bar and on the Remote Desktop toolbar — in
  both the windowed toolbar and the one that floats over the picture in fullscreen, which is where you
  are when you are actually watching the PC's screen.
  A short message on either screen confirms the PC took the picture, and points you at your
  notifications. It says **taken**, not received: the PC saves it straight away, and it reaches your
  phone only once you accept the offer, so it does not claim a file you may yet decline is already
  there. (This message first shipped hedged as "asked the PC", because at the time nothing could tell
  whether the PC had really managed it — see RemEx-66rf above, which fixed that.)
  (`RemoteControlScreen.kt`, `RemoteControlViewModel.kt`, `RemoteDesktopScreen.kt`,
  `RemoteDesktopViewModel.kt`; RemEx-byij, part 3 of RemEx-86nu.)

- **A screenshot the PC takes is now offered to your phone, and sent if you accept.** A screenshot is
  whatever happened to be on the screen, so it is offered rather than pushed at you: your phone asks
  before anything is sent — unless you have previously told it to always accept files from this PC,
  in which case your earlier answer stands.
  If you decline, the picture stays saved on the PC regardless. Taking the screenshot and sending it
  are separate things, and the PC tells you the moment it has been saved rather than making you wait
  on your own answer.
  (`FilePushNegotiation.cs`, `FilePushOriginator.cs`, `TransferSessionManager.cs`, `PingPongHandler.cs`;
  RemEx-y7my, part 2 of RemEx-86nu.)

- **The phone can now ask this PC to take a screenshot.** It is saved as a PNG in a "RemEx
  Screenshots" folder inside your Pictures — where you would look for it, and where a gallery already
  indexes — named so that shots sort in the order they were taken.
  **PNG rather than JPEG**, because a screenshot is usually taken so somebody can read text off it,
  and JPEG's artefacts land hardest on exactly that. The mouse pointer is left out: it records what
  was on screen, not where the pointer happened to be.
  **It would rather give you nothing than give you something wrong.** If the display is rotated or
  resized while the picture is being taken, the result would be a skewed image that looks perfectly
  real — so it checks and refuses. If the PC hands back an older frame because the screen connection
  dropped, it refuses that too: a file saved under the time you asked for it should not be a picture
  of five minutes ago. And two screenshots taken in the same second both survive, rather than the
  second quietly replacing the first.
  It also works on displays with an odd width or height, which the first version did not — those
  machines would have failed every single screenshot.
  Getting the picture onto the phone is separate work with its own consent question, since a
  screenshot carries whatever was on the screen at the time.
  (`ScreenshotService.cs`, `PingPongHandler.cs`, `HostBootstrapper.cs`; RemEx-tjve, part 1 of
  RemEx-86nu. Next: RemEx-y7my.)

- **A "System status" card on Home that tells you whether RemEx can actually do its job.** It checks
  five things — administrator rights, the security certificate, whether RemEx is accepting
  connections, the firewall, and whether it starts when you sign in — and **stays collapsed to a
  single line when all of them are fine**, so it does not become something you learn to scroll past.
  When something is wrong it lists only what is wrong, worst first.
  **"Could not check" is treated as something worth your attention, not as good news.** A check that
  fails to run shows amber and says what that means for you, because a card that quietly rendered it
  as green would hide the first thing you would otherwise have looked at.
  The certificate row **reports and never offers to fix anything**: the only repair for a broken
  certificate would disconnect every phone you have paired, all at once. Starting at sign-in is the
  one row with a button, because that repair is local and reversible — and after you press it the
  card re-checks rather than assuming it worked.
  If the part of RemEx that does the checking is not running, the card says exactly that instead of
  disappearing — that is the situation you would have opened it to discover.
  (`SystemStatusViewModel.cs`, `SystemStatusPresentation.cs`, `HomeView.axaml`, `HomeViewModel.cs`,
  `HostBootstrapper.cs`, `CertificateService.cs`, 9 locale files; RemEx-id37.)

### Fixed

- **RemEx could miss your Pictures, Documents and Desktop folders entirely.** It looked for them by
  name next to your user folder — which is only where they are if nothing has moved them. If you use
  OneDrive's folder backup, the usual setup on a Windows PC, they live under OneDrive instead; and on
  a Linux desktop in any language other than English they have local names like *Bilder* or *Images*.
  In both cases RemEx found nothing there and simply left those folders out, so the phone could not
  browse them at all. It now asks the system where they actually are.
  **This only affects the folders RemEx picks for you the first time.** If you have used RemEx before,
  your folder list was already saved and is left alone — you can add the right folder yourself from
  the file screen.
  (`FileTransferService.cs`; RemEx-ocl9, found while reviewing RemEx-y7my.)

- **Red "danger" buttons were hard to read on three of the four themes, and the obvious fix would
  have broken the fourth.** White on the error colour measures 3.41:1 on Monolith against a readable
  minimum of 4.5:1, 3.67:1 on BaseDarkGlass, 3.88:1 on CyberNOC — and 4.83:1 on SolarFlare, the one
  theme where it was already fine.
  **Red does not follow the accent colour's answer**, which is why an earlier attempt to reuse it
  here had to be undone: on BaseDarkGlass the accent wants white and red wants dark, on SolarFlare
  the accent wants dark and red wants white, and borrowing it fails on both (3.67:1 and 3.81:1) —
  including on SolarFlare, the only theme where red was already fine. Red now has a colour of its
  own, and every theme clears the minimum, worst case 4.83:1. On SolarFlare that is the ceiling:
  nothing beats white on that particular red without changing the palette itself.
  Three bindings in these files also named a plain colour where the brush was meant. That resolved
  correctly either way — Avalonia converts one to the other when the target wants a brush — so the
  pixels are unchanged; they now match every sibling binding.
  The rule that checks for this can finally include red, because there is now something correct to
  point at. One red surface is deliberately still outside it: the canvas "Remove" button is only 15%
  red over glass, a different surface where white is *correct* on three themes and the new colour
  would be far worse — that one is filed separately with its measurements.
  (`ConfirmationDialog.axaml`, `CanvasView.axaml`, 4 theme files, `AccentForegroundContrastTests.cs`;
  RemEx-xb3c, from the RemEx-iegl review. Follow-up: RemEx-1elh.)

- **Eighteen more buttons had white text on a background that made it nearly invisible.** An earlier
  sweep fixed nine and read as though nine was all of them; review of *this* fix then found the same
  undercount again, because the ten obvious ones were only the buttons whose colours are set
  individually. Seven more take their colour from a shared style — File Transfer's four action
  buttons, the About page's two, and the canvas "Add card" — and one is the settings gear icon in the main window,
  whose glyph is drawn rather than written and so needed a different attribute again. On CyberNOC
  white on the accent colour measures 1.38:1 against a readable minimum of 4.5:1; on SolarFlare
  1.73:1. All now use the per-theme accent foreground, whose worst case across the four themes is
  5.10:1 — above the minimum on every one.
  **The two green "success" buttons turned out to be worse, and needed something of their own.** White
  fails on green in *all four* themes (2.28, 1.34, 2.02, 3.30) — and reusing the accent foreground
  would not have fixed it, because on BaseDarkGlass that token is white, correctly, for its purple
  accent. Borrowing it would have left the green button unreadable while looking fixed. Green gets
  dark text in every theme, worst case now 5.59:1.
  **The guard that was supposed to prevent this could not see it.** It read the theme files only, so
  it proved every theme *offers* a readable foreground while eighteen buttons went on ignoring it. It
  now reads the views, in both the ways a colour gets set — on the button itself, and in a shared
  style. It still cannot see a drawn icon whose colour is set separately from its button, which is
  written down rather than glossed over, along with the follow-up that would close it.
  Red buttons are deliberately left alone rather than swept in: the accent colour makes SolarFlare
  *worse* on red (4.83:1 → 3.81:1). Red is not fine, though — white on red is below the readable
  minimum on three of the four themes — it simply needs a measurement of its own, which is filed.
  (`SettingsView.axaml`, `ShellView.axaml`, `ConnectionView.axaml`, `PersonalizationPanelView.axaml`,
  `SecondMetricDialog.axaml`, `SetAlertDialog.axaml`, 4 theme files, `AccentForegroundContrastTests.cs`;
  RemEx-iegl, from the RemEx-tq2e review.)

- **A file appearing inside a folder mid-copy can no longer end up destroying the folder it landed
  in.** Copying a folder creates the destination and then copies the contents; if something dropped a
  file into that brand-new folder in the meantime, the phone was told the ordinary "already exists" —
  the one with a **Replace** button. Replace retries the *whole* copy with overwriting turned on, so
  answering a question about one stray file could overwrite a whole folder. At its worst that is the
  user's own folder: choose "keep both" onto an existing folder, let a stray file land in the new
  one, tap Replace, and the *original* folder is overwritten — the one "keep both" was chosen to
  protect.
  It now reports that the *name was taken*, which offers "keep both" and "skip" and never "replace".
  The message still names the file inside the folder, not the folder itself, so the user is looking
  at the thing that actually clashed. Trying again works: the folder gets a fresh name and the
  contents land inside it, while the half-finished folder from the failed attempt stays behind under
  the original name. One case will not resolve by trying again — copying between two drives that
  disagree about whether `README.md` and `readme.md` are the same name — and there the retries stop
  after three rounds and report an ordinary failure rather than looping.
  (`FileTransferService.cs`, `FileConflictCodeTests.cs`; RemEx-f448, from the RemEx-nhw2 review.)

- **Closed the last way "keep both" could delete the file it was asked to keep.** The host checks the
  destination just before writing, and that check reported the *ordinary* "already exists" — the one
  the phone answers with a **Replace** button. Harmless when the user named the destination; not
  harmless when "keep both" made the host invent the name, because Replace answers the *original*
  request. So the sheet would say `report (2).pdf` is taken, offer Replace, and overwrite
  `report.pdf` — the file the user chose "keep both" specifically to preserve.
  A name the host invented now always reports that the *name* was taken, which offers "keep both"
  and "skip" and never "replace", and trying again re-reads the folder and takes the next free name.
  All eight checks across copying and moving go through one place, and a test reads the source to
  make sure a future check cannot quietly go around it — nothing this suite can set up reaches that
  code path, so no ordinary test could catch a new one.
  (`FileTransferService.cs`, `FileConflictCodeTests.cs`; RemEx-nhw2, from the RemEx-2pyw review.)

- **Moving a file with "keep both" now explains itself the same way copying does.** Copy learned to
  check the name it invents before using it; move never did, so the identical request produced a
  clear, answerable message one way and the operating system's raw *"the filename, directory name, or
  volume label syntax is incorrect"* the other. The phone cannot make sense of that, so no question
  was ever put to the user for a moved file — only a failure.
  **Move is the one where getting this wrong costs the file rather than a retry**, so the check runs
  *before* anything is touched: a name that turns out to be unusable, or claimed by something else in
  the meantime, now leaves the original exactly where it was. That ordering is what the new tests
  assert, and it applies to folders as well as files, on the same drive or across two — though only
  the same-drive paths can be covered by tests, since a second volume is not something a test can
  conjure. Moving across two drives also stopped forcing an overwrite, so a name claimed at the last
  moment is refused there exactly as it already was everywhere else.
  (`FileTransferService.cs`, `FileConflictCodeTests.cs`; RemEx-2pyw, from the RemEx-mu17 review.)

- **A "keep both" name that somebody else claims first can now be answered with "keep both" again.**
  When the host picks `report (2).pdf` and another paired device — or the person sitting at the PC —
  takes that name in the moment before the copy runs, the phone used to reach a dead end: the only
  offer was Skip, and the body text blamed the name's *length*, which was not the problem. Asking
  again is what actually works here, because the host simply re-lists the folder and picks
  `report (3).pdf`.
  The obvious code for "that name is taken" could not be used, and the reason is worth recording: it
  is the code that unlocks **Replace**, and Replace answers the *original* request — overwrite the
  file the user first named — while the sheet is showing the sibling the host invented. Somebody who
  chose "keep both" precisely to preserve that file would destroy it by answering a question about a
  different one. So this is a code of its own, carrying "keep both" and "skip" and never "replace".
  Additive, with no `protocolVersion` bump and no coordinated release needed: the client already
  routes any code it does not recognise to Skip-only, so a phone that has not been updated keeps the
  previous safe behaviour instead of misreading the new one.
  **The batch loop had to change for any of this to be reachable at all.** It ran the operation,
  asked once, retried once, and threw the retry's answer away — so a refusal that can *only* happen
  on a retry was counted as a plain failure and never asked about. The conflict cycle is now a
  bounded loop that re-reads the host's answer each time, capped at three rounds because a remembered
  "apply to all" satisfies the sheet without asking, and an unbounded version could spin against
  something that keeps claiming each name the host picks.
  (`FileTransferErrorCodes.cs`, `FileConflictException.cs`, `FileTransferService.cs`,
  `FileConflictPolicy.kt`, `FileConflictSheet.kt`, `FileTransferViewModel.kt`, 9 locales;
  RemEx-od7s, from the RemEx-mu17 review.)

- **Stopped "keep both" blaming the name it chose for failures that had nothing to do with it.** The
  guard added for RemEx-cirk wrapped the *entire* operation — including a recursive copy over a whole
  tree — and translated five exception types into `resolved_name_unusable`. So a disk filling up
  partway through, a permission denial on a nested child, or a *child* path breaching the length
  limit all arrived at the phone as "the name we picked will not work", which the conflict sheet
  renders as an offer to rename. Renaming fixes none of those, so the user is handed a confident
  wrong diagnosis and a button that cannot help.
  The precondition (we chose a name) never established the attribution (this failure is *about* that
  name). Only a probe does, so the host now creates and removes the exact resolved path first and
  runs the operation unwrapped: the probe touches nothing but the name, which is what makes blaming
  the name honest — with one over-claim now stated in the code rather than hidden, since a
  volume-level refusal (a full disk, a read-only mount) also reaches the probe and is still reported
  as a name problem. Separating it would mean sniffing platform error codes, and the exposure is one
  zero-byte create rather than a whole recursive copy. There is a matching under-claim: a name that
  something else has merely *claimed* in the meantime is reported as unusable rather than taken,
  because the only existing code meaning "taken" unlocks a Replace button that would answer a
  different question and delete the file the user chose Keep both to protect. Skip-only until
  RemEx-od7s adds a code that can say "taken" and still offer Keep both.
  (`FileTransferService.cs`, `FileConflictCodeTests.cs`; RemEx-mu17, from the RemEx-cirk review.
  Follow-up: RemEx-od7s.)

- **Pinned the launch-at-login write-back guard, which a catch-up review found was protecting nothing that any test could see.** Deleting `if (_suppressLaunchAtLoginWrite) return;` restored the original defect — the first Settings open of each run re-registering the logon task with whatever `Environment.ProcessPath` happened to be — while the whole suite stayed green. The test file even declared a `Writes` list whose own comment claimed *"a redundant write cannot hide"*, **and no test ever read it**: a comment asserting coverage that did not exist, which is worse than no comment. That list is gone, and so are two tests the same review flagged as tautological — they asserted against the fake's own reimplementation of the narrowing, so no production implementation could fail them. The handler resolves its service from the static `App.Services`, so no unit test can drive it; the guards read the source instead, which this module documents as its last resort when the alternative is no test at all. **Two of the three mutants turned out to be uncompilable, which is itself the strongest result available:** removing the guard leaves the field assigned but never read, and `TreatWarningsAsErrors` refuses it — so that mutation cannot ship at all. The third, neutering the guard while still reading the field, compiles and is killed by the new test. 484 desktop tests green, zero warnings. (`StartupRegistrationReadBackTests.cs`; RemEx-p2ex, from the RemEx-h5lr review.)

- **The conflict sheet no longer tells users a file "already exists" when the real problem is that the name is too long.** A catch-up review of nine commits that had shipped without a review pass found this, and it is the defect one of those commits explicitly claims to prevent. The host began sending `resolved_name_unusable` when a "keep both" rename produces a name the destination refuses, but Android never learned the token, so it fell through to the unknown-code branch — and the sheet chose its body by testing for a single code and defaulting everything else to *"There is already a file or folder with this name."* **That is factually false**, and it was shown to someone who had just chosen Keep both, with Skip as the only button. The client now knows the code and gives it its own explanation, and an unrecognised code gets a body that says nothing about *why* — saying nothing is the only honest option when the client has no basis for a cause. **Mutation testing then corrected the fix.** An explicit policy branch for the new code was written and removed: the fallback already yields Skip, so no mutant could kill it, and an unkillable branch reads as though it decides something. The actions genuinely are identical, for a real reason — the host already tried the rename and the destination refused the name it chose, so retrying keep-both asks it to choose again from the same too-long stem, and replace was declined a moment ago. What distinguishes the codes is the *explanation*, and that mutant does die. 446 Android tests green (443 → 446); 9 locales, release build, `lintVitalRelease` and `check-localization.ps1` all clean. (`FileConflictPolicy.kt`, `FileConflictSheet.kt`, 9 × `strings.xml`; RemEx-iz6b, from the RemEx-cirk review.)

- **Reverted an accessibility regression introduced by the accent-foreground change.** `AccentForegroundBrush` was applied to four surfaces filled with **error red**, not accent — `ConfirmationDialog`'s destructive confirm and `CanvasView`'s cancel-connect, disconnect and remove buttons. Measured against the opaque error colour, SolarFlare went from **white at 4.83:1 (AA pass) to `#141414` at 3.81:1 (AA fail)**: the change made the very thing it was fixing worse, on the one theme where the original literal had been correct. The token's value on a red surface was coincidence rather than arithmetic — it was derived against `AccentPrimary` and only measured there. Those four sites are back on `White`; the five genuinely accent-filled sites keep the token. **The guard could not have caught this**, because it compares the token to each theme's accent and never looks at which surface a view actually binds it over — recorded on the follow-up bead as the rule worth encoding. (`ConfirmationDialog.axaml`, `CanvasView.axaml`; from the RemEx-tq2e review.)

- **White text on accent-filled buttons was unreadable on three of the four themes, and the fix turned out to be arithmetic rather than a design decision.** Nine call sites carried a literal `Foreground="White"` over a surface filled with the theme's accent. Measured against each theme's own `AccentPrimary`: **CyberNOC 1.38:1**, **SolarFlare 1.73:1**, **Monolith 3.65:1** — all below the WCAG AA threshold of 4.5:1, with CyberNOC's cyan-under-white barely legible — while BaseDarkGlass passes at 5.10:1. **That split is the whole point:** the correct foreground is black on three themes and white on one, so no single literal could ever have been right, which is exactly why the bead recorded this as needing a token that did not exist. What it did *not* need was taste — the value is simply whichever of black or white contrasts better, so each theme now declares `AccentForegroundBrush` with the measured answer and the nine sites bind to it. **The guard reads the theme files directly, because Avalonia hides this failure:** a `DynamicResource` that resolves to nothing is neither a compile error nor a runtime one, so a theme dropping the key would render an unstyled default silently. The test recomputes contrast from each theme's live accent rather than asserting a table, so a future accent change fails until its foreground is revisited — and a control asserts that plain white would still fail on exactly three themes, so the token cannot quietly degrade back into the literal it replaced. 1712 tests green (1709 → 1712), zero warnings. The emoji→`StreamGeometry` half of this sweep remains and is filed as **RemEx-me22**. (`CyberNOC.axaml`, `Monolith.axaml`, `SolarFlare.axaml`, `BaseDarkGlass.axaml`, `CanvasView.axaml`, `ConfirmationDialog.axaml`, `RestorePromptWindow.axaml`, `AddProgramWindow.axaml`, `AccentForegroundContrastTests.cs`; RemEx-tq2e.)

- **The PC transfer queue carries byte counts instead of throwing them away at the boundary.** `FileTransferClient` held `BytesTransferred` and `TotalBytes` and reported `bytes / total`, so a percentage was the only thing that ever crossed — **one line that discarded information nothing downstream could recover**, since speed is bytes over time and time-remaining is remaining-bytes over speed, and neither can be derived from a fraction. **It was a correctness problem independently of any display:** with every producer computing its own ratio, a producer that computed it differently — off by one, clamped, or against the wrong total — would have been invisible. The conversion now happens in exactly one place, `TransferProgress.Fraction`, and is pinned by tests. Two decisions there were chosen for the direction they fail in: **an unknown total yields zero rather than a guess**, because a streamed source has no length and inventing a fraction drives a progress bar that means nothing — the caller shows an indeterminate state, which is what "we do not know how far along this is" actually looks like; and **the fraction is clamped**, because a resumed transfer can report more bytes than the total it was told about, and a bar past 100% reads to a user as a bug in the transfer. Both are mutation-verified. The change is contained — 2 enqueue call sites, one reporting site — and behaviour is unchanged today: the queue still renders the same percentage. What it removes is the blocker. 1709 tests green (1705 → 1709), zero warnings. **This is the structural half only.** Showing speed and ETA on the PC is **RemEx-4lcq**, which is bulk localization rather than plumbing: the PC `Strings.resx` has no plural infrastructure at all, and .NET has no equivalent of Android's `<plurals>`, so Polish and Ukrainian duration words need explicit handling. (`FileTransferQueue.cs`, `FileTransferClient.cs`, `TransferProgressTests.cs`; RemEx-oiah.)

- **"Keep both" can pick a name the destination will not accept, and now says so instead of failing opaquely.** `NextAvailableName` guarantees the chosen name is *absent* from the destination; it never guaranteed it was *creatable*. The suffix lengthens the name, so one at the 255-character component limit comes back at 259 and the create fails with the OS's "filename, directory name, or volume label syntax is incorrect" — precisely the message the conflict sheet exists to replace, delivered **after** the user already chose Keep both, which is worse than delivering it before. **Reproduced before it was fixed**, which is what made this attempt work where an earlier one was reverted: a 255-character name creates fine and the same name plus `" (2)"` throws, and Windows long-path support does not help because the limit breached is the *component* limit rather than the path limit. The regression test was **red against unmodified main** with a raw `IOException` where a coded one belongs. It now carries its own code, `resolved_name_unusable`, distinct from the collision codes because re-opening the sheet would ask the user a question they have already answered — and the only answer that could work is the one they declined. **The wrapper covers only the renamed case:** when the destination is the one the caller asked for, an `IOException` means whatever it has always meant, and this code asserts "the name *we* chose is unusable", which can only be true when we chose one. No clamp was added inside the naming function, deliberately — a correct clamp needs destination knowledge it refuses to guess, since ext4 counts 255 *bytes* rather than characters and exFAT and CIFS differ again. Two mutants, two killed, each with its anchor confirmed applied — the earlier revert was triggered by mutants that silently never applied, so "survived" had been a false signal. 1705 tests green (1703 → 1705), zero warnings. (`FileTransferErrorCodes.cs`, `FileConflictException.cs`, `FileTransferService.cs`, `FileConflictCodeTests.cs`; RemEx-cirk.)

- **The firewall row asked whether *our* rule exists, when the question is whether *anything* permits the app.** It queried two rule names the installer creates, so a machine where those were deleted reported "the firewall is refusing inbound traffic" while the app was in fact fully permitted. **Measured rather than argued:** the test machine carries two GUID-named "Query User" rules — created when a user clicks through the Windows allow-access prompt — covering the agent alongside the two named ones. Four rules permit it; the old check could see two. **The obvious widening does not work, and measuring that first is what saved the change.** `Get-NetFirewallApplicationFilter -Program <path>` matches the *stored string literally*: 299 of 810 filters on that machine store an unexpanded path, and querying the expanded form of one returned **zero** matches where the stored form returned 188. Since `Environment.ProcessPath` is expanded, that filter would have silently missed every such rule — reintroducing the same false alarm one layer down. The query now enumerates and expands each stored path with the OS's own resolver, compares case-insensitively (the prompt-created rules store a lowercased path, so an ordinal compare would miss exactly the rules this exists to find), and skips outbound rules, which cannot permit or refuse an inbound connection. Cost measured at ~550 ms, on an on-demand check that already spawns PowerShell. **It also subsumes RemEx-zmco's fix with a better mechanism:** that one had to inspect `CategoryInfo.Category` to tell "this rule does not exist" from "reading it failed", because both arrived as exceptions from the same call. Enumeration makes them structurally distinct — a rule that does not cover us is simply not enumerated and raises nothing, while a failure to enumerate produces `RULEFAIL` — so nothing has to classify an exception to keep them apart. Verified end to end against the real firewall; four mutants, four killed. 1703 tests green (1700 → 1703), zero warnings. (`FirewallQuery.cs`, `FirewallReadinessTests.cs`; RemEx-4ycq.)

- **Two concurrent commands can no longer have their answers swapped.** When a host echoed no correlation id, the client resolved the *first* pending command — and the code's own comment admitted it was "best-effort and incorrect under concurrency". Two commands in flight at once is ordinary rather than exotic: a widget action landing while a task-manager kill runs. Their responses could be exchanged, so the kill would report the widget's result. **A wrong answer delivered confidently is worse than no answer**, because the caller acts on it. **The unambiguous case is deliberately kept.** An uncorrelated response with exactly *one* command pending has nothing to be confused with, and it is what an older host that never echoed the id produces in the ordinary sequential case — dropping it would break those hosts for no gain. Only the ambiguous case goes. **And an unattributable response is dropped, not broadcast:** failing every pending command would be a guess in the other direction, since some may still receive a correctly correlated answer, so cancelling them would invent a failure. The existing per-command timeout reports honestly that nothing came back. All four host send sites already echo the id (verified in `PingPongHandler`), so no host change was needed and the client stays tolerant of older ones. Three mutants, three killed — restoring the first-pending fallback, never resolving an uncorrelated response, and ignoring a correlated one. 1700 tests green (1693 → 1700), zero warnings.

### Removed

- **`MessageTypes.DesktopFrame`**, a wire constant with zero references outside its own declaration — frames went binary (`DesktopFrameEnvelope`) long ago. Not a wire change, since nothing sent or matched it; the point is that the message table stops advertising a type the protocol no longer has. (`RemexMessage.cs`; RemEx-s8h8.)

- **Written artefacts stopped being pointed at a gitignored directory.** Several beads named `docs/superpowers/specs/` as the home for their spec or spike output, and that path is ignored (`.gitignore:119`, under `# Misc`) — so anything written there is never committed. The task closes, the author believes the artefact exists, and the repo has nothing; the next person finds a closed bead referencing a file that is not in the tree. **It looks like the right home right up until it isn't:** the directory exists locally and already holds a dozen earlier specs, so it genuinely is the precedent — those files are simply untracked too — and nothing warns you at write time. You find out when `git add` silently stages nothing. This caught three separate spikes before it was recognised as a pattern. **Resolved by moving the convention rather than un-ignoring the directory**, which was a real choice and not an obvious one: `docs/superpowers/` also holds a `plans/` tree and a body of historical scratch that un-ignoring would sweep in wholesale, while `docs/` is already the convention by weight — `SPIKE-monitor-brightness.md`, `SPIKE-privacy-curtain-mode.md`, `SPIKE-host-audio-streaming.md` and `MEASURE-font-and-dependency-diet.md` all live there and are all tracked (verified, not assumed). The three beads still naming the old path were corrected, and `CLAUDE.md` now states the convention plus the check that would have caught it: after writing an artefact, confirm it is actually tracked. A closed bead pointing at an untracked file is worse than one that admits it produced nothing. (`CLAUDE.md`; RemEx-0l9x.)

- **A stalled transfer no longer sits there claiming a speed.** The rate estimator only advances when a progress frame arrives, so when bytes stopped — radio dropped, PC asleep, host wedged — the last figure stayed on screen indefinitely while the ETA silently became fiction. A user watching "12.4 MB/s · 38 seconds left" on a transfer that died five minutes ago is being *actively misinformed*, which is worse than the percentage-only display this replaced. **The existing 1 KB/s stall floor could never catch it**, and the reason is worth recording: that floor fires as the average *decays*, and decay needs samples — which is precisely what a stall stops delivering, so the estimate froze rather than falling. **Ageing at READ time is the only shape that stays honest without a timer somebody has to remember to cancel**, and it makes the display going blank the signal that nothing is arriving, rather than a number that quietly stopped being true. The threshold is derived rather than picked: four time constants, by which point the exponential weighting has forgotten ~98% of what the figure was built from — twenty seconds at the default, long enough that an ordinary gap between irregular chunks does not flicker the display, short enough that a dead transfer stops claiming a speed while the user is still watching. Speed and time-remaining age together, because two figures disagreeing about whether the transfer is alive would be worse than either alone. **The fix also separated the arithmetic from the display**, which is what made it tractable: the raw average is now `internal` and explicitly not for rendering — it is *correct*, it is simply about a moment that has passed, and clearing it would destroy the baseline a resumed transfer smooths from. Four mutants, four killed: the staleness check removed, the ETA not aged with the speed, staleness measured from the first sample instead of the last, and the threshold collapsed to half a time constant (which the "ordinary gap" test catches). 442 Android tests green (436 → 442); release build and `lintVitalRelease` clean. (`TransferRateEstimator.kt`, `FileTransferEngine.kt`, `FileTransferViewModel.kt`, `TransferRateEstimatorTest.kt`; RemEx-8c3v.)

- **A firewall rule that could not be READ is no longer reported as a firewall that is REFUSING.** The Windows query wrapped each rule lookup in a `catch{}` that swallowed every failure identically, so "this rule does not exist" and "reading this rule failed" both produced no record — and no records is what the interpreter reads as a definite refusal. If both lookups failed for a reason other than absence (a broken NetSecurity module, a CIM failure, an EDR blocking the cmdlet) the completion sentinel still printed, the parse yielded nothing, and a query that established **nothing at all** was rendered to a non-technical user as "the firewall is refusing inbound traffic on 5005 — the phone cannot reach this PC". That is the same failed-query-as-verdict class the sentinel fixed, one level down. **The premise was verified on a real machine rather than assumed**, which the bead explicitly asked for: `Get-NetFirewallRule` reports a missing rule as `ObjectNotFound` — and so does a malformed name, which is also genuinely not-found — so the script now marks only categories that are *not* `ObjectNotFound`, and a marked run declines to conclude. Absence keeps mapping to a refusal, which matters because a missing rule is the most likely real breakage: `autostart-remex.ps1` wraps its firewall step in a catch that only warns. **Mutation testing found the guard unpinned where it first lived** — inline in a private, Windows-gated method, so deleting it changed nothing any test could see, the third instance of that shape in this area — so the decision is now one internal function covering both ways of having learned nothing, and deleting it fails a test. Three mutants, three killed: the guard removed, the marker matched as a substring, and the script marking absence as failure. 1693 tests green (1690 → 1693), zero warnings. (`FirewallQuery.cs`, `FirewallReadinessTests.cs`; RemEx-zmco.)

- **The launch-at-login switch could show "off" for a PC whose autostart is registered and working — and it is also the control that writes.** The bead described it as write-only; it is actually seeded at load, and the two defects that produced were both worse than a stale label. **First, an unanswerable query was reported as "not registered".** `IsEnabled()` ends in `catch { return false; }`, so an EDR blocking `schtasks`, an unavailable Task Scheduler endpoint or an unreadable `~/.config/autostart` all rendered as a confident "off" — and because the switch writes, a user correcting that false negative issues a real registration against a state nobody established. `SystemReadinessProbe` already documents this exact swallowing as the reason its autostart probe takes a `bool?`; the service now offers `TryIsEnabled()`, and the UI says **"RemEx could not check…"** in a warning row rather than asserting either state. **Second, seeding the toggle wrote straight back.** Assigning the observable property fires its change handler, which calls `SetEnabled` — so the first Settings open of each app run rewrote an already-registered logon task with whatever `Environment.ProcessPath` was at that moment (later opens reuse a cached ViewModel, and seeding `false → false` is a no-op, so it is once per run rather than every trip). The neighbouring keep-session-unlocked toggle has had a suppression guard since RemEx-l6o; launch-at-login did not, and now does. **Mutation testing caught the first version of the tests verifying nothing.** They exercised a fake `IStartupRegistrationService`, so inverting the *production* exit-code mapping — making a failed query report "not registered" — changed nothing any test could see; a test that exercises a stand-in verifies the stand-in. The mapping (`0` → registered, `1` → not, anything else → unknown) and the narrowing direction are now pure, `internal`, and pinned: **unknown must narrow to `false`, never `true`**, because claiming autostart is set up on a machine where nothing established that is the one failure the whole read-back exists to catch, and the user would find out at the next reboot. **Review then caught the same gap a second time, in the desktop half.** Those tests asserted against a private reimplementation of the seeding rule inside the test file, so deleting the suppression guard, or making unknown assert "off", left the whole suite green. The rule is now `internal static` production code that the test calls, and both mutants die. Review also found the warning row placed *after* the switch while all nine translations say "the switch below", and gated only by coincidence — it now sits above it inside the same gated panel, matching the keep-session-unlocked block. Six mutants, six killed. 1689 tests (1677 → 1689), plus one pre-existing skip, zero warnings; 9 locales, `check-localization.ps1` clean; the warning row uses the `SystemWarningBrush` token, verified present in all four PC themes. The Home status card itself is **RemEx-id37**. (`IStartupRegistrationService.cs`, `StartupRegistrationService.cs`, `SettingsViewModel.cs`, `SettingsView.axaml`, `StartupRegistrationReadBackTests.cs`, `SchtasksExitInterpretationTests.cs`, 9 × `Strings*.resx`; RemEx-h5lr.)

### Added

- **Copying onto a name that is taken now asks, instead of failing with a message nobody can act on.** A filename collision used to end the operation with English prose; there is now a sheet offering **Replace / Keep both / Skip**, with "Apply to all remaining" for a batch. It is built on the codes the host started sending — the client branches on `errorCode`, never on the message, because the prose is destined to be translated and matching it would work today and silently stop working later. **The decisions live apart from the sheet, because that is where a mistake costs a file.** Which buttons appear is a pure function, mutation-verified, and three of its rules are ones a screenshot could not reveal. **A different-kind collision never offers Replace** — there the destination is the *other* kind of thing, so replacing means deleting a whole directory tree for one file, or deleting a file to create a folder; the host refuses it outright, but the reason the button is withheld is that it should never have been offered. **An unrecognised code offers only Skip**, since a newer host may send one and guessing which actions it permits is exactly how a client offers a destructive button for a situation it does not understand. And **mkdir offers only Skip**, because the host emits a code there but accepts no resolution — Replace and Keep both would re-fail identically, trapping the user in a loop answering the same question forever. **Fail-closed everywhere it is ambiguous:** a swipe-down, a back press and a tap outside all resolve to Skip, and a dismissal is always treated as a one-off rather than as an answer for the whole batch, so a stray gesture cannot skip everything. **The apply-to-all answer is scoped to its batch by construction** — it lives in a `BatchConflictChoice` created and destroyed inside the loop, not on the ViewModel where forgetting to clear it would overwrite a file in some later, unrelated copy. **And a standing answer is still checked against each collision:** someone who chose "Replace, apply to all" for a run of ordinary collisions has not agreed to destroy a directory tree when the next item turns out to be a different kind of thing, so the remembered answer is discarded and the question asked again. A skip is counted apart from a failure, because reporting a deliberate choice as an error tells the user something went wrong when they chose it; and when the host renames for "Keep both" it says so, since a rename that succeeded silently leaves them believing they have `report.pdf` when the file is `report (2).pdf`. **Review caught the sheet contradicting its own comment: Replace was rendered FIRST.** Its emphasis had been de-weighted, but position is the stronger recommendation and the top button is the one a hurried user taps — and the test asserted that order, cementing it. Keep both is now first, with a swept assertion that Replace is never first for any code or operation. Two more defects came from the same pass, both about a status line nobody would see: `_statusText` is a conflated StateFlow rendered into one label, so the per-item "Saved as report (2).pdf" was overwritten by the batch summary with no suspension in between — **never visible at all for a single-file copy, which is the common case and the exact guarantee the bead asked for** — and skips were subtracted out of both numerator and denominator, so a batch where the user skipped everything reported "Deleted 0 items" with nothing saying their own choice was why. **A second round caught the first attempt at that merely RELOCATING it:** the mid-loop writes were folded into one terminal write that `browseRemote()` — which clears `_statusText` synchronously — then discarded one line later, so the summary was still never rendered, for any batch. The browse now runs first and the summary is written after it. The same round found the summary borrowing the delete-specific wording, so an all-skipped copy read **"Deleted 0 items"** — a file manager that also deletes telling the user it deleted files it never touched; copy and move now have their own words. And it proved the guard for this very defect **vacuous**: it asserted only that the file contained `batchSummary(`, which reinstating a mid-loop write left passing. It now asserts position and uniqueness — exactly two status writes, and the browse before the summary — and fails against that reinstated write. Review also found the standing answer checked against a hardcoded `COPY`, harmless only because copy and move share a rule today — which is precisely why it would have survived until they stopped sharing one. **And it found everything outside the pure policy untested**, including three rules stated here as guarantees; those now have source-reading guards, this module's documented last resort when the alternative is no test at all, with comments stripped so a guard cannot pass on prose describing the rule. Two safety gaps closed on the way: a prompt token, so a torn-down sheet's last dismissal cannot silently skip the NEXT file's prompt, and a `finally` so a disconnect mid-sheet does not strand the spinner up forever. Mutation-checked rather than tallied: the seven policy mutants above, plus dismissal-answers-Replace, dismissal-applies-to-all, first-attempt-pre-answers, canApply-hardcodes-COPY and the reinstated mid-loop status write — each named in the test it fails, since a bare count leaves no artifact a later reviewer can re-run. 436 Android tests green (414 → 436); 9 locales, release build, `lintVitalRelease` and `check-localization.ps1` all clean. (`FileConflictPolicy.kt`, `FileConflictSheet.kt`, `FileConflictPolicyTest.kt`, `FileConflictWiringTest.kt`, `FileTransferViewModel.kt`, `FileTransferScreen.kt`, 9 × `strings.xml`; RemEx-agpn.)

- **A filename collision is now something a client can act on, rather than English prose it would have to string-match.** The host reported these as `errorMessage` — "A file named 'report.pdf' already exists." — which is the only signal a phone had. Matching that breaks the moment the wording improves and cannot work at all once the host is localized, which is a stated goal. So collisions now carry an `errorCode` (`destination_exists`) alongside the unchanged prose, plus the bare `conflictingName` so a sheet can say *which* file it is asking about without leaking the host's directory layout. **The bead's own warning was about sequencing, and it was earned:** an `errorCode` field was written during RemEx-12cj and reverted before commit because it would have shipped unset — the same shape as RemEx-mneb, where a message type is declared and round-trip tested while nothing ever sets it. So the field arrives with its sender in the same change: a typed `FileConflictException` thrown from `FileTransferService` and unwrapped in the handler's catch, verified both against a real temp directory and — after review showed the first was not enough — against the actual `FileManageResponse` that goes on the wire, which is the only test that fails when the assignment itself is removed. **There are two codes, not one, and the difference decides which buttons a client may offer.** `destination_is_different_kind` means the destination is taken by the OTHER KIND of thing — a folder where a file was going, or a file where a folder was going. "Keep both" is still valid, but "replace" would mean destroying the other kind to make room: deleting a whole directory tree for one file, or deleting a file to create a folder. Neither is an outcome anyone intends from a copy and nothing undoes either, so a client treating the two codes alike would offer that button. It is emitted on all four copy/move direction pairs and on mkdir blocked by a file — the mkdir case and the folder-onto-file copy were both found by review, the first reporting the plain code and the second carrying none at all. **The host also gained the one resolution a client cannot perform itself.** `conflictResolution: "keep_both"` makes the host pick the next free `name (n).ext` and report it back as `resolvedName`; the phone must never compose that name, because the host may choose differently — leaving the user shown one filename and given another — or the guess collides again and fails with the same opaque error the feature exists to remove. Only the host can see what else is in that directory, **and only the host knows whether its own filesystem is case-sensitive**: on Windows `Report.pdf` and `report.pdf` are one file, on Linux two, so a single rule is wrong on one platform. That is pinned by a matched pair of tests. Four decisions were chosen for the direction they fail in and each is mutation-verified: a **null resolution changes nothing**, which is the compatibility guarantee for every phone that predates the field; **keep-both never overwrites** even when the legacy `overwrite` flag also says to, because the two can disagree and only one reading preserves the file the user asked to keep; an **unrecognised resolution falls back to the refusal**, since the two things it might mean are the two outcomes a user would most want to be asked about; and **exhausting all 10,000 suffixes falls back to the refusal too**, rather than overwriting or appending a name that collides anyway. **Review then found a real path-escape in the new code, which is the finding most worth recording.** `ResolveWithinRoot` deliberately maps `""`, `"/"`, `"."` and `"x/.."` to *the root itself* — all legitimate ways to name it — and the root's **parent** is outside the share. So a `keep_both` against `"/"` renamed a sibling of the share: a copy wrote a stray file next to it, and a move relocated the entire tree out of it. The property the caller had enforced ("the destination is inside the root") does not imply the one the rename needed ("the destination's *parent* is inside the root"), so containment is now re-established rather than inherited — and the test that was supposed to guard this asserted the wrong invariant, checking that the sibling stayed in the destination's directory, which held while the bug was live because that directory was already outside the root. Review also caught the reverse different-kind case reporting the plain code, and one collision path — a folder copied onto an existing file — carrying no code at all. **And it caught the sender itself being unpinned:** deleting all three response assignments left the entire suite green, because every other test asserted against the service rather than the wire — the exact class of gap the bead's warning is about, one layer up. Eleven mutants, eleven killed, each named in the tests they fail: null-resolution-defaults-to-replace, keep-both-honours-overwrite, unrecognised-falls-through, case-insensitive-token-match, exhausted-suffix-forced, always-report-resolved-name, root-guard-removed, containment-as-plain-StartsWith, and the three response assignments. **And a data-loss asymmetry between copy and move.** Moving a folder onto an existing file honoured `overwrite` by *deleting the user's file* to make room for the directory, while copy refused the same request outright — so one request destroyed data on one path and was rejected on the other. Move now refuses too. The bead's own principle is that the host decides rather than trusting the client to withhold a button, and for an unrecoverable delete of a different kind of thing, refusing is the only reading that cannot lose data. 1677 tests green (1640 → 1677), zero warnings. The sheet itself — Replace / Keep both / Skip with apply-to-all, fail-closed on dismiss, 9 locales — is **RemEx-agpn**, which carries the full wire contract so it is UI and wiring only. (`FileTransferErrorCodes.cs`, `FileConflictException.cs`, `ConflictResolutionPlan.cs`, `FileTransferService.cs`, `FileTransferHandler.cs`, `FileTransferMessages.cs`, `IFileTransferService.cs`, `ConflictResolverTests.cs`, `FileConflictCodeTests.cs`, `FileTransferHandlerTests.cs`, `FakeFileTransferService.cs`; RemEx-6vd8.)

- **A transfer now says how fast it is going and how long is left, instead of only how far along it is.** A 4 GB copy showing a percentage is an anxiety exercise: the number the user actually wants is the one that lets them decide whether to wait. The arithmetic shipped earlier as `TransferRateEstimator`; this is the half where the decisions live. **The estimator returns numbers on purpose and this layer still does not return text** — it picks the *unit* and the *rounding*, which are decisions rather than translations, and stops there. That split is load-bearing rather than tidy: byte-rate symbols are not universal (Ukrainian writes МБ/с, French Mo/s), and second/minute/hour take four plural forms in Polish and Ukrainian, so any function returning a finished string would have to be wrong in at least one of the nine shipped languages. Rendering uses `getQuantityString` with real `<plurals>`, and formats the number against **the locale the resources resolved in** rather than `Locale.getDefault()` — `"%.1f".format(x)` reads the system default, so a French-in-app user on an English phone would have got "12.4 Mo/s" with the wrong separator in the middle of a correctly translated sentence. **The subtle rule is that the ETA is rounded up and bucketed in that order.** Bucket first and 59.6 seconds renders as "60 seconds left", a unit nobody writes; round to nearest instead of up and the display reaches zero while the transfer is still running, which reads as a stuck progress bar rather than a rounding artefact. Both orderings are pinned by mutants that fail. **Three states where the honest answer is to show nothing:** under a second is "Finishing…" rather than "0 seconds left", which reads as a completed transfer that visibly has not completed; an unknown rate stays unknown rather than becoming "0 B/s", because one is a claim about the transfer and the other is a claim about us; and **an ETA beyond 23 hours is refused outright** — the estimator already declines to divide by a rate under 1 KB/s, but a very large file at a rate just above that floor still yields days, and "3 days remaining" that becomes "2 minutes" once the radio wakes is exactly the number the parent bead ruled out, because a user plans around it. The largest figure the display can produce is deliberately **23 hours, not 24**: "24 hours" is a quantity nobody writes — at that size a person says "a day" — and it would sit exactly on the refusal boundary, so an estimate jittering across it would alternate between a number and nothing. Fed `SystemClock.elapsedRealtime()`, never wall-clock time: an NTP correction steps a wall clock backwards and the estimator correctly refuses the sample, so the failure mode would not be a wrong speed but a silently absent one. **Review caught that the first version was wired into the dead v2 fallback path** — `FileTransferHandler` sets `Binary = true` unconditionally, so every transfer against any current host goes through `FileTransferEngine`, and the estimator had been attached to the legacy base64 branch that nothing reaches. The whole feature was unreachable, and two of the three surfaces the bead named had been skipped outright. It now lives on the engine's per-frame funnel, with the rate held **beside** the persisted queue rather than inside it — the queue model is serialized on every state transition, and a throughput figure is the one thing here that is meaningless the moment it is reloaded. Cleanup hangs off the single `updateState` funnel rather than eleven terminal call sites, because the engine is a process-lifetime singleton and a per-site version would leak one estimator per finished transfer for as long as the app runs. **Review also found both sweep tests could not fail:** a `*= 1.05` step walks 57.41 → 60.28 and 3456 → 3629, stepping over every boundary it claimed to guard, and it passed with the bucket-first bug installed. Rebuilt around explicit boundary samples, it now kills that mutant. 414 Android tests green (397 → 414); release build, `lintVitalRelease` and `check-localization.ps1` all clean across 9 locales. One honest limitation is filed rather than hidden (**RemEx-8c3v**): the estimator only advances when a frame arrives, so a truly stalled transfer freezes its last figures on screen instead of clearing them. **PC parity was checked and is not reachable, which is filed rather than skipped (RemEx-oiah):** the desktop queue transports a single `IProgress<double>` fraction and never sees byte counts, so speed and ETA are not derivable there without changing the progress contract at every enqueue site. (`TransferProgressFormat.kt`, `TransferProgressText.kt`, `TransferProgressFormatTest.kt`, `TransferRateEstimator.kt`, `FileTransferEngine.kt`, `FileTransferJobService.kt`, `FileManagerQueuePanel.kt`, `FileTransferNotificationManager.kt`, `FileTransferViewModel.kt`, 9 × `strings.xml`; RemEx-qmiv.)

- **The readiness card can no longer show all-green on a machine the phone cannot reach.** A green port-listening row means *the server is up* — it says nothing about whether anything can reach it, because the firewall sits between the listener and the phone. That gap was the card's one remaining way to be confidently wrong, and it was the exact support case the card exists to prevent. There is now a firewall row, and blocked is a **Problem rather than a Warning**: the connection does not degrade, it fails the same way an offline PC does. **The design problem worth recording is localization.** The obvious Windows implementation parses `netsh advfirewall show rule`, whose field names and values are translated on a localized Windows — so it would silently stop working in eight of the nine languages this app ships in. The escape is that `autostart-remex.ps1` creates its rules with `-Name RemexHostInbound` / `-Name RemexClientInbound` and `-DisplayName "RemEx"`: the **Name is ours and is never translated**, the DisplayName is what the UI and netsh print. The check queries by Name and reads no *localized* output — it parses only a `RULE|…` record format this app defines itself. firewalld has the same trap and the same escape — its messages go through gettext, its **exit codes do not** — so that branch reads `firewall-cmd --state` and `--query-port` exit codes only. **Four Windows states that all look configured and permit nothing** are each pinned: no rule at all (a definite refusal, not an unknown — Windows denies unsolicited inbound by default, and this is where a machine lands when the installer's firewall step failed, which the script only warns about and carries on from); a rule present but **switched off**, which a user reaches through the Windows UI without deleting anything; an enabled **Block** rule, which Windows evaluates ahead of Allow, so an "any rule allows" test would report green on a machine provably refusing us; and the drift case — a rule that survives an update which moved the install directory, still enabled, still allowing, scoped by `-Program` to a file that no longer runs. **Two honest Unknowns rather than guesses, which is most of the Linux story.** `ufw status` requires root and the Linux agent is an unprivileged user process by design (the same fact that gives Linux no elevation row at all), so the row reads `ufw.conf` instead: that file is world-readable and says whether ufw is filtering *at all*, while the rules live in root-only `user.rules`. Disabled is therefore a definite yes and **enabled is Unknown** — guessing "allowed" there would show green on exactly the machines most likely to be blocking, since a user who turned ufw on is the user whose phone cannot connect. Likewise **neither manager present is Unknown, not Ok**: a machine can filter with bare nftables and this process cannot see it. **Mutation testing deleted two branches rather than confirming them, and that is the technique's most useful output here.** An explicit comment-skipping guard in the ufw parser could not be killed by any mutant, because anchoring the match to the start of a trimmed line already excludes comments; a line-level `Trim` in the Windows record parser could not be killed either, because the output is CRLF, so the stray carriage return lands *inside the last field* where the program-scope normalizer trims it anyway. Both were dead code that would have read to a later maintainer as load-bearing. The tests they came from survive and earn their places against the mutants that *are* load-bearing — the `Contains("ENABLED=no")` parse that reads ufw's own documentation as its configuration, and reads it as the green answer; and the normalizer's trim, whose removal would leave every program path ending in `\r` and fail every comparison against the running executable. Every judgement here was mutation-checked rather than assumed green — the named mutants above are the re-runnable record, since a raw tally of "N killed" leaves no artifact a later reviewer can check — and every run asserted at build exit 0 — a discipline that earned itself here, since the first batch reported three meaningless build failures caused by `git checkout` being unable to revert an *untracked* file, so the mutants had silently accumulated. **Mutation testing of pure logic proved insufficient, and review is what caught it: the entire Windows execution path was dead.** The script was passed as a `-Command "…"` argument, and `powershell.exe` argv-parses its own command line and strips the inner quotes — so `Write-Output "RULE|…"` arrived unquoted, failed to *parse* before the `try`/`catch` could run, and exited non-zero. The branch correctly read that as "could not check", so the row degraded to permanently amber and looked like cautious design rather than a bug, while thirteen green unit tests covered code the product never executed. It now uses `-EncodedCommand`, which is right by construction rather than right if every escape is. Two more defects came out of the same review, both invisible to the unit tests because they were about the shape of the *real* data: `Get-NetFirewallApplicationFilter` returns the literal string **`"Any"`** for an unscoped rule — never null — so the null check could never fire from a live query, and the path comparison instead matched `"Any"` against the executable, failed, and reported "the firewall is refusing inbound traffic" for a rule that permits everything (104 such rules on the test machine); and the block-rule check ignored program scope while the allow check required it, so a **stale block rule** left pointing at an old install directory — the very drift the allow path is written to survive — reported a refusal Windows was never applying. Also fixed: `ReadToEnd()` ran before `WaitForExit` with stderr redirected and never drained, the classic pipe deadlock, which made the five-second timeout unreachable — both pipes are now drained on background threads. **A second review round then found the same defect one layer deeper, which is the finding most worth keeping:** the branch now *ran*, but its verdict still could not get out. `powershell.exe`'s exit code reflects **the success of the last statement executed**, not whether any error record was produced along the way — so a handled error partway through exits 0 while a failure in the final statement exits 1. The exit-code gate therefore failed exactly when the *last* rule queried was missing and passed when the first was: **a verdict that depended on the order of the rule names**, which is worse than a consistent failure because it turned the state the row exists for into "could not check" only some of the time. That is precisely the state the row exists for: the installer's firewall step failing is the most likely real breakage, since `autostart-remex.ps1` only warns and carries on. The card went amber on the one machine it should have gone red on, and the partial case discarded a rule that had been read successfully. The script now emits a completion sentinel and the gate reads that instead — the distinction it actually wants is "did the script reach the end", which no exit code can express. **Verified across all three configurations on a real Windows 11 machine**, not only the convenient one: both rules present, one present and one absent, and both absent each produce the sentinel with 2, 1 and 0 rule records — so "no rule at all" now reaches the interpreter and reports Problem, where before it was unreachable from production. 38 new tests; 1640 green (1602 → 1640), zero warnings. **Windows-verified only:** the Linux branch's two factual assumptions — unprivileged `firewall-cmd` exit codes, and `ufw.conf` being world-readable — plus firewalld's zone semantics are filed as **RemEx-oxjm**, with the fix scoped to fact-gathering rather than to the tested interpretation. Two known false-alarm sources are filed rather than papered over: **RemEx-4ycq** — only our two rule names are queried, so a user who allowed the app through the Windows prompt instead has a working GUID-named rule this check cannot see; and **RemEx-zmco** — the per-rule `catch` cannot tell "this rule is absent" from "reading this rule failed", and only the first should report a refusal. (`FirewallReadiness.cs`, `FirewallQuery.cs`, `SystemReadiness*.cs`; RemEx-ksbm.)

- **The Android keyboard edit diff is now written down, before anything replaces it.** RemEx-iyn2 plans to delete `applyRemoteKeyboardEdit` in favour of `InputTransformation`, which hands you the edit deltas the diff reconstructs by hand. That is the right move — but the bead's own acceptance criterion is that IME behaviours the diff special-cases still map to the same host events, and **nobody had recorded what those mappings actually are**. Migrating against an unspecified target is a rewrite, not a migration, so this ships the BEFORE half: 19 characterization tests covering swipe commits, autocorrect word replacement, multi-line and trailing-newline commits, selection replacement and selection deletion, mid-string deletion, caret normalization, the returned value, the hidden buffer cap, composition passthrough, and the send-something-or-nothing invariant. **Writing them corrected a wrong assumption on the first try, which is the argument for the file existing.** Autocorrect `"teh " → "the "` emits **two** backspaces and the text `"he"`, not one and `"h"`: prefix and suffix each match exactly one character, and because positions 1 and 2 are transposed neither match extends. Three more facts that a reading would not have produced: newlines cannot ride inside a text event, so `"one\ntwo"` is text/ENTER/text with ENTER **between** the lines and never after the last; a mid-string deletion costs exactly **one** backspace, where prefix-only matching would cost four events; and `"aa" → "aaa"` resolves the insertion at the END, unobservable for repeated characters and pinned so nobody spends time "fixing" it. Where current behaviour is arguable it is pinned anyway and labelled — the migration's job is to be equivalent first and better second, because a keystroke path that changes silently is one nobody notices until they are typing a password into a remote machine. **Review caught the file's own worst gap, which is worth recording because it is the failure mode characterization tests are most prone to:** the caret test compared the returned value's selection against its own text length — two properties of the same object — so it was satisfied by any self-consistent return, including one that discarded the edit entirely and handed back the old text. That mutant passed all 13 original tests. It now kills 6. The returned value is not decoration: callers assign it back to their state, so it is the baseline the next diff runs against, and a migration that got it wrong would send the right events once and then corrupt every keystroke after it. Two more unpinned behaviours came out of the same pass — the **256-character buffer cap** (nothing came close to reaching it — the longest string literal across all 378 pre-existing Android tests is 108 characters, and no other test file uses `repeat` at all — so a migration could drop it and let the buffer grow for a whole session while every test stayed green) and **composition passthrough**, deliberately suppressing the trim mid-word so the IME is not left pointing at offsets that no longer exist. **Round 2 caught the same class of defect inside a round-1 fix,** which is the honest record of how hard this is to get right: the new trim test used `"x".repeat(300)`, and for a uniform string `takeLast(128)` and `take(128)` are the same value — so it pinned that a trim *happens* while saying nothing about *which half survives*, and keeping the wrong half is worse than keeping none. The fixture is now non-uniform, and both over-limit cases also assert the host still received all 300 characters, since a trim that shortened what was *sent* would drop text off the far end. Mutation-verified rather than assumed green: seven mutants, seven killed, all at zero compile errors — removing suffix matching kills 2, collapsing the newline split kills 2, discarding the edit kills 6, dropping the cap kills 1, dropping the composition kills 2, keeping the wrong half kills 1, and drifting the boundary from `<=` to `<` kills 1. 397 Android tests green (378 → 397), release build and `lintVitalRelease` clean. No production code changed.
