The bundle exists so a user can send their logs to someone who can read them, which is precisely the shape of accident that leaks a secret: the user is being helpful, the recipient may be a public issue tracker, and nobody reads 500 lines of logcat before pressing send. **Redacted always:** base64 runs of 40 or more — both the SPKI pin and the PAIR-1 reconnect secret are base64 of 32 bytes, and the secret is the one that matters because it ANSWERS the host's proof-of-possession challenge — and absolute file paths, reduced to their basename, since a failed transfer naming `C:\Users\Connor\Documents\tax-2025.pdf` says more about the person than the bug. **Redacted unless the user opts in:** addresses, because a network bug is often unreadable without them — but the toggle is off by default and releases ONLY addresses, so a user who wanted their IP included has not thereby agreed to mail their reconnect secret. **Two design points are load-bearing and both are pinned by tests that fail without them.** Keys are scrubbed BEFORE paths: base64 contains slashes, so reducing a secret to a "path" first leaves a recognisable tail behind rather than removing it — reversing the order reddens exactly the test written for it, and only that one. And the threshold is 40 rather than 44, because log lines abbreviate hashes and a secret is not less of a secret for being clipped — raising it past a full base64 SHA-256 reddens four tests (five only at 48 or above, which review measured after an earlier draft here said five). **Most of the suite is negative cases, because that is the failure nobody notices:** version strings like `2.4.0` and `10.0.19041` survive untouched (the IPv4 pattern requires four octets precisely so they do), and ordinary log prose is returned byte-identical. A scrubber that eats useful text defeats the feature instead of the security, and the bundle would still look convincingly clean. **Review found exactly that, twice, and both are now permanent tests.** The IPv6 rule counted colons — and digits are hex digits, so it matched any `HH:MM:SS`. Since the collection step is `logcat -d`, whose every line begins with a time of day, the DEFAULT path would have redacted the timestamp on essentially the whole bundle while looking protective; it ate durations and `a:b:c` triples too. It now requires eight groups or a literal `::`, which a clock cannot produce. Tightening it once was not enough — a word boundary sits happily BEFORE a colon, so `03:04:05` still offered `:04:05` to the compressed branch, and the boundaries had to become hex-aware. Separately the path rule had no notion of a URL scheme and reduced `wss://desktop-pc:5005/ws/desktop` to `wss://desktop-pc:5005desktop` — this repo's own endpoint, mangled in precisely the connection-failure lines a bundle exists to carry. Anchoring the POSIX branch to a token boundary excludes URLs, whose slash follows a port digit or a colon. 16 JVM tests, confirmed to have actually run by reading the JUnit XML rather than trusting a green task — the first two injection attempts reported a false GREEN off a stale report, which is the same trap this branch has now recorded twice. The collection, preview and ACTION_SEND half is **RemEx-3rjf**, along with the requirement that the preview show the SCRUBBED text — otherwise the user approves something other than what is sent. `gradlew clean assembleRelease` green with `lintVitalRelease`. (`DiagnosticsScrubber.kt`, `DiagnosticsScrubberTest.kt`; RemEx-nwnn.)

- **The host can now act on media and volume keys from the phone on Linux, which it silently dropped before.** Phone-as-media-remote needs no protocol change — `InputEventTypes.KeyDown` already carries any virtual-key code — and on Windows the media range worked already, because `MapKeyCodeToVirtualKey` returns any code at or below 255 verbatim and the media keys are 173-179. Linux translates rather than passes through, and had no entry for a single one of them: the phone would have sent a key the host quietly discarded. **Two tables, because there are two backends** — the portal and ydotool paths take an evdev keycode, xdotool takes an X keysym name. A mapping added to one and not the other is a feature that works on Wayland and does nothing on X11, which is the kind of half-wiring that reads as complete. Both are now filled and pinned together, with a test that sweeps the whole 0x00-0xFF protocol range and fails if either table ever knows a key the other does not — it started as a check of just these seven, which review pointed out was true but not general. **Every value was read out of `/usr/include/linux/input-event-codes.h` and `/usr/include/X11/XF86keysym.h` rather than recalled, and that caught a real error before it shipped.** The obvious xdotool name for play/pause is `XF86AudioPlay` — and it is wrong. The header documents it as `KEY_PLAYCD` / `KEY_PLAY`, *start playing*, while `VK_MEDIA_PLAY_PAUSE` is a toggle. X11 has a separate `XF86MediaPlayPause`, annotated `_EVDEVK(0x0a4)` = 164 = `KEY_PLAYPAUSE`, which is the exact counterpart and matches what the evdev table emits for the same key. Written from memory this would have paused correctly on Wayland and restarted the track on X11. **The phone half is not here and is filed as RemEx-hulc**: the row itself needs six new labels and content descriptions across nine locales plus a device test, and none of the host work required either. Nothing has been pressed on real hardware yet — the tables are verified against the headers and pinned by tests, which is not the same as the feature working. 1403 tests green on Windows (1 skipped), 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`; `remex.agent` clean for `linux-x64` under WSL. (`LinuxInputEventTranslator.cs`, `MediaKeyMappingTests.cs`; RemEx-3cnq.)

- **Wake-on-LAN no longer asks the user to find and type their PC's MAC address.** It was fully built on both ends — host verb, native export, quick-settings tile, remote-control card — and still required the one setup step a non-technical user cannot do. The PC has always known its MAC; it just kept it in a desktop view-model that offered copy-to-clipboard. `HostCapabilities` now carries a `MacAddress` and the phone remembers it per connect, so the tile and the card are prefilled with nothing to configure. **Manual entry still wins.** The host-reported value is stored under its own key and `macAddressFlow` prefers a user-set MAC when there is one, so auto-discovery can never overwrite a deliberate choice (a different NIC, a router quirk) — and all four existing consumers — dashboard card, remote-control card, home-screen widget and quick-settings tile — inherit the prefill without a UI change or a single new string to localize. The settings text box deliberately stays blank: prefilling it would promote the host value into the manual key the moment the user pressed Connect, freezing a stale MAC and defeating the precedence rule. **Additive and optional, so no `protocolVersion` bump:** an older client ignores the field, and a newer one treats its absence exactly as it treated every host before this existed. A blank is ignored rather than stored, because blank means "ask the user" — overwriting a good value with it would be worse than not listening. **The discovery moved into `Remex.Core` rather than being copied**, so the answer is the same headless as with a window open, and the card and the capability cannot disagree about which adapter is primary. It prefers a wired adapter deliberately rather than incidentally: most Wi-Fi adapters leave the network entirely when the machine sleeps, so a Wi-Fi MAC is the one least likely to be wakeable, and loopback and tunnel interfaces are excluded outright. Tailscale is excluded on both platforms but for different reasons, which review established by running it: on Linux `tailscale0` reports `Unknown` rather than `Tunnel` and is caught by the six-byte MAC check instead. No new NativeAOT surface — `WakeOnLanService` in the same assembly already links `System.Net.NetworkInformation`. The tests pin the contract the phone depends on rather than the build agent's hardware: the format, that a leading-zero byte is never shortened, and that `Find` returns either a well-formed address or nothing at all. 1386 tests green on Windows (1 skipped), 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`; `gradlew clean assembleRelease` green with the AOT artifacts invalidated, and `remex.agent` clean for `linux-x64` under WSL — the cross-platform leg this bead specifically asked for. (`PrimaryNetworkAdapter.cs`, `HostCapabilities.cs`, `HostCapabilitiesProvider.cs`, `RemoteViewModel.cs`, `SettingsManager.kt`, `RemexClientManager.kt`; RemEx-izuj.)

### Fixed

- **Forgetting a PC no longer depends on the pin still being there to work out which keys to clear.** The previous fix DERIVED the alias set at forget time: look up the pin for the key you were handed, then match every other pin key with the same hash. That works only while the pin is intact — and the population that most needs a clean forget is exactly the one whose pin is already half-gone, from the earlier forget that removed one key and left the rest. **Deriving after the fact fails precisely when it matters.** Pairing now RECORDS the linkage: all three keys a host is stored under (`hostId`, `host`, `spkiHash`) are written to a small `remex_host_aliases` store under each of themselves, so any one of them resolves the whole set. Forget prefers that record and falls back to derivation, clears every alias from both stores and the native cache, and removes the linkage last — otherwise the next forget would resurrect a key set that no longer exists. Written at all three pairing sites (PIN screen, QR scan, and the auto-reconnect re-pin in `RemexClientManager`), so no path creates a host the forget cannot fully undo. **Review caught the first version clearing LESS than the one it replaced.** The record was used INSTEAD of derivation, and `recordAliases` overwrote rather than merged — so re-pairing the same PC at a second address (LAN then Tailscale, or a DHCP change) rewrote the record without the old address while its pin was still on disk, and forget left it behind. That is the exact state the previous bead fixed. Both sources are now unioned, and recording merges with what is already there. The store is deliberately NOT encrypted, and the first justification for that was also wrong: the SPKI hash is NOT a plaintext key in the pin store — there it is the encrypted value; it is a plaintext key in the reconnect-secret store. The values are still not secrets, but the GROUPING is new — this file is the only place linking hostId to address to fingerprint in one record — and review found it was not excluded from cloud backup or device transfer the way the pin store is. Both `backup_rules.xml` and `data_extraction_rules.xml` now exclude it. **What this does NOT fix, stated plainly:** the record is written at pairing time, so a device already half-cleared before this ships has no record and is only repaired by re-pairing. Calling forget with the key that still holds a pin works today via the derivation fallback; calling it with the key that lost one does not. There is no linkage left to recover for those users, which is the whole reason the linkage is now recorded instead of inferred. Direction stays safe throughout — an over-retained pin keeps REJECTING, so the failure mode is "still stuck", never "accepts the wrong certificate". Verified with `gradlew clean assembleRelease`, the run including the fatal `lintVitalRelease` gate: BUILD SUCCESSFUL, no new warnings against the five pre-existing environmental ones. The .NET side is untouched and still 1383 green with 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`. (`PinnedHostStore.kt`, `PairingScreen.kt`, `QrScannerScreen.kt`, `RemexClientManager.kt`; RemEx-uxem.)

- **"Forget this PC" now clears every alias key it can find, both stores, and the native pin cache.** The previous fix cleared the pin and the reconnect secret for the ONE key the caller happened to hold. Pairing writes the pin under two keys and the secret under three (`hostId`, `host`, `spkiHash`), so the rest survived — and the two paths that read them are precisely the ones that reproduce "paired but will not connect": self-healing discovery trusts a host if EITHER pin key is set, and the reconnect-secret read PREFERS the `spkiHash` key. **The aliases are discovered rather than demanded from the caller**, which holds only one of them: every pin key mapping to the same hash is the same PC by definition, so `listPaired` finds them and one loop clears them. **A second cache outlived all of it.** `SetPinnedHostHash` populates an in-memory dictionary in `Remex.Core`, and the connect path falls back to that when the DataStore pin is gone — so a forget did not take effect until the process restarted: tap forget or repair, reconnect, and you are still pinned to the certificate you just rejected. The setter could not serve as its own clear (it ignores an empty hash, so passing one is a no-op), so this adds a `ClearPinnedHostHashNative` export mirroring it. That is a JNI-boundary addition but not a protocol one — it is an export the app calls, not an inbound message type, so nothing needs routing through `OnNativeMessageReceived` and no `protocolVersion` is involved. **One part is deliberately left as a question, not shipped as a guess:** per-host `fileTrust_*` grants — standing permission for a PC to browse the phone's files — also survive a forget. Clearing them is defensible for a deliberate unpair and wrong for a certificate repair, which uses the same code path, so whether those two should diverge is a design decision rather than a one-liner. **RemEx-yza9**. **One case it still cannot reach, which review found and the headline above is deliberately hedged for:** the alias set is DERIVED at forget time from the pin, so when the caller's key has no pin there is nothing to derive from and the loop falls back to that single key. Any device already half-cleared by the previously shipped forget lands there — tapping forget again keeps the other alias, its secret and its native entry. Direction is safe (an over-retained pin keeps REJECTING), but it is the same stuck state, so the durable fix — record the alias set at pairing time, or share one key-derivation helper between pair and forget — is **RemEx-uxem**, along with a second in-memory pin holder (`_lastInitRequest.SpkiHash`) that nothing clears either. Verified with `gradlew clean assembleRelease` with the AOT artifacts invalidated so ILC genuinely re-ran: BUILD SUCCESSFUL with `lintVitalRelease` passing and the 5 pre-existing environmental warnings (4x `XA0033` JDK-version parsing, 1x `IL3053` Mono.Android) and no new ones — an earlier draft of this entry said "zero warnings", which was wrong. 1383 .NET tests still green, 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`, and `remex.core` clean for `linux-x64` under WSL. (`PinnedHostStore.kt`, `RemexCoreClient.kt`, `AndroidNativeExports.cs`; RemEx-1phe.)

- **Forgetting a PC on Android cleared the pin but not the reconnect secret, so "repair" could fail on the very next connect.** The pinned SPKI hash and the PAIR-1 reconnect secret live in two separate DataStores, and `removePin` clears only the first. So after the cert-changed repair button ran, the phone had no pin but still had a secret — and the next connect failed the proof-of-possession challenge, which presents as "paired but will not connect" with no way forward from the UI. **The gap was wider than the bead described.** It named the repair path; there are TWO pin-clearing call sites and both had it, the second being the explicit "forget this PC" button, where a user who has said in as many words that they want the pairing gone was left with a secret on disk. And `removeReconnectSecret` had **no caller at all** — it was written for exactly this and never wired up. The fix is one operation rather than two calls: `PinnedHostStore.forgetHost` clears both, and both sites route through it. Two calls that must always happen together is an invariant nobody can see at a call site; one call is an invariant nobody can break. **Not covered by a test, and the reason first given for that was false.** The claim was that this repo has the test dependencies wired but no `androidTest` sources; review found **seven** instrumented test files, six of them Compose UI tests using `createComposeRule`. The infrastructure is present and in active use. The honest reason is narrower: an instrumented DataStore round-trip needs a device or emulator, which this environment does not have — so the invariant is enforced structurally, and RemEx-1phe records that the test is reachable for whoever has hardware. **The rest of the bead is held back for sign-off, not forgotten** — it also asked for a confirmation dialog showing old-vs-new fingerprints and explaining in plain English when accepting a changed certificate is safe. That copy has to tell a non-technical user when it is reasonable to delete their own security pin, which is Connor's call and needs a device test with a reinstalled host, so it is **RemEx-vnps**. **It is NOT a complete "forget", and review is why that is stated rather than implied.** Pairing writes the pin under two keys and the secret under three (`hostId`, `host`, `spkiHash`); both call sites pass one. So `pin[hostId]`, `secret[hostId]` and `secret[spkiHash]` survive — and the two paths that consume them are exactly the ones that reproduce the symptom: self-healing discovery trusts a host if EITHER pin key is set, and the secret read PREFERS the `spkiHash` key. A native in-memory pin cache and the per-host `fileTrust_*` grants also outlive a forget. All of that is **RemEx-1phe**. What this change fixes precisely: both call sites now clear both stores for the key they are given. Nothing here weakens verification — it only ever clears more client-side state, both callers are explicit user gestures, and no user-facing string moved. Verified with `gradlew clean assembleRelease`, the run that includes the fatal `lintVitalRelease` gate. (`PinnedHostStore.kt`, `ConnectionViewModel.kt`, `ConnectionScreen.kt`; RemEx-j9ei.)

- **A production path ending in `Dispatcher.UIThread.Post` is now covered — and the bead's explanation for why it could not be was wrong, which is the more useful half.** The bead said the blocker was that no `Avalonia.Headless` reference exists, so nothing pumps the dispatcher and a posted delegate is queued and never runs. A headless harness was duly built: the package, an assembly-level `AvaloniaTestApplication`, `[AvaloniaFact]`. **Review then deleted all three and rebuilt clean, and every test still passed.** With no Avalonia application booted at all, `Dispatcher.UIThread.CheckAccess()` is true even on a freshly spawned background thread, and `Post` followed by `RunJobs()` runs the callback. So the dependency was being added on a false premise and has been dropped. **The real gap was that nobody called `RunJobs()`.** The queue was always real; nothing drained it; and a posted callback that never runs looks exactly like an unchanged collection with no error — which does not read as missing coverage, it reads as passing coverage. That is why `CanvasDashboardViewModel` grew an internal `ApplyTelemetry` split from the `ProcessTelemetry` that posts it, and why the destructive-action suite could cover `RevokeTrustAsync` but not the `RevokeRequested` subscription that only happens inside a posted callback. None of it was blocked on infrastructure; each needs three lines. `ProcessTelemetry` is now internal alongside its sibling and one test covers the post site, proven by two injections: replacing the posted callback with an empty one reddens it, and so does deleting the `RunJobs()` call. **A vacuous test was removed rather than kept:** a control asserting `CheckAccess()` cannot fail, since it is true on an unrelated background thread too. Note the same misdiagnosis is already in the shipped RemEx-e1re entry ("no Avalonia headless harness exists anywhere in the repo, so the posted work never runs") — it is wrong there as well. 1383 tests green on Windows (1 skipped), 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`, and no new package reference. (`CanvasDashboardViewModel.cs`, `DispatcherPostedWorkTests.cs`; RemEx-r8c6.)

- **The desktop WSS handshake can be tested at all now, and three security-adjacent paths that nothing could reach are covered.** `RemexDesktopClient.BuildDesktopUri` hardcodes `wss://` and `ConnectAsync` installs a callback that hashes the presented certificate's SPKI, so nothing reached the proof-of-possession exchange, the receive loop, or the live-socket half of pinning — every other test in `remex.core.tests` points at TEST-NET-1 and fails at connect, one step before all of it. **The previous attempt is what makes this bead's answer worth recording.** It hand-rolled a `TcpListener` + `SslStream` + RFC 6455 upgrade and was abandoned: TLS and pinning worked first try, but `ClientWebSocket` rejected `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` even though the value was independently recomputed and matched byte for byte, and the root cause was never found. The bead's own advice was "budget real time for this or use a library rather than hand-rolling" — so this uses Kestrel, which already implements the upgrade, with `UseHttps` and an in-memory certificate giving the same pinnable key. It worked immediately. **What is now pinned:** that a host which upgrades and then goes quiet is classified as a HANDSHAKE timeout rather than as the user cancelling (the catch RemEx-nl0z shipped with zero coverage), asserted against the exact message because the sibling catch one call earlier also throws `TimeoutException` for a host that never answered at all; that a mismatched pin is rejected ON THE LIVE SOCKET, asserted by the server never seeing an upgraded connection rather than merely by something throwing; and a control proving a MATCHING pin does get through, without which "the pin rejected it" and "the fixture never works" look identical. **Three injections were misread before the exit code was checked, and that is the carry-forward.** `TreatWarningsAsErrors` now covers every project (RemEx-3p35), so naive mutations do not compile — deleting the catch leaves `CS1524`, `when (false)` trips `CS8360`, a leading `return true;` trips `CS0162` — and `dotnet test --no-build` then runs the PREVIOUS assembly and reports green, which reads exactly like "the test does not cover this". Rewritten as warning-free mutations (invert a guard, replace a body wholesale) each reddens exactly one test, the right one. The trap is now in `docs/ralph-board-drain.md`, since the change that created it was two beads ago. The private constructor became `internal` so tests hold an isolated client rather than the process-wide singleton, and the ASP.NET reference is test-only — confirmed by `gradlew clean assembleRelease` with the AOT artifacts invalidated, since `remex.core` itself is NativeAOT for Android. 1382 tests green on Windows (1 skipped), 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`; `linux-x64` clean under WSL. (`RemexDesktopClient.cs`, `DesktopWssServerFixture.cs`, `DesktopWssHandshakeTests.cs`; RemEx-u5q0.)

- **The build can finally see a doc comment attached to the wrong thing, which it could not while this branch shipped two of them.** No project set `GenerateDocumentationFile`, so Roslyn emitted NONE of the XML-doc diagnostics — which is why RemEx-wssm inserted a helper between a method's `</remarks>` and its signature, moving a fifty-line comment and five `<paramref>` tags onto a one-line `ToString` wrapper, and RemEx-cxel inserted a property between a field's summary and the field, and both times the build said nothing and a human reading the file caught it. **Coverage is demoted, correctness is not**, which is the entire design: `CS1591` (missing doc) and `CS1573` (undocumented parameter) are about whether a doc was WRITTEN — a style choice, at 3002 and 41 distinct sites, so making them errors would be a documentation project rather than a guard. (Those counts are of distinct file/line/column sites; a first pass reported 6030 and 82 by counting raw log lines, which per-project duplication roughly doubles — the props comment now carries the command.) Everything else stays an error under the repo-wide `TreatWarningsAsErrors`, and those are about whether the doc you DID write points at the thing it describes. **Turning it on found sixteen real defects, all fixed here.** Five test doc blocks in `FileTransferQueueTests` sat BETWEEN `[Fact]` and the method, where C# silently discards them — five explanations that were not documenting anything. Two class-level `<paramref>` tags named parameters belonging to methods. Eight crefs did not resolve. One named `CommandTimeoutSeconds`, which exists nowhere in the repo (the member is `CommandTimeout`). One named `ShowPairingPinCommand` — and review corrected the first fix for it: retargeting to `ShowPairingPin` made the doc point at the property it is written on, saying nothing. The command the prose means is the generated `ShowPairingPinPanelCommand`, so generated `[RelayCommand]` members do resolve after all. One more, `CS0419`, surfaced only when the build was made to fail: an ambiguous cref to `FileFrameCodec.TryRead` silently binding to the `ReadOnlyMemory` overload, which is the one that class does NOT exercise — every call site in it passes a `byte[]`, which binds to the span overload, so the overload is now named in prose. A signature-qualified cref was tried first, short and fully-qualified, and neither binds — Roslyn reports CS1574 for both, which is recorded next to it so nobody retries it blindly — it was missed by the first survey because that grep matched `CS1[0-9]{3}` and this one is `CS0419`, the same too-narrow-pattern error that made "0 warnings" wrong six times earlier on this branch. **How much the guard actually catches was measured by re-injecting both original defects, not assumed** — and the answer is not what the first draft of the props comment claimed. The RemEx-wssm shape IS caught: reinstating a `<paramref>` for a parameter the member does not have fails with `CS1734`. The RemEx-cxel shape is NOT — two `<summary>` tags on one member compile clean, with no diagnostic at all. The comment had listed `CS1571` as covering it; the injection is the only reason that false claim did not ship, and duplicate-summary is now recorded as a review-only catch. 1379 tests green on Windows (1 skipped), 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`; `linux-x64` clean under WSL for all three projects, and `gradlew clean assembleRelease` green with the AOT artifacts invalidated. Review also caught a shipping side effect nothing would have failed on: `dotnet publish` began emitting about 1.3 MB of XML docs, and `installer/RemEx.iss` globs the publish directory with `recursesubdirs` while `build-linux.sh` copies it wholesale — so every end user would have received this repo's verbatim engineering commentary, bead IDs and all, including the elevation, cert-ACL and pairing notes. `PublishDocumentationFile` and `PublishReferencesDocumentationFiles` are now false. (`Directory.Build.props` + ten files; RemEx-3282.)

- **The splash animations' frame-subscription idiom now has a name, and four `@Suppress` annotations are gone rather than relocated.** A Compose `Canvas` re-runs its draw lambda only when a snapshot state it READ is invalidated. The splash particle loops mutate plain `remember`ed lists, which are not observable, so nothing would ever invalidate the draw — the animation is driven entirely by reading a frame counter that the loop increments, as a bare expression whose value is discarded. That is unobvious enough that all four sites carried a `@Suppress("UNUSED_EXPRESSION")`, and a reader who does not recognise it may tidy away the apparently dead line, **which freezes the animation and breaks nothing the build or lint can see.** The sites now call `DrawScope.redrawOnFrame(particleFrame)`, whose doc explains the mechanism once and warns that the call must stay INSIDE the draw block, since it is the argument's evaluation that subscribes. **Better than the bead's suggested shape:** it expected the suppression to move into one documented place, but Kotlin does not warn about an unused parameter on a non-private function, so the helper needs none — checked by compiling without it rather than assumed. Four removed, none added. **A near-miss worth recording, because it is this bead's own trap sprung on the person fixing it.** A scan of `SplashCosmicZoom` found it incrementing the same counter every frame with no read of it in its `Canvas`, and that was filed as a possible frozen starfield. It is not: review found `elapsed`, a `mutableStateOf(0f)` incremented on the line immediately after `particleFrame++` and read at fourteen sites inside that draw block — confirmed in the DEX, where its accessor is inlined thirteen times into the CosmicZoom draw lambda and `particleFrame`'s zero times. So the starfield subscribes correctly and `particleFrame` there is merely a dead counter, now **RemEx-agi0** as a cleanup rather than a bug. **The reason the scan missed it is the whole point of this bead:** it searched for `particleFrame` and for `.value`, and a delegated snapshot read is neither — it is a bare identifier that looks inert, which is exactly the shape the named helper exists to stop hiding. The question was also statically settleable throughout; hedging it as needing a device was wrong in the other direction at the same time. Verified with `gradlew clean assembleRelease`, which is the run that includes the fatal `lintVitalRelease` gate. (`SplashBackgroundFx.kt`, `SplashRemexCommand.kt`, `SplashPong.kt`; RemEx-si3q.)

- **A download that could not flush its last bytes now provably fails and deletes the partial, instead of being promised a test and not getting one.** RemEx-owc3 added an explicit `await fileStream.FlushAsync()` before a download is declared successful, because the writer task returning means every chunk reached the `FileStream`, not the disk — up to 64 KB can still be in memory, and disposal does NOT report write failures (measured on .NET 10.0.10). A destination that filled up or was unplugged in that window otherwise lost the tail while the transfer reported success, because the digest is computed from bytes as RECEIVED and nothing re-reads the file. RemEx-qmnl promised to pin that and could not: its seam fakes the PEER, and this failure is on the filesystem side of the method entirely. **The bead left the design open with three options and the choice is the substance of this change.** A Linux-only ENOSPC test on a loopback or tmpfs mount would break the cross-platform parity rule AND skip on Windows, which is the platform this is developed on — so the case would go untested exactly where it runs most. A filesystem shim is more machinery for the same result. What was added instead is a one-member `DownloadFileOpener` seam, null in production, whose default is the same `FileStream` the inline construction built. **The detail that keeps it from being a mock of itself: the fake WRAPS A REAL FILE.** The bytes go to a genuine file at the caller's path and only `FlushAsync` is overridden, so the partial really exists, the cleanup really deletes it, and `File.Exists` is answering about the real filesystem rather than about the fake. The fake also returns cleanly from `DisposeAsync` while throwing from the flush — reproducing the exact asymmetry the production comment documents rather than smoothing it over. Both halves of the claim are pinned independently, by injection: deleting the `FlushAsync` call reddens the test (the transfer wrongly reports success), and deleting the `File.Delete` reddens it too (the truncated file survives under the final name, where it is indistinguishable from a complete download). No chunks and no expected hash are sent, because the flush sits between the host's end message and the integrity check — a bare successful end reaches it, and adding either would only re-test what already has its own coverage. Review added one assertion that closes a latent hole: the opener runs BEFORE the five registrations, so an IOException escaping the fake stream's own CONSTRUCTOR would leave the counts at zero and no file on disk, and every assertion would have passed without the flush ever being reached. The test now names the exception, and that assertion is itself proven non-vacuous — changing the fake's message reddens it. 1379 tests green on Windows (1 skipped), 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`; `remex.desktop` also builds clean for `linux-x64` under WSL. (`FileTransferClient.cs`, `DownloadUnwindTests.cs`; RemEx-04p8.)

- **The telemetry warm-up guarantee that no fixture could observe is now pinned, and the reason it could not be observed is the interesting part.** `WindowsTelemetryService` skips re-reading the WMI categories HWiNFO already covers, but only once the per-category cache has been seeded — so a tick that did NOT read must not mark it seeded, or those categories never enter the cache and a later stall serves a payload missing them. `TelemetryWarmUpGateTests` could not see that at all: the skip set is `_fallbackCacheSeeded && hwinfoSensors.Count > 0`, and that suite points HWiNFO at a region which does not exist — deliberately, to keep its sibling assertions machine-independent — so the right conjunct is permanently false. Setting the flag inside the skip branch left it green. **The fix needed the opposite fixture and one seam.** A synthetic HWiNFO region covering the `CPU` category makes the conjunct true; observing the effect then needs the cache itself, because `MergeHwInfoOverPerf` drops every WindowsPerf sensor in a covered category, which makes the payloads of a skipped tick and a read tick **identical**. That is why the assertion is on a new internal `CachedByCategory` rather than on `Sensors`: the difference is invisible in the payload by construction, and only surfaces on a much later tick served from the cache. Proven by the exact injection the bead recorded as undetectable — adding `_fallbackCacheSeeded = true` to the skip branch now reddens the new test, and only it. **The control matters as much as the assertion:** the test first asserts an `HWInfo`-sourced sensor is present, because without that it would silently decay into the vacuous test it replaces. The region writer moved out of `HwInfoSamplerTests`, which owned it privately, into a shared `SyntheticHwInfoRegion` — same layout, same writer, same `CPU [#0]: Test CPU` device, and that suite stays green on it. **The bead's second clause is NOT done and is filed as RemEx-k34y**, with the reason verified against the constructor rather than assumed: `_countersReady = countersReady ?? Task.Run(InitializeFallbackCounters)`, so the only seam that can hold the warm-up open also guarantees the counters are never built — `_cpuCounter` stays null and CPU reads `?? 0`, which is the artefact the guarantee is about, while `_activeNic` stays null so no Network sensor exists to assert on. It needs the real warm-up and a way to distinguish pre from post by something other than value magnitude, since an idle machine's first primed CPU sample can legitimately round to ~0%. Review caught the change doing to a doc comment exactly what RemEx-wssm did two beads earlier: the new property was inserted between `_fallbackCacheSeeded`'s `<summary>` and the field, so it acquired TWO summaries — the first describing a `bool` — and the flag this whole bead exists to pin was left undocumented. Same silent failure mode, second occurrence, so the cause is filed rather than just the instance: **RemEx-3282** records that no project sets `GenerateDocumentationFile`, which is why Roslyn emits no CS1571 for either, and that enabling it today fails on pre-existing CS1591s in `remex.branding` — measured, not assumed. 1378 tests green on Windows (1 skipped), 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`. (`WindowsTelemetryService.cs`, `SyntheticHwInfoRegion.cs`, `HwInfoSamplerTests.cs`, `TelemetryWarmUpGateTests.cs`; RemEx-cxel.)

- **Every project now fails its build on a compiler or analyzer warning, not just the test projects.** `TreatWarningsAsErrors` was scoped to `*.tests` by RemEx-t0f3, which stopped there because the shipping projects had not been checked on the build paths a Windows solution build cannot see. They have been now. All of them were already clean on the two that were checkable in isolation: zero warnings on `dotnet build Remex.sln -t:Rebuild`, zero on a `linux-x64` self-contained build of each project under WSL, and zero from `dotnet restore`. `remex.agent.windows` is covered too — it is absent from `Remex.sln` but reached transitively through `remex.agent`'s conditional `ProjectReference`. **The Android NativeAOT build was the one that was not clean, which is exactly why the bead required checking it.** It emits two warnings, neither of them this repo's code: `IL3053`, an ILC-emitted rollup naming `Mono.Android`, and `XA0033`, the Android workload failing to parse `java -version` on Temurin 26. Only `IL3053` needed a carve-out, and the difference between them was measured rather than reasoned: in the build that failed on `error IL3053` with both carve-outs absent, `XA0033` printed as a plain `warning`. **Demoting a rollup sounds dangerous and review checked whether it is, arriving at the right answer for a different reason than the one first written down.** It is not safe because the rollup only ever names a foreign assembly: an AOT-unsafe call planted in `Remex.Core` produced a second `IL3053: Assembly 'libRemexCore'`, demoted by this very line. It is safe because the rsp passes `--warnaserror` alongside `--singlewarn`, and single-warn only folds up diagnostics that stay warnings — the specific one is promoted first and survives, so that probe still failed the build on `IL2026 ... RequiresUnreferencedCode`. The caveat that follows is now written down: this holds only while `IL2026`/`IL2075`/`IL3050` are not themselves added to `WarningsNotAsErrors`. The flag was also confirmed to reach the compiler on the android target framework, by injecting an unused local into `remex.core` and watching `assembleRelease` fail with `error CS0219`. **The part worth keeping is how the first answer came out wrong, and it is not the story this entry originally told.** Three consecutive runs measured "the Android build succeeds with the carve-out removed"; a comment calling the carve-out decoration, and a follow-up bead repeating it, were both written on that basis. The fourth run failed on `error IL3053`, and it now fails reliably: the carve-out is load-bearing, and without it `assembleRelease` fails with `error IL3053` plus an `MSB3077` from ilc. **The first correction then invented a cause** — a stale `artifacts/obj`, by analogy with the `-t:Rebuild` trap already documented on this branch — and review disproved it: editing `WarningsNotAsErrors` rewrites the ILC rsp, and the gradle `Exec` task declares no inputs or outputs, so that step re-runs every time and cannot be measured stale. So the cause of the three green runs is genuinely unknown, and it is recorded as unknown. Attaching a plausible mechanism to an unisolated observation is the exact habit this branch keeps catching, and doing it inside the note about catching it is worth writing down. The props comment, the loop doc and the follow-up bead (**RemEx-go3k**, now scoped to `XA0033` alone) all say that instead, and the guidance is now "one Android build is not a measurement" rather than a mechanism. One authoring trap worth naming, since this file is a props file and this repo comments densely with CLI switches: writing ilc's two dash-prefixed switch names inside the XML comment made `Directory.Build.props` fail to LOAD — `MSB4024: An XML comment cannot contain '--'` — which takes down every project in the repo, the Android build included, from a comment. They are named without their prefixes now. 1377 tests green on Windows (1 skipped), 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`; `linux-x64` clean under WSL for all three projects; `gradlew clean assembleRelease` green with the AOT artifacts invalidated. (`Directory.Build.props`; RemEx-3p35.)

- **The power commands now have tests, and the one they most needed is not the one the bead asked for.** `RemEx-msyn` closed the invariant-formatting series — RemEx-hbma, j7el, tiih, clum, wssm and now this — by routing the two system command services' shutdown arguments through an invariant `Arg` helper. As with the entry below it, **there was no defect**: the Windows delay is clamped to `[0, 315360000]` and the Linux one is `Math.Max(1, ...)`, so neither can be negative, and a positive integer has no culture-sensitive rendering in .NET. Measured, not assumed — reverting `Arg` to a raw interpolation leaves every behavioural assertion green, which is exactly why the routing is enforced by a source check instead. **What the file actually needed was a test of its FLAGS.** `WindowsSystemCommandService` has carried a remark warning that switching `/r` to `/r /g` would arm Windows Automatic Restart Sign-On, signing the user back in unattended and silently falsifying five confirmation strings that promise, in nine languages, that RemEx cannot reach the PC again until someone signs in on it — and that **"no test would fail"** (RemEx-mkq1). That was true when it was written; it is not true now. **The first version of these tests could not have caught it, which is worth recording because the mistake is subtle:** they asserted the argument BUILDER, and the builder is handed its flags, so it can only echo back whatever the call site chose. `BuildShutdownArguments("/r", 0)` cannot produce a `/g` no matter how broken the caller is. The tests now drive the public methods through a `SystemProcessLauncher` seam and record the program and argument list each one would have run, so a call site changing to `"/r /g"` reddens three of them. Proven by injecting exactly that. Both services' dispatch tables are pinned as single assertions, and review was right to count what they actually drove rather than take the first draft's word for "every mode, both platforms": Linux `ForceRestart`, `RestartToUefi` and `MonitorOff` were driven by nothing, which left `systemctl reboot -i` and `systemctl reboot --firmware-setup` — the two most destructive argument lists in the file — as precisely the unpinned ones. They are now driven. Two paths remain deliberately outside, with the reason recorded next to them rather than left to be discovered: Windows `Lock` and `MonitorOff` are P/Invokes rather than processes, and Linux `RestartToUefi` with a positive delay reboots from a `Task.Delay` continuation, so asserting it would mean sleeping for the delay. The tables also pin the delay semantics in place: a sub-minute Linux delay rounds UP to one minute rather than truncating to `now`, because `shutdown` takes minutes and "in 30 seconds" silently becoming "immediately" is the difference between a warning and a surprise. One asymmetry is pinned as a characterization rather than endorsed: Linux `ForceShutdown` takes `systemctl poweroff -i` only when undelayed, and with a delay runs the same non-forced `shutdown -h` as the ordinary `Shutdown`, so "force" stops meaning anything once a delay is supplied. **Review found four things and one of them was a hole in the new test itself, demonstrated rather than argued.** The source check bounded the Windows builder with `";"` as its end marker, which worked only because the builder happened to be an expression body: refactoring it to a block body with a local truncated the scan at the first statement, so it captured zero holes, found zero offenders and passed GREEN while the interpolation sat there raw — contradicting the test's own claim to catch a newly added number. Both rows now end on the next member's signature, which survives that refactor, and the fix is verified by re-running the reviewer's exact demonstration. The body-length floor could not have caught it either (the start marker alone is 45 characters, so a truncated body still cleared 40); it is now per-row and measured — 120 and 250 against real bodies of 153 and 300 — after a first attempt at one shared number, sized from the Linux body, broke the Windows row immediately. Review also caught the `/g` guard's comment having its reasoning **backwards**: it claimed a substring check would let a regression through, when a substring check is in fact STRICTER and the token split was the weaker choice, missing `/g:foo`. The assertion is now on the token prefix, erring toward a false alarm on purpose for a guard protecting a promise made in nine languages. The remaining two were comment accuracy: the launcher delegate claimed every command passes through it, when Windows `Lock` and `MonitorOff` go straight to `LockWorkStation` and `SendMessage` and are outside the seam entirely; and it credited the precedent to "`ISystemCommandService`'s Linux and Windows implementations", which are these two files and reached no prior conclusion — the real precedent is `InputToolLauncher` and `IPortalInputSink` over in `remex.agent`. That is the third misattributed cross-reference this branch has produced, all of the same shape: a plausible citation written without opening the thing cited. **Verified where it actually matters for `remex.core`:** the Android release build was run and regenerated `libRemexCore.so`, so the new delegate and constructor are NativeAOT-safe in practice rather than by inspection. 1377 tests green on Windows (1 skipped), 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`; `remex.core` also builds clean for `linux-x64` under WSL. (`WindowsSystemCommandService.cs`, `LinuxSystemCommandService.cs`, `SystemCommandArgumentTests.cs`; RemEx-msyn.)

- **Scrolling on a Wayland desktop moved 120 times too far, and nothing could see it.** `LinuxInputSimulationService.MouseScroll` has three backends. The two shell ones divide the incoming delta by 120 before using it; the portal one passed it through raw. **Both halves of that mismatch are now verified rather than assumed**, which is the whole of this bead — it was filed as a question, not a fix. The wire value is in Windows' `WHEEL_DELTA` units, 120 per notch: `WindowsInputSimulationService` hands `deltaY` straight to `MOUSEEVENTF_WHEEL`, which is what defines it, and `CoordinateValidation` caps it at `120 * 10`. The portal's parameter is documented as **"the number of steps scrolled"** — `NotifyPointerAxisDiscrete(IN session_handle o, IN options a{sv}, IN axis u, IN steps i)`, checked against the current xdg-desktop-portal API reference rather than from memory. So one notch from the phone asked the compositor for 120 notches: not a subtle mis-scaling, a fling on every flick. The portal branch now shares the ydotool branch's `WheelDetents` helper outright, so the three cannot drift apart again. The neighbouring `NotifyPointerAxis` was considered and rejected: its `dx`/`dy` are a smooth-scroll motion vector in logical pixels, which is the wrong shape for a delta that arrives already quantised to notches. **The more consequential change is the seam that made the fix provable.** The bug survived because the portal backend had none: `LinuxInputSimulationService`'s own constructor remark already stated the rule — "the defect class is not 'the mapping is wrong', it is 'the argv is wrong', and only the argv is worth pinning" — and the shell backends got an `InputToolLauncher` delegate for exactly that while the nine portal branches got nothing. They now go through a narrow `IPortalInputSink`, injectable in the internal constructor and null in production, so a test can assert what the compositor is actually told without a D-Bus session. `WheelDetents` was already correct and already covered; **the mistake was at the call site, which is precisely what a helper-only test cannot reach.** Seven tests drive the service rather than the helper, and six of them redden when the original one-liner is put back — the seventh is a labelled characterization of `(0,0)`, which is unchanged either way and says so. **One thing was deliberately NOT fixed, and that is filed as RemEx-e0b2:** the portal documentation gives the signature and the axis numbering but never says which direction a positive step count means. All three other backends agree that positive is up — `MOUSEEVENTF_WHEEL` forward, `REL_WHEEL` positive up, xdotool button 4 — and the Wayland side conventionally runs the other way, which suggests the portal path may also scroll backwards and always have. Suggests is not knows: settling it needs the compositor's own portal backend traced, or a live session with a paired phone, and inverting on the reasoning alone is the exact failure mode RemEx-nb7c exists to prevent. The seam added here means that once the answer is known it is a one-line assertion. 1361 tests green on Windows (1 skipped), 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`; the agent also builds clean for `linux-x64` under WSL. (`LinuxInputSimulationService.cs`, `IPortalInputSink.cs`, `LinuxPortalInputInjector.cs`, `PortalScrollUnitTests.cs`; RemEx-y45x.)

- **The ffmpeg encoder now formats its arguments invariantly too, and the argument list itself is finally pinned.** `FFmpegH264Encoder.BuildEncoderArgs` interpolated geometry, fps, qp, the VBV rates and the GOP length straight into the argv. **No defect existed and none was fixed** — every one of those operands is structurally non-negative, and a positive integer has no culture-sensitive rendering in .NET, so the old interpolations were correct on all 890 cultures. What changed is that this file no longer has a different convention from the four the preceding beads converted, so a signed operand added here later — an offset, a crop origin, a delta — is safe by construction rather than by whoever reviews it noticing. **The routing is enforced by a source test, which is not a stylistic choice here but the only signal available:** with no negative operand, removing the invariant formatting emits a byte-identical string, so a behavioural test for it could not fail. That test reddens against `HEAD`, which is the strongest form of the proof — the injection is the previous commit. **The more useful half of this change is the shape tests, which close a pre-existing gap:** the existing `FFmpegH264EncoderArgsTests` assert individual flags with `Assert.Contains`, which is right for testing what a flag MEANS but cannot see a swallowed space, a reordered flag, or a scale filter attached to the wrong branch — exactly what a mechanical rewrite of twenty-eight interpolation holes risks. The argv is now asserted whole, per codec, including the VA-API branch that opens its own `-vf` and appends the filter with a comma rather than a second `-vf`, and the AMF branch whose `maxRate * 3 / 4` is the one place arithmetic lives inside an argument hole. Rate values are referenced through the public compute helpers rather than frozen as literals, so a deliberate change to the bitrate formula does not have to touch these tests while a change to the argument layout must. **Byte-identity was measured, not argued:** the new shape tests were run against `HEAD`'s builder with the fix stashed, and all nine cases across the six methods passed unchanged, while the source test went red — so the emitted argv is identical and only the routing differs. One thing worth recording from writing the source test: its two boundary markers are asserted rather than assumed, and that guard immediately earned itself. A marker written with `\n` matched nothing, because the scripted edit that made the change had rewritten the file with CRLF — `.gitattributes` is `* text=auto eol=lf`, so it is LF on a fresh checkout and the normalization now in the test is defensive rather than load-bearing. **The assertion is what made that visible at all:** without it the scan would have run over an empty body, found no offenders and passed green while checking nothing. 1354 tests green on Windows (1 skipped), 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`; the agent also builds clean for `linux-x64` under WSL. Review caught the change doing to a doc comment exactly what the entry directly below records fixing: the new `Arg` block was inserted between `BuildEncoderArgs`'s `</remarks>` and its signature, so C# attached that whole 50-line comment — the GDI+ timing, the bilinear/fast_bilinear PSNR comparison, five `<paramref>` tags — to a one-line `ToString` helper, leaving the method it documents undocumented. No warning fires, because no project sets `GenerateDocumentationFile`. The overloads now sit above that block. Review also narrowed the source test's own claim: it originally matched a list of the nine operand names that exist today, which catches a revert but not the NEW operand the rule is actually about, so it is now an allow-list — anything that is not `Arg(...)` or a named string operand fails, proven by injecting a fresh `{cropX}`. **This is not the last file, which was worth checking rather than claiming:** a sweep of all twenty files that start a process found one more argument builder outside the series, `Windows`/`LinuxSystemCommandService` in `remex.core`, filed as **RemEx-msyn**. It is the same situation again — `NormalizeDelay` clamps to `[0, 315360000]` and the Linux side takes `Math.Max(1, ...)`, so neither can go negative and neither is broken. Everything else the sweep surfaced is a log message, a cache key or a filesystem path (`/proc/{processId}/stat`) rather than a process argument. (`FFmpegH264Encoder.cs`, `FFmpegArgumentFormattingTests.cs`; RemEx-wssm.)

- **On 95 locales a monitor placed above or left of the origin stopped screen capture from starting at all.** `LinuxScreenCaptureService` built its ffmpeg `x11grab` argument with a plain interpolation, `-i {display}+{_screenLeft},{_screenTop}`. That origin is the minimum over outputs, so it goes negative the moment a monitor sits above or left of the primary, and interpolating an `int` uses `CurrentCulture`: 95 runtime cultures render a negative one with a `NegativeSign` that is not the ASCII hyphen — sv-SE, lt-LT and fi-FI use U+2212 MINUS SIGN, and the ar/fa/he families prefix a directional mark. ffmpeg parses none of them, so the process refuses its input and the user gets no frame rather than a wrong one. **This is the mirror of the fix one entry below, and it breaks a different set of locales** — that one was the parse direction and its 57 cultures are a subset of these 95. It was found while fixing that one and deferred on purpose rather than folded in, since the two directions fail differently and deserved separate proofs. **The path is more reachable than "X11 hosts with an unusual layout" suggests:** the `x11grab` call is capture strategy 2 and is not gated on the display server — it runs as the fallback for every session type, so it inherits whatever topology `kscreen-doctor` produced on a KDE session, and both parse patterns admit a negative offset deliberately (`(?<x>[+-]\d+)` for xrandr, `(?<x>-?\d+)` for kscreen). Widths, heights and quality levels in the same argument string cannot be negative and a positive `int` has no culture-sensitive rendering to get wrong; they were routed through the same new `Arg` helper anyway, for the reason RemEx-hbma established — one rule with no exceptions is what keeps the signed cases safe by construction rather than by anyone remembering which values carry a sign. The five copies of the `-q:v` expression became one `FfmpegQualityArgument` helper in passing, arithmetic unchanged. **Only the origin is asserted, because only the origin can fail:** a test for the positive operands could not go red under any culture, so there is not one. Proven by injection twice — reverting both format calls fails both new tests, and reverting only the `y` one fails only the `y` test, so the two axes are pinned independently rather than by one assertion that a half-applied fix would leave green. Review caught two things worth recording: an invented provenance claim in the new doc comment (it said the site had evaded the RemEx-hbma grep; hbma never touched this file), and an orphaned regex comment — which, checked at `HEAD` rather than assumed, this change did not cause: RemEx-tiih separated that comment from `KScreenGeometryRegex` by 43 lines when it inserted the parse helpers between them, this insertion widened the gap to about 88, and it has now been moved back onto its subject. A misattribution inside the sentence reporting a misattribution is the one error this entry could not carry, so it is recorded as inherited rather than caused. 1344 tests green on Windows (1 skipped), 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`; the agent also builds clean for `linux-x64` under WSL. Filed **RemEx-wssm** for the last place the rule does not reach, `FFmpegH264Encoder`, which has the same shape but where every value is structurally non-negative, so nothing is broken there today. (`LinuxScreenCaptureService.cs`, `CaptureArgumentCultureTests.cs`; RemEx-clum.)

- **On 57 locales the host could not read its own monitor layout, and that now aims the mouse pointer.** `LinuxScreenCaptureService` parsed `kscreen-doctor`, `xrandr` and `xdpyinfo` output with culture-blind `int.Parse`/`int.TryParse` across thirteen lines — fifteen call sites, since two of those lines carry two parses each. Those tools emit plain ASCII signs; 57 runtime cultures — the `ar`, `ckb`, `fa`, `he`, `ks`, `lrc`, `mzn`, `pa`, `ps`, `sd`, `ur` and `uz` families — reject one, because theirs carries a directional mark such as U+061C or U+200E in front of it. **The blast radius is wider than the bead said, and finding that out was most of the work.** It was filed as a negative-coordinate problem; `XrandrGeometryRegex` matches `(?<x>[+-]\d+)`, so a sign is REQUIRED and even a primary monitor at the origin arrives as `+0`. Measured here: `"+0"`, `"+1920"` and `"-1920"` are rejected by the same 57 cultures and an unsigned `"1920"` by none — so on an affected host the xrandr path failed for EVERY output, not just for a monitor left of or above the primary. The KDE path is worse again: it uses the THROWING `int.Parse` inside a try/catch that treats any failure as "no displays", so one unreadable geometry line discarded the whole kscreen result and fell through to xrandr, which was broken the same way. **What that costs is not a cosmetic topology error.** The virtual-desktop origin is the minimum over outputs, and RemEx-dyvd made it load-bearing: `MoveMouse` subtracts it before handing coordinates to ydotool, whose `--absolute` is emulated as home-then-move and wants an offset rather than a position. A wrong origin does not merely misreport the layout, it aims the pointer somewhere else, silently. Resolutions, dimensions and priorities cannot be negative and go through the same helper anyway, for the reason RemEx-hbma established: one rule with no exceptions is what keeps the signed cases safe by construction rather than by anyone remembering which values carry a sign. The tests drive the regex and the parse TOGETHER rather than the helper alone, because the helper alone would not have shown that a sign is mandatory in the pattern. Proven by injection, in both tools: reverting the `TryParse` helper fails the three xrandr geometry tests, and reverting the `Parse` helper fails the KDE one. **That second test exists because the first injection exposed a gap rather than a defect** — the kscreen path was initially unpinned, since every other assertion drove the xrandr regex, and KDE is the desktop this project primarily targets. Review found a second such gap: the malformed-token test used a `disconnected` line, which is rejected by a guard before the regex is ever reached, so it passed under both injections and pinned nothing. It now uses a connected line with a truncated token, and asserts the guard separately rather than by accident. The format direction has one site left in this file — the x11grab argument string interpolates the same negative-capable origin — and that is filed as RemEx-clum rather than folded in, since it is the opposite direction and breaks the other 95 cultures. 1341 tests green on Windows (1 skipped), 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`; verified under WSL Linux too. (`LinuxScreenCaptureService.cs`, `DisplayTopologyCultureTests.cs`; RemEx-tiih.)

- **Reading numbers back out of xdotool is culture-sensitive too, and fixing the format side did not fix it.** RemEx-hbma made every number RemEx FORMATS into a shell argument invariant. `int.TryParse` without a provider uses `CurrentCulture`, and a culture whose `NegativeSign` is not the ASCII hyphen rejects the hyphen xdotool actually emits. **The 57 cultures that break parsing are a SUBSET of the 95 that break formatting, and the first draft of this entry called them disjoint — in five places including a test method name.** Review caught it and the claim is impossible by construction: rejecting `"-1920"` requires `NegativeSign` to differ from the ASCII hyphen, which is the same condition that makes formatting differ. Re-measured here: 95 break formatting, 57 break parsing, overlap 57, format-only 38. **The bead's justification survives the correction intact, and is sharper for it**: those 38 use U+2212, so they emit an unparseable argument but read an ASCII hyphen back happily, which means a fix aimed at formatting leaves parsing broken on 57 cultures and repairs nothing on this side. Same condition seen from opposite ends, not the same bug. The 57 are the `ar`, `ckb`, `fa`, `he`, `ks`, `lrc`, `mzn`, `pa`, `ps`, `sd`, `ur` and `uz` families, and their signs take five shapes rather than the one the first draft claimed: U+061C U+002D (26), U+200E U+002D U+200E (16, three characters), U+200E U+002D (9), U+200F U+002D (3) and U+200E U+2212 (3, not ending in a hyphen at all). The test fixture reproduces the largest shape and now says so. **The values that can actually be negative are window X and Y**: a window on a monitor left of or above the primary has a negative origin, the same case RemEx-r29r existed for, and the old parse silently returned false, so geometry went missing with no error anywhere and window control either reported the window wrong or refused to act on it. All nine parse sites in the window-control service, both in the cursor query, and the Windows window-Id round trip now go through invariant helpers — the last of those was already safe, being self-consistent on one machine with handles that are not realistically negative, and is fixed anyway because "self-consistent" stops being true the moment a payload is replayed on a differently-configured host. **A wrong assumption was caught by the control assertion within seconds of writing it**: the parse tests first reused the formatting fixture, whose `NegativeSign` is U+2212, and asserted it broke parsing. It does not. The suite now builds a second, ar-shaped culture and asserts the subset relationship directly, so the next reader cannot treat "culture invariance" as one property, fix one direction, watch the tests go green and ship the other. Review also measured that two of the three fixed sites were shipping untested — reverting either the cursor-query parse or the Windows Id round trip left the whole suite green — so both helpers are now asserted directly. The Windows one still cannot fail on culture, handles being non-negative, and is labelled a characterization rather than presented as coverage. Proven by injection: reverting the helper to a provider-less `TryParse` fails exactly the negative-geometry test. The capture subsystem has the same defect in about a dozen places and is filed as RemEx-tiih, because RemEx-dyvd made the virtual-desktop origin load-bearing — a mis-parsed negative origin there does not merely misreport the topology, it aims the pointer at the wrong place. 1335 tests green on Windows (1 skipped), 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`; verified under WSL Linux too. (`LinuxDesktopWindowControlService.cs`, `LinuxInputSimulationService.cs`, `WindowsDesktopWindowControlService.cs`, `CultureInvariantArgvTests.cs`; RemEx-j7el.)

- **A host set to the wrong language would have sent arguments its own input tools cannot parse.** `NumberFormatInfo.NegativeSign` is culture-dependent — a reviewer scanned all 890 runtime cultures and found 95 that disagree with the invariant one, including `sv-SE`, `lt-LT` and `fi-FI`, which use U+2212 MINUS SIGN — and a bare `int.ToString()` honours that. Mainstream locales, not exotica. Every number the Linux input service formats into a shell argument now goes through one invariant helper, renamed `Arg` to match the sibling router's, because two names for one rule is how the rule gets applied to only one of them. **The site that mattered was an interpolation, not a `ToString()`, which is why it survived the earlier sweep**: `RunTool("key", $"{...}:1")` carries `InputEvent.KeyCode` straight off the wire, and that is an unvalidated `int?`, so a negative arrives without anything having to go wrong first. **The scope is smaller than the bead assumed and the reason is worth writing down: a positive `int` cannot vary by culture at all.** .NET's `int.ToString()` applies neither `NativeDigits` nor `DigitSubstitution`, so `NegativeSign` is the only culture-dependent part of an integer, and only values that can go negative were ever at risk. Measured rather than reasoned — forcing the shared helper to `CurrentCulture` fails five tests and every one of the five carries a negative. Button indices and clamped detent counts are routed through the same helper anyway, and the `F1`..`F12` key name follows the same rule via its own invariant format in a different class, and the tests covering them now say in as many words that they are characterizations of the argv rather than culture coverage and **cannot** fail on culture. That correction came from an injection that was supposed to prove the F-key change and instead proved it a no-op: reverting that one site leaves all twelve tests green, so claiming it as covered would have been a third instance this week of a guard that cannot observe a counterexample. It is kept for consistency, which is a real reason, and labelled as such, which is the honest one. The hostile culture is constructed rather than looked up, because which locales use U+2212 is ICU data that shifts between runtimes and a test naming one would pin the .NET version instead of this code; a control assertion proves the override actually took, so the file cannot pass vacuously. One test also had to be corrected before it meant anything: it asserted `-1:1` for an unmapped key, but the fallback passes the protocol code rather than the `-1`, so it was exercising a positive while claiming the negative case. Both behaviours are now pinned separately. 1330 tests green on Windows (1 skipped), 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`; the new suite and a warning-free rebuild verified under WSL Linux too. **Review found the sweep itself incomplete**, which is the finding worth keeping: `LinuxDesktopWindowControlService` formats `Width`, `Height` and `DesktopNumber` into xdotool arguments with bare `ToString()`, and those are unvalidated `int?` on `DesktopWindowAction` with only `HasValue` checks between the socket and the argument list — the same wire-reachable negative, one directory outside the files the bead named. Fixed here rather than deferred, since it is the same rule. That site has no launcher seam like the two input classes, so flipping its helper to `CurrentCulture` failed nothing behavioural — measured, not assumed. It is covered instead by a direct assertion on the helper plus a source scan asserting NO bare `ToString()` survives in either file, phrased that way on purpose: the failure this bead is about is a NEW formatting site added later by someone who does not know the rule, and naming today's call sites would pass forever while the next one goes in beside them. Both bite — the first injection fails the helper assertion, the second, adding a fresh bare `ToString()`, fails the scan. **The scan's reach is bounded and the bound is the interesting part**: a fresh `$"{limit}"` slips past it, and an interpolation is precisely how the `key:1` argument evaded the earlier sweep. A blanket interpolation ban is not available, because both files legitimately interpolate into developer-facing log messages, so this is recorded as a limitation rather than engineered around — a guard whose reach is overstated is how the next person concludes the class is covered. (`LinuxInputSimulationService.cs`, `LinuxInputEventTranslator.cs`, `LinuxDesktopWindowControlService.cs`, `CultureInvariantArgvTests.cs`; RemEx-hbma.)

- **The Remote Mouse screen was the other, wider way input reached a host that had refused it.** `RemoteControlViewModel.sendInput` emits the same `desktop_input` envelope as the remote-desktop path — mouse move, click, scroll, typed text, key down and key up — and had no capability awareness at all. It needs no video stream, so it is reachable on a host where remote desktop is off entirely, which makes it a **wider** exposure than the path RemEx-q9zw gated rather than a narrower one. That bead's own handover note claimed input was sealed; it was not, and this closes the gap it named. `sendInput` is the only way input leaves this class, so one guard covers all six actions. **The handover worked exactly as designed and that is worth recording.** RemEx-q9zw could not fix this class, so instead of leaving a comment it wrote a test asserting this view model was NOT gated. Closing this bead made that test fail, which is what forced it to be inverted here rather than the two drifting apart. It also survived its own trap: that assertion was keyed on the token `supportsInputSimulation` rather than on the sibling's guard text, and it had to be — the sibling names its holder `_capabilityState` while this class named its own `capabilityState`, so a whole-string match would have stayed green and the handover would have been lost in silence. **Two subtleties in the wiring, both of which fail quietly if got wrong, and both now pinned.** The state is a property rather than an `init` block, because this class has none and `SendDispatcherDeclarationOrderTest` exists precisely because an `init` reaching the send path before `sendDispatcher` was declared was a real defect in the SIBLING view model — this one has never had an `init`, so a new one would import that hazard rather than reintroduce it. And it is shared `SharingStarted.Eagerly`, not the `WhileSubscribed` used by the settings flows above it: nothing ever collects this state — it is read as `.value` at send time — so under `WhileSubscribed` the upstream would never be subscribed to, `.value` would sit at its initial value forever, and the gate would be permanently open while looking correct. The neighbouring flows can use `WhileSubscribed` because Compose collects them, which is what makes the wrong choice look idiomatic. Default semantics match the sibling deliberately — an absent key means assume yes, so an older host keeps working, while an unparseable payload refuses — because two screens disagreeing about the same host would be worse than either answer. Proven by injection: removing the gate fails the test even with the capability plumbing left in place, since the assertion also pins that the guard precedes the launch; swapping `Eagerly` for `WhileSubscribed` fails it; and moving the guard inside the coroutine fails it. **The middle one of those was false when first written, and the way it was false is the more useful half.** The assertion scanned the raw file, and `SharingStarted.Eagerly` appears there twice — once in the code and once in the KDoc explaining why the code says it — so it passed on its own documentation, and the real substitution would have left the suite green with the gate permanently open. The injection that was supposed to have caught this replaced BOTH occurrences at once, so it failed for the wrong reason and read as evidence. Review re-measured with a code-only swap and found it green. `source` now strips comments before every check, which is what `SendDispatcherDeclarationOrderTest` already does and says why: a guard that fails on its own prose gets deleted rather than obeyed — and one that PASSES on its own prose is worse, because nothing draws attention to it. 255 Android unit tests green, release build clean including `lintVitalRelease`. No UI, colour or layout change, so no theming axis is touched. (`RemoteControlViewModel.kt`, `RemoteDesktopViewModelInputGateTest.kt`; RemEx-i8ty.)

- **The client now honours the host's "I cannot inject input" flag, which it had never read.** `supportsInputSimulation` has been produced by the host and consumed by nothing — not the agent, not the desktop UI, not Android, whose capability parse reads six keys and gates every path on `supportsRemoteDesktop` instead. RemEx-jvme made that flag truthful for the first time; until something read it, the fix was inert end to end. `RemoteDesktopCapabilityState` gains the field, and both places input leaves the view model — `sendInput`, which carries mouse, keyboard, scroll and typed text, and `sendPointerBatch` — return early when it is false. **Gating at the two choke points rather than at each caller is what makes the guard total WITHIN THAT VIEW MODEL**: a future input kind is covered by construction instead of by remembering. It is not total for the client, and review caught the first draft asserting otherwise — `RemoteControlViewModel`, behind the Remote Mouse screen, emits the identical `desktop_input` envelope with no capability awareness at all, and that screen needs no video stream, so it is reachable on a host where remote desktop is off entirely. Filed as **RemEx-i8ty**. The handover note this change had already appended to RemEx-vgxv said "a host that cannot inject no longer receives events", which was false for that reason and is corrected in place — the stale-premise failure that RemEx-q9zw itself existed to fix in RemEx-vgxv's original description, repeated one bead later. **THE DEFAULT IS THE PART WITH TEETH AND IT IS DELIBERATELY INCONSISTENT WITH ITS SIBLINGS.** Every other capability defaults to false, because absence means "this host is too old to offer the feature". This one is a refusal, not a feature: the host says false only to state it cannot inject. Defaulting it false would turn a missing key into a session with no input at all, which is a worse failure than the one being fixed. Absence therefore means "assume yes", which is exactly today's behaviour, and the tests exist mostly to stop someone tidying that inconsistency away. The parse was extracted from its collector to make any of this testable: the interesting cases are a key that is absent versus explicitly false, and neither occurs on a developer's own machine. Proven by injection: flipping the default to false fails exactly the backward-compatibility test, and dropping the key from the parse fails exactly the two that assert an explicit false is honoured. The gate lines themselves cannot be exercised behaviourally — the view model is an `AndroidViewModel` reaching JNI and there is no Robolectric here — so they are pinned by a source-reading test, `RemoteDesktopViewModelInputGateTest`, which is the trade this module already makes in `SendDispatcherDeclarationOrderTest`. It asserts both that the gate is present at each choke point and that `sendPointerBatch`'s precedes the consumer being started, and it pins the `RemoteControlViewModel` gap deliberately by asserting that view model is NOT gated — so RemEx-i8ty has to come back and invert it rather than the two drifting apart. **Half the bead is deliberately not done here and has been handed over rather than quietly dropped**: the input affordances are still shown and still respond, they simply send nothing. Hiding them needs the flag threaded into the screen's composables, and per CLAUDE.md a control that disappears has to say why — which is RemEx-vgxv's existing subject, so the two belong together. Doing only the hiding would leave the UI vanishing with no explanation, which is worse than the status quo. RemEx-vgxv now carries that scope explicitly, including the note that it is a Compose layout change needing the Android theming axes and a device, not just a green unit suite. No `protocolVersion` implication: the field already existed in the wire model and both values were always legal. 255 Android unit tests green, release build clean including `lintVitalRelease`. No UI, colour or layout change, so no theming axis is touched. (`RemoteDesktopViewModel.kt`, `HostCapabilityParseTest.kt`, `RemoteDesktopViewModelInputGateTest.kt`; RemEx-q9zw.)

- **A Linux host advertised input it could not perform, and the client believed it.** `HostCapabilitiesProvider.SupportsInputSimulation` answered "can this host inject input?" with `prereqReport.CanStream`, which is `SelectedTier >= X11Degraded` — and `DetermineTier` **never probes xdotool or ydotool**. Any X11 session with a D-Bus session bus reaches that tier, so a machine with neither tool installed reported `SupportsInputSimulation = true` — RemEx-is52's exact shape, a correct-looking advertisement resting on a wrong reason. **What this does NOT do is fix anything the user can see, and the first draft of this entry claimed it did.** Review checked whether the justification rested on a consumer relationship that exists, and it does not: **nothing anywhere reads `SupportsInputSimulation`** — the Android client parses six capability keys and this is not one of them, gating its stream paths on `supportsRemoteDesktop` instead — and its input-send paths on nothing at all, being unreachable until a stream exists. So the phone behaves identically before and after, the lost-taps symptom is caused by the host having no injector rather than by the flag, and this change is currently inert end to end. What it buys is that the advertisement is now true, which is the precondition for wiring a consumer (**RemEx-q9zw**) without shipping the same wrong answer to a client that acts on it. There was no fallback to save it either — the portal injector is constructed only for Wayland sessions, and `RunTool` returns early when no tool is configured. **The check that would have caught it existed and was unreachable**: the tool-aware `SupportsBasicInput` branch sits behind `if (prereqReport is not null)`, and `prereqReport` is assigned on every Linux run, including from `EvaluateLinuxPrerequisites`'s own `catch`. **The obvious fix is wrong in the mirror image, and that is why this is six tests rather than one.** ANDing the tier with `SupportsBasicInput` would deny input on a working Wayland host that simply has no xdotool installed, because there the injector is the portal, not a shell tool. The three tiers need three answers: `Unsupported` has nothing to inject into; `PortalNoPen` and `WaylandNative` inject through the portal, and `DetermineTier` already required that same portal to select them, so the tier is itself the evidence; `X11Degraded` has no portal injector, so a shell tool is the only mechanism and its absence is decisive. The enum's own doc agrees — it defines that tier as "shell-tool capture and xdotool input only". **Deliberately not expressed by making `DetermineTier` refuse the tier**, and the real reason is stronger than the one first written here. "Capture and input are separate capabilities" is not supported by this codebase, since nothing consumes the input flag at all.
