What rules it out is that `SelectedTier` drives things that ARE consumed — `SupportsRemoteDesktop`, which the client reads and gates streaming on, plus `GetInputBackendName` and `HostDoctor`'s exit codes — so probing for a shell tool there would have turned an X11 box with no xdotool from "streams, cannot inject" into "cannot stream at all", and made `--doctor` exit 1 on a machine that works. The bead's first suggestion would have shipped a regression. The Linux decision was also split out of the OS dispatch into a pure function, without which none of this is testable from Windows: a test would have hit the `OperatingSystem.IsWindows()` branch and answered a different question, so the only possible coverage was a Linux runner — and this decision was wrong for months with nobody noticing. Proven by injection, both directions: restoring `return prereqReport.CanStream` fails exactly the X11-without-a-tool test, and applying the naive AND fails exactly the Wayland one. Two follow-ups filed rather than bundled: **RemEx-q9zw** to make the client honour the flag at all, and **RemEx-vgxv** to tell the user what to install once it does — the latter needs a new user-facing string, which is a nine-file localization change rather than a rider on a correctness fix. RemEx-vgxv's own premise was corrected in the same pass, since it had been written on the same wrong assumption that the client already reacts to this flag. 1318 tests green on Windows (1 skipped), 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`; the new suite and a warning-free rebuild verified under WSL Linux too. (`HostCapabilitiesProvider.cs`, `LinuxInputCapabilityTests.cs`; RemEx-jvme.)

- **The Stage 5 Linux input router is not wired up, and three places in the codebase said otherwise.** `LinuxInputBackendRouter` has no production construction site: DI registers `LinuxInputSimulationService` as the `IInputSimulationService`, and the only way in is its `SetRouter`, which has no callers anywhere. **The wiring was never written rather than written and lost**, which is worth establishing rather than assuming: `git log -S"SetRouter("` across all history returns exactly one commit, the one that introduced the method, and `LinuxInputCapabilitySet` has no production construction site either, so the capabilities it routes on are never computed. The rest of the codebase already agrees — `RemoteDesktopHandler` says stylus data "will be preserved end-to-end once Stage 5 lands", present tense, still true. So this is documentation, not wiring: the router's own doc described a routing table nothing selects, the `_router` field said it "is set when a WaylandNative/PortalNoPen session is active", and `SetRouter` promised that "all input events are routed through the router". **The last of those was never true even in principle**, and it is the part that would actually bite: the router is consulted by four members only — `BackendName`, `EnqueuePointerSample`, `KeyDown` and `KeyUp` — so setting one routes the KEYBOARD through it while every mouse event keeps going to the shell path. Whoever wires Stage 5 up would set a router, watch keystrokes start flowing through libei, and reasonably conclude the pointer did too. **That asymmetry is now a test rather than a sentence, because a comment cannot fail.** Both classes gained launcher seams in the two preceding beads, so a service and a router can each be given their own recorder and the assertion becomes simply which one received the call. Five tests pin it, including the deliberately-inverted `AMouseButtonBYPASSESTheRouterEvenThoughOneIsSet`; when Stage 5 is wired they must fail, and that is the handover. Proven by injection: routing `MouseDown` to the router — what Stage 5 would do — fails exactly the bypass test, and removing `KeyDown`'s router branch fails exactly the one asserting the router IS connected, so neither passes by accident. **One of the three was a comment inside a capability decision, and asking a reviewer to verify its conclusion rather than accept it turned up a live bug.** `HostCapabilitiesProvider` justified advertising input support on Linux with "With Stage 5 input router: portal/EIS or legacy tools are all valid". The first draft of this fix replaced that with a correct attribution — the portal injector, not the router — and asserted the conclusion still held. It does not. `DetermineTier` **never probes xdotool or ydotool**: any X11 session with a session bus returns `X11Degraded`, `CanStream` is `SelectedTier >= X11Degraded`, so on an X11 box with neither tool installed the host advertises input it cannot perform and every tap becomes a log line. There is no fallback there — the portal injector is constructed only on Wayland. The tool-aware check that would catch it exists and is unreachable, because `prereqReport` is assigned on every Linux run. Filed as **RemEx-jvme** and the comment now scopes its claim to the Wayland tiers instead of asserting it generally; changing what the host advertises is a behaviour change that wants its own review, not a rider on a documentation bead. This is RemEx-is52's exact shape — a correct-looking advertisement resting on a wrong reason — found this time by a comment being made specific enough to be checkable. **Reading the bead's option (1), wiring it up, would have shipped a regression**, which is worth recording because the bead presented the two options as equally open. `remex.agent.native.linux/src/libei_sender.c` is a scaffold: it loads libei and then returns `REMEX_OK` from every send function after discarding its arguments, with the real `ei_device_*` calls left as comments. On a WaylandNative host, where the EIS branch is checked first in every router method, wiring today would route input into that stub and it would vanish while reporting success. The router's doc now names that as the third obstacle, alongside the missing capability-set construction and the four-member asymmetry. The router is kept rather than deleted on the strength of "no callers": libei/EIS is the strategic Wayland input path, this is most of the work for it, and its argv went under test one bead ago. 1312 tests green on Windows (1 skipped), 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`; the new suite and a warning-free rebuild verified under WSL Linux too. (`LinuxInputBackendRouter.cs`, `LinuxInputSimulationService.cs`, `HostCapabilitiesProvider.cs`, `Stage5RouterWiringTests.cs`; RemEx-7tkg.)

### Added

- **The Wayland input router's argument vectors are under test, and unifying them removed a latent quoting bug.** `LinuxInputBackendRouter` built its shell arguments the way this repo has now shipped wrong twice — `RunXdotool($"mousedown {ButtonToXdotoolButton(button)}")` — in the sibling class to the one RemEx-fu9n put under test, in the same interpolate-into-a-process shape, with no seam. **It is also not currently reachable, which review established and I had asserted the opposite of**: `SetRouter` has no callers anywhere, so the router is never constructed in production and every tier falls through to the legacy shell path. That is filed as RemEx-7tkg. Pinning the argv before it is wired is still the right order — the alternative is pinning it after something breaks — but the entry should not have claimed it was live. Twelve tests now assert the exact argv for buttons, click composition, absolute and relative moves, all four scroll directions, keys by XKB name, the unmapped-key fallback and typed text, with no process started. **Finding along the way: there were two launchers, and the one carrying eight of the nine call sites was unsafe.** `RunXdotool(string)` handed a single space-joined command line to `ProcessStartInfo(fileName, arguments)`, which re-splits and re-quotes it — so any argument containing a space or a quote would have been silently re-parsed into different arguments. Nothing sent through it happened to contain one, which is why it never failed; `type` already used the argument-list form precisely because its payload is attacker-chosen text. Everything now uses one launcher taking a real list, which is also what makes the argv assertable. Numbers are formatted invariantly for the same reason as RemEx-r29r: relative deltas are signed and `NegativeSign` is culture-dependent — including the unmapped-key fallback, which review noticed had been left culture-sensitive while the helper introduced to prevent exactly that sat two lines away. **One behaviour change came with the unification and is disclosed rather than buried**: the two launchers had different timeouts, 1000ms on the string form carrying eight call sites and 2000ms on the list form carrying only `type`. (Both figures read "six of seven" in the first draft and no counting convention yields it — eight string-form call sites across seven methods, plus `type`. Review had repeated the number in its own round-1 report before counting it, which is a fair description of how it survived.) Collapsing onto 2000 would have doubled the worst-case block on a synchronous input path that spawns up to ten processes per scroll, so `type` moves to 1000 instead. The wait is backpressure, not a kill — `WaitForExit` returning false leaves the process running and `Dispose` does not terminate it — so a long `xdotool type` still finishes. The first draft called that costless, which review sharpened and I then recorded as taken without actually taking it: what it costs is a wider window in which `TypeText` returns while xdotool is still emitting, so a following event can interleave keystrokes. Not a new window — at roughly 12ms per keystroke, 2000ms already stopped covering text past about 166 characters, and it now opens past about 83. **Deliberately not sharing a launcher or a suite with the sibling class**, because the two have already diverged where it matters — this one has its own `ClickCount` since RemEx-hnin and still uses X11 wheel buttons where the ydotool path had to stop — and a shared helper would assume the agreement these tests exist to check. Two of the assertions cover fixes that were made in other beads and never pinned here: `int.MinValue` scroll (`Math.Abs` overflow, RemEx-hnin) and the ten-process ceiling on a loop that spawns one process per detent. Proven by injection, each measured separately with a forced rebuild: passing the protocol index straight through instead of xdotool's 1-based numbering fails 3 — press, release and the composed click. (That figure was 2 in the first draft because the injection had been applied to `mousedown` alone while the sentence described the mapping generally; review caught the mismatch between what was measured and what was claimed.) dropping the end-of-options marker from relative moves fails 1, reverting `ClickCount` to the `int` overload fails 1, and transposing the horizontal wheel buttons fails 1. **The injection recipe in `docs/ralph-board-drain.md` was itself wrong and is corrected here**, having been written one bead ago: it said not to use `--no-build`, but letting `dotnet test` build is not enough either — that is also incremental, and two consecutive injections silently measured the same stale assembly and agreed for the wrong reason. The recipe is now `dotnet build -t:Rebuild` followed by `dotnet test --no-build`, and it only came to light because the guidance also says to print the failing test NAMES, which made an impossible result visible instead of plausible. 1307 tests green on Windows (1 skipped), 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`; the new suite and a warning-free rebuild verified under WSL Linux too. (`LinuxInputBackendRouter.cs`, `LinuxRouterArgvTests.cs`, `docs/ralph-board-drain.md`; RemEx-n3z6.)

### Changed

- **Test projects now fail the build on any warning, because the check that was supposed to catch them structurally could not.** Six consecutive changelog entries claimed "0 warnings" while two xUnit analyzer warnings sat in the build. The command behind the claim grepped for `warning CS`, which matches compiler diagnostics and nothing else — so no number of analyzer warnings could ever have appeared in the output. That is worse than not checking: a check unable to observe a counterexample still reads as evidence, so it stops anyone asking. **Documenting the right grep was the bead's ask; it is the weaker half of the answer**, because it only helps whoever reads the doc. `TreatWarningsAsErrors` on `*.tests` removes the question instead — the warning cannot exist to be miscounted. Proven by injection: restoring the `Assert.NotEqual` argument order that hid for six entries now produces `error xUnit2000` and **fails the build**, where before it produced a warning nothing was looking at. **Scoped to test projects deliberately, not timidly.** They do not ship, so a hard failure costs a developer two minutes; and the analyzer rules that fire here — xUnit's argument-order and assertion rules — are precisely the ones that catch tests quietly asserting less than they appear to, which is the failure this loop has hit repeatedly. Extending it to the shipping projects is filed as RemEx-3p35 rather than bundled, because `Remex.Core` is compiled as a NativeAOT JNI library and the trim/AOT analyzers emit during the **Android** build, which a solution build never exercises — so that change needs `gradlew assembleRelease` verified alongside, and possibly the warnings themselves are the deliverable. NuGet's vulnerability audit warnings are demoted rather than suppressed — they still print and still need acting on — because they arrive on someone else's clock: `NU1901`–`NU1904` are advisories published against already-committed packages, and **`NU1900`/`NU1905`, which review found missing from the first draft, are not about this repo's packages at all** but about the audit source being unreachable. Review reproduced the consequence rather than arguing it: `build-remex.ps1` restores the SOLUTION, which includes these projects, and hard-aborts on failure, so an offline machine or a DNS blip would have taken down the canonical build entry point with a message about vulnerability data that explains nothing. Verified on both platforms per the parity rule — all three test projects build with 0 warnings and 0 errors on Windows and under WSL Linux. **The documented command itself had the defect it was written to prevent, which review caught and I then reproduced**: MSBuild does not re-emit diagnostics for a project it considers up to date, so the same command run twice with the same warning still in the tree reports 2 and then 0. `-t:Rebuild` is therefore not optional in it, and the repo's own CI already carried a comment saying exactly that. The claim that a green `dotnet test` proves the test projects clean is removed for the same reason — `--no-build` compiles nothing, and even a building run is incremental. Two further verification traps this loop actually hit are also written into `docs/ralph-board-drain.md` beside the grep: `dotnet test --no-build` can measure a stale assembly on this share, so two different injections can "agree" for the wrong reason (which happened, and was caught only because the agreement was impossible); and injection counts must be re-measured after the last test edit, since adding a test during a review round silently invalidates them (which also happened, in the entry directly below this one). The condition matches case-insensitively, since MSBuild's one-argument `EndsWith` is `CurrentCulture` (case-sensitive, and culture-sensitive too) and this repo must build on a case-sensitive filesystem — a future `Remex.Foo.Tests.csproj` would otherwise be skipped silently, with the PascalCase spelling already live in these projects' assembly names. **The obvious way to write that does not work, and only running the Linux build revealed it**: review suggested `EndsWith('.tests', 'OrdinalIgnoreCase')` and I took it as free, but MSBuild's property-function binder does not resolve the two-argument overload on every SDK — `error MSB4184: Method 'System.String.EndsWith' not found` on SDK 10.0.104, where 10.0.302 accepts it. The honest attribution is the SDK version rather than the OS: it was found by running the Linux leg, but those two machines also differ by SDK, and the binder's allow-list is platform-neutral code. That matters in the direction that bites — a Windows box on the older SDK would fail too. Lower-casing before the comparison is portable and verified on both. A one-line suggestion that looked free, from a review that had already caught two real defects, would have broken every Linux build. 1295 tests green on Windows (1 skipped, so 1296 in the suite), 0 warnings on a `-t:Rebuild`. (`Directory.Build.props`, `docs/ralph-board-drain.md`; RemEx-t0f3.)

### Fixed

- **ydotool absolute pointer targets are now translated into what ydotool actually wants, which is not a coordinate.** `--absolute` is emulated, not implemented: `tool_mousemove.c` slams the pointer to the minimum of the **relative** space with two `INT32_MIN` REL emits and then moves by the operands. So the operands are an **offset from the desktop's top-left**, and passing a virtual-desktop coordinate is correct only when that origin happens to be `(0,0)`. Where it is not, every target landed off by exactly the origin — **positive coordinates included**, which is what makes this a different defect from RemEx-r29r rather than more of it: with the desktop starting at `x = -1920`, a target of `300` on the primary monitor homed to `-1920`, moved `+300`, and landed at `-1620`, on the other monitor. `MoveMouse` now subtracts the origin for the ydotool branch. **Being straight about how much this fixes today**: on X11 the origin is `(0,0)` by construction — the root window is 0-based — so there the change is a no-op, and that is precisely why the assumption survived unnoticed. Whether any compositor RemEx supports reports a non-zero origin was not established; `LinuxScreenCaptureService` computes it as the minimum over enumerated outputs and its own parser accepts `[+-]\d+`, so the code path is real, but this is a correctness change that removes an unstated assumption rather than a confirmed field failure. **The xdotool branch is deliberately left alone**, and a test asserts that with a non-zero origin so the two branches cannot later be "unified": xdotool takes X11 screen coordinates, and on an X11 session the coordinates arriving here *are* X11 screen coordinates, so subtracting an origin there would introduce the very error it removes for ydotool. Relative motion and scroll are untranslated for a different reason worth stating once — a delta is a displacement, not a position, so an origin does not apply to it, and translating one would turn every drag into a jump toward the desktop corner. The origin arrives as an internal `VirtualDesktopOrigin` delegate supplied by the composition root rather than as an `IScreenCaptureService` dependency: the value wanted is `GetVirtualDesktopBounds`, which is on the concrete Linux capture service and not on the shared interface, and a default implementation there would be wrong on Windows, where the active capture region and the virtual desktop genuinely differ. The public constructor is unchanged. Proven by injection: dropping the translation fails 3 tests, translating the wrong way (adding instead of subtracting) fails the same 3, and applying the translation to the xdotool branch fails the one test that exists to forbid it. (Those figures were 2 and 2 until review pointed out that adding a test during the review round had changed them and they had not been re-run — the same defect this entry is otherwise about, committed while writing about it. Re-measured, not recounted.) **This is the third and last layer of the same call site**, which is worth recording as a sequence: RemEx-fu9n made the argument list visible, RemEx-r29r made the coordinate survive `getopt`, and this makes it mean the right thing on arrival. Not verified on hardware — that needs a multi-monitor Wayland layout with a left-of-primary display and `ydotoold` running, and upstream's own help text warns that pointer acceleration must be off for absolute movement to be correct at all, which is noted on the bead. Review also found that the "0 warnings" this entry and its five predecessors all claimed was never checked: the verification command grepped for `warning CS`, which matches compiler warnings and nothing else, so two xUnit analyzer warnings (`xUnit2000`, an `Assert.NotEqual` argument order in a test written three beads ago) sat in the build unseen while six consecutive entries asserted there were none — every entry from RemEx-nb7c, which introduced them and claimed zero in the same commit, to this one. (That span was first written as "two predecessors" and "three consecutive entries"; review checked it against `git log` and it was twice as long. Understating it cut against the point being made, which is the more interesting half of the error.) A verification that cannot observe a whole class of result is worse than no verification, because it reads as evidence. Both are fixed, so the claim now holds for every prefix rather than one. 1295 tests green on Windows and 0 warnings, this time measured with `grep ': warning '`. (`LinuxInputSimulationService.cs`, `HostBootstrapper.cs`, `LinuxInputArgvTests.cs`, `YdotoolClickArgumentTests.cs`; RemEx-dyvd.)

- **On the ydotool backend, every leftward or upward mouse movement did nothing at all.** Both `mousemove` invocations passed their coordinates as bare positional arguments, and a bare `-5` is not a coordinate to `ydotool`: `Client/tool_mousemove.c` calls `getopt_long` with the optstring `"hawx:y:"`, which has no leading `-` or `+`, so `-5` is read as an option cluster, every character of it is discarded by `case '?': break;`, and only the remaining operand reaches the positional loop. That leaves one coordinate where the `if (i == 2)` guard needs two, so the tool prints its usage and emits **no uinput event whatsoever**. Rightward and downward drags worked, which is the worst possible shape for noticing it. The coordinates now go through `-x` / `-y`, because getopt takes the next argv as a required option's argument unconditionally, dash or no dash — the same shape the scroll path already uses since RemEx-nb7c. **The absolute half is the one that strands a whole monitor**: virtual-desktop coordinates are legitimately negative for a display positioned left of or above the primary, which this repo documents in `ClampToRange`'s summary — flooring at zero "makes left/top monitors unreachable" — so the cursor could not be placed anywhere on such a display. That is RD-D's failure one layer down, in the argument list rather than the clamp. Coordinates are also now formatted with the invariant culture: `NumberFormatInfo.NegativeSign` is culture-dependent, and a culture rendering U+2212 MINUS SIGN would produce an argument neither tool can parse — the same failure for the same values on the same lines, so fixing one and leaving the other would have been arbitrary. (The remaining non-coordinate sites stay with RemEx-hbma.) **Surviving getopt is not the same as landing in the right place, and the distinction is now written down rather than assumed.** Reading the emulation rather than only the parser showed a second, separate defect: ydotool has no absolute mode at all — it slams the pointer to the relative minimum and then moves by the operands — so those operands are an offset from the pointer space's top-left, not a coordinate. On any desktop whose origin is not `(0,0)` the cursor lands off by exactly that origin, for positive coordinates too. Filed as **RemEx-dyvd** rather than folded in, because the fix needs an origin this method does not currently receive, and the test that would have quietly implied otherwise says so explicitly instead. Proven by injection, measured per call site rather than stated once and generalised: reverting both call sites to bare positional coordinates fails 4 tests, and swapping the `-x`/`-y` pairing fails 2 in whichever call site it is swapped in — the two absolute tests for `MoveMouse`, the two relative ones for `MouseMoveRelative`, so 4 if both are swapped. The first draft of this sentence said "fails 2" beside the 4 without saying which, which reads as both. Worth recording how that survived a check: the injection runs used `dotnet test --no-build`, and on this share the restore-then-repatch cycle left MSBuild's up-to-date check satisfied, so two different injections were measured against the same stale assembly and agreed with each other for the wrong reason. Re-run without `--no-build` and with the failing test NAMES printed, they separate cleanly. All six coordinate arguments in the file, scroll included, now go through the one helper, and breaking that helper fails 5 tests — so the consolidation is regression-protected rather than cosmetic. The two tests that RemEx-fu9n deliberately pinned to the broken output now assert the fix, which is the handover that pinning was for. Not verified on a live ydotool session — that needs a Wayland machine with `ydotoold` running and no working portal, and is noted on the bead. 1289 tests green on Windows, 0 warnings. (`LinuxInputSimulationService.cs`, `LinuxInputArgvTests.cs`; RemEx-r29r.)

### Added

- **The Linux input service's argument vectors are under test, and writing that test immediately found a live bug.** Every method in `LinuxInputSimulationService` ends in a list of words handed to another program, and RemEx-nb7c was two of those lists being wrong for as long as the backend existed — `0x00110D` to press and `0x00110U` to release, neither carrying an action bit, so clicking did nothing at all on ydotool. That fix moved the string into a pure function and covered it thoroughly, and it *still* was not enough: re-introducing the original broken interpolation at the **call site** failed no test, because everything under test was the function the call site had stopped using correctly. The unit worth pinning is not the mapping but the argv, because the argv is the only thing the other program sees. `RunTool` and the cursor query now go through an `InputToolLauncher` delegate, defaulted to the real process launcher and injectable through an internal constructor alongside the probe result. **Both have to be injectable together**: which branch runs is decided by which tool was probed, and the two backends want genuinely different words for the same action — `mousedown 1` against `click 0x40` — so a test that could only observe whichever tool the build machine happened to have would cover one branch on Linux and neither on Windows. The sweep asserts click, scroll, absolute and relative move, key down/up, typed text and the cursor query, on both backends wherever they differ, without starting a process. Proven by injection, and this is the number that matters: restoring the original RemEx-nb7c interpolation now fails **3** tests where before it failed **zero**; dropping `--absolute` from the ydotool move fails 2, dropping the end-of-options marker from `type` fails 1, and dropping `--shell` from the cursor query fails 1. (That `--absolute` figure was 1 in the first draft of this entry, carried over from before a second test began asserting the same production line and described as re-run when it had not been. Review caught it, which is the entry's own thesis applied to the entry.) **The moment the argv became visible it exposed a defect nobody had been able to see** — reported by review of this change and then confirmed against upstream source. On ydotool a bare `-5` is not a coordinate: `Client/tool_mousemove.c` calls `getopt_long` with the optstring `"hawx:y:"`, which has no leading `-` or `+`, so `-5` is read as an option cluster, every character of it is discarded by `case '?': break;`, and only the remaining operand reaches the positional loop — leaving one coordinate where the guard needs two, so the tool prints its help and emits **nothing**. Every leftward or upward drag silently does nothing while rightward and downward ones work. The worse half was not in the report and is RD-D's failure one layer down, in the argument list rather than the clamp: virtual-desktop coordinates are legitimately negative for a monitor left of or above the primary — this repo says so itself in `ClampToRange`, whose summary records that flooring at zero "makes left/top monitors unreachable" — so on ydotool the cursor cannot be placed anywhere on such a display. That is filed as **RemEx-r29r** rather than fixed here, because changing how production addresses a shell tool is a behaviour change in a fenced high-risk path and wants its own review; the tests pin the current broken output deliberately and say so, so the fix will fail them and force both to move together instead of drifting apart again — which is exactly how the original argv bug survived its own fix. Review also corrected two overstatements: ydotool did not *reject* the old click arguments — it parses with `strtol` and never checks an endptr, so `0x00110U` truncated to `0x110` while `0x00110D` parsed in full to `0x110D`. Neither was truncated *and* wrong in the same way; what made both no-ops is that neither carried an action bit. 1289 tests green on Windows, 0 warnings. (`LinuxInputSimulationService.cs`, `LinuxInputArgvTests.cs`; RemEx-fu9n.)

### Fixed

- **One unexpected exception no longer costs a remote-desktop session every input it will ever receive.** `ProcessInputQueue` is the only consumer of a session's input queue; it is created once in the handler's constructor and nothing restarts it. So an exception escaping `DispatchInput` did not drop an event — it ended the `GetConsumingEnumerable` loop, and from that moment every mouse and keyboard event the client sent was queued and never drained **while the video kept streaming**. The remote user sees a live desktop that ignores them. **The catch lists could never have been complete and that is the actual defect**: behind that switch are three platform backends that shell out, P/Invoke, and talk to a portal over D-Bus, and the list named three exception types. RemEx-hnin was this bug with `OverflowException` as the instance; this is the other half, so the next unknown trigger costs an event instead. Guarded twice on purpose, because the two guards catch different things: a catch-all in `DispatchInput`, plus one around the call site, which is the only thing that can contain a throw from *inside* one of `DispatchInput`'s own catch arms — sibling clauses do not catch each other, and the logging call and its Windows hint builder are exactly that kind of code. Swallowing is defensible for this payload specifically and not as a habit: input events are independent and already explicitly best-effort — `InputEvent`'s own remarks say the queue drops them under flood and a client must not assume delivery — so losing one is within the contract and losing the session is not. **It was silent at every layer, including the last one, which is now fixed too.** The faulted task was observed only at teardown by a `catch (AggregateException)` whose entire body was the comment "expected", after which `Dispose` reported that the queue had not drained "within 2s" — blaming a slow dispatch for a thread that had been gone for minutes. `Dispose` now distinguishes three outcomes, and needs a flag to do it, because a loop that catches its way out completes its task *successfully*: `Task.Wait` returns true and nothing downstream has anything to report. **Review caught the first draft reintroducing the exact defect it was fixing.** That draft excluded `OperationCanceledException` from the catch-all "so shutdown still unwinds", pointing at the queue's arm that logs cancellation as a graceful stop — but that arm is unreachable from the queue, which is constructed and enumerated with **no cancellation token** and shuts down via `CompleteAdding`, ending the loop normally. The exclusion preserved nothing and built a fresh silent path for a backend cancellation to kill the session's input while the log called it orderly. The same wrong claim had been copied into `PingPongHandler`; both are corrected, along with a third comment that credited `Task.Wait` with throwing for an already-completed task, which only a *faulted* one does. Review also caught a vacuous test that asserted only the absence of a throw, so deleting all three specific catch arms would have left it green; it now asserts the log level, paired with one asserting an unpredicted failure is Error rather than Warning. `PingPongHandler` itself needed no change and got a comment saying why: it dispatches inline on the receive loop, so there is no consumer thread to lose — checked rather than assumed, per the bead. Proven by injection, including on the two arms that should be unreachable: removing the call-site guard fails 2 tests, suppressing the teardown report fails 1, and removing both guards at once fails 3 — the last being the only mutation that can open the cancellation hole, which is stated in the test rather than left to look like an untested claim. One spurious failure under solution-wide CPU contention was tracked down rather than re-rolled: the new waits assert liveness, not latency, so their budget is now 30s and five consecutive full-suite runs are clean. The second review round found the fix's own guarantee still had a hole of the same shape — `ObjectDisposedException` derives from `InvalidOperationException`, so one arriving outside teardown lands on the named arm rather than the catch-all, and that arm ended the loop without recording it, leaving teardown silent exactly as before. Every arm that ends the loop now keeps `Dispose` honest. 1274 tests green on Windows, 0 warnings. (`RemoteDesktopHandler.cs`, `PingPongHandler.cs`, `InputThreadContainmentTests.cs`, `ScrollDeltaClampTests.cs`; RemEx-q4wm.)

- **One scroll message could permanently disable mouse and keyboard for a remote-desktop session.** `mouseScroll` deltas went from the wire to the input backends unclamped, and `int.MinValue` reached `Math.Abs`, which has no representable result and throws rather than saturating. The interesting part is not the throw but what it cost. `RemoteDesktopHandler.DispatchInput` catches `Win32Exception`, `InvalidOperationException` and `ArgumentException`; `OverflowException` derives from `ArithmeticException` and is none of them, so it escaped into `ProcessInputQueue`, whose own catch list is narrower still, and ended its `GetConsumingEnumerable` loop. That thread is started once in the handler's constructor and nothing restarts it — so every subsequent mouse and keyboard event for that session was queued and never drained **while the video kept streaming**: a desktop that looks alive and ignores you. It was silent at every layer, including the last one: the faulted task is observed only in `Dispose`, by a `catch (AggregateException)` whose whole body is the comment "expected", and the resulting warning blames a slow dispatch. **Fixed at the wire boundary rather than in the branch that threw**, because that is the only place that covers all four backends at once — the two dispatchers now pass deltas through a new `CoordinateValidation.ClampScrollDelta`, joining the absolute coordinates already clamped by `ClampToActiveBounds` (RemEx-lq6h) and the pointer deltas already clamped by `ClampDelta` (RemEx-q6u). No wire change and no `protocolVersion` implication: the format is byte-identical and a host clamping untrusted input is not a contract change. **The bound is not arbitrary and not a behaviour change where anything was already bounded** — 1200 is ten wheel detents, which is exactly what both of `LinuxInputSimulationService`'s scroll branches already saturate at, so it is invisible there. It exists for the two paths that bounded nothing: Windows passes the value straight to `MOUSEEVENTF_WHEEL`, and the Linux backend router's xdotool fallback spawned one process per detent with **no ceiling at all**, so a large delta could ask for millions of them — which is why a magnitude bound rather than an `int.MinValue` special case. Real gestures are nowhere near it: the Android mouse pad sends ±100 per tap and ±500 at maximum sensitivity, and the remote-desktop surface would need more than 160px of two-finger travel inside a single event to reach it. Both `Math.Abs` sites now widen to `long` first, as a second line of defence for any future caller reaching a backend without a handler. **Review corrected four over-broad claims in the first draft's comments**, three of which came from taking the bead's own wording at face value: `PingPongHandler` dispatches inline behind a `catch (Exception)`, so the session-killing consequence was never possible there and only the remote-desktop dispatcher was affected; the router's fallback was **not** among the paths that "already saturate"; and `LinuxInputSimulationService`'s xdotool branch negates rather than taking a magnitude, and unary minus on `int.MinValue` is unchecked, so that branch never threw — it quietly emitted one click instead of ten. Proven by injection: restoring the original code reproduces the real `System.OverflowException: Negating the minimum value of a twos complement number is invalid` and fails 4 tests, and widening the bound fails the test that pins it. Disclosed rather than papered over: nothing test-pins `PingPongHandler`'s clamp (its 14-argument constructor includes five concrete types, so a harness for it is its own piece of work), and the "session dies permanently" half of the diagnosis is verified by reading rather than by a test. The containment gap itself — one bad event should cost that event, not the session — is filed as RemEx-q4wm rather than folded in here. 1267 tests green on Windows, 0 warnings; Android release build clean, which is also the NativeAOT link check for the `Remex.Core` addition. (`CoordinateValidation.cs`, `RemoteDesktopHandler.cs`, `PingPongHandler.cs`, `LinuxInputBackendRouter.cs`, `LinuxInputSimulationService.cs`, `ScrollDeltaClampTests.cs`, `CoordinateValidationTests.cs`; RemEx-hnin.)

- **Mouse clicking and scrolling did nothing at all on the ydotool backend, and the arguments being sent were not valid in any grammar.** `ydotool click` takes a small button index OR'd with `0x40` (press) or `0x80` (release). It was being handed an evdev `BTN_*` code with a literal letter stuck on the end — `0x00110D` to press, `0x00110U` to release. The two were not even wrong in the same way: `D` is a hex digit, so the press form parsed; `U` is not. Neither was *rejected* — ydotool parses with `strtol(..., NULL, 16)` and never checks an endptr, so the release form was silently truncated to `0x110` — but the mismatch is what made the bug findable by inspection. It is not what broke clicking. Upstream's `Client/tool_click.c` masks the argument to a low nibble and ORs it onto `BTN_MOUSE` (`keycode = (key & 0xf) | 0x110`), then emits **only** inside `if (key & 0x40)` and `if (key & 0x80)`. The old argument set neither bit, so both guards failed and nothing reached `uinput` — the man page's own note that a bare `0x00` "chooses left button, but does nothing", arrived at from the other direction. The bead asked whether this was P3 or P1 depending on that answer; it was P1. **The mapping came with a trap that the naive fix walks straight into.** ydotool orders `0x00 LEFT, 0x01 RIGHT, 0x02 MIDDLE`, while the protocol vocabulary and every other table in this repo use `0 left, 1 middle, 2 right`. Passing the shared index through — the obvious thing to do now that RemEx-upxn has unified those tables — would have swapped right-click and middle-click on this backend only, silently, which is precisely what RemEx-kie3 already cost this project once. So `ToYdotool` is a deliberate transposition rather than a reuse, and a test pins it against upstream's own worked examples (`0x41` right down, `0x82` middle up, `0xC0` left click) instead of against this repo's opinion. **Review found the same defect a second time, fifty lines below, in the scroll path.** `MouseScroll` sent X11's wheel buttons 4/5/6/7 to `ydotool click` — a comment in the code even admitted it was copying "the xdotool fallback pattern". ydotool has no wheel button: those numbers masked to EXTR/FORWARD/BACK/TASK and, again carrying no action bit, emitted nothing, so every scroll gesture spawned up to ten processes to accomplish nothing. The real mechanism is `mousemove --wheel`, which emits `REL_HWHEEL`/`REL_WHEEL` using its arguments verbatim as detent counts — so one invocation replaces the whole loop. **That option is absent from ydotool's man page and present in its source**, which is the likeliest reason the click-based workaround was written at all. **Everything asserted here was fetched from upstream rather than recalled**, deliberately: a recent change in this area invented a tool name from memory and shipped it in a source comment. Doing so caught a fabrication in the first draft of this one too — a claim that `0x0D` "selects FORWARD", when FORWARD is `0x05` and `0x0D` is outside the documented range entirely — and the same fetch showed the man page documents three more buttons (`0x05` FORWARD, `0x06` BACK, `0x07` TASK) than the citation first written down, none of which `MouseButtons` can reach. The argument is now built by one `YdotoolClickArgument` function rather than interpolated at each call site, because the bug lived precisely in that interpolation and no test could see it: the first version of these tests pinned the mapping functions, and restoring the broken argument form failed **nothing**. It now fails 12. Inverting the wheel sign fails 11 of 12 detent tests, and dropping the sub-notch minimum fails 4. This path only runs on a Wayland session with no portal and `ydotoold` present — the portal is preferred and xdotool is the usual fallback — which is why it went unnoticed. 1246 tests green on Windows, 0 warnings. Not verified on a live ydotool session; that needs a Wayland machine with the daemon running and is noted on the bead. (`MouseButtonCodes.cs`, `LinuxInputSimulationService.cs`, `YdotoolClickArgumentTests.cs`, `YdotoolWheelDetentTests.cs`; RemEx-nb7c.)

### Changed

- **Windows had a complete window-control backend that the client could never see, because the host told it the feature did not exist.** `WindowsDesktopWindowControlService` is a full Win32 implementation — list, activate, raise, minimize, close, resize — and `HostBootstrapper` registers it for `IDesktopWindowControlService` on Windows, overriding the unsupported default. `RemoteDesktopHandler` dispatches `desktop_window_query` straight to it with **no capability check of its own**, so the host would have answered those queries correctly all along. But `HostCapabilitiesProvider.SupportsAdvancedWindowControl` opened with `if (!OperatingSystem.IsLinux() ...) return false` and was never revisited when that backend landed — and the Android client hides its **entire** window-control section on that flag. A working, registered, dispatched feature was invisible on the platform it was written for. Nothing failed and nothing logged; two independently-correct-looking halves simply disagreed. **This was very nearly closed as "not a bug".** The investigation that found it started from a device pass that could not locate the panel, correctly established it was gated on a capability the host reports false on Windows, and stopped there — concluding the gating was "consistent end to end" and Windows-absence was "by design". Review pushed one layer further and found the registered Win32 service the conclusion had assumed away. The same draft also invented `wmctrl` as the Linux tool and baked it into a source comment; the probe looks for `kdotool` and `xdotool`, so a Linux user following that comment would have installed the wrong package. Both are corrected. Virtual-desktop *moves* remain unsupported on Windows — the COM API is undocumented — but that one action already returns a clear, non-fatal error, which is a property of the action rather than grounds for withholding the other six. Guarded by tests holding both halves together: that Windows advertises the capability, and that the very service registered there really does enumerate windows. Reverting the gate fails the first. (`HostCapabilitiesProvider.cs`, `RemoteDesktopScreen.kt`, `AdvancedWindowControlCapabilityTests.cs`; RemEx-is52.)

### Added

- **The prime-before-read invariant in telemetry is now guarded by a test instead of by one line nobody would miss.** Moving counter construction off the startup thread (RemEx-z447) left the whole guarantee resting on a single bounded wait in `GetTelemetryAsync` — delete it and the suite stayed green while the artefacts that got RemEx-48kh reverted came straight back: a constructed but unprimed CPU rate counter reporting 0% from an empty sample window, and a live NIC whose byte baseline was never taken, making the first delta one stray frame divided by the process uptime. `TelemetryWarmUpGateTests` holds the warm-up open through an injected task and asserts a tick meanwhile reads **no** counters at all. That assertion has real teeth rather than being a null-counter tautology: the read emits six WindowsPerf sensors even with every counter null, three of them from a P/Invoke that needs no counter at all — so an empty result can only mean the read never happened. **The warm-up is injected rather than raced**, because the real window is short precisely when the machine is warm, which is the worst possible property for a regression guard; and HWiNFO is pointed at a region that does not exist, because where it *is* running its readings displace the WindowsPerf sensors being asserted about and the test would pass or fail by hardware. Proven by injection: removing the wait fails the guard. **Review caught the second test claiming something its own fixture cannot see** — it was named for the cache-seeding flag, but the skip set is `seeded && hwinfoSensors.Count > 0`, and making HWiNFO absent pins that conjunct false, so setting the flag wrongly left the test green. The very choice that makes the first test machine-independent blinds the second; they want opposite fixtures. It is renamed to what it proves (the gate releases rather than permanently disabling), and the two clauses this fixture structurally cannot reach are filed as RemEx-cxel with the reason each obvious approach fails. Also fixed on the way: the first version of these two tests added **12 seconds** to the agent suite by waiting out the real 2-second fallback timeout twice, so that timeout became an instance field a test can shrink — 27s back down to 18s. (`TelemetryWarmUpGateTests.cs`, `WindowsTelemetryService.cs`; RemEx-s999.)

### Changed

- **Sign-in no longer waits for the machine's performance-counter catalog to load.** `WindowsTelemetryService`'s constructor runs inside the serial `IHost.StartAsync`, and building the fallback `PerformanceCounter`s there blocked it. **The cost was measured rather than inherited, and it is worse than previously recorded**: the first construction in a process takes **510–888 ms** warm across three separate runs, and **4.9 seconds** on the first run against a cold OS cache — which is precisely the sign-in case. A second construction in the same process costs 9 ms, so what is being paid for is the counter catalog, loaded once. After the change the constructor measures **0 ms**. **The work is moved, not skipped, and that distinction is the whole design.** Making it lazy was tried before and reverted (RemEx-48kh) for a reason that still stands: this path does more than construct counters — it primes the CPU rate counter and takes the NIC byte baseline, and both are only meaningful *ahead of* the first read. Prime microseconds before the first `NextValue` and the counter reports 0% from an empty sample window; take the network baseline inside the call that consumes it and the elapsed divisor is near zero, turning one stray frame into a multi-megabyte-per-second reading. Per-counter laziness would also buy nothing now, because the first successful tick reads every category to seed the fallback cache (RemEx-c2g4) — so nothing would go unbuilt anyway. Instead the warm-up runs on a background task and the tick waits on it, which preserves the prime-before-read ordering exactly. **Review corrected the mechanism, and the first draft's stated one was simply wrong**: it claimed a slow warm-up would surface as the read's existing 2-second timeout, but `Task.Run(func, token)` observes its token only for *scheduling* — once the delegate is running, `CancelAfter` cannot interrupt it, so the first read would have blocked for the whole warm-up. The wait is now bounded and awaited before the read is dispatched, and on timeout it **skips** the read rather than falling through to it. Falling through is the trap worth naming: the warm-up assigns the NIC before it takes the byte baseline, so a half-finished one leaves a non-null adapter with an unset poll timestamp — one stray frame divided by the process uptime — alongside a constructed but unprimed CPU counter. A skipped tick also deliberately does not mark the cache seeded, so the next tick still performs the full seeding read. Disposal now checks the result of its bounded wait rather than discarding it, since `Wait(TimeSpan)` returns `false` on timeout instead of throwing, which would have made a wedged warm-up undiagnosable while leaking counter handles. The ordering invariant itself is still unpinned by any test — deleting one line would leave the suite green — and that is filed as RemEx-s999 rather than left implied. Verified on Windows; the class is `[SupportedOSPlatform("windows")]` and never instantiates on Linux. (`WindowsTelemetryService.cs`; RemEx-z447.)

### Fixed

- **A stalled telemetry read no longer serves a payload with whole categories missing.** This closes a regression introduced one commit earlier: once a tick reads only the categories a healthy HWiNFO is not already covering, the cached fallback stores a *partial* read — so on the tick where HWiNFO stopped producing **and** the now-full read exceeded its 2-second timeout, the cache served only the categories HWiNFO had *not* been covering, dropping the rest. A double fault lasting one tick, but before the skip existed the cache had always been complete. The cache is now keyed **by category**, each entry refreshed only when that category was actually read, so a timeout serves the freshest available reading for every category regardless of which ticks read which. **The obvious alternative is worse and the code says so**: "only cache complete reads" sounds safer, but a machine with good HWiNFO coverage never performs a complete read, so its fallback would freeze at whatever the first tick produced and stay there. Two directions are pinned by tests, because they pull opposite ways — a *skipped* category keeps its previous reading, while a category that was read and produced **nothing** is cleared rather than left stale, so a machine whose only NIC disappears stops showing traffic on it instead of serving the last rates forever. The map is replaced wholesale rather than mutated, keeping the same atomicity for a concurrent reader that the single-field cache had, and a test pins that updating leaves the previous map untouched — including the carried-over case, where old and new maps share the same list object. **Review caught the fix being self-defeating in the commonest configuration**, which is worth stating because the first draft's headline was simply wrong: where HWiNFO has been healthy since process start and covers CPU and Memory, those categories are *never read*, so they never entered the cache and a stall still served a payload missing them — exactly the hole being closed. The first successful tick now reads every category regardless of coverage, seeding the cache; that costs one extra read once per process. Uptime is recomputed on the stall path rather than cached, since it is `TickCount64` formatting that cannot stall and a stale value would be strictly worse. Proven by injection: restoring the whole-payload semantics fails exactly the regression test. 1216 tests green on Windows, 601 passed / 8 skipped on Linux. (`WindowsTelemetryService.cs`, `TelemetryCategoryCacheTests.cs`; RemEx-c2g4.)

### Changed

- **A machine with healthy HWiNFO stops paying for telemetry it throws away every second.** `GetTelemetryAsync` read the WindowsPerf fallback unconditionally on every tick — three `PerformanceCounter` reads, `GlobalMemoryStatusEx`, a NIC statistics read and whatever WMI does — and then overlaid HWiNFO on top of the result, at 1 Hz for the life of the process. **The obvious fix is wrong, and finding out why was most of the work.** The bead proposed "the pieces are there; what is missing is the branch", but a branch on `_hwinfoAvailable` would have deleted sensors: the overlay is **category-scoped**, dropping a WindowsPerf reading only when HWiNFO also supplies its category, and HWiNFO's categories come from the user's own hardware and configuration. A desktop reporting rich CPU and Memory data but nothing for Disk or Network is ordinary — and on that machine a wholesale skip removes the only Disk and Network sensors there are, silently, on exactly the machines that look healthiest. So the fix is a **reorder, not a branch**: HWiNFO is read first (cheap — the reading addresses were resolved once, so a tick is a handful of `ReadDouble` calls against a mapped view), the categories it actually covered become the skip set, and only the uncovered WindowsPerf sections are read. The bead's two secondary worries turned out to be non-issues, verified rather than assumed: nothing here assumes a fixed interval, since a rate `PerformanceCounter` averages over the gap since its own previous call and the NIC block divides by **measured** elapsed time from `_lastNetworkPoll`, so a resumed category reports an average over the skipped window rather than a spike. The merge rule is now one extracted, pure, tested function instead of an inline filter, and the skip set is proven to be *exactly* what that merge would have discarded — which is the argument that skipping and reading-then-merging are equivalent. Proven by injection: implementing the naive wholesale skip fails 4 of the 5 new tests. **Review found a counter that was pure overhead**: `_ramCounter` — a `PerformanceCounter("Memory", "Available MBytes")` — was constructed at startup and disposed at shutdown but **never read**, since the memory sensors come from `GlobalMemoryStatusEx`. It is deleted, which also corrects the "four counters" figure inherited from the bead to three. No measured wall-clock claim is made here; what is eliminated is structural, and the tests assert behaviour rather than timing. One narrow regression is filed rather than hidden: the cached fallback is now a partial read, so a tick where HWiNFO stops *and* the WMI read times out can serve fewer categories than before — double-fault, one tick, self-healing, and the naive fix is worse than the bug (RemEx-c2g4). 1210 tests green on Windows, and the new ones are pure enough to run on Linux too. (`WindowsTelemetryService.cs`, `HwInfoCategoryOverlayTests.cs`; RemEx-rxth.)

- **A stylus axis the device never reported is now omitted rather than reported as zero.** The pointer-batch writer replaced any NaN or infinity with `0`, on every axis. For the five **required** axes that is still right — `logicalX`, `logicalY`, `dx`, `dy` and `pressure` are non-nullable on the host (`float`, not `float?`), so "absent" is not a state they can express, and `0` beats losing the whole stroke to an exception. For the four **optional** axes it was wrong: `hoverDistance`, `tiltX`, `tiltY` and `orientation` are `float?` on the host, so absence is a supported wire state meaning exactly *"this device did not report it"*. Writing `0` instead asserts something specific and false — a stylus lying perfectly flat, or touching the glass — and nothing downstream can distinguish that fabricated zero from a real measurement. The null case was always omitted; a non-finite value now takes the same path, via an `appendOptionalNumber` whose name states which rule applies where. Verified against the host model rather than assumed. **This is wire fidelity, not a behaviour change today, and review insisted on saying so plainly**: no current host consumer distinguishes an absent axis from a zero one — the Linux tablet router coalesces `?? 0f`, the Windows input bridge drops tilt/hover/pressure entirely until the stylus backend lands, and `orientation` has no reader at all. What changes is that the JSON stops asserting "flat, touching the glass" when the truth is "the driver said nothing", which is the shape the eventual stylus backend needs. No `protocolVersion` implication: absence was already valid for these four, so this narrows what goes on the wire without changing what the wire means. Proven by injection — restoring the old fallback fails the new test and nothing else. 246 Android unit tests green including the 23 pre-existing serializer tests; release build clean with `lintVitalRelease`. (`RemoteDesktopPointerSerializer.kt`, `PointerBatchSerializerTest.kt`; RemEx-unda.)

### Fixed

- **The test suite is now actually green on Linux, and the cross-platform parity rule can be checked instead of promised.** CLAUDE.md has always required the repo to work equally on Windows and CachyOS, but the suite had apparently never been *run* on Linux — and it was not clean there: 590 of 598 agent tests passed, with 8 permanent failures. **None was a product defect.** Seven were `HwInfoSamplerTests`, every one dying on `PlatformNotSupportedException: Named maps are not supported` — the *test* fabricates HWiNFO's shared region using a **named** memory-mapped file, which is a Windows-only .NET feature (as is HWiNFO). The eighth failed on its *sanity precondition* rather than its security assertion: it asserts a UNC path would match the launcher allowlist verbatim, which needs Windows path semantics, since `IsLaunchAllowed` compares `OrdinalIgnoreCase` on Windows and `Ordinal` elsewhere and a backslash is not a separator on Linux. The guard it actually protects is platform-independent and is covered on every platform by the sibling theory, which passes. Those 8 are now marked with a dependency-free `WindowsOnlyFact` that takes a **mandatory reason** and skips only off-Windows. (Review caught the first draft shipping an unused `Theory` counterpart alongside it — deleted, since this repo does not carry speculative code, with a note recording the xUnit quirk that would complicate adding one: a skipped theory collapses to a single case rather than one per `[InlineData]`, which is exactly what would break the skip-count arithmetic relied on below.) **Deliberately not the other fix**: relaxing the assertions so they also pass on Linux would have meant testing less on Windows, where the code runs. Windows still executes all 598 with **zero** skipped, which is the evidence that no coverage was traded away; Linux now reports 590 passed / 8 skipped / 0 failed. The other two suites turned out to be Linux-clean already (260 core, 347 desktop), so the whole solution now passes on both. Why this had gone unmeasured is itself worth knowing and is now in CLAUDE.md: the obvious `dotnet test` fails under WSL because that .NET install has no `Microsoft.AspNetCore.App`, and the fix — `-p:RuntimeIdentifier=linux-x64 -p:SelfContained=true` — needs no package install or other change to the machine. (`WindowsOnlyAttributes.cs`, `HwInfoSamplerTests.cs`, `AppLauncherServiceSecurityTests.cs`, `CLAUDE.md`; RemEx-z17h, RemEx-lrk4.)

### Changed

- **The file-transfer receive loop no longer allocates three buffers for every inbound frame.** Each frame cost a growable `MemoryStream`, its `ToArray()`, and then a third `payload.ToArray()` before the handler — at the 256 KB frame cap, Large Object Heap allocations several times per frame, for buffers discarded moments later. The loop now fills **one** rented buffer per channel and passes a `ReadOnlyMemory` view of it straight through. **The `ToArray()` at the call site was never defending anything**, which is the detail that made this tractable: `TryRead` yielded a `ReadOnlySpan`, and a `ref struct` cannot cross an `await`. A `ReadOnlyMemory` overload of `TryRead` removes the reason for the copy; it delegates parsing to the span version so the two cannot disagree about what a valid frame is. **The ownership question the bead posed was settled by reading before any code was written**, since this is the shape that has reverted the capture-path pooling three times: the loop `await`s its handler, which `await`s `WriteChunkAsync`, which writes the stream awaited and appends to the hash synchronously and retains nothing — so no frame outlives its iteration. That property is not enforced by any compiler, so `FileChannelReceiveBufferTests` drives the **real** receive loop over a scripted socket with four differently-sized, differently-filled chunks and compares the staged bytes; removing the `await` makes it fail. **Review caught the oversize-bound test being vacuous** — it asserted on a path the receive loop never touches, and passed with the bound deleted — so it now asserts on the staging partial's length, and deleting the bound fails it. The reuse test's teeth turned out to depend on chunk sizes exceeding the partial stream's 64 KB buffer, since that is the handler's only suspension point; that is now written down beside the data rather than left as an accident waiting for someone to "simplify" it. It asserts on the staging partial rather than completing the transfer, because `RunChannelAsync`'s teardown suspends the receive session — correct behaviour, and what keeps a partial resumable across a dropped socket. One trap avoided along the way: `buffer[..length]` on an **array** uses the range indexer, which allocates and copies, quietly reinstating the very allocation being removed — and it compiles either way. 1205 tests green, 0 warnings; Android release build clean, which is also the NativeAOT link check for the `Remex.Core` change. (`FileFrameEnvelope.cs`, `TransferSessionManager.cs`, `FileChannelReceiveBufferTests.cs`, `FileFrameWriteIntoPooledBufferTests.cs`; RemEx-8su9.)

- **File transfer no longer allocates a Large Object Heap buffer for every frame it sends.** Each outbound `/ws/files` frame was built with `new byte[4 + header + payload]`; at the 256 KB payload cap that is an LOH allocation, and a transfer running at 100 MB/s produces roughly 400 a second — pure Gen2 pressure for a buffer that is dead the instant the send completes. The frame is now written into a rented buffer. **The safer of the two options in the bead was taken deliberately, and the reason is worth recording.** The alternative — sending the header and payload as two WebSocket fragments — is genuinely zero-copy, but its correctness rests on every receiver reassembling fragments, and that could not be proven here: the only production reader of these frames on the far side is Android's OkHttp, and the test project has no MockWebServer to demonstrate it with. On a wire path whose last silent breakage bricked all of v3 file transfer with "Peer did not respond" (RemEx-y6x6), an unprovable assumption is not worth the extra copy it saves. Renting achieves the same allocation win with **no wire change at all**, and its lifetime argument is trivial rather than delicate: `WebSocket.SendAsync` does not retain the buffer, and the send is awaited before the `finally` returns it — the opposite shape to the capture-path pooling that has reverted three times, where the buffer outlives its producer. **One trap came with it and is now pinned from both ends, and review sharpened what it actually is**: `ArrayPool` returns an array *at least* the requested size, so the send must be bounded by what was written. `new ArraySegment<byte>(buffer)` would ship the tail as well — and because the pool is not cleared on return, that tail is whatever the *previous renter* left, realistically bytes of an earlier frame and possibly from a different file or transfer. So the bound is load-bearing for **confidentiality**, not merely for a well-formed frame, and neither failure announces itself. (Not clearing on return is the deliberate other half: clearing would memset the full bucket on every frame, which is the throughput this change exists to stop wasting, and the bound already prevents anything past the frame from leaving.) `FileFrameCodec` gained `SerializeHeader`/`GetFrameLength`/`WriteFrame` so the frame layout has one definition that both the allocating and the pooling caller go through, rather than two that must agree. Proven by injection: restoring the unbounded segment fails four of the five new sender tests. The inbound half of the original bead is **not** included — the receive buffer is handed to a consumer, so its lifetime is the unresolved ownership question rather than a settled one — and is filed as RemEx-8su9 with that distinction spelled out. 1198 tests green, 0 warnings; Android release build clean, which is also the NativeAOT link check for the `Remex.Core` change. (`FileFrameEnvelope.cs`, `TransferSessionManager.cs`, `FileFrameWriteIntoPooledBufferTests.cs`, `FileChannelSendFramingTests.cs`; RemEx-npdm.)

### Added

- **A host-reported download failure is now covered by a test, because the client no longer needs the whole view model to be driven.** `FileTransferClient` took a concrete `ConnectionViewModel`, and one consequence was absolute rather than awkward: a C# event can only be raised by the class that declares it, so **no test could ever hand the client an inbound `file_transfer_end`** — which is the ordinary way a download goes wrong. It now takes `IFileTransferConnection`, two members wide (the message event and `SendAsync`), which `ConnectionViewModel` satisfies **without gaining a single member** — both signatures were already exactly what the interface declares. The unwind this unblocks is worth covering rather than reasoning about: RemEx-gyf4 found two real defects on it by reading, and every failure mode there is a silent leak or a wrong file on disk, never a crash. **Review corrected the justification, and the correction is the point**: the first draft claimed the unwind path "could not be exercised from a test at all", which is false — `FileTransferCancelOrderingTests` and `FileTransferClientLeakTests` already drive `DownloadAsync` end to end through the existing `IWebSocketSender` seam and through local-file failures that never reach the connection. Two of the four tests written were duplicates of those and were removed rather than left to be two things that must agree; what remains is the host-failure case that genuinely needed the seam, plus a faulted Start send that was reachable before but uncovered. **Teeth proven by injection, twice**: dropping two of the five dictionary reaps from the `finally` fails them on the registration count, and dropping only `File.Delete` fails them on the partial file surviving — each restored afterward. Also disclosed rather than quietly skipped: the flush-failure case this bead promised is *not* delivered, because it needs a broken `FileStream` handle rather than a fake socket, and is filed as RemEx-04p8. No production behaviour changed — the seam is a type swap. Explicitly no flow-control change; that half of RemEx-wfim still needs an operator decision. 1187 tests green, 0 warnings (desktop 345 → 347: four were drafted, two deleted as duplicates of tests already in the repo). (`IFileTransferConnection.cs`, `FileTransferClient.cs`, `DownloadUnwindTests.cs`; RemEx-qmnl.)

### Fixed

- **The pairing QR code could encode an address the phone can never reach.** `GenerateQrCodeAsync` substitutes this PC's LAN IPv4 when the configured host is loopback, so the phone scanning the code gets somewhere it can actually connect. It decided that with `host is "localhost" or "127.0.0.1" or "::1"`, and that list misses two forms: `Uri.Host` returns the **bracketed** `"[::1]"` for an IPv6 literal, so the `"::1"` arm had never matched anything, and all of `127.0.0.0/8` is loopback while only `127.0.0.1` was listed. On a miss the loopback host went into the QR payload unchanged and the user scanned a code that silently cannot work — no error, just a pairing that never completes. This one **ships**: the command is bound in both ConnectionView and SettingsView. **The bug was found in a property that turned out not to be the one that mattered.** It was filed against `LanHostAddress`, which has the identical defect — and which review then established has *no consumer at all*, no binding and no caller, making it latent. The same review found the fourth copy of the predicate sitting in the QR path, bound and shipping, 146 lines below. Both are fixed; whether the unbound property should be wired up or deleted is filed as RemEx-19al. **What made one bug into four copies is now written down rather than left to be rediscovered**: five sites in `remex.desktop` decide "is this loopback", and the remarks on the shared predicate list all five by name. Two literal copies remain and both gate trust-on-first-use, so both are behind the operator sign-off tracked by RemEx-19pj — including `RemoteDesktopService.cs:423`, a second TOFU gate that bead had not been scoped to cover. The QR substitution was extracted to a small pure `ResolvePhoneReachableHost` because the command's only output is a rendered bitmap; asserting on the host through it would have meant decoding a PNG under an Avalonia render stack. Both fixes were proven by injection — restoring the old predicate fails exactly the `[::1]` and `127.0.0.2` cases and nothing else. No security gate was touched, which is the entire reason this was split from RemEx-19pj. 1185 tests green, 0 warnings. (`ConnectionViewModel.cs`, `LanHostAddressTests.cs`, `QrPairingHostSubstitutionTests.cs`; RemEx-eskd.)

### Added

- **Two concurrent Remote Desktop clients are now actually exercised against one shared capture service, instead of being reasoned about.** `IScreenCaptureService` is registered `AddSingleton` on both platform branches and resolved per `/ws/desktop` request, so two connected phones run independent stream loops against one capture instance — the finding that ruled out "Design B" in RemEx-lcp8's second investigation and constrains the rest of the pooling work. Nothing in the suite had ever run it, so every claim about it was unverified. `ConcurrentDesktopClientsTests` drives two real `/ws/desktop` sessions through the genuine handler and socket path against a capture double that hands both clients the SAME array, and asserts each client's frames arrive with their payload intact. A second test has a client join while another is already mid-stream, which is where a pooled backend's window for handing out a buffer still being sent is widest. **Both assert the two sessions genuinely OVERLAPPED in time** — every other assertion in the file is satisfied by two sequential sessions too, so without timestamps "concurrent" would have been decoration in a test name. **It took two review rounds to get the file's own accuracy claims right, and that argument is now recorded in it**: the first draft implied broader coverage than it had, the correction over-swung into asserting that MJPEG never aliases in production, and neither was true. `WindowsScreenCaptureService` has three MJPEG tiers — WGC and the GDI fallback encode into a fresh stream per call and do not alias, but the DXGI tier caches its encoded frame and returns that identical memory on every static-desktop replay, with `isLive` set, so two concurrent clients genuinely are handed one array today. (`ScreenCaptureResult`'s "every producer allocates a fresh stream per capture" is about stream *allocation*; the replay path allocates nothing.) The header now carries that tier split instead of a blanket claim in either direction, and scopes out the raw-to-H.264 path, which aliases the same way but needs ffmpeg or an encoder injection seam the handler does not have. What the file earns is therefore concrete: on the tier where production really does share a buffer, the host neither mutates it nor lets one client's stream corrupt another's. **The teeth are permanent this time**: a `RecyclingCaptureService` control refills the shared array in place on every capture, and a test asserts zero frames survive intact — so if the checks ever stop being sensitive to a recycled buffer, that says so out loud rather than passing quietly. Test-only; no production code changed. 1167 tests green, 0 warnings; verified on Windows — the `/ws/desktop` endpoint takes an additional PipeWire lifetime-acquire branch on Linux that this run never enters, so a Linux confirmation is still owed. (`ConcurrentDesktopClientsTests.cs`; RemEx-c5an.)

- **A harness that makes a recycled video buffer fail loudly instead of producing an artifact nobody can see.** Three separate attempts at pooling the Remote Desktop capture buffers (RemEx-lcp8, with RemEx-wpk9 and RemEx-dfhq stacked behind it) have been implemented and reverted, always for the same reason: the failure mode is a buffer reused while ffmpeg is still reading it, which yields **corrupted video rather than a crash or a red test**. The third attempt is the instructive one — its buffer pool's contract held perfectly under the pool's own unit tests and still broke, because nothing exercised the BOUNDARY between a caller that caches frames and a writer loop that consumes them asynchronously. `FrameInputPipelineTests` drives that boundary: the genuine `EncodeFrame` → bounded drop-write channel → `StdinWriterLoop` path, against a recording stream instead of a live ffmpeg child, so it runs headless with no encoder process and no GPU. The recorder copies each write at the **end** of the write window on purpose — snapshotting at the start would miss every mid-write recycle, which is the only thing worth catching here. Four behaviours are pinned: frames arrive intact and in order; `EncodeFrame` does **not** copy, so ownership belongs to the writer loop from a successful `TryWrite` until its `WriteAsync` returns; an aliased replay array — the static-desktop case where the capture backend hands the same buffer out on consecutive ticks, which is exactly what broke the third attempt — is delivered intact both times; and a full channel silently discards frames while `AcceptedInputFrameCount` still counts them, proving `DropWrite` makes `TryWrite`'s return value a lie and leaves a "the writer returns the buffer" scheme leaking on the busy path. **The teeth were proved by injection, not asserted**: a temporary probe resubmitting one refilled buffer, and another overwriting the replay array after submit, both went red naming the offending byte index. **The file is explicit about the limit of its own guarantee**, because a harness that oversells itself would recreate the false confidence it exists to end: these tests are NOT an automatic gate on the pooling beads, since that pool lives in the capture backend which is not in this harness — they pin the encoder-side contract and supply reusable detection machinery, and a pooling attempt has to route its pooled producer through them to get the benefit. Two gaps are recorded rather than glossed: `RemoteDesktopHandler` is absent because it constructs its encoder directly with no injection seam, and the two-concurrent-clients-against-the-singleton-capture-service hazard is filed as RemEx-c5an. Production behaviour is unchanged — the only non-test edits are extracting the channel construction so the harness exercises the real options rather than a copy, a documented internal test seam, and widening the input-channel capacity constant from `private` to `internal` so the drop assertion is bounded by the real value instead of a duplicate of it. 1164 tests green, 0 warnings. (`FrameInputPipelineTests.cs`, `FFmpegH264Encoder.cs`; RemEx-13se.)

### Changed

- **Stylus inking no longer allocates a JSON object graph and a coroutine per touch sample.** The pointer path is unthrottled on purpose — fidelity beats bandwidth for handwriting — so every `MotionEvent` built its batch through `JSONObject`: one map per sample, ~15 autoboxed `put` calls each, a `JSONArray`, and an intermediate `JSONStringer` buffer, then `viewModelScope.launch` for the send. Thousands of short-lived allocations per second, producing GC pressure at exactly the moment latency is what the user feels. The batch is now written straight into one `StringBuilder`, and the per-event launches are replaced by a single consumer draining an unbounded `Channel`. **Ordering is preserved for a stronger reason than "channels are FIFO"**: every producer is the Compose main thread and the consumer runs on the same `limitedParallelism(1)` dispatcher the launches already serialized through, so the dispatch order is identical. The buffer is `UNLIMITED` deliberately — a bounded channel must drop or suspend, and dropping loses exactly the stroke fidelity this path exists to protect; it is not a new risk, because the old per-event launches queued without bound on that same single thread. **A hand-rolled JSON writer is the obvious way to silently break a wire format**, so the 23 pre-existing serializer tests were kept working by reimplementing the now test-only `sampleToJson` as a *parse of the real writer's output* rather than as a second copy of the schema — two implementations that must agree is a bug this codebase has been bitten by before. Seven new tests compare against a rebuilt reference tree instead of a literal string, since key order is not part of the contract and pinning it would be brittle for no gain. Two of them pin the classic locale trap under `Locale.GERMANY`, where anything built on `String.format` emits `1,5` and breaks the host's parser for some users only. **One behaviour genuinely changed, and it is an improvement**: `JSONObject.put` *threw* on a NaN axis, uncaught, on the main thread, inside a `pointerInteropFilter` lambda — a driver reporting no tilt could crash the app. A non-finite axis is now written as `0`, which the host already clamps, turning a crash into a one-sample glitch that self-corrects. Review also caught that collapsing thousands of coroutines into one costs the failure isolation `SupervisorJob` was providing for free: a single escaping `Throwable` would end the consumer permanently and silently, killing pointer input for the ViewModel's whole life, so the loop body is wrapped in `runCatching`. Verified on the release variant (`lintVitalRelease` included), 244 unit tests green. (`RemoteDesktopPointerSerializer.kt`, `RemoteDesktopViewModel.kt`, `PointerBatchSerializerTest.kt`; RemEx-ugvo.)

### Added
- **A guard against silently unwiring the cleanup that unsticks held keys.** Both WebSocket endpoints build their handler with `using var handler = …`, and disposing that handler is what releases keys a disconnecting client left physically held down on the user's desktop — a phone that vanishes mid-chord otherwise leaves Ctrl or Alt pressed, and only the host can clean that up because the client is what went away. **Deleting the single `using` keyword left every existing test green**: the handler tests construct and dispose directly, so they covered dispatch → tracker → Dispose but never connection-end → Dispose.
