That is a one-token edit that disables a user-visible guarantee with nothing going red, and a plausible one — anyone extracting the endpoint delegate into a helper would drop it without noticing. **The stronger option was tried first and rejected on evidence**: enabling CA2000 scoped to that one file does catch this, but it also errors on two pieces of correct code in the same file, where ownership is deliberately transferred to the host. A rule that reports correct code gets suppressed rather than obeyed. The reasoning, including the `#pragma`-scoped variant that was weighed and passed over, is recorded in the test so nobody runs the experiment a third time. **Review then caught the guard committing the same sin it was written to prevent**: the first version's regexes rejected three *correct* ways of writing the same thing — the `using` statement form, an explicitly typed declaration, and a namespace-qualified constructor — and failed with a message that dumped 30 KB of source. They now accept every form, name the consequence in the failure text, and the one remaining gap (a target-typed `new()`, which names no type to match) fails loudly as "the endpoint moved" rather than passing silently. Also corrected: locating the repo root by walking up from the build output, which a previously closed issue had already removed elsewhere because it breaks with an out-of-repo artifacts path; the same defect was fixed in a guard added one commit earlier. (`HandlerDisposalWiringTests.cs`, `DxgiVtableCacheGuardTests.cs`; RemEx-kqje.)

### Added

- **Two command-correlation behaviours that had been described but never tested since 2.0 are now actually tested, and the last `TODO` comments in the C# tree are gone.** `ConnectionViewModelTests` carried two `[Fact(Skip = …)]` placeholders explaining what should be verified and why it could not be: a command whose response never arrives must fail rather than hang, and two concurrent commands must each receive **their own** response. The second is the entire reason `_pendingCommands` is a dictionary — it replaced a single pending field because concurrent callers overwrote each other — so it was worth being able to prove. A narrow `IWebSocketSender` seam plus a settable timeout makes both writable. **The seam is deliberately one method.** A full socket abstraction would have to model connect, receive, close and state, none of which correlation cares about, and each of which becomes a fake that can drift from the real socket. **The more important choice was not writing a second copy of the matching logic**: the correlation branch was lifted out of the receive loop into `DeliverCommandResponse`, which the loop and the tests now both call — a test that re-implemented that matching would have kept passing while the real loop broke. The concurrency test answers the two commands in **reverse order**, so a pass cannot mean “the replies happened to arrive in order”. Both were proved by injection: rethrowing the raw `TimeoutException` instead of converting it fails the first, and bypassing the correlation lookup so the first waiter takes any response — the pre-dictionary behaviour — fails the second. The timeout became a `TimeSpan` rather than a count of seconds purely so the timeout test costs 150 ms instead of adding ten seconds to every run. **The desktop suite now reports 0 skipped**, 218 passing where it was 216 passing and 2 skipped; 883 across the solution, 0 warnings. (`IWebSocketSender.cs`, `ConnectionViewModel.cs`, `ConnectionViewModelTests.cs`; RemEx-h01r.)
- **A test that catches the stale-label-on-language-switch defect, after four separate fixes failed to prevent a fifth.** RemEx-6h3q, RemEx-4f30, RemEx-si0h and RemEx-4p27 all fixed the same shape — a bound property whose getter resolves its text from `LocalizationService` when it is *got*, so switching language changes what it would return while nothing on the view-model has changed, no notification fires, and the control keeps rendering the previous language. **Each fix was correct and none could prevent the next**, because the defect is the *absence* of a subscription elsewhere in the file: the property reviews as correct in isolation. `LocalizedPropertyRefreshTests` intersects the property names bound in `Views/*.axaml` with the `public string` properties in `ViewModels/*.cs` whose getter reads the localizer, and requires each survivor’s file to subscribe, **re-raise that property from the locale handler**, and detach with `-=`. **It found two real defects on its first run.** `ConnectionStatusAccessibleName` — a screen-reader name, where stale text is heard rather than seen — is derived from `IsConnected`, so its `[NotifyPropertyChangedFor]` only fired when the connection flipped, never on a language switch. `HostRuntimeSummary` was re-raised only when host capabilities change, so on a stable connection it would hold the old language indefinitely. `PairingPinExpiresInText` was fixed alongside them even though its one-second countdown makes it self-heal, because a rule with an exemption list is a rule nobody can check mechanically. **Three design points decide whether this test is worth having.** It requires the re-raise to be reachable *from the locale handler* rather than merely present in the file — the weaker check passes `HostRuntimeSummary`, which was the defect. It follows one level of same-file calls, because `FileTransferQueue`’s handler correctly fans out through `RaiseLocalizedLabels()` and a stricter rule would fail working code. And it **excludes methods by construction**, which is the trap that made RemEx-4f30’s first scan report 26 candidates of which 2 were real: a method re-reads the localizer on every call and is already correct. Both binding syntaxes are scanned, including the `<Binding Path="X"/>` element form the localized `MultiBinding`s use — omitting it would have exempted exactly the properties most at risk. Proved by injection in both directions: deleting the `HostRuntimeSummary` re-raise failed with “the locale handler never re-raises HostRuntimeSummary”, and deleting `FileTransferViewModel`’s `-=` failed with “never detaches with -=, so it is pinned for the process lifetime”. (`LocalizedPropertyRefreshTests.cs`, `ConnectionViewModel.cs`; RemEx-6ddx.)

The Personalization picker only ever exposed the coarser *screen-class* buckets, so "make all my temperature cards a Gem" was expressible in the code and not in the UI. **The precedence question was the real decision, and my own bead note had it backwards.** It specified class → category → built-in; reading the resolver made clear that is wrong. A class preset says "all telemetry cards"; a category preset says "all RAM cards" — the narrower statement, so it must win. Ordered the other way, a user who sets RAM to Oval *and* telemetry to Square gets Square, and the more specific of their two choices vanishes with nothing to explain why. Resolution is now per-card override → user category → user class → built-in default, with the reasoning written at the resolver. **Defaulting to INHERIT is what makes this migration-free**: an untouched install stores nothing, the map comes back empty, and every card resolves exactly as before. One Kotlin detail worth recording: the mapper has to be typed `@Composable ((String) -> String)?` — a plain function type cannot call `stringResource`, and the compiler reports that as "@Composable invocations can only happen from the context of a @Composable function" at the call site rather than at the declaration. That is the right failure direction and precisely what makes it invisible. Two checks, deliberately separate because they fail for different reasons and one masks the other: every declared code must map to something other than the English fallback, and none may resolve to a resource *key name* — `LocalizationService`'s indexer ends in `?? key`, so a branch can exist and still render the developer string `TaskManager_KillErrAccessDenied` if the `.resx` entry is missing, which is what RemEx-2s91 actually shipped. - **The file-transfer idle watchdog is now a class of its own, and has the regression test it shipped without.** RemEx-l519 added the watchdog — which fails a transfer when the peer goes *silent*, rather than bounding total duration, because any deadline generous enough for a 4 GB file over Wi-Fi is far too generous to notice a dead peer — with no test at all. Its review then found a real leak **inside the watchdog itself**: the receive path marked activity through the `ConcurrentDictionary` indexer, which *inserts*, so a chunk arriving after a cancelled transfer's teardown resurrected an entry nothing would ever reap. That is the ordinary cancelled-download path rather than an exotic one, because the peer keeps streaming until it has processed the cancel — one leaked entry per cancelled download, for the life of the process. The fix shipped unguarded, and this is the guard. The bead asked for the two-minute limit to be made injectable, calling a const that exists only for tests to override a smell. It is right, but the better move was extracting the whole thing: the watchdog is a self-contained state machine that had been living inside a 900-line class that owns a socket, so pulling it into `TransferIdleWatchdog` made the limit a constructor parameter *as a side effect* and left a unit with no `ConnectionViewModel`, no message envelope and no I/O — testable without the fake the bead had planned for. **The regression guard was proved by reintroducing the exact defect**, not by watching green ticks: `Mark` was changed to `GetOrAdd`, which still updates a live transfer's timestamp so the deadline keeps sliding but inserts one for a dead transfer. Exactly one test failed — the leak test — with the other four still passing, confirming the injection isolated the leak rather than breaking the watchdog wholesale, which is precisely the bead's acceptance criterion. The sliding-deadline test doubles as the positive control for `Mark`: without it, the leak test would pass just as well if `Mark` did nothing at all, since a watchdog that never records activity cannot leak an entry either. Review (PASS) confirmed the extraction is behaviourally identical against `HEAD` — the timing loop, cancellation handling, exception and `finally` ordering all unchanged — and found one real gap: the cancellation path, which the class's own remarks call its subtlest, was covered by reading the code rather than running it. It now has a test that wires the same `ct.Register(() => tcs.TrySetCanceled(ct))` contract the real callers use and bounds the unwind at five seconds against a thirty-second idle limit, so a regression that made cancellation wait for the timer fails fast instead of hanging the suite. `FileTransferClient` had no test file at all before this, despite being the entire PC file-transfer path. 840 tests green, 0 warnings. (`TransferIdleWatchdog.cs`, `TransferIdleWatchdogTests.cs`, `FileTransferClient.cs`; RemEx-sf27.)
- **A new pairing failure cause on the C# side can no longer go unmapped on the Android side without anything noticing.** `PairingErrorCodes.cs` declares fourteen machine-readable causes; `PairingErrors.messageRes` turns each into a localized sentence. Nothing connected the two lists mechanically, so adding a fifteenth cause and forgetting the Kotlin branch would render it as "Pairing failed for an unexpected reason" — no crash, no log, no build error. The same shape as the stale allowlist that bricked all of v3 file transfer: a value the other side did not recognise, dropped with nothing reporting it. The existing test hand-mirrored the code names, so it could only prove that the mappings which *exist* do not fall through — it could never notice a cause that was never added to it. A new JVM test parses the C# file instead and asserts every declared code either maps to a specific message or appears in a two-entry `intentionallyGeneric` set (`ARG_MISSING`, a caller bug not expected to reach a user, and `UNEXPECTED`, which by definition has nothing specific to say). Keeping those explicit rather than skipping them is the point: a new code must be triaged into one column or the other rather than quietly joining them. Reading a file outside the Gradle module is a deliberate call — the two are already coupled by construction, since `libRemexCore.so` is built from `remex.core` and packaged into this same APK, so the test only makes an existing coupling checkable — and the repo root arrives as an injected system property rather than a guessed working directory. **The interesting part was that the first version of this guard did not work, and said it did.** Adding a fifteenth code to prove the test would catch it reported `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`: Gradle considered the task up to date, because a file read at runtime is invisible to its input tracking, so the test never ran. Only `--rerun-tasks` revealed it failing correctly. The C# file is now a declared task input, after which the same edit failed *without* `--rerun-tasks`. That is the same class of trap as MSBuild skipping Avalonia's XAML compilation, and it is now recorded alongside it: whenever a check reaches outside its own module or language, ask what the build system thinks its inputs are — and verify a guard by breaking the thing it guards, because a new test that passes may simply not have run. (`PairingErrorCodesCoverageTest.kt`, `app/build.gradle.kts`; RemEx-odkk.)
- **All five destructive actions are now covered by the fail-closed confirmation tests, and three of them turned out not to need the test seams they were budgeted for.** The remaining four sites — reboot to UEFI, remove a launcher card, delete on the connected device, restore default shared folders — each get the three cases: no delegate declines, a delegate returning `false` declines identically, and confirming actually gets past the guard. **The survey this bead was planned from was wrong in the expensive direction.** It listed `CanvasDashboardViewModel`, `AppLauncherViewModel` and `SettingsViewModel` as needing seams because their constructors "demand a `ShellViewModel`, which `Guard.NotNull`s five services". They demand the *type*, not a live instance: all three only assign `_shell = shell` and never dereference it, which is the exact property that made `DiagnosticLogsViewModel` free in the first place. So `null!` worked at all three, and the interface, the DI graph and the fake shell that were budgeted for were never written. `SettingsViewModel`'s only `Guard.NotNull`'d dependency is its savefile service, which is the one thing built for real. **Each site's difficulty was finding an observable, not constructing the ViewModel.** Reboot to UEFI reaches `SendCommandAsync`, which returns "Not connected" immediately when the socket is closed — no network, no hang — and surfaces it into `StatusText`. Removing a launcher card is the cleanest of the five: past the guard the entry leaves `Launchers`, an `ObservableCollection` on the ViewModel itself. **Restoring default shared folders is deliberately given a null settings service**, because the real one writes the machine-wide shared-roots store under ProgramData — the file the host reads — so a positive control built on it would reset the developer's actual shared folders on every run; with it null the confirmed path throws past the guard and the ViewModel's own catch reports it, making guard passage observable while writing nothing. That is the same shape as the Kill Process site below, where the observable is a re-verification failing rather than a kill succeeding. **The delete positive control cost 61 seconds until it was measured**: nothing answers a manage request when disconnected, so awaiting the command sat out `FileTransferClient`'s 60-second `ManageRequestTimeoutSeconds`, and a plain fire-and-forget did not help either because xUnit waits for outstanding async operations posted to its own synchronization context. Starting it via `Task.Run` and polling for the status change instead took the same test to 32 ms. Polling is used *only* there and only in the safe direction — waiting for a change that must happen fails only when it genuinely does not, whereas polling for an absence is sound only probabilistically, which is why the two fail-closed cases still await normally. All of it proved by **inverting each guard to fail-open**, which failed exactly the four "no dialog wired" tests, one per site, with messages naming the real symptom: "❌ Not connected." for a reboot that was actually sent, and a null-reference report for a restore that actually ran. **Two Settings actions are recorded as NOT covered rather than half-covered**: revoke device trust and remove a shared folder are `async void` event handlers, and while their two fail-closed cases would in fact be deterministic — both short-circuit before any real await — the positive control cannot be, so it would have to poll for an absence. Two-thirds of the pattern without the control that makes the other two mean anything is false confidence at a security-adjacent site, so the gap and the fix (give each handler an awaitable core) are written into the test file and filed as RemEx-e1re. 928 tests green, whole suite still about ten seconds. (`DestructiveActionFailClosedTests.cs`; RemEx-w9ui.)
- **Kill Process is now covered by the fail-closed confirmation tests too.** Ending a process discards whatever that program had not saved and there is no undo, which makes it the most destructive of the confirmed actions and the right second site after `DiagnosticLogsViewModel`. As before they were proved by **inverting the guard to fail-open**, which failed with the right message rather than by watching green ticks. The non-obvious part was finding an observable that needs no socket: past the guard, `KillProcessAsync` re-verifies that the PID still belongs to the program the dialog named, and a freshly built view-model has an empty process list, so that check always fires and sets `KillError` — making "did we get past the guard" directly visible. The remaining three sites are surveyed on RemEx-w9ui rather than guessed at: `FileTransferViewModel` is cheap to construct but needs a populated selection before its delete path is even reached, while `CanvasDashboardViewModel`, `AppLauncherViewModel` and `SettingsViewModel` were surveyed as demanding a live `ShellViewModel` that `Guard.NotNull`s five services and so could not be handed nulls the way `DiagnosticLogsViewModel` could. **That last part was wrong; see the entry above for the correction** — all three only assign the shell and never dereference it, so `null!` worked there exactly as it did here and no seam was needed. (`DestructiveActionFailClosedTests.cs`; RemEx-w9ui, partial.)
- **The fail-closed property that makes every destructive-action confirmation safe is now tested.** Each of these actions follows the same shape: the ViewModel owns no UI, so it exposes an `OnConfirmationRequested` delegate and the View supplies a dialog. The entire safety of that arrangement rests on what happens when the delegate is *missing* — an unwired ViewModel, or a View whose window is not visible, must **decline** rather than proceed unconfirmed. Nothing tested it: RemEx-6p1f guarded five destructive actions across four ViewModels and added no test, and RemEx-07jx, which established the pattern, added none either. Four tests now pin it at `DiagnosticLogsViewModel` — no delegate declines, a delegate returning `false` declines identically, a delegate returning `true` actually performs the action, and the dialog receives resolved text rather than a raw resource key (which matters because `LocalizationService`'s `?? key` fallback would silently show `Confirm_ClearLogs_Title` verbatim). **They were proved by inverting the guard to fail-open**, which made exactly one of them fail with the right message, rather than by watching four green ticks. The third test is a deliberate positive control: without it, the first two would still pass if the action were broken outright and cleared nothing under any circumstances. That site was chosen because it is genuinely free to construct — its constructor stores the shell it is handed without ever dereferencing it, and it is `IDisposable` so the static log subscription cannot outlive the test — whereas the other five sites take live dependencies and need real test seams, filed as RemEx-w9ui. Recorded there too is the limit of this approach: these tests prove a site *with* a guard fails closed, but cannot catch a new destructive action that forgets the guard entirely — which is precisely what RemEx-5vcb turned out to be. Catching *that* needs an inventory of destructive commands asserted against the set carrying confirmation, which is the higher-value test and the harder one. 822 tests green. (`DestructiveActionFailClosedTests.cs`; RemEx-d5d8.)
- **The `*Format` naming trap is settled — by detecting it rather than renaming anything.** `string.Format` against a placeholder-free string **silently drops the argument**: no exception, no warning, just a sentence shown to the user with the filename, count or reason missing. Five keys named `FileTransfer_*Format` stopped taking an argument when RemEx-p9fn reworded them, leaving names that promise a placeholder they no longer have. The bead offered two ways out — rename 45 entries across 9 resx files, or add comments at each call site — and a third turned out to be better than both: a test that detects the actual call shape, which makes the name irrelevant. **The naming convention could not have been trusted anyway**, and that is what decided it: six keys end in `Format` while carrying no placeholder, and one of them is `Status_InvalidMessageFormat` — "Invalid message format from PC" — where the word is part of the *meaning*. A suffix rule would have demanded renaming that one too, and still would not have stopped the mistake being made against a key named anything else. The check parses .NET composite format syntax properly, which matters more than it sounds: **the first version searched for the literal `"{0}"` and reported three false positives**, because `"Zoom: {0:F1}×"` carries a format specifier — the check had the same class of bug it exists to catch. Across 72 `string.Format` call sites the trap is currently live at **zero** of them, and the test was proved by injecting one, which it reported with the key, its value and the file. The other half of that bead — seven sites still interpolating a raw exception into user-facing text — is split out as RemEx-mznc, carrying the caveat that makes it non-mechanical: two of the seven surface genuinely actionable copy from the phone ("Adding a shared folder must be done on the phone"), and collapsing those into a generic message would repeat a regression a previous review already caught. 827 tests green. (`LocalizationKeyReferenceTests.cs`; RemEx-udq9.)
- **A test now catches a localization key that code asks for but no `.resx` defines — and writing it exposed a hole in the checker meant to catch the same thing.** `LocalizationService`'s indexer ends in `?? key`, so a key missing from every file is not an exception: it renders the developer string on screen, in every language. RemEx-2s91 shipped exactly that, and users saw the literal text `TaskManager_KillFailed`. A cross-locale parity test cannot catch it, because parity is never broken — the key is absent from all nine files equally. The new test collects every key named in `remex.desktop` and `remex.agent` source across all four reference shapes (`Instance["Key"]`, the XAML `Localize` markup extension, the generated `Strings.Key` accessor, and the confirmation keys that reach `ConfirmAsync` and `CommandPaletteEntry` as plain positional strings with no compiler check at all) and asserts each exists in the base `Strings.resx`. **The hole:** the checker's own axis 3 matched only `{local:Localize …}`, but this repo uses two prefixes — 528 `local:` and **116 `conv:`** — so 116 references had been invisible to it the whole time. That is precisely the blind spot the axis exists to remove. Fixing it raised the visible reference count from 690 to 778; all 88 newly-visible keys turned out to be defined, so the gap was real but had not yet been stepped in. **The test was proved by making it fail**, not by watching it pass: a reference to a deliberately undefined key was injected into `ShellViewModel`, and the test named both the key and the file before it was reverted. Two limitations are documented rather than hidden — a key named in a comment counts as a reference (fails safe: it can only demand a key exist, never hide a missing one), and keys built by concatenation such as `"Splash_Style_" + id` cannot be checked statically at all, so they remain the one way to reach the `?? key` fallback undetected. The reverse direction — defined but unreferenced — is deliberately not asserted, since that is a different judgement with a real backlog behind it (RemEx-b5kx). 818 tests green. (`LocalizationKeyReferenceTests.cs`, `scripts/check-localization.ps1`; RemEx-fxkg.)
- **Nothing built or tested this repository except a developer's own machine; now CI does.** Before this, `.github/workflows/` held two Claude-assistant workflows and the localization check — no job compiled `remex.agent`, `remex.desktop` or `remex.core`, and nothing ran the 811-test suite. Every build and test result in the project's history was a local one. The new workflow runs a Windows build-and-test leg and a Linux build leg on pull requests and pushes to `main`. **The build step is `dotnet build -t:Rebuild`, and that is load-bearing rather than cautious:** Avalonia's XAML compilation is skipped by MSBuild's incremental up-to-date check, so a plain `dotnet build` can report "0 Errors" on a `.axaml` file that does not compile, and `dotnet test` then runs the stale assembly and passes too. Compiled bindings are on solution-wide, so every binding error is a compile error that this blind spot can hide — RemEx-5vcb was exactly that, and a CI running a plain build would have merged it. The comment above the step says so, so nobody simplifies it later. The Linux leg exists because the PC side must build on both platforms and because it is the only thing that can catch the case-sensitive-path class of bug that CLAUDE.md's hard rule 4 exists for. **Both legs were verified green before being committed, not assumed:** the exact Windows command sequence was run locally (build exit 0, then `dotnet test --no-build` exit 0, 811 passed), and the Linux build was run under WSL against `Remex.sln` (exit 0, 0 errors). That Linux run also turned up a genuine defect nobody knew about, because nobody had ever run the tests there: two `remex.desktop.tests` cases cannot pass on Linux — one hardcodes `C:\Windows\System32` paths and asserts no warnings, where the product correctly warns that the paths do not exist. So the Linux leg deliberately ships **without** a test step rather than red on arrival, with the commented-out step and the reason left in place, tracked as RemEx-6i1l. An Android job is likewise omitted rather than guessed at: `assembleRelease` pins NDK `30.0.14904198` and shells out to `dotnet` for the NativeAOT `libRemexCore.so`, none of which was verified to exist on a hosted runner (RemEx-t4zr). The residual risk is honest and stated: the workflow's *commands* are verified, but the workflow itself has never executed on GitHub. (`.github/workflows/dotnet.yml`; RemEx-jx7r.)
- **The localization check gained a fourth axis, for the failure that slipped past the first three.** A value can exist in all 9 files, be genuinely translated, be current, and be referenced correctly — and still be broken from the inside, if it does not take the same arguments as its English source. That is how a literal `{0}` reached Spanish users (RemEx-xn7l): parity was intact because the key existed everywhere, staleness ignored it because it was properly translated and too short to judge, and the undefined-key axis never fired because the key was defined. The defect lived *inside* a value all three axes considered healthy. Axis 4 compares placeholders per key against English: a locale carrying an argument English does not supply is an **error** (it renders literally, or throws `FormatException` in that language alone), a locale dropping one English has is an **error** (the number or name is silently lost in that language alone), and a malformed brace is an error. **The two platforms get separate extractors, because sharing one would be wrong in both directions:** `.resx` uses .NET composite formatting where literal braces are doubled — a regex that does not consume `{{`/`}}` in pairs reads `{{0}}` as a placeholder — so that side is hand-scanned rather than regexed; Android uses printf, where the unit of comparison is the *(index, conversion)* pair, since a locale turning `%1$d` into `%1$s` changes number formatting without crashing. That last case is deliberately a **warning**, not an error, because it degrades rather than breaks. Repeating a placeholder stays legal in both syntaxes — sets are compared, not counts — so `"Delete {0}? {0} is gone"` is not flagged against a single `{0}`. One deliberate leniency is documented in the code: the printf space-flag is not accepted, because it would make the `% d` inside ordinary prose like `"100% done"` parse as a format specifier. **A detector that finds nothing is indistinguishable from a broken one, so it was proved by positive control rather than by its clean run:** seven values were injected into the real files and reverted via git — extra `{0}`, missing `{0}`, unclosed brace and extra `%1$s` were all caught, while `{{Sayfa}}`, `100% done` and `50%%` were all correctly ignored, and a `%1$d`→`%1$s` swap produced a warning rather than an error. The current tree is clean on this axis, so it was switched on with **zero** new baseline suppressions. (`scripts/check-localization.ps1`; RemEx-ozep.)
- **A localization check that catches the three separate ways a translation can go wrong, on both platforms, and a CI job that runs it.** RemEx ships 1080 PC keys and 754 Android keys across 9 languages each, and nothing verified any of it. `scripts/check-localization.ps1` checks three independent axes, because passing one says nothing about the others. **(1) Parity** — every key exists in all 9 files. **(2) Staleness** — parity only proves a key *exists*; two detectors ask whether it is still *correct*. An English-similarity pass flags values that are still mostly English words, comparing against both the current English and every historical English value recovered from git, so that a value stranded by the repo's own Host→PC find-replace — English text matching no version of the English file — is still caught. A freshness pass compares the commit that last touched each key's line in English against the same key's line in each translation; that is the only way to catch a value which is perfect prose in the target language but describes behaviour the app no longer has. **(3) Referenced-but-undefined** — a key used in code that *no* file defines. Axes 1 and 2 are structurally blind to this because parity is never broken: the key is equally absent from all nine files. This axis found 16 live defects on the PC side (`Status_PairingFailed`, `Status_InvalidHostAddress`, six `RemoteDesktop_Window*` keys and more) where `LocalizationService`'s `?? key` fallback means the user is shown the raw key name — the literal text "Status_PairingFailed" — in every language; they are filed as RemEx-qug7 rather than fixed here. Three false-positive traps are handled deliberately rather than tuned away: Polish and Ukrainian carry four plural quantity buckets where English carries two, so only the plurals *name* is required across locales; `translatable="false"` inverts the parity rule for that key; and the technical vocabulary that inflates similarity scores (`ipconfig`, `Linux`, product names) is *derived* — a token every one of the 8 translators left verbatim is by definition non-translatable — rather than kept in a hand-maintained list that would rot. Values under 40 characters are not judged for similarity at all, because cognates and loanwords ("Client Android", "Mode Palette") are indistinguishable from untranslated text at that length. The 397 findings that already existed are recorded in `scripts/localization-baseline.json` and reported as known, so the check could be switched on today and no *new* defect can be introduced; the suppressed count is always printed, the script names which baseline entries have since been fixed so the file shrinks, and `-NoBaseline` shows everything. `git blame --line-porcelain` once per file replaces the `git log -L`-per-key approach the design called for — the same answer in 18 subprocesses instead of roughly 16,000 — and the whole run takes 19 seconds. Cross-platform pwsh per the parity rule; the GitHub job checks out with `fetch-depth: 0`, without which blame reports one commit per line and the freshness detector silently finds nothing. (`scripts/check-localization.ps1`, `scripts/localization-baseline.json`, `.github/workflows/localization-check.yml`; RemEx-km0i.20.)
- **Both FAQs now tell you how to stop RemEx launching itself at sign-in.** Both already said it "starts automatically at sign-in" without saying how to change that, so a user who wanted RemEx off their startup had no in-app answer and no way to check what it had installed. The new entries (PC `Faq_Q14`, Android `faq_q15`) lead with the switch rather than the plumbing: Settings → "Launch RemEx when you sign in", quoted in each locale exactly as that file ships the label, because `SettingsViewModel.IsLaunchAtLoginEnabled` → `StartupRegistrationService.SetEnabled` is what actually creates and deletes the autostart registration — pointing a non-technical user at Task Scheduler when a toggle exists would be poor guidance. Both mechanisms are still named for anyone verifying or repairing by hand, as the bead required: on Windows a Task Scheduler task literally named `RemEx` (created via `schtasks /Create /TN "RemEx"`, visible under Task Scheduler Library), on Linux an autostart entry at `~/.config/autostart/remex-agent.desktop`. Both entries give the repair step — toggle it off and back on to recreate the registration — and the Android one then closes with the consequence a phone user needs to know: the phone can only reach the PC while RemEx is running, so with autostart off it has to be started on the PC first. Each locale also names its own Settings screen as that file labels it (`Configuración`, `Налаштування`, `Ayarlar`…), matching the sibling pairing entry rather than inventing a synonym. Translated in all 9 files per platform (key parity 1044 PC / 767 Android). (`AboutViewModel.cs`, `FaqScreen.kt`, 9 resx files, 9 `strings.xml`; RemEx-36n4.)
- **Both FAQs now explain why RemEx needs elevated permission, and what to do when that is why the phone will not connect.** Elevation is load-bearing on Windows — a non-elevated `remex.agent` cannot read the machine-wide `cert.pfx`, so every paired phone is refused while still showing as paired — yet the words "administrator", "elevated" and "UAC" appeared nowhere in either FAQ. New entries (PC `Faq_Q13`, Android `faq_q14`) explain that the certificate is stored where nothing else can read it, that this is what stops another program impersonating the PC, and how to recover. The guidance is split per host OS, because the two are opposites: on Windows the fix is to restart RemEx elevated, while on Linux RemEx deliberately runs unprivileged with a `0600` cert in `~/.local/share/Remex`, `sudo` is the wrong move, and the cause is almost always a root-owned `/var/lib/remex/cert.pfx` left by the retired `remex-host` service — so the answer points at re-running the installer, which repairs that automatically, rather than at a raw `chown` on a path that does not exist yet in that state. Translated in all 9 languages on both platforms (key parity 765 Android / 1042 PC). (`FaqScreen.kt`, `AboutViewModel.cs`, 9 `strings.xml`, 9 resx files; RemEx-csfz.)
- **The PC FAQ now explains the "phone suddenly refuses to connect" certificate-pinning failure.** A new entry (`Faq_Q12`, mirroring Android's `faq_a13` from the PC's perspective) covers why the phone refuses after a RemEx reinstall, backup restore, or hardware move — the phone pins this PC's certificate fingerprint at pairing — and walks through the unpair-then-re-pair fix using the QR code or 6-digit PIN. Certificate pinning is the most likely hard failure a user will ever hit, and the PC previously had no user-facing explanation at all. Translated in all 9 languages (key parity 1040). Reviewed by Opus (PASS). (`AboutViewModel.cs`, 9 resx files; RemEx-a6to.)

### Security

- **The Remote Desktop channel now actually enforces certificate pinning, instead of computing the answer and discarding it.** `ValidateServerCertificate` derived the presented SPKI hash, looked it up in `PinnedCertStore`, and then returned `true` regardless — with a comment reading “Fallback for RemoteDesktop connecting” sitting where the rejection belonged. **Every certificate was accepted on the H.264/MJPEG channel** while the control channel beside it enforced pinning properly. It also called `GetAllPinsAsync().GetAwaiter().GetResult()` from inside a TLS callback, blocking on async I/O from the handshake thread — moot, since the result was thrown away. **The fix copies a sibling rather than inventing a rule.** `ConnectionViewModel.AcceptSelfSignedCertificate` had already been hardened: snapshot the pins before connecting, fail closed with no snapshot, require a match when pins exist, and permit an empty store only for loopback. Adopting that verbatim is what makes this safe — the two channels talk to the same host, and disagreeing about its certificate would be its own defect. **Why it does not brick the PC’s own session, checked rather than assumed**: `SetPinAsync` is reached only inside ConnectionViewModel’s pairing block, and loopback sets `_isPairedWithCurrentHost` *before* that block — so a PC that only talks to its own embedded host never pins anything, its store stays empty, and the loopback branch accepts. **The decision is now a pure function** (`IsCertificateAcceptable`), which matters more than usual here: the defect was never a wrong rule, it was an unused one, and a rule nobody consults reads exactly like a rule that works. Six tests cover the decision table and a seventh checks the call site — **proved by re-introducing the original bug**, where all six decision tests still passed and only the call-site test failed. RemEx-xmgw is updated: deduping the two validators is now a genuine dedupe rather than a choice about which behaviour survives. 896 tests green, 0 warnings. (`RemoteDesktopService.cs`, `RemoteDesktopCertificatePinningTests.cs`; RemEx-mlce.)
- **An incoming file push can no longer skip the consent prompt on the phone.** The v3 push flow is two steps: the PC sends `file_push_offer`, the phone prompts the user, and on acceptance the phone mints one transfer id per file and returns them; the PC then negotiates each file with `file_transfer_offer(mode="push")` carrying its assigned id. **Nothing tied the two steps together.** `handleOffer` accepted any PUSH offer whose destination root happened to be writable, so a paired PC could skip the offer entirely, invent an id, and write files into a shared folder with **no prompt ever shown**. The consent dialog was a step a well-behaved client chose to take, not one the protocol required — and the code said so, with a comment asserting per-file offers "ride this after the `file_push_offer` was already consented" that nothing enforced. A `PushConsentRegistry` now makes the id unforgeable: only an accepted offer puts ids in it, and a PUSH offer whose id is absent is declined with "This push was not accepted on the device." **The gate is on PUSH only, and that boundary is the substance of the fix.** `UPLOAD` shares the same `beginHostReceive`, but an upload targets a folder the user already shared for writing — the share *is* the consent — so gating it would have broken every ordinary upload while protecting nothing. A test asserts an upload with no grant still proceeds, because over-gating is the likelier mistake here than under-gating. **Grants are released on completion and cancellation** rather than consumed on first use: a resumable transfer legitimately re-offers the same id after an interruption, and consuming it would fail resume with a consent error the user cannot act on. The registry is bounded at 256 outstanding grants — growth already requires a person tapping Accept, but an unbounded set a peer can influence at all is the wrong shape. Ids are recorded **before** the acceptance reply is sent, since the PC may negotiate the first file the instant it lands. Proved by injection: bypassing the gate fails `pushOffer_withAnIdTheUserNeverAccepted_isRefused`. 189 Android unit tests green (was 185), `assembleRelease` and `lintVitalRelease` clean. (`PushConsentRegistry.kt`, `FileHostHandler.kt`, `AndroidFileTransferHost.kt`, `FileHostHandlerTest.kt`; RemEx-z6lh.)
- **The launcher allowlist can no longer be rewritten over the wire, closing a gap that made VULN-3’s mitigation self-referential.** VULN-3 hardened `LAUNCHAPP` so a launch target must match a persisted launcher entry — a mitigation that is only worth something while the list is curated by the person at the PC. It was not: `PingPongHandler` accepted `launcher_add`, `launcher_remove` and `launcher_sync` from **any paired client**, with `launcher_sync` replacing the entire list in one message. A paired client could append an arbitrary local path and then launch it as the always-elevated host, so the allowlist was measuring a list the caller controlled. **Not exploitable by the shipping product** — Android has no add/remove UI — but it is exactly the kind of protocol-surface gap that outlives the assumption that no client happens to use it. Those three types now require a **loopback** connection, which is the PC’s own UI talking to its embedded host and the only sender that legitimately writes the list. **The bead offered two designs and the deciding fact settled it**: `isLoopback` is already a parameter of `HandleAsync`, so the gate needed no new plumbing, and CLAUDE.md’s hard rule that a PC-side client connecting to a PC-side host is unsupported means gating to loopback breaks no supported configuration. **Only the inbound direction is restricted** — the host still emits `launcher_sync` to clients on connect, which `PairingHandlerTests` depends on. `RequiresLoopback` deliberately mirrors the existing `RequiresPairing` predicate, because the two answer different questions: one asks whether the connection authenticated, the other whether it is the PC itself. **The test asserts the count, not just the members** — checking only the three known types would still pass if a fourth allowlist-mutating type were added ungated, which is how this arose, `launcher_sync` having been added after the others — **and it checks the call site**, because every other assertion would pass if `HandleAsync` never consulted the predicate. That is not hypothetical here: RemEx-mlce is a cert-pin check that computes its pins and returns true regardless. Proved by injection both ways: unwiring the gate fails the call-site test, and ungating `launcher_sync` fails both the theory and the count. `AppLauncherService`’s comment claiming the owner "added themselves" is now true, and says what makes it true. 889 tests green, 0 warnings. (`PingPongHandler.cs`, `AppLauncherService.cs`, `remex.agent.csproj`, `LauncherAllowlistAuthorizationTests.cs`; RemEx-q6xt.)
- **Ending a process now also checks it is the same *instance* the user confirmed, not just a process with the same name.** RemEx-druh had the host verify the process NAME immediately before killing, which closed the case where a recycled PID belonged to an unrelated program. It could not close the narrower one: the dialog says "chrome (PID 1234)", the user confirms, the original chrome exits, a new chrome is handed 1234 — the name check passes and the wrong window dies, with different tabs and different unsaved work. Closing that needed a start time, which `ProcessInfo` did not carry. It does now, and both clients echo it back so the host can compare it against the live process in the same step it kills. **The type is a `long` of Unix milliseconds rather than a `DateTime`, unlike the `InstallDate` field beside it, and that is deliberate:** the Android client parses this JSON by hand, so a `DateTime` would arrive as an ISO 8601 string it must parse with precision that differs by platform, whereas a millisecond count is a plain number on both sides and survives the kill command's string dictionary exactly. **Compared with a tolerance, never for equality** — testing equality here would look like rigour and behave like a trap, because the two reads happen at different moments from sources that may round differently, and any drift would refuse a legitimate kill *permanently* while telling the user to refresh a list that keeps producing the same value. Two seconds sits far below the window being defended and far above any plausible representation drift, and both edges are tested. Unknown means unchecked on either side, for two independent reasons that would each be a bug if it refused instead: a client older than the field sends nothing, and `Process.StartTime` genuinely fails for protected and system processes even from an elevated host — refusing would quietly make exactly those processes unkillable. Proved by disabling the comparison, which failed the four tests that assert a refusal while all seventeen allow-cases stayed green. **One known cost, filed rather than hidden:** review found the Linux listing now reads `/proc/<pid>/stat` twice per process per poll, once by hand and once via `Process.GetProcessById`. The correct fix reuses the `starttime` field already sitting in the parsed array, but converting it needs boot time and `USER_HZ` — arithmetic that cannot be verified from Windows, and getting it subtly wrong would yield plausible-but-wrong timestamps that refuse legitimate kills through this very guard. That is a worse failure than a redundant read, so it is RemEx-nchu with the exact fix recorded. 873 tests green, 0 warnings, `assembleRelease` succeeds. (`ProcessInfo.cs`, `ProcessKillGuard.cs`, both process monitors, `PingPongHandler.cs`, `ConnectionViewModel.cs`, `TaskManagerViewModel.cs`/`.kt`; RemEx-on4n.)
- **The PC now checks that a process is still the program you confirmed before ending it — which also protects Android, whose kill path had no check at all.** A PID is not an identity: operating systems recycle them, so between a client rendering its process list and the user tapping Confirm, that number can belong to something else entirely, and ending the wrong program discards whatever it had not saved with no undo. RemEx-2s91 had the PC re-check its own last-polled list before sending, which removed the grossest case, but a client cannot close this on its own — its check is separated from the kill by a network round trip, and the list is only as fresh as the last poll. Android sent a bare PID with no check whatsoever. The kill command now carries the process name the user was shown, and every host implementation verifies the live process still has it immediately before killing. Doing it on the host covers **both** clients at once, which is a far better place for the guarantee than a heuristic duplicated in Kotlin. The parameter is optional on the wire and blank counts as absent, so an older phone against a newer PC still works exactly as before — it simply does not gain the protection — and a newer phone against an older PC is ignored harmlessly. That backward-compatibility hinge is tested in both directions, because getting it wrong would silently break Kill Process on every phone that had not updated yet. The comparison is ordinal, case included: the name round-trips from the host's own process list, `Chrome` and `chrome` are genuinely different programs on Linux, and the failure directions are not symmetric — a wrong refusal costs a retry, a wrong kill costs unsaved work. **Review found a real regression in the first version of this, and it is the interesting part.** The rule was right; the *inputs* were mismatched. Linux exposes a process's name twice — `/proc/<pid>/stat`'s `comm` field, which the kernel truncates to `TASK_COMM_LEN - 1` = 15 characters and which is what the process list actually sends to clients, and `Process.ProcessName`, which is not truncated. Comparing the client's echoed (truncated) name against the untruncated one refused **every** Linux process whose real name exceeds 15 characters, every time, while telling the user their list was stale when it was not — `gnome-terminal-server`, `xdg-desktop-portal` and most Electron helpers are all over that line. No unit test of the comparison could have caught it, because both values were correct in isolation; the defect lived in two independent code paths disagreeing about what "the name" is. Confirmed empirically on a real Linux .NET runtime rather than taken on trust: `ProcessName` 21 characters, `comm` 15, not equal. The Linux host now accepts either host-derived spelling, which costs nothing because a genuinely different program matches neither. The handler's forwarding is tested for the elevated action as well as the ordinary one — two branches, two chances to forget one — and was proved by deleting the forwarding, which failed the ordinary case while the elevated case stayed green. Start-time verification, which would also close a *relaunch* of the same program into the same PID, needs `ProcessInfo` to carry a start time it currently does not and is filed as RemEx-on4n; the unlocalized English refusal messages this extends are filed as RemEx-r37a. 853 tests green, 0 warnings. (`ProcessKillGuard.cs`, `IProcessMonitorService.cs`, both process monitors, `PingPongHandler.cs`, `ConnectionViewModel.cs`, `TaskManagerViewModel.cs`/`.kt`, `TaskManagerScreen.kt`; RemEx-druh.)
- **The Indonesian FAQ told users to pipe a script from the wrong domain into their shell.** `Faq_Q11_Answer` in `Strings.id.resx` gave the Tailscale install step as `curl -fsSL https://scale.com/install.sh | sh` — `scale.com`, not `tailscale.com`. That is a live, unrelated third party's domain, and the instruction pipes whatever it returns straight into `sh`, aimed at a non-technical user following a help page. Corrected to `tailscale.com`, matching what the other eight locales already said; `scale.com` now appears nowhere in the repo. Found while converting that value's line-break escapes (RemEx-mqwx) and fixed inline rather than deferred, since the fix is one token inside bytes already being rewritten and leaving it meant knowingly shipping it. (`Strings.id.resx`; RemEx-mqwx.)
- **The `/ws/desktop` and `/ws/files` channels now require cryptographic proof-of-possession, not bare clientId presence (VULN-2).** These secondary channels — live screen capture + input injection into the always-elevated desktop, and bulk filesystem read/write — gated only on `IsClientPaired(clientId)`, a presence check, not authentication: a `clientId` is an unguessable-but-not-secret identifier. They now perform the same PAIR-1 HMAC-over-nonce handshake the `/ws` control channel already enforces (new shared `ChannelReconnectAuth`): the host issues a fresh 32-byte nonce and services the socket only when the client returns `HMAC-SHA256(reconnectSecret, nonce)` for the presence-checked clientId. Loopback still bypasses; legacy secret-less paired clients must re-pair. Client side: the native `RemexDesktopClient` answers the challenge synchronously on connect (before any stream-control frame, reusing the reconnect secret the `/ws` client already holds — no new JNI plumbing), and the Kotlin `/ws/files` client answers before any binary frame. **This is a coordinated change — the host, `libRemexCore.so`, and the Android APK must be deployed together, and an on-device round-trip (remote desktop + a file transfer succeed; an un-updated client is rejected) is the release gate.** Covered by 6 new host crypto tests. The 8338 external-script command channel is tracked separately (RemEx-ng5z) because its clients are external automation scripts, not the app. (`ChannelReconnectAuth.cs`, `HostBootstrapper.cs`, `remex.core/Native/RemexDesktopClient.cs`, `remex.core/Native/RemexNativeClient.cs`, `FileTransferChannelClient.kt`; RemEx-s032.2.)
- **The unauthenticated `GET /debug/logs` endpoint has been removed (VULN-1, closes the primary auth-bypass chain).** It served up to 3000 buffered in-memory log lines to any network-reachable caller — Kestrel binds `0.0.0.0:5005` with no auth or loopback gate — and those lines retained the live 6-digit pairing PIN (logged at Information) plus full paired `clientId`s in cleartext. An unpaired LAN/Tailnet peer could read the PIN during the pairing window to complete pairing, or harvest `clientId`s to feed the secondary channels. The endpoint is deleted (diagnostics read the buffer in-process via `InMemoryLogSink.GetEntries()`; there was no remote consumer). Independently: the PIN is no longer written to any log sink at all (removed from `PairingHandler` and `PairingService` — it is shown on the host screen only), and `clientId`s are now redacted to an 8-char prefix everywhere they are logged via a new shared `LogRedaction.RedactClientId` helper. (`HostBootstrapper.cs`, `PairingHandler.cs`, `PairingService.cs`, `PairedClientRegistry.cs`, `TransferSessionManager.cs`, `FileTrustService.cs`, `WindowsInteractiveSessionGuard.cs`, new `LogRedaction.cs`; RemEx-s032.1.)
- **`LaunchApp` now enforces an allowlist and rejects network paths (VULN-3).** The `LAUNCHAPP` command passed the client-supplied `TargetPath` straight to `ProcessStartInfo` after only a `Path.GetFullPath` + existence check, so a paired client could launch *any* file — including a remote `\\attacker\share\evil.exe` — as the always-elevated host (admin RCE). `AppLauncherService` now normalizes the path, rejects UNC / `\\` / `//` / mapped-network-drive targets outright (before any other check), and requires the normalized path to match a persisted launcher entry (`ILauncherStorageService.LoadEntriesAsync`) the PC's owner added themselves. Covered by 8 new tests. (`AppLauncherService.cs`; RemEx-s032.3.)
- **A shared root derived from a read-only root now inherits the parent's permissions instead of escalating to full write/delete (VULN-4).** `AddRootFromPathAsync` pinned every new root with `IsWritable/CanRename/CanMove/CanDelete = true` unconditionally, so a paired client could browse a read-only default root (Documents/Desktop/Pictures/Downloads), pick a subfolder, and re-pin it as a fully writable/deletable root — defeating the read-only designation. The derived root now inherits the parent root's capability flags (a read-only parent yields a read-only child); `CanRemoveRoot` stays true as it is a UI-management flag, not a filesystem-write grant. Covered by 2 new tests. (`FileTransferService.cs`; RemEx-s032.4.)
- **The native TLS client now fails closed when no certificate SPKI pin is supplied (VULN-5).** The SPKI-pinning `RemoteCertificateValidationCallback` was installed only `if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(spkiHash))`; with an empty pin, `SslStream` fell through to the OS trust manager, which the JNI trust-manager overrides force to accept *any* certificate (full MITM). This was latent (shipping callers gate the empty-pin path) but had no fail-closed backstop. Both `RemexNativeClient` and `RemexDesktopClient` now throw before connecting when the pin is null/empty/whitespace, and the validation callback is *always* installed and rejects when no pin is configured — so an empty pin can never reach an accept-any state. NativeAOT-safe (no reflection). Covered by 10 new tests. (`remex.core/Native/RemexNativeClient.cs`, `remex.core/Native/RemexDesktopClient.cs`; RemEx-s032.5.)
- **Residual unauthenticated info-disclosure endpoints trimmed (VULN-6).** `GET /` no longer returns the full remote-desktop diagnostic report (OS, capture backend, capability/failure detail) to anonymous callers — it is now a minimal `{service, status}` handshake, and capabilities reach paired clients over `/ws` as before. The dead `GET /download/apk` endpoint (which served a hardcoded `Z:\` debug-APK path) is deleted. `GET /pairing-qr` was reviewed and exposes only public-by-design data (host id + certificate SPKI hash); no machine name is disclosed. Covered by new endpoint tests. (`HostBootstrapper.cs`; RemEx-s032.6.)

### Changed

- **Audited every sync-over-async call in the repo for deadlock against Avalonia's `SynchronizationContext`, after RemEx-rbfq established that one exists.** No live defect found, and the useful output is where the hazard *would* be. The certificate-pin store's synchronous `GetPin` is the only site that could deadlock at all: it blocks on a lock that `EnsureLoadedAsync` holds across `File.ReadAllTextAsync`, awaited without `ConfigureAwait(false)` because that is banned repo-wide — so an instance started on the UI thread posts its continuation back there, and blocking that thread would strand it and hang the app holding the pin store. It has no production callers, and the hazard is now written at the method so nobody wires one up. `RemexDesktopClient.Dispose` is likewise unreachable — a process singleton nothing owns — and now says so. **Review found three of my recorded claims wrong, which is the part worth reading.** "`GetPin` has no callers" was false (a test calls it, and deleting the API means deleting the test). The deadlock mechanism was stated too widely: the two write paths also hold the lock across an await, but they await the loader *before* taking it, so the sync path returns at its own guard and never participates — only the first-load window is constructible. And "not a blocking call, returns at once" for the FFmpeg stderr read was over-confident: `WaitForExit(int)` does not wait for redirected-stream EOF, so it can block briefly while the reader drains; it cannot hang or deadlock, but the reason was wrong. **The enumeration was also incomplete, so "every site checked" was false when written** — five more were missed, four of them safely pre-Avalonia. The fifth is the one that matters and is now documented: the host shutdown in `Program.cs` blocks on the `[STAThread]` Main thread in the `finally` *after* the dispatcher loop has ended, which is the only blocking task-wait in the repo that provably runs on a thread Avalonia gave a context. Nobody has reported a hang on exit, but it is precisely the shape this audit was looking for, and the call site now names the fix that would apply. Three further `SemaphoreSlim.Wait` sites are recorded as unexamined rather than implied clean. Comments only, no behaviour change; 1157 tests green. (`PinnedCertStore.cs`, `Program.cs`, `RemexDesktopClient.cs`, `FFmpegH264Encoder.cs`; RemEx-r9tv.)

- **The PC agent is now ahead-of-time compiled on publish, so signing in no longer pays to JIT Avalonia and ASP.NET Core from cold.** A Task Scheduler logon task starts it during the busiest moment of the session, and the work was identical on every boot. `PublishReadyToRun` is set in the project rather than on the publish commands — there are five publish call sites across four scripts, and a flag repeated five times is a flag that will be missing from the sixth. It is guarded on a runtime identifier being present, so a RID-less publish still works instead of failing. **The cost is measured, not waved at:** the publish output grows 175.2 MB → 227.4 MB (+29.8%) on disk, and the LZMA2-compressed installer payload — what a user actually downloads — grows 49.3 MB → 61.9 MB (+25.4%). 279 of 382 assemblies are compiled, including Avalonia, Kestrel and CoreLib, and cross-publishing linux-x64 from Windows produces the same, so both platforms benefit. **The bead's second item was attempted and reverted, which is the more useful result.** Building the WindowsPerf fallback counters lazily looked like ~414 ms off the serial startup path — the counter-catalog load, measured. Two things killed it. Its stated precondition had never landed: `GetTelemetryAsync` calls the WindowsPerf read *unconditionally* and HWiNFO merely overlays the result, so the claim that a healthy HWiNFO makes the fallback unnecessary — which I had written into two comments in capitals — is simply false, and I had confirmed it against the wrong gate. And the constructor does more than build counters: it primes a CPU *rate* counter and takes the network byte baseline, both of which are only meaningful ahead of the first read. Deferred into the call that consumes them, the CPU sensor reports a confident 0% from an empty sample window and the network divisor becomes the few milliseconds since the baseline, turning one stray frame into megabytes per second. Reverted to behaviour identical to before, with the reasoning recorded in the constructor so the next attempt starts from it, and the real prerequisite filed as RemEx-rxth — skipping the fallback read entirely while HWiNFO is healthy, which is both the larger win and what makes the deferral correct. 1157 tests green, 0 warnings. Not verified: nobody has timed a cold sign-in. (`remex.agent.csproj`, `WindowsTelemetryService.cs`; RemEx-48kh.)

- **Four places told you the wrong reason for the repo's own async rule, and correcting them took three tries.** `docs/ASYNC_GUIDELINES.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.editorconfig` and two code comments all said Avalonia installs no `SynchronizationContext`, so `ConfigureAwait(false)` "has no effect". Avalonia 11 installs one via `AvaloniaSynchronizationContext.Ensure` from the dispatcher's main loop, and nothing in the `AppBuilder` disables it. **The rule is unchanged; its justification is now the opposite of what was written.** Far from having no effect, on the desktop side the captured context is LOAD-BEARING: `SendCommandAndWaitAsync` builds its `TaskCompletionSource` with `RunContinuationsAsynchronously` and is completed by the receive loop, so the continuation cannot run on the completing thread — the captured context is what returns it to the UI thread before callers assign bound properties like `TaskManagerViewModel.KillError`. `ConfigureAwait(false)` there would move a bound-property write onto a thread-pool thread. It is harmful, not redundant; only the ASP.NET Core host side is genuinely context-free. **Three wrong replacement claims were written and cut before this shipped, and the discarded ones are recorded** — a wrong correction reads as freshly checked and is worse than the error it replaces. "Nothing here blocks on a task" would have justified the ban outright and is false (`Dispose`, several Linux host paths, and the JNI exports all block; they are safe because no context is captured *there*, which is a different statement from "no context exists" — the exact collapse that produced the original error). "Capturing the context buys nothing" contradicted, in the same commit, the comment explaining that the capture is what keeps a write on the UI thread. And the evidence first cited was `AutoInstall`, which is the Designer's hook with no caller on the app path — proving only that the type exists. **One comment had reached the right conclusion from an inverted mechanism**, asserting a continuation runs on the UI thread *because* Avalonia never captures a context; it now names the two awaits separately, since only one of them actually depends on the capture. The follow-up audit was corrected too: its headline site turned out not to block at all (a `.Result` read after `Task.WhenAll`), which makes that audit weaker than when filed rather than stronger. No behaviour change; 1157 tests green. (`ASYNC_GUIDELINES.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.editorconfig`, `FireAndForgetExtensions.cs`, `TaskManagerViewModel.cs`; RemEx-rbfq.)

- **The last `ConfigureAwait(false)` in the repo is gone, and the ban that had been restated in three places is now enforced by something.** CA2007 — the analyzer that would catch it — is deliberately suppressed in `.editorconfig`, precisely because the rule here is the opposite of its default advice, so nothing checked. The lone survivor sat in `LoadPinSnapshotAsync`, which populates the snapshot the TLS validation callback reads, and had lasted long enough to look deliberate — which is the actual harm, since a single exception to a stated rule reads as considered and invites copies. **The removal is behaviour-neutral, but not for the reason the docs give, and that turned out to matter.** `docs/ASYNC_GUIDELINES.md` says Avalonia has no `SynchronizationContext`; Avalonia 11 ships `AvaloniaSynchronizationContext` with `AutoInstall` — verified against the packaged binary, not inferred — and the connect commands start on the UI thread, so a context is installed and the flag was never a no-op. It is safe because the CALLER already awaited without the flag and so resumed on the captured context regardless; the removed flag governed one field assignment, nothing blocks anywhere on the path, and the sibling pinning path in `RemoteDesktopService` has always been written this way. The two are now textually identical. **The first draft of the guard test repeated the wrong claim in its own failure message** — the sentence someone reads while the build is red — which review caught; the docs and two further comments still repeat it, filed as RemEx-rbfq with instructions to verify against the binary rather than trust either the docs or the bead. **Two holes in the guard were also closed before it landed:** it scanned three projects and missed `remex.agent.windows`, a real ProjectReference kept out of the solution because it is Windows-only — and WinRT interop is the likeliest place someone reaches for the flag; and a `//` inside a string literal (a URL) would have read as a comment and hidden a real call, a false negative, which is the direction that matters for a guard whose whole job is not to go quiet. Both are proved by injection, the second from inside `remex.agent.windows` itself. A liveness test asserts the scan actually reaches the repo, since a source scan passes identically whether it found nothing or looked nowhere. 1157 tests green, 0 warnings. (`ConnectionViewModel.cs`, `ConfigureAwaitBanTests.cs`; RemEx-8phl.)
- **A navigation route can no longer be required to carry a label nothing will ever render.** `Screen` demanded `titleRes` and `icon` from all sixteen destinations, but only the eleven listed in `navItems`/`moreItems` ever have them read. The other five — Splash, Connection, Tutorial, QrScanner, Pairing — are reached programmatically and appear in no navigation surface, so their title and icon went nowhere. **The cost of that was not untidiness, it was manufactured work that looked mandatory.** `screen_splash_title` and `screen_tutorial_title` were translated into every locale for a constructor argument no user could ever see, and were unremovable, because deleting the keys would break compilation of an argument that is never read. A QR-scanner title existed only to feed the same unread argument and was separately filed as a screen-reader accessibility bug — a bug that could not exist, since nothing displayed the string. The type could not tell the two cases apart because the unreachability was expressed by a list literal further down the file rather than by the type itself, so a reader at the definition site had no way to know which kind they were looking at. `Screen(route)` is now the base and `NavDestination(route, titleRes, icon) : Screen(route)` the subclass for the rendered eleven; `navItems`/`moreItems` are typed `List<NavDestination>`, so a destination without a label cannot be added to them and a plain route cannot carry one. **The `NavDestination` objects stay nested under `Screen` on purpose**: moving them would churn roughly twenty `Screen.Dashboard`-style call sites for no functional gain and bury the actual change. **Both list contents and their ORDER are unchanged, which is load-bearing rather than incidental** — `AppNavigation` derives pager indices from `navItems.indexOfFirst`, and the pager's own dispatch is a `when (navItems[page].route)`, so reordering silently lands a swipe on the wrong tab; that warning is now written at the declaration. Review verified all eleven `(route, titleRes, icon)` triples are identical old-to-new and both lists match `HEAD` element for element, which is why **the rendered bottom bar, rail and "More" sheet cannot have changed** and were not device-checked: there is no expression in this diff capable of producing a different one. `assembleRelease` succeeds including the fatal `lintVitalRelease` gate, unit tests pass, localization check clean. (`NavRoutes.kt`; RemEx-5reo.)


- **The two TLS channels this app opens to the host now ask one shared question about the host's certificate, instead of each keeping its own copy of the answer.** The control channel (`ConnectionViewModel`) and the Remote Desktop stream (`RemoteDesktopService`) each carried their own `AcceptSelfSignedCertificate`, and the copies had already diverged once for real: until RemEx-mlce the stream's version computed the SPKI hash, looked it up and returned `true` regardless, so one channel enforced pinning while the channel beside it accepted anything. The rule now lives once in `CertificatePinPolicy`, along with the SPKI hash computation both were also duplicating. **The dedupe's one genuinely dangerous cell is the pairing flag.** `_isPairedWithCurrentHost` used to fall out of the branch structure — assigned `true` in exactly one branch (matched pin) and `false` in the other four, *including the branch that accepts under trust-on-first-use*. Collapsing that to `_isPairedWithCurrentHost = accepted` would have been the obvious refactor and would have marked the trust-on-first-use window as a verified pairing. It is instead a named, separately tested predicate, `IsPairedHost(accepted, pins)`, and the asymmetry is asserted by a truth table rather than left implicit. A second trap avoided in the same rewrite: the logging is `else if (accepted && pins.Count == 0)`, not `else if (accepted)`, because the matched-pin path is the only silent case in the original and a bare `accepted` would have logged "First-time pairing" on every successful *pinned* connect. **Equivalence was checked as a table, not by eye** — all eight cells of {pins null, empty, matching, non-matching} × {first-time-trust on, off} were compared against the pre-change code on three axes at once (returned bool, resulting `_isPairedWithCurrentHost`, and which log statement fires); zero cells differ. `ComputeSpkiHash` keeps the `X509Certificate2` copy-constructor semantics, so disposing the copy still never disposes the caller's certificate. The new `NeitherChannel_ReimplementsThePinLookup` guard is what makes the dedupe stick, and it is not vacuous: it fails against the previous commit, where `ConnectionViewModel` still contained its own lookup. Also filed on the way past, deliberately not fixed here to keep a pinning diff scoped: RemEx-8phl, the repo's lone surviving `ConfigureAwait(false)`. 914 tests green, 0 warnings. (`CertificatePinPolicy.cs` (new), `ConnectionViewModel.cs`, `RemoteDesktopService.cs`, `RemoteDesktopCertificatePinningTests.cs`; RemEx-xmgw.)
- **The QR and pairing-PIN panels are one piece of markup again, but their cards are deliberately still two.** Both panels existed twice, wholesale, in `ConnectionView.axaml` and `SettingsView.axaml`, differing only in the `Connection.` binding prefix — so any fix to the PIN display had to be made twice or silently applied to one screen. The contents now live in `PairingQrPanelView` and `PairingPinPanelView`, and `SettingsView` passes `DataContext="{Binding Connection}"` into them, which is what lets the shared markup drop the prefix that was the entire difference. **What was NOT unified is the more useful half of the finding.** The bead described the duplication as wholesale, but the outer cards are genuinely different: `ConnectionView` uses the `glass-card` style (`CardBackgroundBrush` plus a box shadow and its transitions) while `SettingsView` hand-rolls a flat `GlassBaseDarkBrush` card with no shadow. Merging them would have silently restyled one of the two screens across all four PC themes — a design decision wearing a dedupe's clothes — so each host keeps its own `Border` and only the identical interior is shared. `IsVisible` stays on those hosts too, so the two panels still show and hide independently. The QR plate's hardcoded `Background="White"` moved across unchanged and is documented in place as a deliberate exemption: a QR quiet zone needs a fixed light plate to stay scannable, so it must not follow the theme. (`PairingQrPanelView.axaml` (new), `PairingPinPanelView.axaml` (new), `ConnectionView.axaml`, `SettingsView.axaml`; RemEx-xmgw.)
- **The Android release build compiles with zero Kotlin warnings, and two of the twenty would have been silently wrong if fixed the obvious way.** `compileReleaseKotlin` emitted 20 warnings in four families: six `WebSocketListener` overrides in `FileTransferChannelClient` naming their socket parameter `ws` instead of the supertype's `webSocket`, one `@FlowPreview` opt-in for `sample()`, three `Icons.Filled` icons with AutoMirrored replacements (`Send`, `Sort`, `HelpOutline`), one redundant `!!`, and nine deprecated Material 3 / platform APIs. **Every replacement was read out of the artifacts on the classpath rather than taken from the warning text**, which is what caught the two traps. `rememberPlainTooltipPositionProvider`'s own `ReplaceWith` points at `rememberTooltipPositionProvider(spacing)` — *also deprecated in 1.5.0-alpha24*; the live overload is the one taking a `TooltipAnchorPosition`, so `RemexTooltip` now passes `TooltipAnchorPosition.Above` to reproduce the old placement rather than landing on a second deprecation. And swapping `rememberModalBottomSheetState()` for `rememberBottomSheetState(SheetValue.Hidden)` is only behaviour-preserving if the new function's default enabled-value set still contains the partially-expanded detent — the deprecated call defaulted `skipPartiallyExpanded` to `false` — so that default was disassembled and confirmed to be `setOf(Hidden, PartiallyExpanded, Expanded)` before the swap. **The `SHOW_IMPLICIT` fix is a behaviour question, not a rename**: there is no drop-in constant, the documented replacement is to call `showSoftInput` *without* a flag, and the flag has no effect at all from Android B onward. Passing `0` makes it an explicit show request, which is what the RemEx-46q comment above it already says the call is for — the user tapped the keyboard button. The six `ws` parameters were renamed rather than suppressed, and the rename deliberately shadows the enclosing `webSocket` field; a comment records that this is correct, because a callback must act on the socket it was handed and not on whatever the field now points at after a reconnect. Four `ListItem` call sites moved `headlineContent` into the trailing `content` lambda. Verified by deleting the Kotlin incremental caches and recompiling non-incrementally — an incremental pass would only have re-reported files it happened to rebuild — giving 0 warnings, with `lintVitalRelease` clean. (`FileTransferChannelClient.kt`, `FileTransferJobService.kt`, `ShareToPcActivity.kt`, `ShareToPcViewModel.kt`, `FileManagerToolbar.kt`, `RemexFlexibleTopBar.kt`, `AboutScreen.kt`, `ConnectionScreen.kt`, `DashboardScreen.kt`, `DashboardShapes.kt`, `TelemetryViews.kt`, `RemoteDesktopScreen.kt`; RemEx-62s7.)
- **Whether a remote command needs confirming is now derived from the command, not typed out beside it.** `RemoteCommandCard.requiresConfirmation` was a bare positional Boolean among six positional arguments, and the original values had been assigned **by category** — every POWER card `true`, every SESSION and ENERGY card `false`. Sign Out sits in SESSION beside Wake and Lock, so it inherited `false` by association and shipped a destructive action with no prompt (RemEx-awks). **That specific bug was already fixed; this removes the reason it happened.** A new card is written by copying a neighbour, and copying the wrong neighbour is precisely how it occurred — the property that actually matters, *does this discard the user’s work?*, was never expressed, only proxied. The flag is now a derived property reading one `actionDiscardsWork(action)` classifier, and the positional Boolean is gone from all 11 call sites. **The fallback direction is the interesting decision.** A `when` over a wire string cannot be exhaustive the way an enum can, so `else` **confirms**: an action nobody classified gets a prompt rather than running silently. On its own that would let cards accumulate unnoticed in the fallback, so `RemoteControlConfirmationTests` requires every action a card actually uses to appear in one of the two explicit arms — giving the “adding a command forces a decision in one place” property by test where the compiler cannot. Proved by injection in both directions: moving Sign Out to the non-confirming arm — reproducing the original defect exactly — fails with *“SignOut closes programs or discards unsaved work, so it must require confirmation”*, and deleting Hibernate from both arms fails with *“These actions fall through to the fail-safe `else` branch”*. The bead’s larger second payoff — one shared notion of “destructive” spanning the PC and the widget — is recorded as deliberately out of scope, because it has to decide where that list lives and `remex.core` is the only place all three could read it from. 184 Android unit tests green (timestamp-checked), `assembleRelease` and `lintVitalRelease` clean. (`RemoteControlScreen.kt`, `RemoteControlConfirmationTests.kt`; RemEx-q4sm.)
- **Two dashboard menu items stopped being named as though they were screen-reader-only text.** `cd_customize_cards` and `cd_reset_zoom` carried the `cd_` prefix that marks content descriptions in this codebase, but both label **visible** items in the dashboard dropdown. **The bead flagged a real risk and it turned out not to apply**: it asked whether the other two of the four references were genuine content descriptions, which would have meant those controls needed a label *and* a description rather than a rename. All four are `text = { Text(stringResource(...)) }` on `DropdownMenuItem`, and the leading icons beside them are `contentDescription = null` — correct for a decorative icon on an already-labelled item — so it is a straight swap. **The new names differ from the ones proposed**, on evidence from the surrounding code: these two items are interleaved in source with `dashboard_menu_options`, `dashboard_menu_undo`, `dashboard_menu_redo`, `dashboard_menu_unlock_layout` and `dashboard_menu_clear_cards` — the same dropdown — so they became `dashboard_menu_customize_cards` and `dashboard_menu_reset_zoom` rather than `dashboard_customize_cards`. Matching the immediate siblings is what makes a key say where its string appears. Android resource lookups are compile-time, so a half-finished rename fails the build rather than shipping broken; both halves landed together across 9 `strings.xml` and 4 Kotlin references, with 0 stale references remaining. `assembleRelease`, `mergeReleaseResources` and `lintVitalRelease` all re-ran, 182 Android unit tests green against this edit (timestamp-checked, not assumed), and `check-localization.ps1` confirms the new keys exist in all nine files.
