### Changed

- **The phone stopped copying every Remote Desktop frame a second time just to skip a 28-byte header** — roughly 12 MB/s of extra garbage at 60 fps and 200 KB frames, on top of the unavoidable native→Java copy. `RemoteDesktopFrameEnvelope` now hands back a *range* into the arriving array rather than a trimmed copy, and both consumers already take one: `BitmapFactory.decodeByteArray(bytes, offset, length)` and `MediaCodec`'s `inputBuffer.put(bytes, offset, length)`. **Deferring a copy across a thread boundary is the whole risk here**, because the H.264 path queues the range and a different thread drains it later — so the safety claim was verified at source rather than taken from the comment that asserts it: the WebSocket loop's pooled buffer is only receive scratch and every message is materialised with `ms.ToArray()`, then the JNI layer allocates a fresh `jbyteArray` per frame. No pooling on either side, so nothing can mutate a queued frame. Worth recording that this **widens the exposure window** — the old `copyOfRange` snapshotted the bytes within microseconds of arrival, whereas the raw array is now held until the decode backlog drains — so the invariant that was nearly self-healing is now genuinely load-bearing, and it is commented at all three points that depend on it. **The NAL index scan was deliberately left alone.** Threading offsets into `findNalUnits` would have put the change inside the logic with a history of black-screen bugs, so the queued access unit exposes `materialize()` instead: the per-frame path (`feedInput`, `containsNalType`) works on the range and never copies, while the two rare paths that need a standalone array — initial configure and a mid-stream SPS change, both IDR-only — take one. Review also caught an asymmetry worth closing: `BitmapFactory` throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`, which is *not* an `IllegalArgumentException`, so a bad range would have escaped the existing catch and cancelled the frame collector — stopping video with nothing logged. A range check now drops the frame instead. Not yet exercised on a device; the three things worth ten minutes there are a sustained H.264 session, a mid-stream scale change, and an MJPEG session — that last one because `decodeByteArray` receives a non-zero offset for the first time on that path. 199 Android tests green (10 new), `assembleRelease` and `lintVitalRelease` clean. (`RemoteDesktopFrameEnvelope.kt`, `H264StreamDecoder.kt`, `RemoteDesktopViewModel.kt`, `RemoteDesktopFrameEnvelopeTest.kt` (new); RemEx-t8ku.)
- **The host's HWiNFO sampler stopped rebuilding its entire view of the sensor universe every second: measured 648 KB → 44.5 KB allocated per tick against real HWiNFO with 460 sensors.** Everything HWiNFO reports about a reading except its *value* is fixed for the session — label, unit, parent device, classification — yet the sampler reopened the memory-mapped file, re-marshalled every sensor and reading element (three fixed-length strings each), lower-cased four or five times per reading to classify it, and interpolated an Id string, once a second, forever. The mapping and the per-reading templates are now built once; a tick reads only the value doubles at recorded offsets. **The dangerous part of that is not the offsets — it is that caching the handle silently deletes the only "HWiNFO stopped" signal.** A Windows section object lives as long as any handle references it, so the previous open-and-close-per-tick code got its liveness check for free: when HWiNFO exited the name was reclaimed and the next open threw, and the WMI fallback re-engaged. Hold a handle and none of that happens — the signature still reads `HWiS`, the geometry is unchanged, and `ReadDouble` cheerfully keeps returning the last bytes HWiNFO ever wrote. **Review caught this by writing a probe program and running it**, proving the section survives the producer's exit and that our own handle is what keeps it alive. Left as-was, the dashboard would have shown frozen temperatures and clocks presented as live *and* kept suppressing the working fallback, because the sampler would keep reporting success — strictly worse than before the optimisation, and invisible to any test that has HWiNFO running. The fix reads `poll_time`, HWiNFO's own poll counter, and drops the mapping when it stalls for 30 seconds. The same review also noted our permanently-held handle would stop a restarting HWiNFO from resizing its section, which the staleness drop resolves. **The tests were rebuilt around that**: the original pair were near-tautological — both the test and the production code called `Marshal.OffsetOf`, so a layout change moved them in lockstep — and neither could catch a struct that disagrees with HWiNFO's real C layout. There is now a fixture that synthesises an entire shared-memory region, which covers off-device what a live smoke test cannot: value-only re-reads keeping their labels, the temperature sanity filter dropping a placeholder 127 °C and *recovering* when the sensor returns, layout-change template rebuilds, a rejected signature, and above all the frozen-producer case that would otherwise only appear in the field. Verified against live HWiNFO on the reference box — 460 sensors, plausible values — with the caveat that the "before" figure comes from forcing a full rebuild per tick and so includes some fallback-counter setup; treat it as an upper bound. Not verified: killing and restarting HWiNFO under a running host, which needs a deliberate manual pass. 982 tests green. (`WindowsTelemetryService.cs`, `HwInfoSamplerTests.cs` (new), `HwInfoReadingLayoutTests.cs` (new); RemEx-8coq.)
- **The PC dashboard stopped rescanning every card for every sensor reading, once a second, on the UI thread.** `ProcessTelemetry` ran a `Where + Concat + Distinct + ToList` over both card collections *per reading* — and because every sensor ever seen leaves a staged template card behind, the staged count tracks the sensor count, so the work grew as N² with ~5 LINQ allocations and a closure per reading. One index is now built per tick and each reading is a dictionary lookup. **Rebuilt per tick rather than cached and invalidated on card add/remove, which is what the bead asked for**, because a `SensorViewModel` has no identity until its first `Update` — identity is read from `RawReading` — so a view-model created mid-tick would be filed under the wrong key by any cache built when its card was added. A per-tick rebuild is O(cards), cannot go stale, and the quadratic term is the one that mattered; caching across ticks would only remove a linear pass in exchange for a new stale-index failure mode. **The refactor had to reproduce the old LINQ exactly**, since the failure mode is a card that silently stops updating and just freezes — so the index keeps first-seen order, skips non-sensor and sensor-less cards, and deduplicates by *reference*, which is what the old `Distinct()` did given `SensorViewModel` has no equality override. Review confirmed all of that against the previous revision and found no card that could be missed, double-updated, or reordered. Two things changed on review: an `Any(lambda)` in the new index builder became a plain loop, because a closure per sensor card per tick is an allocation in the exact hot path this is meant to stop allocating in; and **a scaling test was deleted rather than kept** — it asserted a wall-clock ratio between 200 and 400 sensors, but its per-reading lookup loop lived in the *test*, so it would have gone on passing if a scan were reintroduced into the real code, all while carrying the flake profile of timing a few milliseconds. In its place `ProcessTelemetry`'s body was split into a testable `ApplyTelemetry` (the original is queued on Avalonia's dispatcher, which never pumps in a unit test) and the tests now drive the real tick — including the case none of the isolated tests could see, where the same sensor appears twice in one payload and the create branch must find the bucket it just inserted rather than making a duplicate card. Also filed while in here: RemEx-228x, a pre-existing bug where two sensors whose identities differ only by case get two cards but only one alert subscription, so the second one's threshold alerts silently never fire. The rest of the original bead — updating only visible view-models, keeping staged entries as plain data, and gating the tick on window visibility — is RemEx-4q6l; all three are behaviour changes rather than refactors and wanted their own review. 973 tests green. (`CanvasDashboardViewModel.cs`, `SensorIndexTests.cs` (new); RemEx-8tdf.)
- **Every message in both directions stopped carrying ~55 dead `"field":null` entries — a pong went from 1.5–2 KB to under 200 bytes.** `RemexMessage` is one envelope with a payload slot per message type and exactly one ever set, so `DefaultIgnoreCondition = WhenWritingNull` on the source-generated serializer context removes the rest. Pointer-rate input events and telemetry paid that tax on every frame. **NOT YET VERIFIED ON A DEVICE — the bead stays open for that**, and the reason is sharper than caution: the Android unit tests resolve `org.json:json` (JSON-java), whose `optString` returns the supplied default for an explicit null, while Android's *runtime* `org.json` returns the literal string `"null"`. Those are opposite behaviours, and this change turns on exactly that difference — so a green `testDebugUnitTest` says nothing about it, and only a real pairing / telemetry / file-transfer / Remote-Desktop round-trip can confirm it. **What has been done is the audit the bead demanded, rather than an assumption.** All 100 Kotlin files were scanned for `org.json` access patterns and every hit classified: the strict `get*()` calls (which throw on a missing key) all land on fields that are non-nullable in C# and therefore still written; `has() && !isNull()` pairs are unchanged because `isNull()` is true for an absent key as well as an explicit null; and the QR-pairing payload turned out to be built by a *reflection-based anonymous type*, not this context, so scanning a QR is untouched. Compatibility was also executed rather than argued — a test round-trips a message serialized both ways and asserts the results are equal, which is why no `protocolVersion` bump is needed. **The change is mostly a bug fix, which was the surprise.** Android's `optString` on an explicit null returns the string `"null"`, so the eight `if (has(k)) optString(k) else null` sites in the file-transfer host were producing `"null"` instead of null — `FileTransferViewModel` already carries a `takeUnless { it == "null" }` guard that exists purely to undo it, and `FileHostHandler` would otherwise browse a folder literally named `"null"`. Likewise `optInt("desktopNumber").takeIf { has("desktopNumber") }` was yielding `0` for a null desktop number, because `has()` is true for an explicitly-null key; it now yields the null the code was evidently written to produce. Review corrected two of the stated reasons in the process: `getString` on an explicit null does *not* throw on Android (it returns `"null"`), and "non-nullable in C#" is a convention rather than a runtime guarantee — nullable reference types are not enforced at run time, so the invariant to protect is "these are never null", not "the compiler prevents it". Note this also changes the ON-DISK format for the dashboard profile and launcher stores, which persist through the same context; readable in both directions, but worth knowing. 962 tests green; `assembleRelease` and `lintVitalRelease` clean. (`RemexJsonSerializerContext.cs`, `NullFieldOmissionTests.cs` (new); RemEx-bcgr, pending device verification.)

### Changed (docs)

- **The JNI boundary and the Remote Desktop input/display models are documented, and writing the documentation found two real bugs.** `remex.core`'s undocumented public surface went 502 → 378 of 887, but the count is the least interesting part: `AndroidNativeExports` (37 → 0), `InputEvent` (18 → 0), `DesktopDisplayModels` (44 → 0) and `JniHelper`'s raw ABI structs (4 → 0) are now fully covered, which is the surface where a wrong assumption costs the most. **Every claim was derived from the CONSUMER, not from the field names** — what `InputEvent.X` means came from `RemoteDesktopHandler.DispatchInput`, what `KeyCode` means from `LinuxInputEventTranslator` — and that is exactly why it turned up defects. **The mouse button index has no consistent meaning**: Windows maps `1` to MIDDLE and `2` to RIGHT, Linux maps `1` to RIGHT and `2` to MIDDLE, and the Android client matches neither — `RemoteMouseScreen` sends `1` for "Left click", so left click does not left-click on either platform (RemEx-kie3, P1). **And `PersistentDisplayKey` was not persistent on Windows**: Linux derives it from the display's UUID, but the Windows host assigned it the same string as the session-scoped `DisplayId`, so a client that persisted it to reselect "the monitor I was watching" could silently land on a different screen after a re-plug (RemEx-zftu — fixed below in this same release; the tense here is historical). Both were found by the reviewer checking a documented claim against both host implementations — the first draft had asserted a single canonical button mapping that neither host fully implements, which is the failure mode a docs bead has to guard against, since nothing in the compiler or the 932 tests checks a comment. Three further inaccuracies were corrected the same way: the pairing-PIN and pinning exports return bare `OK:…` / `ERROR: {code}: {message}` status strings rather than the JSON the class-level convention claimed, and the "given a constant you can find its payload slot and vice versa" symmetry does not hold in reverse for payload-free types. **What was deliberately NOT written is the other half of the work.** `RemexMessage`'s 100 undocumented members are 35 payload slots whose property name IS the payload type name and 65 constants whose name IS their value; the bead's own rule is "focus on semantics, not restating names", so the CONVENTION is documented once at class level — slot name = type name = snake_case constant, adding a slot is backward compatible while renaming is not, an unrecognised type is silently dropped and needs JNI routing — instead of 100 summaries that could only repeat their own identifiers. The reviewer measured that convention before accepting the argument: it holds for 35 of 35 slots and 73 of 73 constants, and the 27 members where it does NOT hold were already documented. The same reasoning leaves 13 file-transfer action constants alone under parents that already explain them. `dotnet build` 0 warnings, 932 tests green, `assembleRelease` clean — the last of those being the NativeAOT link check that any `remex.core` change has to pass. (`AndroidNativeExports.cs`, `JniHelper.cs`, `InputEvent.cs`, `DesktopDisplayModels.cs`, `FileTransferMessages.cs`, `RemexMessage.cs`; RemEx-cnwu.)

### Changed
- **The screen-capture path stopped rebuilding its COM plumbing for every frame.** Both Windows capture backends resolved each Direct3D vtable slot through `Marshal.GetDelegateForFunctionPointer` at the point of call — building a fresh marshalling stub every time, several times a frame, roughly a thousand a second at 120 fps for function pointers that never move — and additionally malloc'd and freed two fixed-size native structs per frame purely to give a COM call somewhere to write. The slots are now read once and the scratch buffers live for the object's lifetime. No behaviour change; this is allocation only. **The interesting part is how the cache decides it is still valid.** The obvious design — clear it wherever the COM pointer is released — turns out to be unsafe here: the DXGI access-lost recovery releases and re-creates the duplication output *without* going through the shared teardown, and can then return early on its own throttle gate, so a hand-invalidated cache would have been stale on exactly the recovery path. Each delegate instead records the pointer it was read from and re-reads when that changes, exposed through properties so the check happens at the point of use and no future call site can forget it. **Review supplied a stronger safety argument than the one this was built on**: a cached delegate is never invoked against a *captured* pointer — every call site passes the live field, re-read at the call — so a released object is structurally unreachable through the cache, and the pointer check is only there to stop a delegate read from one object being used against another. Since each field has a single assignment site, any non-zero value in it is the same COM type, whose vtable is that type's static table, so even address reuse is harmless. **Stated accurately rather than generously**: three per-frame resolutions deliberately remain (`QueryInterface` and two `Release`, on objects that are genuinely new each frame and so cannot be keyed on identity), so this removes most of the per-frame delegate churn, not all of it. None of this is executable without a GPU and a Desktop Duplication output, so the accompanying tests are a source scan guarding the realistic regression — someone adding a per-frame call and reaching for the old helper out of habit — with their own limits documented rather than implied. Not run against real hardware. (`DxgiDesktopCapture.cs`, `WgcDesktopCapture.cs`, `DxgiVtableCacheGuardTests.cs`; RemEx-8c1l.)

### Changed
- **The H.264 reader stopped scanning its output a byte at a time.** Both Annex-B start-code searches — the one deciding where each access unit is cut, and the one asking whether an access unit contains a keyframe — were hand-rolled scalar loops running over every access unit the encoder emits, 120 or more a second across buffers up to a megabyte. They now use a vectorized span search. Measured at review on this hardware: **9.4× faster**, 39 GB/s against 4.3 GB/s on a worst-case full traversal. **The risk here was framing, not speed** — cut in the wrong place and the encoder emits access units that are not independently decodable, which reaches the user as tearing or a frozen picture with no error anywhere, because a malformed access unit is still a perfectly well-formed WebSocket message. So review verified equivalence by differential-testing the old and new scanners over **1.26 million inputs**, comparing the complete list of cut positions rather than just the search results: zero disagreements. The keyframe check also collapsed from two interleaved branches to one pass, on the observation that the four-byte start code contains the three-byte one a byte in, so a single scan finds both forms with the NAL header always the byte straight after the match. The delimiter scan deliberately still matches the four-byte form only, because that is what the encoder is started to emit and accepting the short form would change where the stream is framed rather than how fast it is found. **A comment of mine was wrong and is now corrected**: it claimed the scanner must advance one byte at a time because matches can overlap in a run of zeros. An injection test that failed nothing exposed it — Annex-B start codes provably cannot overlap, since a match needs a byte to be `01` that an overlapping match would need to be `00`. The test file now records why no test can distinguish that choice, rather than implying one does. The delimiter scan was also extracted from the reader loop so it is testable at all; it had no coverage before. **Three further items filed under the same issue were split out rather than bundled**, because they are different changes in different risk classes: pooling the encoder's output buffers (blocked on the same ownership question that reverted an earlier attempt, and worse here because that channel also drops), sending the frame envelope as two WebSocket fragments (verified safe at review — the client's receive loop already reassembles on `EndOfMessage`, and that is now recorded as a load-bearing invariant), and avoiding a copy on the MJPEG path (which the issue described as a local swap but is really a public-interface change, and would silently ship a zero-padded tail if done the easy way). Not run against real ffmpeg or a device. (`FFmpegH264Encoder.cs`, `AnnexBScanTests.cs`; RemEx-rpu2.)

### Changed
- **Video frames are no longer copied in full just to put a header in front of them.** Every frame sent to the phone was concatenated into a fresh `28 + payload` array so a 28-byte envelope header could precede it — at full frame rate, the entire stream's bytes copied a second time, plus a Large Object Heap allocation per frame. The header and payload now go out as two fragments of a single WebSocket message, which is a transport-level detail: the bytes the client parses are byte-for-byte what the old path produced, asserted rather than argued. No protocol version bump, because nothing about the format changed. **The safety of this rests entirely on both fragments going out under one acquisition of the send lock.** A WebSocket carries one message at a time per socket, so releasing between them would let the cursor channel — which shares the socket — splice its own packets into the middle of a video frame. The client would reassemble one corrupt message, and because the envelope validates by exact length it would not error: it would fail to parse and fall through to the legacy untagged path, feeding header bytes to the decoder as though they were video. A test drives two concurrent senders through a socket that suspends mid-send and asserts the messages stay whole; releasing the lock between fragments fails it. **Review found one hazard this change introduces and it is now closed.** If the payload send fails after the header is already on the wire, the message is never terminated — and .NET marks the *next* data send on that socket as a continuation of it regardless of the message type requested, so a later send from the input loop (which runs on a different cancellation token and can still fire during teardown) would be spliced onto an orphaned header. That path now aborts the socket, which is already unusable for framed data. Review also independently re-verified the receiving side rather than taking it on trust: both consumers accumulate until `EndOfMessage` before parsing, and because the receive buffer is 256 KB, any access unit larger than that has *already* been arriving fragmented in production — this adds no new reassembly path. Not observed on a device. (`DesktopFrameEnvelope.cs`, `RemoteDesktopHandler.cs`, `DesktopFrameFragmentSendTests.cs`; RemEx-41xu.)

### Fixed

- **JPEG capture stopped copying every frame out of its encoder stream, which at MJPEG sizes was a Large Object Heap allocation per frame.** The three encode sites returned `ms.ToArray()` — a second frame-sized array plus a copy. They now hand back the stream's own buffer. **That could not be a one-line swap, and the reason is the interesting part:** `GetBuffer()` returns the stream's whole capacity, not the frame, so returning it as a `byte[]` would make every consumer's `.Length` read the capacity — the frame header would declare the wrong size and the zero-padded tail would go to the phone. It compiles, it runs, and it corrupts. Carrying the length in the type is what makes it safe, so the capture result, the encoder input and the send path are `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>` throughout. The wire format is untouched: the envelope already took a span, and the bytes and declared length are identical. **Review caught that the type change silently destroyed an atomicity invariant** — the defect that would actually have shipped. The DXGI capture replays its cached frame on a deliberately unlocked fast path, taken *precisely* when another thread holds the lock, i.e. when the writer may be mid-store. As a `byte[]` that was race-free by construction: a reference store is atomic and the length is intrinsic to the array. A `ReadOnlyMemory` is a 16-byte struct whose copy is several moves and may tear — and a torn read pairing the old array with the new length makes `Span` hand out a span past the end of that array, because `Span` does not re-validate. That is a send reading adjacent heap: either a fault in the elevated agent or heap bytes transmitted to the paired device. The frame and its length are now published as one immutable reference, restoring the atomicity the array had. Review also caught the source guard passing when one of two sites in a file regressed — it counts occurrences now, proved by injecting exactly that masked case — and a frame-sized copy I had reintroduced on the Linux path while removing it on Windows. 1160 tests green, 0 warnings, `assembleRelease` and `lintVitalRelease` green (the NativeAOT link check, since `remex.core` changed). Not verified: no live stream; MJPEG is the fallback codec. (`IScreenCaptureService.cs`, `DxgiDesktopCapture.cs`, `WindowsScreenCaptureService.cs`, `LinuxScreenCaptureService.cs`, `RemoteDesktopHandler.cs`, `FFmpegH264Encoder.cs`; RemEx-hgox.)

- **The last two destructive actions without fail-closed coverage now have it: revoking a device's file trust, and removing a shared folder.** Both are `async void` EVENT handlers rather than commands, so a test could raise the event but never know when the handler finished. RemEx-w9ui had recorded that as an honest gap rather than ship two-thirds of the pattern — the two fail-closed cases were deterministic, but the POSITIVE CONTROL awaits a real service call and would have needed a polling timeout, and the positive control is precisely what stops the other two passing against an action that is broken outright. Each handler is now a one-line forwarder over an awaitable core, so the same three cases apply here as at the other four sites. **Both halves of that claim are proved by injection, not asserted:** making the guards fail open fails exactly three tests including both new no-dialog cases, and no-op'ing the two actions after their guards fails exactly the two new positive controls — nothing else. A test-only seam supplies the trust service, because the real resolution reaches into the embedded-host locator, which finds nothing under test, so without it every case returned at the same early guard and proved nothing. **The residue is stated rather than implied.** The forwarders themselves — one line each — are still uncovered, and this was tried rather than skipped: the only thing that subscribes a device item to its handler runs inside a `Dispatcher.UIThread.Post`, and no Avalonia headless harness exists anywhere in the repo, so the posted work never runs and the collection stays empty. Subscribing by hand would exercise a wiring production does not use, which is worse than the gap. That is a far smaller residue than the one it replaced — "the entire action is untestable" became "the one-line forwarder is" — and it is filed as RemEx-r8c6, which several other view-model paths would also benefit from. Production behaviour is unchanged: no input distinguishes the old combined guard from the new split one, and the `async void` exception exposure is identical, since the same statements sit outside the same try. 1155 tests green, 0 warnings. (`SettingsViewModel.cs`, `DestructiveActionFailClosedTests.cs`; RemEx-e1re.)

- **The host's operating system was shown to the user as a raw wire token — "2.4.0 (windows, Interactive)" — lowercase mid-sentence and untranslated in all eight non-English locales.** `GetPlatform` emits `windows` / `linux` / `macos` for the wire, and two user-facing strings interpolated one straight into a sentence. The runtime half of that same string had been given a localized label by RemEx-9z0f; the platform half was left behind. **The second defect in the same line was the worse one:** `HostRuntimeSummary` built its text as `$"{runtimeLabel} on {platform}"` — an English word hardcoded between two localized values, with a word ORDER several languages do not use. Hindi and Turkish both place the platform first, so no translation of "on" could have produced a correct sentence; it had to become a positional format string, and there is now a test asserting the two orders differ rather than spellchecking the resource file. An unrecognised platform keeps its raw token rather than becoming a generic "Unknown" — a host on "freebsd" should still say so, since that is imperfect but diagnosable. **Review reproduced a test-isolation race this change introduced, and measured it.** `remex.desktop.tests` had no `AssemblyInfo.cs`, so unlike the other two test assemblies it ran classes in parallel; `FileTransferQueueTests` was the only class mutating the `LocalizationService` singleton, and this added a second. The pair failed about one run in eight, in both directions, and because both capture the culture at entry an interleaved restore could park the singleton in the wrong language for whichever class ran next — surfacing somewhere else entirely and reading like a bad translation rather than a test bug. Parallelization is now disabled for that assembly, matching the two that already did it for the same reason against their own singletons. **Review also caught the About page's fallback branch becoming a comparison of an English wire sentinel against a nominally-translated label** — correct only until somebody localizes the unknown case, at which point it breaks with every test still green. It reads the raw token now, and the branch that had no test has two. One Ukrainian string corrected from `у` to `на`, which is the idiomatic preposition for an operating system. Known and left: with a blank platform AND an unrecognised runtime mode both halves fall back to the same key, giving "PC on PC" — unreachable from any host this repo builds. 1147 tests green, 0 warnings, localization check clean, and the desktop suite run eight times to corroborate the race fix. Not verified on a running UI. (`ConnectionViewModel.cs`, `AboutViewModel.cs`, 9 resx, `AssemblyInfo.cs`; RemEx-6s34.)

- **The About page labelled one machine two different ways, one divider apart.** RemEx-nll1 fixed the app's own row to read "2.4.0"; the host row below it still read "2.4.0.0", because the host builds that value from `GetName().Version`, which .NET always widens to four components. Before nll1 both rows were consistently wrong — after it, the same PC was described as two versions on one screen, which to a non-technical user reads as two different things being installed. Normalised at the DISPLAY layer, as the bead required: the wire payload the Android client parses is untouched, and the reduction is the one `AppVersion` already applied to this app's own version rather than a third copy of "what a version looks like here" — a third copy being how the two rows diverged in the first place. A value that is not a version parses as such and is returned unchanged, which matters because the host sends the literal `unknown` when it cannot determine its own and the page branches on exactly that string. **The tests are at the view model, not the helper, and that distinction is the point:** asserting that the helper shortens a string proves the helper works and says nothing about whether the About page calls it. Reverting the call site leaves all fifteen helper tests green and fails two view-model ones. **Review caught the new test asserting a wire shape the host never sends** — the fixture used `Platform = "Windows"`, copied from the bead's prose, where `GetPlatform` actually returns lowercase `windows`. It also caught that an existing test hand-rolled a copy of the trimming it was meant to verify, so it passed only because our version happens to be three-part and would have diverged silently on a four-part one; it now asks the same reduction the code uses. That lowercase, untranslated platform token is itself a user-facing defect sitting in the same interpolated string — the runtime half beside it was localized by RemEx-9z0f and the platform half was not — filed as its own issue rather than folded in here. 1138 tests green, 0 warnings. Not verified on a running UI. (`AppVersion.cs`, `AboutViewModel.cs`, `AboutHostVersionTests.cs`, `AppVersionTests.cs`; RemEx-8jzu.)

- **Six copies of the mouse-button table became one, so the two ends of a click agree by construction rather than by coincidence.** Three tables lived in `LinuxInputSimulationService`, two in `LinuxInputBackendRouter`, one in `LinuxInputEventTranslator`, and the `MOUSEEVENTF_*` switch was written out twice — once for press, once for release. They agreed only because RemEx-kie3 had just corrected the one that did not, and what held them together was a test comparing their SOURCE TEXT. **The failure mode is why this was worth doing:** a wrong entry in one of these never crashes and never fails to work — it silently performs the wrong click, which is exactly what kie3 was, a left click that middle-clicked. The evdev codes invite it, since BTN_MIDDLE is 274 and BTN_RIGHT is 273, so they run out of index order; transcribe that six times and one copy eventually goes wrong. There is now one `MouseButtonCodes` on the host and a shared `MouseButtons` vocabulary in `Remex.Core` mirroring the Kotlin object, so the mapping can be asserted by CALLING it instead of by matching literals — worth strictly more, because it survives the table being rewritten in any style. One reduced source-text check remains, guarding the property that makes the behavioural tests sufficient: that no backend regrows a copy. It fires on a reintroduced table even when its values are RIGHT, which is the point — duplication is the defect, not just divergence. **Review caught two things, one of them the same class of error this bead exists to remove.** The new shared file — the one both ends are meant to treat as authoritative — claimed the side and extra buttons were reachable from the pointer path. They are not: that path carries a button MASK, read as stylus barrel state, and never produces an index at all. A comment three lines above the function being edited said so correctly, and the false version had already been mirrored into the Kotlin. And unifying the tables would have left index 3 pressing BTN_SIDE through the portal and ydotool while LEFT-CLICKING through xdotool — one service, three backends, two answers — a divergence the first draft pinned with a test rather than closing. Side and extra now map to xdotool 8 and 9, which are back and forward; 4 and 5 are the scroll wheel, and that trap is recorded where someone would fall into it. 1125 tests green, 0 warnings, `assembleRelease` and `lintVitalRelease` green. The unreachable `LinuxInputBackendRouter` path was unified but deliberately not deleted — `SetRouter` has exactly one occurrence in the repo, its own definition, and removing a whole backend is an operator's call. (`MouseButtons.cs`, `MouseButtonCodes.cs`, `LinuxInputSimulationService.cs`, `LinuxInputBackendRouter.cs`, `LinuxInputEventTranslator.cs`, `WindowsInputSimulationService.cs`, `MouseButtons.kt`; RemEx-upxn.)

- **Stopping an upload left a truncated, locked copy of the file on the PC under the name of the one it was replacing.** `UploadAsync`'s cancellation registration only ever cancelled the local wait — there is exactly one `FileTransferCancel` send site in the whole client and it was in `DownloadAsync` — so the host was never told. **The bead asked for the host's reaping behaviour to be measured before deciding whether this was a correctness fix or just diagnostics, and the measurement settled it.** The host opens the destination with `FileMode.Create` and `FileShare.None`, so the target file is truncated and locked before the first chunk arrives; the only bulk reap is called from a single place, the session-end `finally`, and a search for any idle timeout on that side returns nothing. So a cancelled upload replaced the user's file with a locked fragment that survived until the app disconnected. The client now sends the cancel, which the host already handles correctly — it disposes the stream and deletes the partial. **The gate added for the download case is now shared by both directions**, because the two differed by accident rather than design: download sent its cancel too early and upload sent none at all, and the two were found months apart. One object means the next change cannot fix one direction and miss the other. **Review measured my test and found it proved the opposite of its own comment** — the second time in two beads. It used an 8 MB file and cancelled 100 ms after the Start, claiming to catch the chunk loop mid-flight; instrumented, the entire file *and* the `FileTransferEnd` were on the wire at ~22 ms, so it exercised the final await and would have needed a five-times slower machine to do otherwise. It now cancels from inside the sender on chunk 3 of 8, which runs the registration callback inline on the sending thread with the loop provably still going, needs no sleep, and cannot drift with machine speed — and it asserts that no `FileTransferEnd` was sent, so the label fails rather than lies if it ever drifts back. 1123 tests green, 0 warnings. (`FileTransferClient.cs`, `FileTransferCancelOrderingTests.cs`; RemEx-o5cz.)

- **A download cancelled before it began told the host to stop a transfer the host had never heard of, so the host streamed the whole file anyway.** `DownloadAsync` registers its cancellation callback before sending `FileTransferStart`, and `CancellationToken.Register` runs the callback *synchronously inline* when the token is already cancelled — so the first thing on the wire was a `FileTransferCancel` naming an id the host had never seen. The host discards an unknown id, the `Start` follows, and nothing cancels it again. The local unwind was always clean; the entire residual was message ORDER. An already-cancelled download now says nothing at all rather than announcing a transfer and retracting it, and a three-state gate makes the cancel emit exactly once and only after the `Start` — with a re-check after the send so a cancel that lands *while the Start is in flight* is not swallowed instead, which would have reached the same broken end state from the other side. **Making this testable meant widening a seam, and that is the part worth recording.** `SendGuardedAsync` returns early when the socket is not open, so against a disconnected view model every send silently no-ops: the existing tests could observe leaked registrations but not one byte of what reached the wire, which is exactly how a bug whose only symptom is ordering survived a green suite. The `IWebSocketSender` seam added for correlated commands is now `OutboundSender` and covers the plain send path too. **Review then proved my own test was aimed at the wrong path** — by deleting the cancel emitter from the registration callback and watching the whole suite stay green. Cancelling from inside the sender runs the callback while the `Start` send has not returned, so the gate is still shut and the cancel observed came from the post-send re-check, not the callback: the real user-taps-cancel-mid-transfer path had no coverage at all. That test is renamed to what it reaches and a third added for the mainline, verified by the same injection, which now fails exactly one test. The first test also gained the assertions that justify putting the guard *inside* the `try` — the six registrations reaped, the partial file deleted — which the existing leak tests cannot make, since they all fail above the registrations and prove "registered nothing" rather than "registered, then reaped". **One correction to the bead:** it says the defect applies to `UploadAsync` too. There is exactly one `FileTransferCancel` send site in the whole client, in `DownloadAsync` — upload's callback is bare, so cancelling an upload tells the host nothing whatsoever. Different symptom, and an upload is client-driven so nothing keeps streaming; filed as RemEx-o5cz, now testable through the same seam. 1121 tests green, 0 warnings. (`FileTransferClient.cs`, `ConnectionViewModel.cs`, `FileTransferCancelOrderingTests.cs`; RemEx-mubp.)

- **The words "TAP TO CONNECT" were the one part of the connection card that did nothing when tapped.** On the Android dashboard, only the 72dp status orb carried a hit area — device capture had it clickable at [259,504][475,720] with the caption below at [228,744][544,804] and `clickable=false`. So a user who read the instruction and tapped the words it is written in got no response and no feedback that they had missed, which matters more than an ordinary hit-target nit because the label is an imperative aimed at someone non-technical. The hit area now covers the orb and its caption together, well past the 48dp accessibility minimum. **The bead's stated fix was to hoist the click to the whole card, and doing that would have caused a worse bug than the one being fixed.** Every card is wrapped by `DraggableDashboardCard`, and Compose dispatches pointer events leaf-to-root, so a clickable child outranks the card's own gestures. In selection mode the card toggles multi-select through `detectTapGestures`, which awaits an *unconsumed* down — a card-sized clickable consumes it first, and the PC status card would have become the only card that cannot be added to or removed from a multi-select, navigating the user away instead. Separately, `detectPickUpGesture` arms on a long press and selects on release without consuming it, while a plain `clickable` has no long-press timeout and fires on release regardless of hold duration, so a long press inside the hit area both selects the card and activates it. Both predate this change over the orb; widening to the caption is the smallest area that fixes the reported bug, and leaving the card's outer ring untouched is what keeps it selectable and draggable. Both are filed as RemEx-7o8r, where the fix belongs — the gesture layer, since it affects every in-card control including the Wake-on-LAN button. **Three smaller things came out of review.** The ripple is clipped to the card's morphing shape rather than landing as a hard rectangle on a card whose entire visual language is rounded, which shows worst under the monochrome palette at contrast 1.0 where ripple alpha is highest. `mergeDescendants` makes the card one node for a screen reader instead of an unlabelled button beside a stranded caption, with a localized click label across all nine locales, because once connected the merged label reads "ONLINE" and activation silently means reconnect. And the connecting state is now genuinely disabled rather than a no-op branch that still rippled and still announced as actionable — `toggleConnection` already returned early in that state, so nothing was ever cancellable. Not device-verified: the gesture-timing claims are derived from the Compose dispatch model and the code as written. `assembleRelease` and `lintVitalRelease` green, localization check clean. (`DashboardScreen.kt`, 9 `strings.xml`; RemEx-g9mq.)

- **A remote-desktop connection that failed because the PC was asleep told the user nothing at all — not English, nothing — and the bead filed against it had the symptom wrong.** RemEx-nl0z was raised to translate the connect timeout's English text, which was described as rendering untranslated in all eight non-English locales. Tracing where it actually surfaced showed it did not surface: `StartDesktopStream` runs the connect through an ordered work queue whose only failure handler writes to logcat, and `ErrorReceived` — the one channel that reaches the UI — is raised solely for an error message arriving over an **already-established** stream. A connect that never reached the host could not use it. The phone sat on a stalled screen with no way to tell a sleeping PC from a broken app. **Fixed by using the mechanism that already existed** rather than inventing one: host-originated desktop errors already travel as `code␟arg␟englishFallback` and are mapped to string resources on the Kotlin side, so the connect failures now join them as `connect_timeout` and `handshake_timeout`, with the English kept as a fallback for a client too old to know the codes. **The bead's second half was real too**: the proof-of-possession exchange that runs immediately after connect had its own ten-second deadline linked into the caller's token, so a host that completed TLS and then went quiet escaped as a bare cancellation — telling the user they had stopped it themselves, the exact inversion the connect-side filter had been added to prevent one call earlier. The two codes are kept distinct because reaching the handshake proves the address, the network path and the pinned certificate are all good, so "check your network" would send the user the wrong way. **Review caught that surfacing these fed them into a retry loop that could not terminate.** The client's reconnect budget is reset by every stream start, so routing connect failures through it unchanged meant an unbounded retry pinned at its first backoff step — roughly a fifteen-second connect against a sleeping PC every sixteen seconds, forever, with the new message wiped one second after it appeared and the terminal "connection lost" state unreachable. The repo already documented that reset trap in the same file, for the same reason, forty lines from the code that was read. Connect failures now use a counter that survives stream starts, exactly as the existing decode-stall escalation does, and the give-up path deliberately leaves the explanation on screen. A second round then found the message was still being cleared on the *other* start path — the one taken whenever the display catalog has not loaded, which is permanent rather than transient for a host with an empty or unparseable catalog — so both exits now go through one function that cannot diverge again. **Known gap, stated rather than hidden:** the handshake catch has no automated coverage, because reaching it needs a live `wss://` endpoint whose certificate matches the pin and every test in that file targets an unroutable address. A hand-rolled TLS listener was written for it and abandoned when debugging the WebSocket upgrade became the work; what it proved and where it stuck is recorded in RemEx-u5q0, scoped as a shared fixture because several remote-desktop paths need the same thing. 1118 tests green, 0 warnings, localization check clean, `assembleRelease` and `lintVitalRelease` green. (`RemexDesktopClient.cs`, `DesktopErrorCodes.cs`, `RemoteDesktopViewModel.kt`, 9 `strings.xml`; RemEx-nl0z.)

- **A dashboard performance issue was measured instead of assumed, and the measurement says leave it alone — so what shipped is the evidence and a guard, not an optimisation.** RemEx-4q6l proposed three narrowings of the telemetry tick: update only view models bound to placed cards, keep staged entries as plain data until placed, and gate the whole tick on window visibility with a ~10s fallback. Its own text made the first two conditional on a measurement nobody had taken. **Taken, the tick costs well under a millisecond**: 0.087–0.139 ms at 250 sensors and 0.272 ms at 500, i.e. linear and about 0.01% of one core at the 1 Hz telemetry rate — with run-to-run spread larger than most of the effect being argued about. The harness is checked in as a skipped benchmark rather than deleted, because a decision resting on a number nobody can re-run is not a decision. **The finding that outranks the timings is a coupling**: `SensorViewModel.CheckAlert` has exactly one call site, the last line of `Update`, so threshold alerts are evaluated only as a side effect of the same per-sensor work the bead proposed to skip. Gating the tick on window visibility stops evaluating alerts while the window is hidden — the state a tray-resident monitor is in nearly always, and the state its alerts exist for — reporting crossings up to ten seconds late and missing any spike that begins and ends between two fallback ticks. **Review corrected two load-bearing claims before this could be closed, both of which had been written into permanent source.** A closed staging drawer costs nothing to lay out because its container is `IsVisible=false`, which drops the subtree from measure and arrange — not because the `ListBox` virtualises; the distinction matters because `IsVisible=false` does *not* stop binding evaluation, and the list sits inside a redundant outer `ScrollViewer` that measures with infinite height, which is the classic way to defeat virtualisation. And "gating would cause a regression" was too strong: splitting `Update` into an evaluate half and a present half keeps alerts at full rate and is perfectly correct — it is simply not worth thirty lines and a resync-on-show path to reclaim a fraction of a millisecond per second. Both corrections are now recorded where the wrong versions were. **One of the two guard tests was also caught claiming more than it does**: item [4] gates `ProcessTelemetry`, one level above the `ApplyTelemetry` seam the test can reach, so a faithful implementation would leave it green. It is kept, renamed, and says so. The unbounded growth of the staging drawer — nothing ever evicts a staged sensor, and the host switches sensor sets mid-session — is split out as RemEx-yqpa, a usability defect rather than the allocation cost it was filed as. 1115 tests green, 0 warnings, no behaviour change. (`DashboardTickCostTests.cs`, `SensorViewModel.cs`; RemEx-4q6l.)

- **Card customization stopped being saved from the first reconnect onward, and the fix for its identical twin one commit earlier is the reason it was findable.** Disconnecting detaches two handlers per sensor — the threshold-alert one and the customization one — and both were re-attached only inside the *first time we have seen this sensor* branch. Reconnecting skips that branch, because the staged card keeps its view model, so neither came back. RemEx-k74x fixed the alert half; this is the other half, and it is the quieter one: theme, custom title, value-overlay toggle and graph type still applied on screen, so nothing looked wrong, and were simply gone at the next launch. **They are now attached in the same guarded block, deliberately**, so the pair cannot be separated again — which is precisely how one got fixed and the other did not. **A second, intended effect that is easy to misread as a regression**: the attach now happens after the persisted-state restore rather than before it. `ApplyPersistedSensorState` sets five properties that all match the save filter, so the old position made every restored card request a save while the canvas was still half-materialized — several redundant writes of `dashboard_layout.json` on the first tick after launch, now gone. Nothing is lost: a load has nothing new to persist, and the other restore path still requests its save explicitly. **The test seam is a notification counter rather than an observed save**, because the view model takes the sealed concrete layout service and the harness has none, so a provoked save throws instead of writing the operator's real layout file — the alternative is not merely inconvenient but unavailable. Its known limit is written where the counter is defined: counting before the save filter proves the handler is *attached*, not that the filter still routes the right property names. **The double-attach test states what it actually catches, having been measured rather than assumed** — the two detaches compensate for each other, so it goes red only when both are gone, making it a guard on the pair rather than on either half. It also failed on its first run for a reason worth keeping: first sighting populates name, unit and category as well as value, so it raises strictly more than a steady tick and is not a valid baseline for one. **Review caught three defects in the delivered text**, two of them the same class of error this bead exists to correct: a duplicated comment block left dangling by the injection revert, a doc comment the new property had silently taken from the method below it — leaving it saying the exact opposite of what the counter does — and a rewritten lifetime comment that had the direction of an event subscription backwards. 1113 tests green, 0 warnings. (`CanvasDashboardViewModel.cs`, `SensorIndexTests.cs`; RemEx-9qgb.)
- **Threshold alerts work again after the PC reconnects.** Disconnecting detaches every sensor's alert handler and forgets which sensors were wired — but the handler was only ever attached on the "first time seeing this sensor" path, and the template card keeps its sensor across a disconnect. So on reconnect that path was skipped and nothing re-attached: threshold alerts were dead for **every** sensor from the first disconnect onward, for the rest of the session. Silent, and it looked healthy — cards kept updating normally, the connection showed connected, and nothing was logged. The wiring now happens on the shared path every tick, still guarded so it attaches once per sensor rather than once per second. **The guard is what stops the cure being worse than the disease**: attaching unconditionally would give the user two notifications per crossing after one reconnect and four after three. Both directions are tested — alerts fire after a reconnect, and three reconnect cycles still produce exactly one alert — and each fails against the corresponding mistake. Review confirmed the safety argument independently and more strongly than it was made: there is exactly one place in the whole PC UI that constructs a sensor view model, and every card for a sensor aliases that same instance, so re-wiring cannot multiply alerts by card count. It also identified the ordering risk that actually mattered — the wiring moved past the persisted-card restore, not just past the value update — and confirmed nothing in that restore can raise an alert. **One thing is deliberately left**: the same function detaches a second handler, the one that saves per-card customization, and that one is still attached only on the first-sight path. So card themes, custom titles and graph types stop being saved after a reconnect too, by the identical mechanism. It is filed separately rather than folded in here, and the comment that claimed it was safe — citing a reconnect path this change proves does not exist — is corrected to say so. Not observed against a real PC disconnect. (`CanvasDashboardViewModel.cs`, `SensorIndexTests.cs`; RemEx-k74x.)
- **Two sensors whose identifiers differ only in capitalisation each get their alerts again.** The dashboard matched cards to readings case-sensitively but tracked which sensors had an alert handler attached case-INSENSITIVELY, both keyed by the same string. So a pair like `CPU` and `cpu` produced two cards and two live readouts — correctly — while only the first ever got its handler wired, and the second sensor's threshold alerts silently never fired. No error, nothing in the log. **The issue asked for a decision rather than an alignment**, warning that if identities were meant to be case-insensitive then the matching side had to change instead, which would drag in how cards are persisted. They are not: an identity is the PC-stamped sensor id, a machine token like `wmi:cpu:load`, and case is meaningful in it. Review confirmed that by tracing every producer — the only sensors given no id at all are ones whose names are fixed English literals, so the fallback can never split one logical sensor in two, and every producer whose names *can* vary in case stamps an id, so those names never become identities. The alert-threshold store was checked separately and is correctly case-insensitive, because it is keyed by the user-facing *name*: a PC relabelling "CPU Total" to "Cpu Total" should keep the alert rather than drop it. **The two now share one comparer so they cannot drift apart again**, and the field that held identities while being named for names — the mismatch that allowed this — is renamed. **Review rejected the first set of tests**, and rightly: they asserted the shared comparer and the card index, so re-introducing the exact bug by giving the subscription set its own case-insensitive comparer would have left them both green. The injection that appeared to validate them had only changed the shared comparer, proving sensitivity to that rather than to the drift. There is now a test that drives the whole path — two sensors over threshold, assert two alerts fire — and it is the only one of the three that fails when the drift is re-introduced. A separate and worse problem review found next door, where alert handlers are never re-attached after a disconnect, is filed rather than folded in. Not reproduced against a real PC with case-colliding sensor ids. (`CanvasDashboardViewModel.cs`, `SensorIndexTests.cs`; RemEx-228x.)
- **The phone no longer offers to stream a single monitor from a PC that cannot do it.** The combined "both screens" option was already offered only when the PC said it supported that mode, but the per-monitor options were built regardless — so a PC that could not enumerate its displays, and therefore advertises only whole-desktop capture, still presented a monitor picker whose every entry it would refuse. **The result was worse than a confusing picker.** With a single display that host produced exactly one monitor option, so the picker stayed hidden and the user simply pressed start: the stream then failed outright with "the host does not support 'Monitor' capture mode". With the option suppressed there is nothing to select, the phone omits the target fields entirely, and the PC falls back to its own default — which is the one mode it can actually serve. A failed start becomes a working one. **The rule is now fail-closed**: a catalog that does not say which modes it supports is treated as supporting none, rather than assuming both. Review confirmed that costs nothing real — every current host populates the field, and a host old enough to omit it does not answer the display query at all, so it never reaches this code. **Review also found this change promoting a dormant bug into a live one, which is now fixed too.** The "no usable targets" branch returned without clearing the previously known displays, which are deliberately kept across a disconnect so the picker does not blank out. That was harmless while the branch was effectively unreachable; now that it is the normal path for a degraded PC, reconnecting to one after a monitor-capable one would leave a stale monitor selected and send it anyway — reproducing the exact refusal this fixes. The list is cleared there now. Not exercised on a device or against a PC with failed display enumeration. (`RemoteDesktopViewModel.kt`, `CaptureModeOfferingTest.kt`; RemEx-e1x4.)
- **A download that cannot open its destination no longer leaks a stalled-transfer lease every time it is tried.** The transfer-end waiter, the progress reporter and the idle-watchdog lease were all registered *before* the destination file was opened, while the block that releases them started well after — so an ordinary failure to open the destination stranded all three permanently, once per attempt. That matters more now that those failures finally say something a user can act on: the natural response to "the folder is protected, try another" is to try again, and every retry leaked again. All the registrations now happen immediately before the block that reaps them. The upload path never had the bug — its file opens *before* its registrations — and that asymmetry is what gave it away. **The leak was invisible from outside**, which is how it survived a previous fix whose own comment already asserted the invariant it broke: nothing errors, nothing logs, the download reports its failure correctly and the user sees exactly what they expect. Only the watchdog's own counter can see it, which is what that counter is documented as existing for. **Review then caught the first version of the test measuring one sixth of the fix.** The counter it asserted on watches the watchdog lease alone, so moving the other five registrations back outside the reaping region would have left every test green while most of the leak returned — and the injection that appeared to prove the test worked had only reverted the watchdog. There is now a second counter covering all five dictionaries, and the injection that reproduces the original leak exactly (waiter and reporter above the open, watchdog left correct) fails all three tests. Every such upload would have been reported as "the download could not be saved, the drive you chose may be out of space", where every clause is false. Nothing visible went wrong (those branches describe a single display, and a client that remembers nothing selects the primary, which is that display), but it taught clients that a key they cannot trust is a key — the habit removed on Windows earlier in this release. The three copies of that literal are now one shared helper, which is how they came to disagree with the contract in the first place. **The larger half of this issue was a decision, and the answer was to change nothing.** Mirroring the Windows fix on Linux looked obvious, since its key is likewise equal to the session-scoped display id — but the two are not the same kind of identifier. A Windows adapter name is an *enumeration index*: unplug one monitor and the survivor renumbers, so a stored key resolves to a different screen. A DRM connector name like `DP-1` names a *port*: it does not renumber when other monitors change. The telemetry decision now uses `Uri.IsLoopback`, which is the precise client-side mirror of what the host applies. **That existing predicate was deliberately left alone**: it also gates the pairing bypass and trust-on-first-use, which this repo places behind explicit sign-off, so aligning it is filed separately rather than slipped into a performance change — even though the host already treats every loopback connection as paired, making the client the narrower of the two today. Review also caught that `Dispose` runs a deliberate subset of the normal teardown and never calls it, so an unsubscribe placed only in the latter would have left a process-lifetime singleton firing into a disposed view model every second for the rest of the run. - **Telemetry is now serialized once per sample instead of once per connected client.** Every client's stream built and encoded its own copy of the identical payload every second; with HWiNFO running that envelope is 60-100 KB, so each connection meant another Large Object Heap allocation per tick — and the PC's own dashboard connects as a client too, so a single phone already meant two. The sampler publishes the bytes alongside the sample and the streams send those. **The pair travels as one immutable object deliberately**: the sampler writes on its own thread while every stream reads on theirs, so publishing them as two fields would let a reader take a new payload with the previous tick's bytes and send telemetry that disagrees with itself — no error, just quietly stale numbers. Sharing the bytes also means sharing the envelope's timestamp, which changes it from "when this was sent" to "when this was sampled"; nothing anywhere reads it (the only consumer of that field is the ping round-trip measurement, on a different message type, and the telemetry envelope never even crosses the JNI boundary — the phone receives only the payload), and sample time is the more truthful thing for a telemetry frame to carry anyway. (`TelemetryBackgroundService.cs`, `MessageSerializer.cs`, `PingPongHandler.cs`, `TelemetrySnapshotTests.cs`; RemEx-0zbj.)
- **A received file is now moved into place instead of being written a second time.** A verified upload was re-read from its `.remexpart` staging file and streamed into the destination shared root, so a 5 GB push cost 10 GB of writes plus a 5 GB read to relocate bytes already sitting on the right disk — and because completion is awaited from the `/ws` reader loop, the connection sat idle for the whole of it. Promotion is a rename when staging and destination share a volume. **The bigger gain is not speed.** The old copy opened the destination with `FileMode.Create`, which truncates before the first byte arrives, so a failure part-way through a large transfer left the user's pre-existing file destroyed and replaced by a fragment; a rename replaces atomically. It also closes a quieter hole: root containment is checked lexically and does not resolve reparse points, so `FileMode.Create` would happily write *through* a symlink or junction planted inside a shared root to a target outside it, where `MoveFileEx`/`rename()` replace the link itself. **Landing a file in a shared root is a write grant, so the checks that gate it — size cap, root writability, root-escape safety — were extracted rather than duplicated.** Adding a second way to write is exactly how such a check gets bypassed: not by deleting it, but by a new path that never had it. Both paths now go through one `ResolveForWrite`, and giving promotion its own resolution fails the read-only and size-cap tests. **Review caught two real defects in the first attempt, both confirmed by measurement rather than argument.** NTFS does not recompute inherited permissions on a cross-directory rename, so a file promoted out of machine-wide staging arrived in the user's Documents carrying ProgramData's ACL — **read-only to the person who received it, and readable by every other local account** — and overwriting an existing file replaced its permissions wholesale. Inheritance is now re-applied from the destination, which reproduces byte-for-byte what creating the file in place produced. Separately, `Path.GetPathRoot` returns `/` for *every* absolute Unix path, so the same-volume test was unconditionally true on Linux and a genuinely cross-device promotion took the rename branch, where .NET's internal fallback copy is synchronous, uncancellable and not atomic — a regression against the old `CopyToAsync`. Volumes are now compared by mount point there, which as a side effect fixes cross-mount directory moves, since `Directory.Move` on Unix has no such fallback and simply threw. **Left undone, deliberately**: the bead also asks for promotion to run off the reader loop. Same-volume promotion is now effectively instant, so the blocking it complains about is no longer material, and moving completion off the reader loop changes when the client is told the transfer finished — a protocol-timing change that wants a device round-trip rather than a drive-by. Not exercised against a real transfer, a device, or a second physical volume. (`FileTransferService.cs`, `IFileTransferService.cs`, `TransferSessionManager.cs`, `FileTransferPromotionTests.cs`; RemEx-fq6f.)

A ~87 KB v2 file chunk cost worse: at 4 KB it took 22 reads and about six doubling reallocations of the accumulator, then a Large Object Heap copy on top. The receive buffer is now pooled, and a message that arrives in a single frame — which is nearly all of them — is parsed straight out of that buffer with no accumulator and no copy whatsoever. Only genuinely multi-frame messages allocate, and even those lost the `ToArray` duplicate in favour of a bounded span over the accumulator's existing backing array. The same pattern in the Android native client's own receive loop got the same treatment. No wire change: this is receive-side buffering only and `protocolVersion` is untouched. **The risk here is entirely in what the fast path might swallow.** `gitnexus` rates this symbol CRITICAL with 29 impacted callers — it is the inbound path for pairing, telemetry, remote-desktop input and file transfer alike — and the failure it could cause is not a crash but a truncated message or a desynced socket. (`MessageSerializer.cs`, `RemexNativeClient.cs`, `MessageSerializerReceiveTests.cs`; RemEx-tfi6.)

The position is now streamed as a `Flow` parameter and collected inside non-restarting `LaunchedEffect(Unit)` blocks with `collectLatest`, which reproduces the old cancel-and-retarget behaviour without paying for a recomposition to get it. **`collectLatest` only does that if the work is actually its child**, and the first attempt got this wrong: its action has no `CoroutineScope` receiver, so a bare `launch` bound to the enclosing effect's scope instead, the action completed immediately with nothing to cancel, and the code carried a comment claiming semantics it did not have. The old keyed effect had hidden this by rebuilding the closure every packet. `rememberUpdatedState` restores the live reads; a full audit of both effects' captures found nothing else frozen. **The three cursor flows also became one.** A consumer needing position *and* visibility had to `combine` three `StateFlow`s, which can emit three times per packet and hand out torn intermediates — composition used to hide that by batching per frame, and a flow collector does not. `hostCursor` is now a single `HostCursorSample` written in one assignment at all three view-model sites, preserving the existing contract that a visibility-only update leaves the last-known coordinates alone rather than overwriting them with a sentinel. **Verification limits, stated plainly**: this module has no Compose UI tests and the change was not run on a device, so nothing *asserts* the recomposition count or the coroutine parentage — compilation plus review reasoning is the whole of it, and the `contentRect` mis-mapping in particular is only observable on a non-16:9 host stream on real hardware. `assembleRelease` succeeds including the fatal `lintVitalRelease` gate. (`RemoteDesktopScreen.kt`, `RemoteDesktopViewModel.kt`; RemEx-zc9r.)

The fallback ladder is gone: the key is the interface path or **empty**, and empty is a real answer meaning "no stable identity available". Clients must not substitute `DisplayId` for it — that is session-scoped by definition — and the Android client already treats a missing key as "remember nothing", which turns a silent wrong answer into a visible lost preference. **The capability trade is real and worth stating**: in environments where the interface-path lookup fails, users lose the ability to remember a monitor at all. That is the right direction, because the fallback only ever worked when the topology was unchanged — which is exactly when the plain `DisplayId` worked too. It added no capability, only false confidence, and failed silently the moment topology changed. Eleven tests; the injection that reinstates a fallback fails four of them. **A claim in the shared model doc was scoped after review caught it overreaching**: it asserted the host sends empty rather than a plausible-but-unstable value, which is true of Windows and *not* of Linux, whose xrandr path sets the key to the output name unconditionally.
