(`WindowsScreenCaptureService.cs`, `DesktopDisplayModels.cs`, `PersistentDisplayKeyTests.cs`; RemEx-i50k.)

- **"The monitor I was watching last time" now actually means that monitor.** The app remembered a display by a token embedding `displayId` — the identifier the host documents as renumbering whenever monitors are added, removed or replugged. So after a re-plug the stored value still *resolved*, just to a different physical screen: the user silently got someone else's monitor, with no error anywhere. RemEx-zftu gave the host a stable `persistentDisplayKey`; this is the half that stores it. `DisplayTargetOption` now carries both identities on purpose — `token` selects within a session, `persistentKey` is what survives one — and conflating them was the whole bug. **The migration is the part that had to be right.** Every existing install holds a `monitor:<displayId>` string, and reading one of those as a persistent key would reintroduce the same wrong-screen bug through the new code path. The new format is `monitorkey:<key>`, and legacy values are deliberately left unrecognised so the selection falls through to the primary display — the honest handling of "we no longer know which monitor you meant". Review confirmed that collision is impossible by construction rather than by luck: the two prefixes differ at index 7, so no legacy value can match whatever the display id contains. **When the host is too old to send a key, nothing is remembered rather than something wrong** — and review caught that the first version wrote an empty string, which would wipe a good key the user had set on a *different* PC, since the preference is global rather than per-host. Skipping the write is behaviourally identical in that session and keeps the good value. Seven tests, proved by injection: restoring the old token-based storage failed exactly the three that depend on the stable key, while the migration guard correctly stayed green since it exercises the matching side. **One residual is filed rather than glossed**: on Windows the host's key silently degrades to the adapter name when the monitor's interface path is unavailable — which is byte-identical to the session id — so a degraded key would be stored under the new prefix and be just as unstable. The client cannot detect that, because the wire carries no confidence marker, so the fix belongs on the host (RemEx-i50k). The `persistentKey` doc was also softened to match the host's own stated limits rather than calling it flatly stable. `assembleRelease` succeeds including the fatal `lintVitalRelease` gate; localization clean. Not tested with real monitors. (`RemoteDesktopViewModel.kt`, `SettingsManager.kt`, `RememberedDisplayTargetTest.kt`; RemEx-ynur.)

- **Stopping the remote desktop no longer leaves a hidden capture session running.** `SendInputAsync` and `SendPointerBatchAsync` auto-start a stream when one is not running, and since desktop work became serialised on a single queue a straggler could be queued *behind* the stop — a keyUp, or the tail of a burst of pointer samples from the user's last touch. Each one reconnected and started a **whole new capture session**: the phone encoding and receiving frames nobody asked for, the host holding a session open with its keep-awake engaged so the PC would not sleep, and the UI showing the stream as stopped throughout. **The auto-start is not the bug and was deliberately kept.** It is how a stream recovers from a transient socket drop — the receive loop clears the streaming flag when the link dies, and the next input brings the session back. Deleting it would have traded a zombie stream for input that silently stops working after a blip. The flag simply cannot distinguish the two reasons for not streaming, since it reads false for both, so the client now records the *intent*: stopping sets it, starting clears it, and the send paths return early when it is set — checked before connecting, so a straggler cannot even reopen the socket. **Both the set and the clear sit above their method's early return**, which matters and was half-missed on the first pass: asking to stop expresses intent whether or not a stream was running, and the not-running case is precisely where a straggler would start one; review caught that the same argument had been applied to the stop side only, leaving a window where a start could early-return with the flag still set and silently drop input — a worse failure than the one being fixed. Three tests, proved by injection: removing the guard failed exactly the two input cases while the pointer-batch case, whose guard was left in, stayed green. They are honest about their limits — the singleton is never connected, so they pin the reachable half (a stop records intent, a later send honours it without opening a socket) rather than a real stop-of-a-running-stream, which needs a fake host the private constructor rules out. `libRemexCore.so` links cleanly under NativeAOT. (`RemexDesktopClient.cs`, `StoppedStreamDoesNotResurrectTests.cs`; RemEx-yzbb.)

- **The one remaining input path that could leave keys held on the PC now cleans up after itself too.** RemEx-e2p4 taught the Remote Desktop handler to release keys a vanishing client never released; `PingPongHandler`, which serves the `/ws` control socket, had the same shape and no cleanup. It now tracks and releases the same way, reusing the tracker rather than a second copy of it. **The bead's user-facing claim turned out to be wrong, and the entry says so rather than repeating it.** The bead described a phone dying mid-chord on the Remote Control screen leaving Ctrl down — but verification found that no shipping client sends `desktop_input` over `/ws` at all: the Android side short-circuits it into `HandleDesktopMessage`, which routes to `/ws/desktop`, so those keystrokes were **already** covered by the earlier fix. What shipped here is defensive symmetry on a protocol branch that is still reachable and still presses real keys — worth closing so it is not the one input path without cleanup, but not a live bug, and the code comment and test now record that distinction instead of overstating it. Three tests pin the wiring (dispatch → tracker → `Dispose`), proved by injection: removing the tracking call fails the Alt+Tab case. One gap is filed rather than papered over — nothing pins the `using` keyword at either handler's construction site, so deleting that one token would silently unwire the release at *both* handlers with every test still green (RemEx-kqje). (`PingPongHandler.cs`, `HostBootstrapper.cs`, `PingPongHeldKeyReleaseTests.cs`; RemEx-73dc.)

- **A disconnecting phone can no longer leave keys held down on your PC.** A key press from the phone is two independent messages and a chord is six, and nothing guarantees the client sends the closing half — it can be force-stopped, lose Wi-Fi, or tear the stream down before its own keyUps have drained. The host had already told Windows the key was down, so a modifier ended up **physically held on the user's desktop**, turning every subsequent keystroke into a chord, with no way to clear it from the phone because the phone is what went away. The Remote Desktop handler now remembers which keys the client pressed and did not release, and releases them when the session ends. **The three client-side ordering fixes in this release do not cover this and could not**: RemEx-3uhp, RemEx-7rq3 and RemEx-krvz make the messages arrive in order when they arrive at all — this is the case where they never arrive, and only the side holding the state can clean it up. **The release runs after the input queue drains, which is the part that has to be right**: doing it earlier races the input thread, and a queued keyDown landing afterwards would silently re-hold the key just released. The 2-second drain wait now logs a warning when it times out rather than passing quietly, because in that window the guarantee genuinely does not hold. **Verification found the fix reaches further than expected**: `StopDesktopStream` closes the socket, so *every* stream end is a connection end — meaning this covers the bead's ordinary case (a stop overtaking its own keyUps) and not only the crash and Wi-Fi ones. Nine tests. Six pin the bookkeeping — including that repeated auto-repeat presses release once, that a release for a key never pressed is harmless, and that concurrent teardowns each get a key exactly once — and three pin the **wiring**, which is the part that could otherwise be deleted with every other test still green: removing either the tracking call or the release call fails them, and both were proved that way. That gap is the shape of RemEx-y6x6, where a stale allowlist silently dropped every v3 file transfer and nothing went red. Only keys this host injected are tracked, so a key the user presses on the PC's own keyboard never enters the set — though the doc is careful not to over-promise, since Windows keeps one keyboard state and releasing ours would lift a physically-held duplicate too. Two adjacent gaps are filed rather than folded in: the Remote Control input path has no equivalent cleanup (RemEx-73dc), and a straggler keyUp arriving after a stop can reconnect and start a whole new capture session the UI shows as stopped (RemEx-yzbb). Not tested on a device — nobody has confirmed a stuck Ctrl actually clears on disconnect. (`HeldKeyTracker.cs`, `RemoteDesktopHandler.cs`, `HeldKeyTrackerTests.cs`, `HeldKeyReleaseOnDisconnectTests.cs`; RemEx-e2p4.)

- **Keyboard chords sent from Remote Desktop can no longer arrive scrambled, which was leaving modifier keys held down on the PC.** Every send from `RemoteDesktopViewModel` launched on plain `Dispatchers.IO`, a 64-thread dispatcher, so each raced the others through JSON build and JNI marshalling. That matters more than it sounds, because one keystroke is several messages: **Ctrl+Shift+C is six** — keyDown Ctrl, keyDown Shift, keyDown C, keyUp C, keyUp Shift, keyUp Ctrl — and any permutation was reachable. Two of them are bad in ways the user cannot fix from the phone: a modifier keyUp landing before the key's keyDown sends a plain `c` instead of the copy they asked for, and a modifier keyUp landing before its own keyDown leaves the modifier **physically held down on the host**, turning every later keystroke into a chord until they walk over to the PC. It also desynced the app's own record of which modifiers the host is holding. All seven send-carrying launches now share one `limitedParallelism(1)` dispatcher, which keeps the work off the main thread while restoring submission order. **This completes a guarantee that needed both ends**: RemEx-krvz made the native side preserve whatever order it is handed, and this is what makes the order it is handed the order the user actually acted in — neither half is sufficient alone. **The first draft of this shipped a crash, caught in review.** Kotlin runs initialisers in declaration order, and the property was declared ~670 lines below the `init` block that reaches a send synchronously — `viewModelScope` is `Main.immediate`, so its collector runs inline in the constructor and a `StateFlow` delivers its current value before suspending. The dispatcher was still null there, so a connected user opening Remote Desktop for the first time got a null-parameter exception inside the view model's constructor and a screen that never rendered. `Dispatchers.IO` was an object, so the old code could not hit it, and neither `assembleRelease` nor `lintVitalRelease` can see it. The declaration moved above `init` and **two source-text guards now hold the line**: one asserts the declaration precedes any `init`, the other that no `launch(Dispatchers.IO)` remains to race the serialised sends. Both were proved by injection, and the first attempt at that proof was itself wrong — the injected `init` went *after* the declaration, so the guard correctly passed and had to be re-injected properly before it meant anything. A test that constructs the view model would be the direct check and is not available: it is an `AndroidViewModel` needing a real `Application`, and this module has no Robolectric. Three senders that run inline rather than launching are deliberately untouched and their residual is recorded rather than implied — `pushConfigIfStreaming` does not matter (capture config is idempotent state, not an ordered event), but `stopStreaming` does, and is filed as RemEx-e2p4: it can tear the stream down before its own modifier keyUps drain, leaving Ctrl held. `assembleRelease` succeeds including the fatal `lintVitalRelease` gate. Not tested on a device — nobody has typed a chord over a real connection. (`RemoteDesktopViewModel.kt`, `SendDispatcherDeclarationOrderTest.kt`; RemEx-7rq3.)

- **A stuck key on your PC, and silently dropped mouse and keyboard input.** Every Remote Desktop operation the phone sent — key presses, clicks, pointer batches, stream start and stop, window queries — was handed to a fire-and-forget `Task.Run`, twelve separate call sites of it. That re-parallelises onto the thread pool, so two operations issued microseconds apart started on different workers and reached the socket in whichever order they got there. A key press is sent as a **separate** keyDown and keyUp, so an inversion tells the host to release a key it was never told to press: the key is left physically held down on the user's actual desktop, recoverable only by walking over to the PC. And the send took no lock, while a `ClientWebSocket` permits exactly one outstanding send — an overlap threw into a `catch` that only wrote to logcat, losing the message outright. Both failures are invisible from the app. **A lock alone would not have fixed it**, which is the part worth remembering: serialising execution prevents overlap but does nothing about order, because whichever thread wakes first takes the lock first. Order can only be preserved by not re-parallelising, so the twelve sites now enqueue onto one ordered queue with a single consumer that awaits each item in turn; the send gate added alongside is defence for callers that do not come through it. **Serialising then created a worse failure than the one it fixed, which review caught before it shipped.** Two of those operations are request/*response* round trips that waited on a reply with no timeout, and the receive loop did not fail pending waiters when it ended — so one dropped socket during a window query blocked the single consumer *forever*, with the stream-stop that is the only route to teardown queued behind it. That would strand a keyDown's keyUp permanently: the same held-down key, now unreleasable, for the life of the app process. Fixed at the root (the receive loop now cancels every in-flight waiter when it ends, for any reason), with a 10-second backstop for a host that stays connected but never answers, and — because the next person to add a call site should not have to know any of this — the queue itself abandons any item that exceeds 30 seconds rather than let it strand the work behind it. Seven tests, proved by injection: replacing the consumer's `await` with fire-and-forget fails exactly the three that assert ordering and non-overlap. The queue's guarantee is one `await`, and without a test it is one keystroke away from being deleted by someone tidying up. Ordering starts at the queue, and the docs now say so rather than claiming more: it inherits whatever order the caller submitted in, which `RemoteControlViewModel` guarantees and `RemoteDesktopViewModel` does not yet (RemEx-7rq3). `libRemexCore.so` links cleanly under NativeAOT. Not tested on a device. (`AndroidNativeExports.cs`, `RemexDesktopClient.cs`, `OrderedAsyncWorkQueue.cs`, `OrderedAsyncWorkQueueTests.cs`, `RemoteControlViewModel.kt`; RemEx-krvz.)

- **The Remote Mouse trackpad now moves the pointer when you drag it slowly, and stops doing JSON work 120 times a second on the main thread.** The bead filed this as performance. It was also a plain functional bug: the trackpad called `onMouseMove(dragAmount.x.toInt(), …)` on every pointer frame, **truncating each frame independently** — so a drag of 0.6px per frame, which is ordinary careful pointing at 120 Hz, truncated to zero every single frame and the pointer did not move at all. Deltas are now floats, accumulated, and emitted only in whole pixels, so a drag of any speed eventually delivers every pixel the user asked for. **The throttle gates sending, not accumulating, and that distinction is the design.** The Remote Desktop screen throttles by *dropping* the callback, which is right there because it throttles stylus hover — absolute positions, where only the newest matters. These are relative deltas: drop one and the movement is gone permanently and the pointer drifts away from the finger. So every frame is accumulated (two float adds) and the clock only decides when the accumulated total is flushed, about 30 times a second instead of 120. A drag that ends mid-interval flushes its tail, or every gesture would stop fractionally short. **The accumulator already existed and had never been called** — `RemoteControlViewModel` carried a `sendMouseMove(Float, Float)` that nothing reached, because the screen's callback was typed `(Int, Int)` and the overload silently resolved to the truncating one; that overload is now private, which is what made the dead code possible in the first place. **Review caught a serious regression in the one part of this the bead prescribed verbatim.** "Dispatch on IO to match `RemoteDesktopViewModel`" moves each send to a 64-thread dispatcher — and `sendKeyPress` issues keyDown and keyUp as two *separate* sends, which then race through tens of microseconds of JSON and JNI work. If keyUp wins, the host releases a key it was never told to press and **the key is left physically held down on the user's PC**, recoverable only by walking over to it. This never happened before because `viewModelScope.launch {}` defaults to `Dispatchers.Main.immediate` and the send does not suspend, so bodies ran inline and in order. Sends now use `Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1)`, which keeps the work off the main thread while preserving submission order. **That order holds only as far as the JNI call, and the code says so rather than implying more**: `desktop_input` bypasses the outbound queue and is handed to a fire-and-forget `Task.Run` that re-parallelises onto the .NET thread pool, where the send takes no lock — so two ordered sends can still reach the socket inverted, or overlap and have one dropped. That was pre-existing and untouched by that change; the single-threaded dispatcher existed to avoid stacking a second, far wider race on top of it. **The underlying one is fixed below in this same release** (RemEx-krvz), so the two halves now compose into an actual end-to-end guarantee. The identical latent bug in `RemoteDesktopViewModel` — the very code the bead pointed at as the reference — is filed as RemEx-7rq3 rather than fixed as a drive-by. Ten tests, proved by injection: restoring per-frame truncation failed exactly the five that depend on accumulation while the five that do not stayed green. One of them pins the send count at **48** for a two-second drag, not the 60 that 2000/33 suggests, because a send can only land on a frame — the effective interval is always the frame time rounded up. Wire format unchanged: `deltaX`/`deltaY` are still integers. `assembleRelease` succeeds including the fatal `lintVitalRelease` gate. Not tested on a device. (`MouseMoveThrottle.kt`, `RemoteControlViewModel.kt`, `RemoteMouseScreen.kt`, `MouseMoveThrottleTest.kt`; RemEx-3uhp.)

- **A download that lost its last 64 KB no longer reports success.** `DownloadAsync` writes through a 65536-byte `FileStream` buffer, so the writer task returning meant every chunk had reached the *stream*, not the disk — and the only flush was the implicit one when `await using` disposed at method exit. **Disposal does not report write failures.** Measured on .NET 10.0.10: a `FileStream` whose underlying handle had been killed returned normally from `DisposeAsync`, while `FlushAsync` on an identically broken stream threw. So a destination that filled up or was unplugged in that window dropped the tail silently — and nothing downstream noticed, because the SHA-256 is accumulated from chunks as they *arrive* and never re-read from the file, so the integrity check compared a complete digest against a short file and passed. One explicit `await fileStream.FlushAsync()` before success is declared turns that into a real error, and `completed` stays false so the partial file is deleted instead of being left under the user's chosen name looking finished. **The comment says what the fix does NOT buy, which matters more than what it does**: `FlushAsync` hands the buffer to the OS with a write call and does not `fsync`, so it surfaces out-of-space and device-gone — the two cases this was filed for — but a write-back failure once bytes are in the OS cache is still invisible. It is deliberately not escalated to `Flush(flushToDisk: true)`: that blocks synchronously, and the host does not fsync its side either, so a plain flush is honest parity rather than a false guarantee on one end. It is also deliberately untokenised, because `FlushAsync(ct)` with an already-cancelled token returns a cancelled task **without flushing** — the identical failure this exists to remove. Review moved it below the host-error check, since a throwing flush there would displace `FileTransferHostException`, whose message is the only text the transfer queue shows verbatim. **A claim was retracted rather than shipped**: a reviewer reported the truncated file ends up zero bytes, and that did not reproduce — reading `FileStream.SafeFileHandle` flushes the buffer as a side effect, so the probe had already written the bytes. Only the throw/no-throw asymmetry, which reproduces, is asserted. No test: making a flush fail deterministically needs a device failure or a seam this class does not have, tracked on RemEx-wfim with this case added to its list. The unhelpful generic message the new failure currently produces is filed as RemEx-6tvh. (`FileTransferClient.cs`; RemEx-owc3.)

- **A download to a slow drive can no longer consume unbounded memory — and two failure paths that were quietly leaving corrupt files behind now clean up.** Downloads hand every arriving chunk to a channel drained by one writer task, which is what keeps the file in order. Nothing in the file protocol lets the receiver slow the sender, so when the destination writes slower than the network delivers, that channel accumulates the ENTIRE difference: a large file onto a USB stick queued gigabytes of managed arrays inside an always-running elevated process. There is now a 256 MB ceiling on unwritten backlog, past which the transfer is abandoned with a message naming the cause. **The obvious fix was the wrong one, and the reasoning is recorded because it is not obvious in hindsight.** Switching to a bounded channel looks right until you notice the producer is a *synchronous* dispatch handler: there is nowhere to await room, so `TryWrite` would return false and silently **drop** the chunk, producing a corrupt file that surfaces much later as an integrity failure blaming the wrong thing. Byte accounting keeps the ordering guarantee the channel exists for while still refusing to grow forever. **This is honestly a trade, not a free win.** With no flow control the backlog has no fixed point, so *any* finite ceiling eventually fails a sustained mismatch — USB-2 against Wi-Fi reaches 256 MB in about thirteen seconds — where the old code would have completed by spending the whole difference in RAM. Losing one download beats losing the process, but the fix that gets both is receiver-driven flow control, filed as RemEx-wfim with three costed options. **Review caught two defects on the new failure path, and one of them turned out to be older than this change.** The abandon claimed to remove the partial file and did not: `File.Delete` ran only after the wait returned *normally*, so the exception skipped it. Chasing that down showed the two pre-existing delete sites — host error and integrity failure — never worked either, because the file is opened `FileShare.None` and `await using` disposes it at method exit, so on Windows every one of those deletes threw a sharing violation into a best-effort `catch` and left a truncated file under the user's chosen name looking complete. (On Linux it happened to work: `FileShare` maps to an advisory `flock` and `unlink` ignores it, so the delete succeeded and the stream wrote on into an unlinked inode.) All three now close the stream first. The abandon was also not the fast failure its own documentation claimed: completing the channel makes the reader drain, so it wrote the entire backlog to the disk that could not keep up before the user saw the error. The writer now has its own cancellation — deliberately NOT linked to the caller's token, which the verification pass caught as a data-loss bug in the first attempt at this: linked, a cancel landing during the FINAL drain stopped the writer mid-flush, and nothing downstream noticed, because the digest is accumulated from bytes as they are RECEIVED and never re-read from the file. The integrity check would have compared a complete hash against a truncated file, passed, and reported a short download as finished. Cleanup is now driven from a single flag in the `finally` instead of a delete at each throw site, which also covers the two ordinary exits that were silently stranding partial files all along — user cancellation and the idle timeout. **The user-facing string was reworded after review too** — the first draft called the same machine "this device" and "your PC" in one sentence, while its sibling messages use those words for the *peer*, so the one thing it had to convey (which machine to change) was ambiguous. Ten tests over the accounting, proved by injection: deleting the rollback failed exactly the five that depend on the counter not drifting, while the other five stayed green. The reserve/retire pair is unit-tested; the writer's single call to retire, and the unwind itself, need a seam the client does not have and are tracked in RemEx-wfim rather than claimed as covered. 1005 tests, 0 warnings, localization clean. (`FileTransferClient.cs`, `FileTransferBacklogException.cs`, `FileTransferQueue.cs`, 9 resx, `DownloadBacklogTests.cs`; RemEx-gyf4.)

- **`PersistentDisplayKey` is now actually persistent on Windows.** `DesktopDisplayInfo` carries two identifiers with deliberately opposite contracts: `DisplayId` is session-scoped and renumbers when monitors change, and `PersistentDisplayKey` is the one a client may store to reselect "the monitor I was watching last time". The Windows host assigned them **the same string** — `\.\DISPLAY1`, or a `monitor-N` ordinal — so the persistent key was exactly as session-scoped as the id it exists to outlive, while Linux had been deriving its key from the display's own UUID all along. **The failure was silent, which is what made it worth fixing**: a stored key still resolves after a re-plug, it just resolves to a different physical screen, so the user gets someone else's monitor and nothing anywhere reports an error. It now comes from the monitor's device interface path (`EnumDisplayDevices` with `EDD_GET_DEVICE_INTERFACE_NAME`), which is registry-persisted and identifies the panel rather than its place in an enumeration. **The doc comment states the limits rather than overselling them**, because review caught the first draft overselling exactly this: the path embeds the manufacturer and *model*, not a unit serial, so it survives reboots and same-port re-plugs but not moving a monitor to a different port — and it cannot tell two *identical* panels apart when they are swapped, where both keys still resolve, each to the other's screen. The EDID serial is reachable over WMI but is blank or constant on plenty of panels, so it is not the better source it looks like. **The key is deliberately computed where it is consumed, not where displays are enumerated**: `EnumerateDisplays` is reached from `GetActiveBounds` on the per-frame capture path, so resolving it there would have meant an `EnumDisplayDevices` call per monitor per frame — marshalling an 840-byte struct into four managed strings — for a value only `GetDisplayCatalog` ever reads. The fallback ladder and the enumeration walk are pure and unit-tested (13 tests, proved by injection: restoring the old source failed exactly the three that assert panel identity, while the two-panels-differ control correctly stayed green, since it passes under the old behaviour too). The Win32 marshalling needs real hardware and is honestly untested. **This does not yet fix the symptom the bug describes**, and that is filed rather than implied: `PersistentDisplayKey` is write-only across the whole repo, and Android's "remember my monitor" flow persists `"monitor:$displayId"` — the session-scoped id — so the host now emits a correct key nobody reads (RemEx-ynur). No protocol change: the field keeps its name, type and optionality, only its value changes, and it has no consumers to migrate. (`WindowsScreenCaptureService.cs`, `DesktopDisplayModels.cs`, `PersistentDisplayKeyTests.cs`; RemEx-zftu.)

- **A pairing prompt no longer arrives while the app is in the background.** Three small correctness fixes, of which the middle one turned out not to be the change it was written as. `pairingRequired` (navigate to the PIN screen) and `wakeStatus` (show a snackbar) were both collected in `LaunchedEffect(Unit)` with no lifecycle gating, so an event arriving while the app was stopped was acted on regardless — in `pairingRequired`'s case by driving navigation behind the user's back. **The two flows are not alike, and gating them identically would have made one of them worse.** `wakeStatus` has no replay, so gating genuinely drops what is emitted while stopped — correct here, because a snackbar announcing a wake the user triggered several minutes ago is worse than no snackbar. `pairingRequired` has `replay = 1`, and `repeatOnLifecycle` re-subscribes on every return to foreground, so gating it *alone* would have redelivered the retained request every single time the app resumed and walked the user to the PIN screen each time. It is gated **and** consumed: `consumePairingRequest()` drops the retained value once the navigation site has acted on it, which makes the event one-shot in fact rather than by convention and demotes the pre-existing stale-request guard from sole defence to second line. **Review caught the interesting mistake:** the first version also consumed in that guard's early-return branch, where nothing had been acted on. `isConnected` is cleared only when the native layer *notices* the link is gone, so it can be stale-true after a phone leaves the LAN — and `connect()` has no already-connected early return, so a genuine request can be emitted in exactly that state. Consuming there would have silently destroyed it, leaving a Connect button that does nothing until the staleness resolved. Consumption now happens only where the request was actually handled. Alongside: `PairingScreen`'s startup effect keys on `(host, port)` rather than `Unit`, which it reads — unreachable today because the route embeds both, so a change always builds a new nav entry, but a `Unit` key asserts an independence from its inputs that is false; and `WidgetDataCache.startCaching` is `@Synchronized`, because its check-then-act guard has three callers that are not all on one thread — `MainActivity`, `RemexConnectionService`, and a Glance widget update running from a broadcast — and two arriving together would each read a null job and start a permanent duplicate collector on a second scope. That scope is process-lifetime and never cancelled, which is deliberate and now says so: a widget outlives every Activity and Service that might have started it. The consumption contract is pinned by a JVM test that reflects the private flow to emit — the ordinary routes are all unreachable without the native library, and eight lines of reflection in a test beat adding a second test-only seam to a class the project marks high-risk. **Verification depth, stated plainly because this is the pairing path:** `assembleRelease` succeeds including the fatal `lintVitalRelease` gate and 211 unit tests pass, but **none of this has been exercised on a device**. Confirming it needs an unpaired PC and a background/foreground cycle, and the bead stays open until someone runs it. (`AppNavigation.kt`, `DashboardScreen.kt`, `PairingScreen.kt`, `RemexClientManager.kt`, `WidgetDataCache.kt`, `PairingRequestConsumptionTest.kt`; RemEx-zlpm.)

- **The Task Manager sort row now wraps onto two lines instead of squeezing its chips until they ellipsize.** Its label, four equal-width sort chips and the direction button could not share one line at large font scales: the chips carry `weight(1f)` each, so they absorb whatever the label and button leave, and past a certain size that is less than the text needs. RemEx-0pxq made the failure graceful rather than mid-glyph, but a capacity problem cannot be fixed by an overflow mode. When the chips do not fit they now get a full-width line of their own, with the label and direction button on the line above — and the label switches from a 120dp cap to `weight(1f)` there, so the longer translations stop truncating at exactly the scale where they are hardest to read. **The decision is measured, not thresholded**, which is the substantive choice: a font-scale threshold is one number that has to be correct for nine languages at every scale, and being wrong is silent in both directions — too high and the labels clip, too low and the row wastes a line forever. A `BoxWithConstraints` plus a `rememberTextMeasurer` asks the only question that matters, whether these four labels at this size in this language fit beside the label and the button, and the arithmetic lives in a pure `sortControlsFitInline` that is unit-tested on the JVM rather than only visible on a device at a font scale nobody remembers to try. **The bead's own numbers were wrong and were corrected against the code:** both its line references had rotted, and it assumed the system scale is clamped to 1.5, giving a worst case of 1.4. `clampedAppFontScale` clamps only the app's OWN contribution so the combined scale stays under 1.6, and its documentation is explicit that it never counteracts the system setting — so on API 34+ non-linear scaling the system alone reaches **2.0** and wins. The tests assert 1.6 and 2.0. **Two consequences are pinned by tests rather than left to be rediscovered as bugs:** a locale whose "Sort by" reaches the 120dp cap stacks at *default* font scale on a 360dp phone, and English needs a 324dp-wide window to stay inline — both cases were already clipping before, so this is the fix reaching further than the bead scoped, not a regression. And stacking does not *guarantee* a fit: a full-width chip row on a 280dp screen at 2.0x still overflows, which is the floor of this approach and is written at the function. Ten tests, proved by injection — restoring the always-inline behaviour failed exactly the four that assert stacking while all three positive controls stayed green. `assembleRelease` succeeds including the fatal `lintVitalRelease` gate. (`TaskManagerScreen.kt`, `SortControlsFitTest.kt`; RemEx-k0vy.)

- **Five labels that hard-clipped mid-glyph at large font scales now ellipsize.** A Compose `Text` with `maxLines = 1` and no `overflow` defaults to `TextOverflow.Clip`, which cuts the string at the pixel boundary — often part-way through a character, with nothing to signal that text is missing. At `fontScale` 2.0, or simply with a longer translation of the same label, five sites did that: the shape names in the 72dp Personalization grid cells, the Remote Desktop `SettingSlider` labels (two of which sit side by side in landscape), the user's own shared-folder display name in Settings, and the display-mode and palette-mode `ToggleButton` labels. **The bead's list was wrong in both directions, which is why the tree was audited rather than the four named sites patched.** Its Task Manager entry was already fixed by RemEx-0pxq — both the "Sort by" label and the chip labels carry `Ellipsis` today — while the two Personalization `ToggleButton` labels it never mentioned are the *identical* shape it describes: a `Text(label, maxLines = 1)` inside a `Modifier.weight(1f)` button, where any label longer than its share of the row is what gets clipped. Fixing the four as written would have left two live instances of the exact defect the bead exists to remove. **Six further `maxLines = 1` sites were found and deliberately not touched**: they are in `HardwareInfoWidget` and `RemoteControlWidget`, which are Glance widgets, and `androidx.glance.text.Text` has no `overflow` parameter at all — the fix is not expressible there, so their clipping is a separate problem needing a different mechanism (RemEx-4g8g). That leaves the app's own screens uniformly on `Ellipsis`, which is what the rest of the codebase already did. `assembleRelease` succeeds including the fatal `lintVitalRelease` gate; unit tests pass. (`DashboardShapes.kt`, `RemoteDesktopScreen.kt`, `SettingsScreen.kt`, `PersonalizationScreen.kt`; RemEx-wdit.)


- **The default Remote Desktop configuration was spending 20.7 ms per frame downscaling on the capture thread — enough on its own to cap the stream near 48 FPS against a 120 FPS target.** `BgraFrameConverter` only has a fast path (one row-wise copy) when it is *not* resampling, and the default scale is 0.6, so every frame took the `System.Drawing` fallback instead: two `Bitmap` allocations, a GDI+ bilinear `DrawImage`, and another full `byte[]` — the exact pattern the type's own regression-guard comment says capped streaming near 30 FPS. **The premise was measured before anything was written**, at the real resolution on the reference box: GDI+ path **20.69 ms/frame** at 2560×1440 → 0.6, versus **1.68 ms** for the full-res row copy. That is where the bead's "~10-20 ms" estimate actually lands, at the top. The capture now runs at full resolution and ffmpeg does the resize with a `scale` filter on its own threads; the capture backend needed no change at all, because passing scale 1.0 makes it take the existing fast path automatically. The trade is pipe bandwidth — 14 MB/frame instead of 5.3 — and it is worth it because the capture thread is what gates frame rate. **Review measured the things that were only assumed.** The pipe was the main worry and it is a non-issue: a real Win32 anonymous-pipe write sustains 5.2 GB/s, three times what 120 FPS needs (a `cat |` benchmark suggesting otherwise turned out to be an MSYS emulation artifact). The scaler flag, however, was wrong: `fast_bilinear` scores 28.93 dB against a lanczos reference while plain `bilinear` scores 42.87 dB for +0.32 ms — free against an 8.3 ms budget — and the original rationale had the rate-distortion argument backwards, since scaler aliasing costs *more* bits at a given QP. **And review caught a defect that would have broken H.264 outright.** `BuildEncoderArgs` correctly declared `-s 2560x1440`, but `RunEncoderProbe` still wrote `width * height * 4` — the *encoded* size — so ffmpeg rejected the short frame (`packet size 5308416 < expected frame_size 14745600`), the probe failed for **every** codec, and H.264 fell back to MJPEG permanently with no error surfaced. Six passing argument-string tests said nothing about it, because none of them looked at the code that writes bytes; there is now a guard that does. Three of the six codec branches — including `h264_nvenc_bgra`, the one tried first — were also missed in the first draft and would have silently encoded at the capture resolution, so the test that covers them is exhaustive over the codec list by construction. Confirmed on real hardware that the scale filter keeps `h264_nvenc_bgra` in BGRA end to end, so that path still hands NVENC raw BGRA for fixed-function conversion rather than gaining a CPU colorspace pass. An odd-width surface now stays on the old route, since `ScaledEven` rounds it down and full-res would land back on GDI+ at *full* resolution — slower than what it replaced. Left as follow-ups in RemEx-zs7l: a bytes-per-frame budget for very large multi-monitor surfaces (7680×2160 would be 66 MB/frame), and the fact that `AdaptiveScaleController` now moves only the encode size, so it cannot relieve a capture- or pipe-bound stream. 957 tests green. (`FFmpegH264Encoder.cs`, `IH264Encoder.cs`, `RemoteDesktopHandler.cs`, `FFmpegH264EncoderArgsTests.cs`; RemEx-evzv.)
- **Streaming stopped burning a whole CPU core doing nothing. The Remote Desktop pacer was spinning every interval instead of sleeping it — measured 99% of a core before, 18% after.** `PrecisionPacer` coarse-sleeps most of each tick and busy-spins the tail for sub-millisecond accuracy, but the spin margin was 16 ms — **larger than an entire tick at 90 Hz (11.1 ms) or 120 Hz (8.3 ms)**. The coarse sleep could therefore never run at either rate, so the tail *was* the interval: the 90 Hz cursor loop pinned a core for as long as a stream was open, on the same machine trying to hold NVENC boost clocks, and held a thread-pool thread hostage while doing it. **The margin can only shrink if the sleep underneath it is accurate**, so the coarse wait is now a Windows high-resolution waitable timer (`CREATE_WAITABLE_TIMER_HIGH_RESOLUTION`, Win10 1803+) awaited without occupying a thread. `timeBeginPeriod(1)` was the other option in the bead and was rejected: it raises the timer resolution for the *entire machine*, and `remex.agent` runs from logon, so it would tax the box even when nobody is streaming — which is most of what this bead is trying to save. **Where the timer cannot be created the old 16 ms margin is kept deliberately**, because a 2 ms margin over a 15.6 ms-granular sleep overshoots the tick and drops the frame rate, which is worse than the CPU cost. Linux was spinning identically and is fixed too — at 11.1 ms `remaining > 16` was never true there either, which the bead undersold. **Pacing semantics are untouched**: the absolute timeline, `Reset()`, the overrun path and the never-throw cancellation contract are byte-for-byte the same, and the pre-1803 branch is the previous code exactly. **The review found a handle leak in the first version of this fix** — `WaitHandle.SafeWaitHandle`'s setter does *not* close the handle it replaces, so every pacer orphaned one until a finalizer happened to run (500 disposed pacers left 504 handles outstanding). It also found that a failed `SetWaitableTimer` was returning the same value as cancellation, which would have ended a stream silently on a transient Win32 error; arming failures now fall back to `Task.Delay` for that tick and log the error code. The wait is bounded rather than infinite, so a lost signal degrades into one late tick the absolute timeline reclaims instead of freezing the stream. **The first version of the regression test had to be thrown away too**: it measured `Process.TotalProcessorTime`, which is process-wide and read ~105% under the full suite whether the pacer spun or not — it was measuring xUnit. It now asserts on the pacer's own accumulated spin time, which is the mechanism itself; injecting the old margin fails it at "spun 100% of the wall time" for both rates. 941 tests green across three consecutive runs. (`PrecisionPacer.cs`, `PrecisionPacerTests.cs` (new), `RemoteDesktopHandler.cs`, `AGENTS.md`; RemEx-ccen.)
- **Left click now left-clicks on the phone's Remote Mouse screen. It was sending a middle click, on every platform, from both the button labelled "Left click" and the trackpad tap.** `RemoteMouseScreen` sent button index `1`, and `1` is the MIDDLE button — the protocol uses the W3C `MouseEvent.button` order (`0` left, `1` middle, `2` right), which both hosts implement. Right-click was correct all along, and the Remote Desktop screen was correct all along, which is why this survived: the broken screen still *did* something on every tap. **The bead's own diagnosis was wrong and had to be discarded first.** It was filed (by the previous iteration of this loop, off a reviewer's finding) claiming the two hosts disagreed — Windows `1`=middle, Linux `1`=right — citing `LinuxInputEventTranslator.ButtonIndexToLinuxCode`. That method has NO production callers. The live Linux path is `LinuxInputSimulationService`, whose three backends (xdotool, ydotool, portal) all match Windows exactly, as do the two further tables in `LinuxInputBackendRouter`. So the hosts never disagreed; a dead method had been mistaken for the platform's behaviour, and **the earlier entry below that repeats the "Linux maps 1 to RIGHT" claim is wrong and is retracted here.** The dead method's order was inverted too, and a unit test pinned that inversion — which is how it looked verified rather than wrong. It is corrected to match, because wiring it up for a future evdev path would otherwise have silently swapped right and middle. **The real defect is that there are SIX button tables and nothing compared them**; `EveryHostButtonMapping_AgreesOnLeftMiddleRight` now does, asserting both that the correct pairs are present and that the inverted ones are absent, deliberately without pinning how many tables exist so that correctly adding a backend does not fail with a message about arity. Proved by inverting a live table and watching it fail naming `1 => 0x111`. The Android side no longer sends bare digits at all: `MouseButtons.LEFT/MIDDLE/RIGHT` replaced every literal across both screens, including the stylus/absolute-click twins and the drag-button state, because "nothing about `1` looks wrong at a call site" is the whole reason this shipped. **No protocol break**: the host's live behaviour is byte-for-byte unchanged, so an old phone against a new host behaves exactly as before, and a new phone works against an *unpatched* host — the fix needs no coordinated release and no `protocolVersion` bump. The structural fix, one shared constant behind all six tables, is filed as RemEx-upxn. 933 tests green, `assembleRelease` and `lintVitalRelease` clean. (`MouseButtons.kt` (new), `RemoteMouseScreen.kt`, `RemoteDesktopScreen.kt`, `LinuxInputEventTranslator.cs`, `LinuxPointerSampleTranslatorTests.cs`, `InputEvent.cs`; RemEx-kie3.)
- **The code-built parts of the PC UI follow the theme now, and the bead that blocked this for months was blocked by a typo in its own research.** The minimap, the colour picker, the window's non-transparent background, the sparkline's "running hot" colour, the card-customisation fallbacks and the Home link-card tints were all painted from hex literals compiled into the control, so they were only ever right for one of the four themes — a dark slab sitting on SolarFlare being the usual symptom. **The bead recorded a hard blocker: "THERE IS NO ACCENT BRUSH KEY IN ANY OF THE FOUR THEMES … verified by counting x:Key matches", concluding that anything accent-coloured needed a palette designed first and must not be done autonomously.** That search looked for `AccentBrush`, `AccentColor` and `SurfaceBrush`, none of which are this repo's naming convention. The actual key is `AccentPrimaryBrush`, and all **49** theme keys are defined in all four theme files with zero divergence — so every site had something to point at the whole time. The lesson is not about accents: a "verified by counting" claim that returns zero is as likely to be a wrong query as a real absence, and this one cost the bead an unknown number of sessions. **The three-line lookup existed twice already** (`LogLevelToBrushConverter`, `SensorColorConverter`) and is now one `ThemeResources` helper — `TryGetResource` so a missing key degrades instead of throwing inside a `Render` override, the variant passed explicitly, and resolved PER CALL, because a `static readonly` brush is captured once at type-initialisation and then survives every theme switch for the life of the process, which is the bug in miniature. Every conversion keeps its original literal as the fallback, so a missing key degrades to exactly what the control drew before. **Two things the review caught that neither the build nor 932 tests could.** First, the redraw fix was dead code for the majority of switches: `ThemeService` sets `RequestedThemeVariant` to Dark for BaseDarkGlass, CyberNOC *and* Monolith and Light only for SolarFlare, so switching between the three dark themes assigns the variant a value it already held and raises no event — the drawing controls now listen to `ResourcesChanged`, which fires on every switch because the merged dictionaries are always swapped, and additionally covers the accent-override path that changes colours with no variant change at all. Second, `SolidColorBrush.Opacity` MULTIPLIES with the colour's own alpha, and `GlassBaseDark` is already translucent on two themes (`#A00A0A10`, `#D90A0A10`) — so asking for it at 0.92 produced 0.58 on the default theme, *more* transparent than the literal it replaced. `ThemeResources.OpaqueColor` strips the theme's alpha where a site means "this plate is 92% opaque". **Making a fill theme-aware without its foreground is its own bug**: the colour picker's confirm button took the theme accent, which is amber on SolarFlare, under a white tick it had inherited from a fixed deep blue — 1.73:1, against a 4.5:1 requirement. Its label is now derived from the resolved background by sRGB relative luminance, since no "on-accent" key exists to look up. The guard against all of this is `EveryKeyAskedForByCode_ExistsInAllFourThemes`, and it earned its keep twice: a mistyped key resolves to the fallback **silently and forever**, which is indistinguishable from working, and the guard's first version scanned only `Brush|Color` — so adding `OpaqueColor` as a third entry point moved call sites out of coverage without failing anything, and keys passed through `CanvasMinimap.Plate`'s parameter were never in scope at all. Proved by injecting a typo through the parameter path and watching it fail by name. **The same blind spot then repeated one level up**: consolidating the two converters onto the shared helper did not bring their keys into scope, because their call sites still went through a local `Resolve(key, fallback)` wrapper that the scan cannot see either — the wrapper had to go, not just its body. Coverage went 7 keys to 10, and a scanner that follows only what it can see needs every indirection removed rather than special-cased. Left alone deliberately: the theme preview tiles and accent swatches, which are meant to show their own colour; and `SparklineControl`'s two `StyledProperty` defaults, which are baked in at static registration before any theme exists and so want a style setter instead (RemEx-qljv). Two listed sites needed no work — an earlier bead had already fixed the hover ring and the font-warning banner. 932 tests green, 0 warnings; the four themes were NOT visually inspected, which is why every conversion is fallback-preserving and every colour claim above was checked against the four theme files rather than by eye. (`ThemeResources.cs` (new), `ThemeResourcesTests.cs` (new), `CanvasMinimap.cs`, `SparklineControl.cs`, `ColorPickerPopup.cs`, `CardCustomizationConverters.cs`, `LogLevelToBrushConverter.cs`, `SensorColorConverter.cs`, `MainWindow.axaml.cs`, `HomeView.axaml`; RemEx-fy0a.)
- **The PC About page labels a release the way Android labels it — "2.4.0", not "2.4.0.0".** `AboutViewModel` read `Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly().GetName().Version` and rendered it with a bare `.ToString()`, which always widens to four components, while `Directory.Build.props` declares `2.4.0` and Android's About screen shows `BuildConfig.VERSION_NAME` — so the same build was labelled two different ways depending on which device the user was looking at, and the trailing `.0` meant nothing to anyone. The version was correctly wired to the build on both platforms; only the formatting differed. The fix reads `AssemblyInformationalVersionAttribute`, which carries the declared `<Version>` verbatim, and trims the `+<git sha>` the SDK appends by default since .NET 8 (`IncludeSourceRevisionInInformationalVersion`) — a commit hash is not something the target user has any use for. **The logic was extracted rather than copied, because a second copy would have preserved the exact drift being fixed.** `SkiaSplashControl.ResolveVersion` already did this same resolve-and-trim for the splash label; pasting it into the view-model would have left two independent answers to "what version is this", which is how the About page and the splash could have disagreed. Both now call `AppVersion.Display`, resolved once. **The extraction also removed a latent crash nobody had hit**: the old `Version.ToString(3)` fallback throws `ArgumentException` when the third component is undefined, so a two-part `<Version>` such as `2.5` would have taken down the splash — the shared helper falls back a component instead. Nothing on the wire changed: `caps.Version` and `PairingRequest.ClientVersion` are untouched, and the `Remex.Core` NativeAOT rules do not bind this code because `remex.desktop` is PC-only and never compiled into `libRemexCore.so`. The three load-bearing tests assert the *observable output* rather than restating the implementation — three components, no `+` suffix, and not equal to the four-part assembly version that the old code produced — with the three-part regex left as a deliberate tripwire, since a prerelease or two-part version would need an answer for Android's `versionName` too. The host-version row one divider below still shows `2.4.0.0 (Windows, …)` from `caps.Version`; that is a display-layer fix in `UpdateHostVersion` filed separately as RemEx-8jzu, deliberately not conflated with an optional wire change the Android client also reads. 907 tests green, 0 warnings. (`AppVersion.cs` (new), `AppVersionTests.cs` (new), `AboutViewModel.cs`, `SkiaSplashControl.cs`; RemEx-nll1.)
- **Pull-to-refresh on the phone's App Launcher now actually refreshes, instead of spinning for exactly five seconds and re-showing the same list.** `AppLauncherViewModel.refreshApps()` sent `{"type": "launcher_sync_request"}` — a type that existed **only** as a hand-built literal on the Android side. There was no `MessageTypes` constant naming it and no `case` in `PingPongHandler` answering it, so every Refresh tap fell through the switch to `default:` and was dropped. **What hid it is that the symptom looks like success.** The host pushes `launcher_sync` proactively on connect, so the launcher list does populate — just never because the user asked — and the phone then cleared its spinner from a hard-coded 5s safety-net delay. The visible result was a refresh that took five seconds and returned unchanged data, which reads as slow-but-working rather than dead. The host had in fact been logging `"Unknown message type: launcher_sync_request"` on every tap since the feature shipped; nobody was reading for it. The fix is the constant plus the host case, which mirrors the existing `LayoutRequest → LayoutSync` pair and is deliberately **not** added to RemEx-q6xt's `RequiresLoopback` set: asking for the list is a read, and re-reading a list the host already pushes on connect grants a remote client nothing it did not have a second earlier. **The generalisation is the more valuable half.** Android builds its JSON by hand in Kotlin and cannot reference the C# constants, so a type can exist on the phone with no counterpart on the host — and `RequiresLoopback` matches on **constants**, meaning a hand-built literal cannot be gated at all even where it needs to be. `EveryMessageTypeAndroidSends_HasAMatchingConstant` scans every `put("type", "…")` literal in the Kotlin tree and requires a declared constant for each; it deliberately ignores `put("type", variable)` dispatchers, where there is no string to check. That audit found `launcher_sync_request` was the **only** drifted literal — the other 22 all map to existing constants — so the guard is cheap and currently green by one edit. It also names the offending literal and file in its failure message rather than reporting a count. Both tests were proved by injection: disabling the host case fails the round-trip with the user's exact symptom (`Timed out waiting for a 'launcher_sync' message`), and typo-ing the Kotlin literal to `launcher_sync_requst` fails the parity guard naming that string. The round-trip test changes the stored list **after** the on-connect push, so a reply that merely echoed the connect-time snapshot would fail — asserting only "a `launcher_sync` arrives" would have passed on the broken build. 902 tests green, 0 warnings, `assembleRelease` and `lintVitalRelease` clean. (`RemexMessage.cs`, `PingPongHandler.cs`, `AppLauncherViewModel.kt`, `LauncherSyncRequestTests.cs` (new), `LauncherAllowlistAuthorizationTests.cs`; RemEx-vpxx.)
- **Downloading a file found by browsing a bare drive works from the phone, which is the one place it never did.** Full-device browsing was extended to downloads in RemEx-39jw, that change shipped with its tests green, and the user-facing repro — browse `C:\`, walk into a folder that is *not* a pinned shared folder, download a file — still failed on device with “Unknown shared root”, on a host build that verifiably contained the fix. **There are two host download paths and the fix landed on the one the phone does not use.** The legacy v2 `file_transfer_start` flow through `FileTransferHandler` got the pinned-root-or-consented-volume fallback; the v3 `file_transfer_offer` flow through `TransferSessionManager.BeginSendAsync` — the one every real Android download takes — called `OpenForReadAsync` with the client’s raw rootId, so `FileTransferService` looked `C:\` up in the pinned-root registry, threw, and the sender turned that into a `file_transfer_ready(accepted: false)` carrying the exception text straight to the phone. **The duplication was the actual defect, so the fix removes it rather than pasting the fallback a second time.** `SharedRootReadResolver` is now the single place a client-supplied rootId becomes a readable location, and both paths call it — the handler’s two private helpers delegate to it instead of holding their own copy. Read-only by construction: there is no write counterpart, because full browse still never exposes write/delete on a bare volume (RemEx-hb1t) and un-pinned writes still refuse with the plain-English pointer to the shared-folders list (RemEx-hb1t.3). Consent is re-verified inside the resolver on every call, so a rootId naming a real drive is not sufficient on its own, and an unidentified peer — `HandleOfferAsync` passes `clientId ?? string.Empty` — cannot inherit another device’s grant. **Why the original tests could not have caught this**: `TransferSessionManagerTests` stubbed *both* `OpenForReadAsync` and `OpenVolumeForReadAsync` as `throw new NotSupportedException()`, so v3 download root-resolution had no coverage at all and RemEx-39jw’s 419 green tests were green about the other path. The four new tests build the real `FileTransferService` / `FileTrustService` / `VolumeEnumerator` instead of the fake, against the temp directory’s own drive root so the same test is `C:\` on Windows and `/` on Linux. Proved by injection: restoring the pre-fix call fails three of the four with the user’s verbatim `UnauthorizedAccessException : Unknown shared root 'C:\'`, while the pinned-root test keeps passing — the discrimination that matters, since that branch was never broken. 900 tests green across all three projects. (`SharedRootReadResolver.cs` (new), `TransferSessionManager.cs`, `FileTransferHandler.cs`, `HostBootstrapper.cs`, `TransferSessionManagerTests.cs`, `FileTransferHandlerTests.cs`; RemEx-hb1t.6.)
- **Five languages stopped hearing an English word explaining a Latin key legend they already could not read.** RemEx-qykh made every on-screen key announce “LEGEND (gloss)” so the name contains what the cap draws — but the gloss was whatever was there before, so a Ukrainian user heard “PgUp (Page Up)”: an all-Latin name with an English parenthetical that adds nothing in their language. es/fr/in were already right. **The candidate list was 12 keys; the real scope was five.** Only escape, delete, pageup, pagedown and insert actually carry a gloss in hi/pl/pt-BR/tr/uk — the other seven are bare legends with nothing to translate, so this is 25 values, not 60. **The values needed a stated principle, which is that the gloss is what a speaker of that language *calls* the key.** Where the language has its own word it is used; where the language simply says the Latin abbreviation the gloss is **dropped** — pl/pt-BR/tr/uk now carry a bare `Esc`, which is exactly the deliberate choice `es` already made and which the bead warned against "fixing" into the pattern. Hindi is the exception, taking `Esc (एस्केप)` because Devanagari gives a Hindi screen reader something to pronounce. Delete is anchored to each locale’s **own existing vocabulary** (`file_transfer_delete` → Usuń / Excluir / Sil / Видалити / हटाएं) rather than translated afresh. **The constraint that justifies the whole feature is now a test.** The bead records that a reviewer checked all 108 legend-first pairs by hand under RemEx-qykh — and nothing re-checked them since, while this change rewrote 25. `KeycapAccessibleNameTests` asserts all 108 mechanically, excludes the seven glyph-only keys by construction (`cd_key_enter` must never gain a Latin prefix), and accepts a bare legend as legitimate. Proved by inverting uk `pageup` to “Сторінка вгору (PgUp)”, which fails naming locale, key and value — an injection that also confirmed the new `build.gradle.kts` input declarations, since a `strings.xml`-only edit re-ran the guard instead of reporting `UP-TO-DATE`. **A mechanical “the gloss must not be English” check was written and then removed**, with the reasoning left in the test file: `es` “Ctrl (Control)” and `in` “Ins (Insert)” are byte-identical to English and correct, so that property is not decidable from the string and the test would have needed a hand-maintained exemption list. 185 Android unit tests green, `assembleRelease` and `lintVitalRelease` clean, `check-localization.ps1` clean. (5 `strings.xml`, `KeycapAccessibleNameTests.kt`, `build.gradle.kts`; RemEx-jcbw.)
- **Every Remote Desktop status message now follows a language switch, because the view-model stopped storing resolved text.** `StatusText` and `WindowControlStatusText` were plain properties assigned already-localized strings in 26 places — “Connecting…”, “Streaming”, “Stream failed”, “Loading displays”, “Switching display”, “Frame decode error” and the rest. A language switch could not reach any of them: whichever message was showing simply stayed in the previous language until the next user action replaced it. **Patching the one site the bead originally named would have fixed a twentieth of it while making the file look handled**, and nothing distinguished that site — several messages set `HasStreamError`, so a conditional refresh would have overwritten whichever error was actually on screen with the wrong message. Both properties now hold a `Func<string>` resolver and resolve on each get, so **re-raising the property is the entire refresh** and the view-model never has to know which message is current. **The host-authored case is deliberately separate.** `SetStatusLiteral` exists so text the host wrote is shown verbatim and never re-resolved — the same distinction RemEx-mznc and RemEx-s4p4 settled for file transfer by dispatching on exception *type* rather than message text, because the host’s own wording is the most useful sentence in the flow and must not be replaced by a generic one. **The change pays for itself in coverage**: because the getters now read the localizer, `LocalizedPropertyRefreshTests` picks both properties up automatically — proved by deleting the `StatusText` re-raise, which fails with “the locale handler never re-raises StatusText”. They were invisible to that guard while they were snapshots. One mechanical trap worth recording: the rewrite pattern initially matched `StatusText =>` as well as `StatusText =`, turning the expression-bodied declaration into nonsense — `=(?!>)` is what separates an assignment from an expression body. 881 tests green, 0 warnings. (`RemoteDesktopViewModel.cs`; RemEx-qlfj.)
- **The Settings host-info labels follow a language switch while connected, which is the state they were never refreshed in.** `SettingsViewModel.OnLocaleChanged` recomputed `HostRuntimeText` and `HostCapabilityText` **only when `HostCapabilities == null`** — that is, only while *disconnected*. Connected, which is where a user actually spends time, both properties held a snapshot taken from the connection’s localized summaries and kept the previous wording until host capabilities next changed. This is the variant `LocalizedPropertyRefreshTests` cannot see by construction: the bound property is a plain `[ObservableProperty]`, its getter a field read with no localizer call anywhere near it, while the staleness a user sees is identical. **The handler also picked up the guard `AboutViewModel` was alone in having** — `SetCulture` raises `Item`, `Item[]` and `""` in sequence, so an unguarded handler runs three times per switch; harmless when the body only re-raises notifications, wasteful when it re-reads state. **The new pinning test caught a hole in the test I shipped one iteration earlier.** Injecting the removal of the recompute call left it green, because the reach-expansion matched *call sites* as well as declarations: `Post(() =>` parsed as a “declaration” of `Post` whose body was an unrelated lambda that happened to mention the method. Requiring an accessibility prefix fixed it, and the same injection now fails — as does deleting `FileTransferQueue`’s `RaiseLocalizedLabels()` fan-out, so the deliberate one-level indirection still works. **The remaining site was deliberately not patched**: `RemoteDesktopViewModel.StatusText` was filed as one bad line, but it is assigned in about twenty places and every one is a localized snapshot. Fixing the named line would have covered a twentieth of the defect while making the file look handled, and no condition distinguishes it — several messages set `HasStreamError`, so a naive refresh would overwrite whichever error is actually showing. That needs a key-based status model, filed as RemEx-qlfj with the note that `StatusText = errorText` must stay a verbatim passthrough because it carries host-authored text. 881 tests green, 0 warnings. (`SettingsViewModel.cs`, `LocalizedPropertyRefreshTests.cs`; RemEx-q3h0.)
- **The file manager now explains why uploading is unavailable on a read-only shared folder, instead of leaving the user to find out by failing.** `FileTransferViewModel.RemoteRootHint` existed, carried a `[NotifyPropertyChangedFor]` attribute, and resolved three localized strings — “Choose a shared folder to browse.”, “Uploads from this PC go into {0}.”, “{0} is read-only. Choose a writable shared folder to upload.” — and **nothing in any view bound it**, in any of the nine languages. **Which way to fix it was the whole question**, and the triage bead deliberately refused to assume: the same evidence supports deleting a dead property or adding a missing binding. Reading what the strings actually say settled it — the read-only line explains a disabled Upload button, which is otherwise discoverable only by trying it and failing, and that is squarely the plain-English hand-holding this project targets. So the property was the finished half and the binding was the missing half. It now renders under the shared-folder selector it describes, in `TextMutedBrush` like the rest of that view’s secondary text, so all four PC themes restyle it along with everything else rather than it needing a colour of its own. **Binding it as-is would have shipped a fresh instance of a defect this loop has now fixed three times**: the getter resolves its text from `LocalizationService` when it is *got*, so a language switch changes the value with nothing on the view-model having changed and therefore no notification — the stale-label bug of RemEx-6h3q, RemEx-4f30 and RemEx-si0h. The subscribe / re-raise / detach trio went in with the binding, the detach being non-optional because the localizer is a process-lifetime singleton that would otherwise pin the view-model forever. **That is four occurrences of one shape, so RemEx-6ddx is filed** to catch it by test rather than by a fifth fix — including the traps its predecessors hit, chiefly that methods reading the localizer are correct by construction and must not be flagged. Verified: the view sets `x:DataType`, so bindings are compile-checked — proved by injecting `RemoteRootHintTypo`, which failed the build with `AVLN2000: Unable to resolve property or method`. A clean `-t:Rebuild` is therefore real evidence the binding resolves. 878 tests green, 0 warnings. (`FileTransferViewModel.cs`, `FileTransferView.axaml`; RemEx-4p27.)
- **French UI text now spaces its punctuation one way instead of two, and the measurement reversed the intended fix.** The bead was filed as “50 plain spaces vs 2 non-breaking spaces before a colon” and proposed converting the 50. Counting every punctuation class first showed why that would have been wrong: `?` (26), `!` (7) and `;` (7) are **already 100% plain**, and there is a second rule the bead never mentioned — spacing inside guillemets, which is 17 plain vs 2 NBSP. Converting only the colons would have made that one rule uniform while leaving the others plain, **trading one inconsistency for a new one between punctuation classes**, at a cost of ~51 invisible-character edits. NBSP turned out to be the outlier file-wide, present in just **three values out of roughly eight hundred**. Normalizing those three to a plain space — 6 NBSP → 0 — makes the whole file follow a single rule for every class, in three edits, with a diff a reviewer can actually read. **What that trades away is stated rather than hidden**: strict French typography does want U+00A0 before `:` `;` `!` `?` and inside guillemets, and that remains available as a deliberate ~110-edit change — but it wants someone able to look at the rendered UI, and it must do all five classes at once or it lands straight back here. 878 tests green, 0 warnings, `check-localization.ps1` clean. (`Strings.fr.resx`; RemEx-gd5z.)
- **Twelve localization suppressions that no longer matched anything were removed, closing silent holes in the check.** `check-localization.ps1` had been ending every run with “12 baseline entr(y/ies) no longer occur — somebody fixed them”. **A stale suppression is not clutter, it is a hole**: the entry stops matching, stays in the file, and if that exact finding ever recurs it is suppressed on arrival and never reported. **The filed count of 4 was right when written and wrong by the time it was fixed** — this session’s own RemEx-9vcw retired the other eight, which is why every one of the twelve is an `android/behind-english` staleness finding for exactly the two keys it rewrote: `tutorial_page6_body` in eight locales and `faq_a8` in four. Rewriting a translation is precisely what stops it being behind English, so those suppressions had nothing left to suppress. **Verified purely subtractive**, which was the bead’s own condition and the thing worth checking: `git diff` on the file is 12 deletions and 0 insertions, 203 → 191 known findings, and a re-run afterwards reports no stale entries and no new problems — so nothing was quietly suppressed on the way through. An `-UpdateBaseline` run that ADDS lines would have meant real defects being hidden rather than fixed, which is the opposite of the point. (`scripts/localization-baseline.json`; RemEx-j8i1.)
- **French and Polish now describe an upload the same way everywhere in the file-transfer feature.** The same event was labelled two ways: French said “Envoi de %1$s…” in-app and “Téléversement de %1$s” in the notification, while Polish said “Przesyłanie %1$s…” in-app and “Wysyłanie %1$s” in the notification. **The bead’s counts were wrong for the third time, and the fresh measurement inverted its own recommendation.** It reported French as envoi 16 / téléversement 1 / chargement 9; word-boundary counting gives envoi 24 / téléversement 5 / chargement 2 — the “9” was a substring artefact, since `chargement` sits inside `téléchargement`, so that count was mostly **downloads**. Polish was filed as przesyłan 13 / wysyłan 5 and is actually 4 / 12. **Two matches were false positives and were deliberately left alone**, which is the part a bulk find-and-replace would have got wrong: French `Chargement` in `screen_splash_title` and `file_manager_requesting_volumes` is genuine French for *loading*, not uploading; and Polish `podczas przesyłania` in `rd_err_target_switch_unsupported` describes **streaming a display**, not sending a file — rewriting it would have been a mistranslation dressed as consistency. **The stem choice departs from the bead, on the bead’s own criterion.** It proposed téléversement because the button used it; but its central complaint is that “Téléversement de %1$s” and “Téléchargement de %1$s” differ mid-word and are hard to tell apart at a glance — so adopting téléversement would have maximised exactly the confusion being fixed. Envoi/Envoyer differs from the first letter, which is the same prefix-contrast the bead praises in Ukrainian, and it already carried the feature 24:5 including the failure counterpart of the very notification being changed. Polish took wysył- for the same two reasons, przesyłanie reading as “transferring” without saying which direction. `faq_a12` moved with the button, since it quotes the label. Real scope: **5 French values and 3 Polish**, not the ~26 the filed counts implied. Verified: `télévers` 0 remaining, `chargement` 2 (both the loading strings), `przesyłan` 1 (the streaming string); `assembleRelease` and `lintVitalRelease` clean; `check-localization.ps1` clean. 182 Android unit tests green — **re-run deliberately**, because the first run reported them up-to-date and a timestamp check showed the results predated the edit. (`values-fr/strings.xml`, `values-pl/strings.xml`; RemEx-bpqh.)
- **The tutorial and the Wake-on-LAN FAQ now name the home screen by asking it its name, instead of repeating a copy that goes stale.** Both said “the dashboard” in prose while `screen_dashboard_title` said something else — “Accueil RemEx”, “Pusat RemEx”, “RemEx - Strona główna”, “Base RemEx”, “RemEx होम बेस” — so a first-run user was pointed at a screen name the UI never displays, in five locales for the tutorial and in **all nine including English** for the FAQ. **This is the recurrence the filing bead reserved judgement for.** RemEx-7gwa fixed the English tutorial line by hand and explicitly declined the durable fix as disproportionate, noting “if this recurs a third time, that calculus changes” and warning that the coupling — retranslate the title, silently break the prose — is invisible. Since all eighteen strings had to be rewritten either way, the placeholder cost almost nothing on top and removes the coupling permanently: `tutorial_page6_body` and `faq_a8` now carry `%1$s`, and `TutorialPage.bodyArgRes` / `FaqItem.answerArgRes` pass `screen_dashboard_title` at render time. **The grammar is the substantive part of the translation work.** The substituted value is a proper noun in its nominative form, so the sentence around it must not demand a case ending — dropping `%1$s` into the old phrasing would have produced “Z poziomu RemEx - Strona główna”, which is not Polish. Polish and Ukrainian therefore inflect the word for *screen* (`ekranu`, `екрана`) and leave the name alone, and Turkish hangs its ablative suffix on `ekran` rather than on the title. **The change introduces a new failure mode, so it ships with a guard for it**: `stringResource(id)` with no argument returns the raw string, so a body declaring `%1$s` whose page forgets `bodyArgRes` renders a literal `%1$s` on screen — and nothing else reports it, because it compiles, lints clean, and `check-localization.ps1` is *satisfied* by the placeholder being present in all nine files. `ScreenNameSubstitutionTests` checks the pairing in both directions (a supplied argument for a placeholder-free string is discarded silently, losing the name) and pins the two converted strings so removing placeholder and argument together — which the pairing check would accept as consistent — still fails. Proved twice: deleting the page-6 wiring failed with the actionable message, and deleting `%1$s` from **only** English also failed, which is what confirms the new `inputs.file` declarations work — a values-only edit does not change the R class, so without them Gradle would have left the guard unrun and reported success (the RemEx-odkk trap). It then caught a botched restore of mine during that very exercise. 182 Android unit tests green, read from the JUnit XML rather than from `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`; `assembleRelease` clean. (`TutorialScreen.kt`, `FaqScreen.kt`, `build.gradle.kts`, 9 `strings.xml`, `ScreenNameSubstitutionTests.kt`; RemEx-9vcw.)
- **A screen-reader button that announced itself as a toggle can only do one thing, so it now says which.** The Remote Desktop toolbar’s fullscreen button was described as `cd_toggle_fullscreen` — “Toggle fullscreen”. **The code did read as a toggle**, `onSetFullscreen(!uiState.isFullscreen)`, which is why this needed tracing rather than reading: the whole top bar is rendered inside `topBar = { if (!uiState.isFullscreen) { … } }`, so at the only moment the button exists `!isFullscreen` is always `true` and it can only ever ENTER. Exiting belongs to a separate `cd_exit_fullscreen` control on the fullscreen overlay. Someone relying on the description was told the control does two things when it does one. Renamed to `cd_enter_fullscreen` in all nine locales and changed the call to `onSetFullscreen(true)` — **the point of passing a constant is that it makes the description true by construction** rather than true only while the enclosing guard happens to hold. **The translations had already drifted apart, which the rename resolves as a side effect**: five said “toggle” (en/hi/in/pt-BR/uk) and four were bare nouns (es “Pantalla Completa”, fr “Plein Écran”, pl “Tryb pełnoekranowy”, tr “Tam ekran”) — and Indonesian had left the English word “Toggle” sitting untranslated in “Toggle layar penuh”. Each new value mirrors **that locale’s own** `cd_exit_fullscreen` phrasing so the pair reads as a pair (`Salir de Pantalla Completa` → `Entrar en Pantalla Completa`; `Wyjdź z pełnego ekranu` → `Przejdź do trybu pełnoekranowego`), instead of each being translated afresh from English. Per the filing bead this is **not** a WCAG 2.5.3 Label-in-Name issue — the control is icon-only with no visible label — it is a plain wording-accuracy defect. Verified: `compileReleaseKotlin` and `lintVitalRelease` both re-ran rather than reporting `UP-TO-DATE`, no references to the old key remain (11 → 0), and `check-localization.ps1` confirms key parity across all nine files. (`RemoteDesktopScreen.kt`, 9 `strings.xml`; RemEx-kqh9.)

Not blocking, since the card is on the dashboard too, but strictly less help than everyone else gets on a feature people reach for when they cannot get to the machine. **The clause names the screen by the app’s own Spanish title** — `screen_remote_control_title` is “Control Remoto” — rather than by a fresh translation of the English words.
