That is the deliberate part: fr and pl both reference their own screen titles, and inventing a synonym here would have recreated RemEx-9vcw exactly, where a tutorial body and a screen title drifted apart per-locale once the title was translated. Verified beyond a green build: `mergeReleaseResources`, `processReleaseResources` and `lintVitalRelease` all re-ran rather than reporting `UP-TO-DATE`, so the string was genuinely reprocessed and lint-gated, and `check-localization.ps1` reports no new problems across all four axes on both platforms. That run also surfaced **4 baseline entries that no longer match anything** — filed as RemEx-j8i1, because a stale suppression silently re-hides its own finding if it ever recurs. (`values-es/strings.xml`; RemEx-rvj3.)
- **The canvas selection counter is now translatable at all, which it was not before — the layout made three earlier “fixes” impossible to get right.** `CanvasView.axaml` rendered the count and the word as two adjacent `TextBlock`s, hardcoding the order as *[number][adjective]*. That structure, not any one translation, is what made `Canvas_SelectedLabel` unfixable: a bare adjective must agree with a count that is 1 as often as it is 3, so French and Spanish were plural (wrong at one, after RemEx-zupl and RemEx-xn7l), pt-BR was singular (wrong above one, RemEx-z2t6), and **Polish needs three forms, so no word choice could have worked there at all**. Three beads had each been fixing one cell of a grid whose shape was the real defect. Replaced with a single `Canvas_SelectedCountFormat` carrying `{0}`, so every locale controls **word order as well as wording**: Polish and Ukrainian lead with an impersonal verb (`Zaznaczono: {0}`, `Вибрано: {0}`), Romance locales use a count-independent noun (`Sélection : {0}`), and the four locales that were already invariant keep their natural trailing form (`{0} selected`, `{0} dipilih`, `{0} seçili`, `{0} चयनित`). The key was renamed rather than redefined so a missed consumer fails loudly — `LocalizationService`’s indexer ends in `?? key`, so a stale reference renders the key name rather than a literal `{0}`. **The new guard matters more than the fix.** `NoStringFormatCall_TargetsAKeyWithoutAPlaceholder` reads only the neutral `Strings.resx`, so it proved English was formattable and said nothing about the other eight files — and a translator who drops `{0}` gets no exception, just a sentence with the number missing, visible only to speakers of that language. `EveryTranslationOfAFormatKey_KeepsThePlaceholders` now compares placeholder *indexes* across every locale for every format key, deliberately ignoring absent keys so it does not collide with the parity question. Proved by removing `{0}` from Ukrainian: it failed naming `uk/Canvas_SelectedCountFormat`, the expected set and the found set. **One review catch**: the French value first used a non-breaking space before its colon, which is correct French typography but would have been the third style in a file that uses a plain space 50 times to NBSP twice — matched to the house convention and the inconsistency filed as RemEx-gd5z rather than widened here. `SelectionSummary` re-raises on both the count and a language switch, and detaches in `Dispose`. RemEx-z2t6 is closed by this. 878 tests green, 0 warnings. (`CanvasDashboardViewModel.cs`, `CanvasView.axaml`, 9 resx, `LocalizationKeyReferenceTests.cs`; RemEx-si0h.)
- **A remote-desktop test that failed about one run in six now passes deterministically, and the product turned out to be right all along.** `DesktopStart_WhenWindowsDesktopBlocked_SendsActionableDesktopError` threw `ObjectDisposedException` on `TestWebSocket` — **from the test’s own send**, which is the detail that located it. `RemoteDesktopHandler` checks the Windows diagnostic report *before* entering its receive loop: on a blocked desktop it sends the error unsolicited and immediately closes the socket, never reading a request. The test sent a `desktop_start` anyway and raced that close. **The bead’s first diagnosis was wrong and is corrected on the record**: it blamed parallel test classes, but xUnit runs tests within a class sequentially and the flake reproduces running this class alone (2 failures in 6). It passed 8/8 as a *single* test only because that is the one case with nothing before it — the trigger was ordering, not concurrency. Deleting the send is the whole fix, and it makes the test assert the stronger contract: the host reports a blocked desktop **without being asked**, which is what a real client depends on. Renamed to `DesktopConnect_WhenWindowsDesktopBlocked_ReportsWithoutBeingAsked` so the name stops implying a request, with a comment recording why re-adding one reintroduces the flake. **A second defect surfaced from the injection test and was fixed too.** Flipping `CurrentDesktopReady` to true — to prove the assertion was load-bearing — did not fail the test, it *hung it*: the receive used `CancellationToken.None`, so a regression that stopped sending the error would block CI forever rather than report anything. Bounded at 10s, matching the five other timeouts already in the file; the same injection now fails in 12s with `OperationCanceledException`. Verified over 18 consecutive clean runs (10 class-only, 8 full-assembly) against a prior rate of roughly 1 in 6. No retries and no widened catch — both would have hidden the race. 877 tests green, 0 warnings. (`RemoteDesktopHandlerTests.cs`; RemEx-0v3w.)
- **The canvas selection counter now agrees with what it is counting in French.** `Strings.fr.resx` had `Canvas_SelectedLabel = « sélectionnés »` — masculine plural — rendered immediately after `SelectionCount` in the multi-select action bar, whose sibling buttons pin and remove the selected *cartes*. `carte` is feminine, so it read “3 sélectionnés”. **An invariant masculine is demonstrably not the house style in this file**, which is what settles it: `FileTransfer_SavePathUnavailable` already reads `La destination sélectionnée`, agreeing with a feminine referent, while the eight masculine ones agree with `dossier`, `fichier` and `élément`. All nine were checked rather than assumed, and all nine are correct. **The more useful finding is what this fix cannot reach.** `HasSelection` is `Count > 0`, so the bar is shown at a selection of one, and the label must therefore be right at N=1 *and* N>1 — which no single bare adjective can be. French is now correct above one and wrong at one; Spanish has had the identical problem since RemEx-xn7l; pt-BR is wrong in the opposite direction (RemEx-z2t6); and Polish needs three forms, so no word choice fixes it at all. That is a plural-handling problem rather than a vocabulary one, filed as RemEx-si0h with the three candidate strategies weighed, and z2t6 annotated as its pt-BR slice. Fixing it here by picking a different single word would have moved the error to a different count and looked like a fix. **A pre-existing flaky test was also caught and filed** (RemEx-0v3w): `DesktopStart_WhenWindowsDesktopBlocked_SendsActionableDesktopError` fails about one full-assembly run in six on a disposed `TestWebSocket`, yet passed 8/8 in isolation — an interaction with parallel tests, not this string. 877 tests green, 0 warnings. (`Strings.fr.resx`; RemEx-zupl.)
- **The transfer queue’s direction and state labels now follow a language switch, and the triage found the defect was a fifth the size the bead claimed.** RemEx-6h3q fixed two Remote Desktop labels and filed this bead listing five more view-models with 26 candidate members. **Almost none of them were the defect.** The scan counted expression-bodied members that read the localizer, but only members *bound in XAML* can go stale — a method that reads the localizer each time it is called, such as `DescribeFailure`, `LocalizeKillFailure` or `BuildEntries`, is already correct by construction. The switch-expression arms also inflated the count, each continuation line reading as its own member. Checking every candidate against the views left **two real ones**: `ModeLabel` and `StateLabel` on `FileTransferQueueItem`, both bound in `FileTransferView.axaml`. `RemoteRootHint` was flagged and is declared with a `[NotifyPropertyChangedFor]` attribute but bound nowhere, so it cannot render stale text — filed as RemEx-4p27 rather than “fixed” here, because a property nothing binds is a dead-code question and the evidence points equally at a missing binding. **The subscription belongs on the queue, not the item**, and that is the substantive design point: the labels are per-item, but `LocalizationService.Instance` is a process-lifetime singleton, so subscribing each item would create one subscription per transfer and pin every completed transfer alive for the life of the process. The queue subscribes once and fans the notification out to its items, and `FileTransferViewModel.Dispose` now disposes the queue — the detach is not optional for the same reason. **The regression test was wrong before it was right, in an instructive way.** It first asserted no notifications arrive after `Dispose`, and failed intermittently — not on the localizer at all, but because the queue pump runs on a background task and the item was still raising `State`/`Progress` when the assertion ran. Awaiting completion first makes both tests deterministic; they now pass five runs in a row. The guard was proved by removing the subscription, which fails exactly the language test. 877 tests green, 0 warnings. (`FileTransferQueue.cs`, `FileTransferViewModel.cs`, `FileTransferQueueTests.cs`; RemEx-4f30.)
- **Two Remote Desktop labels no longer keep their old-language text after a language switch.** `LocalizationService` raises `PropertyChanged` for its indexer on `SetCulture`, which refreshes bindings that read the indexer directly — but **not** properties that merely *call* it inside an expression body. Those have to be re-raised by name. Three sibling view-models already did that; `RemoteDesktopViewModel` did not, so its capability labels stayed in the previous language until something unrelated happened to re-raise them. **No cascade rescued it**, which is the part worth knowing: `ConnectionViewModel.OnLocaleChanged` reassigns its own `StatusText` and never touches `IsConnected`, `HostCapabilities` or `SupportsRemoteDesktop` — the only three triggers that would have re-raised these two. So the defect was invisible to the obvious "surely something refreshes it" reasoning. The unsubscribe in `Dispose` is not housekeeping: `LocalizationService.Instance` is a singleton, so a view-model that subscribes without detaching is pinned alive for the process lifetime. **A scan for the same shape found five more view-models with no locale subscription**, and it is filed as a triage rather than a fix list, because the count overstates it: the scan matches any expression-bodied member containing the indexer, which includes *methods* like the `DescribeFailure` added by RemEx-s4p4 — evaluated on every call and perfectly fine. Only bound properties go stale, so each site needs checking rather than patching. That is RemEx-4f30. 875 tests green, 0 warnings. (`RemoteDesktopViewModel.cs`; RemEx-6h3q.)
- **The shape reset buttons now say what they reset.** Every one announced the same "Reset to default shape", and the enclosing Row sets no `mergeDescendants`, so the heading naming the category was a separate node — leaving a screen-reader user with a column of identical controls and no way to tell which resets telemetry, which resets the launcher, and so on. Each now names its own row. **The bead says six buttons; there are fifteen, and that is partly my doing** — RemEx-mycn added eight per-category rows this session, so a defect that was awkward at six became unusable at fifteen. Worth stating plainly: the change that widened it landed a few iterations ago with no note of the interaction, because I was looking at the shape model rather than at the a11y tree the model happened to render into. The existing key was given a `%1` rather than a second key being added beside it. It has exactly one call site, so repurposing is safe, and the alternative would have orphaned a string in nine locales — the kind of leftover RemEx-b5kx spent an iteration removing 233 of. The nine translations were adapted from the existing wording rather than rewritten, so the phrasing each locale already used survives. Verified specifically by the localization check's **placeholder-parity axis**, which is the one that matters here: a locale that dropped or duplicated the new `%1` would render a literal token or throw `FormatException` in that language alone, and no other check would see it. `assembleRelease` succeeds, unit tests pass. (`PersonalizationScreen.kt`, 9 `strings.xml`; RemEx-pmo4.)
- **The Wake-on-LAN FAQ entry no longer implies that waking the PC restores remote access.** It described how to enable WoL and enter a MAC address, and stopped there — from which a reader reasonably concludes that waking the machine gets RemEx working again. It does not follow: WoL powers the machine on and it stops at the **sign-in screen**, where the per-user logon task (Windows) and the XDG autostart entry (Linux) do not run, so the agent never starts. Both entries now say so. **The FAQ was saying less than a confirmation dialog**, which is the wrong way round for a reference surface. RemEx-mkq1 had already put the consequence in front of users at the moment of danger — the shutdown dialogs read "Waking it with RemEx is not enough on its own — RemEx cannot reach it again until you sign in on the PC itself" — while the page a user consults *to understand the feature* omitted it entirely. Someone reading the FAQ before shutting down would have been misled by the more considered document. **Fixed on both platforms rather than only the one the bead names**, because the entry is item 8 of the canonical list RemEx-6kr1 just established, and correcting the PC alone would have re-opened the divergence that bead closed — with the added trap that the two would then disagree about a safety-relevant claim. 18 values across both platforms. 875 tests green, 0 warnings, `assembleRelease` succeeds, localization check clean. (`Faq_Q8_Answer` in 9 resx, `faq_a8` in 9 `strings.xml`; RemEx-0j6z.)
- **The remaining five connection status dots are now announced instead of skipped.** RemEx-x12a fixed the one dot with a *wrong* accessible name; these five had none at all, so a screen-reader user simply never learned whether the PC was connected — on the connection screen, the home screen, settings, the shell rail and the tray flyout. All six now share one localized two-state name. **Two judgement calls decided which element gets it, and both were nearly wrong.** `HomeView` stacks four ellipses at the same point — a radar-sweep ring, a 0.1-opacity halo and the 12px dot. Naming all of them would announce the same fact three times, which is precisely the decorative double-announce defect RemEx-xqli removed; only the 12px dot is named, the rest stay decoration. And four of the five sit beside a `TextBlock` bound to `StatusText`, which looked like grounds for leaving the dot silent to avoid duplication — **until you notice `StatusText` is the transient message property**, which is the whole reason x12a existed. It may read "Sleep command sent" rather than anything about connection state, so the neighbouring text is not a status label and the dot genuinely adds information. Each binding mirrors the path its own `Classes.connected` binding already uses, so the same edit works whether the data context is the shell view-model or the `ConnectionViewModel` itself — one file needed no prefix and four needed `Connection.`, which a uniform find-and-replace would have got wrong. No new strings: the keys and the notifying property already existed. 875 tests green, 0 warnings. (`ConnectionView.axaml`, `HomeView.axaml`, `SettingsView.axaml`, `ShellView.axaml`, `TrayFlyoutWindow.axaml`; RemEx-1j0r.)
- **The canvas connection indicator no longer announces command results as its own name.** The status dot took its accessible name from `StatusText`, a general-purpose transient message property — so a screen reader announced whatever that last held, a power-command result or a pairing note, as the **name of the connection indicator**. Both wrong and unstable: the same element answered to a different name minute to minute, which makes it unusable as a landmark. It now has a two-state name tracking `IsConnected` — the very thing the dot conveys visually through its `connected` class — so sighted and screen-reader users get the same fact from it instead of two different ones. The name says what the element **is** as well as its state ("Connection status: connected"), because a bare "Connected" gives a screen-reader user no idea what is connected. Two new keys, 18 values. **A related but distinct defect was found and filed rather than swept in**: the other five status dots — Connection, Home, Settings, Shell and the tray flyout — have no accessible name *at all*, so they are passed over silently. The property to bind already exists, making each a one-attribute change, but it needs per-site judgement rather than a sweep: `HomeView` stacks three ellipses at the same spot, and naming all three would announce the same fact three times, which is the decorative double-announce defect RemEx-xqli existed to remove. That is RemEx-1j0r. 875 tests green, 0 warnings, localization check clean. (`ConnectionViewModel.cs`, `CanvasView.axaml`, 9 resx; RemEx-x12a.)
- **The transfer queue panel stopped showing developer English to every user.** `RunItemAsync` assigned `ex.Message` straight to the item the panel renders, which quietly made **every exception thrown anywhere beneath a transfer** user-facing text — including "Download failed: SHA-256 integrity check failed." and the idle watchdog's timeout, in all nine languages. **Dispatch is by TYPE, never by message text**, and that is the load-bearing choice: matching on content would work today and silently revert to raw English the first time a message was reworded. A host refusal (`FileTransferHostException`) is shown **verbatim**, because it is the one message written for a user by the phone; the two failures the PC detects itself get localized sentences; anything else falls back to a generic one with the detail left to the log. The SHA-256 case needed a type of its own, `FileTransferIntegrityException`, for exactly that reason — it had to be distinguishable without inspecting its wording. **A test was asserting the bug.** `Work_ThatThrows_MarksItemFailedWithMessage` expected the raw text "nope" to reach `ErrorMessage`, which is precisely the defect. It now asserts the opposite contract, and two more tests cover the dispatch it never had: that a host refusal survives verbatim, and that the integrity failure gets its own sentence rather than the generic one. Each also asserts the result is not the resource key name, since `LocalizationService`'s `?? key` fallback would otherwise let a missing entry pass as a string. 3 new keys, 27 values. 875 tests green, 0 warnings, localization check clean. (`FileTransferIntegrityException.cs`, `FileTransferClient.cs`, `FileTransferQueue.cs`, `FileTransferQueueTests.cs`, 9 resx; RemEx-s4p4.)
- **Dashboard cards no longer claim to be collecting data when nothing is connected.** With no PC connected every Home Base sensor card sat at `--` under a perpetual "Collecting data…" shimmer — an assertion that work was in progress when the app was not even talking to anything. The App Launcher and Task Manager already drew this distinction; the dashboard did not. The placeholder now reads the same connection state the rest of the app uses and says "Not connected" instead. **The spinner is dropped rather than relabelled, and that is the substance of the fix.** A motion indicator *is* the claim of progress — leaving it turning under the words "Not connected" would keep asserting exactly what the text had just denied, which is a worse kind of wrong than the original, because it contradicts itself. "Collecting data…" and its spinner survive untouched for the genuinely-connected warmup, where they are accurate. The change sits in one place: `CollectingData` is the single placeholder behind `ChartOrCollecting`, so every card in the ten-view catalog picks it up without threading connection state through any of them. One new string across nine locales. `assembleRelease` succeeds, unit tests pass, localization check clean. (`TelemetryViews.kt`, 9 `strings.xml`; RemEx-5mkc.)
- **Three Android text-entry surfaces no longer let the keyboard cover the field you are typing into.** The app runs edge-to-edge, which means nothing is inset automatically, and these three never applied IME insets: the pairing PIN dialog, the six connection fields, and the shutdown/restart delay field. **The pairing screen was the worst of them** — a fixed centred column with no scrolling at all, so at large font scale or in landscape the keyboard could cover both Submit and Cancel with no way to reach either. It now scrolls as well as insetting, because on a short screen inset alone is not enough. **Modifier order carries the fix, and getting it backwards looks almost identical in code.** `imePadding()` is applied *before* `verticalScroll()` so the scroll **viewport** shrinks when the keyboard opens, letting content move above it. After the scroll, it would pad the scrollable content instead and leave the viewport itself sitting behind the keyboard — the fields would still be unreachable, and the diff would look like the bug had been fixed. Each site records that reasoning inline. The remote-control grid keeps its existing floating-toolbar inset and gains `imePadding` alongside it; the delay field sits mid-grid, so the toolbar inset alone never helped it. The bead's line numbers had drifted on all three, so each container was re-located by content. Verified by build and unit tests; the behaviour itself needs a device at fontScale 2.0 and in landscape, which is where the pairing case actually bites. `assembleRelease` succeeds. (`PairingScreen.kt`, `ConnectionScreen.kt`, `RemoteControlScreen.kt`; RemEx-a9ci.)
- **The pairing dialog, the keyboard-shortcut list and several status messages are no longer English in the locales that had missed them — 56 values.** These sit on the paths where a stuck user is most likely to be reading carefully: the six-digit PIN dialog and its hint, the tooltip explaining what that PIN is for, the shortcut reference in About, and the status lines for connecting and for remote-desktop availability. **Two values were deliberately left identical to English, and the reasoning is the useful part.** `Status_ZoomFormat` ("Zoom: {0:F1}×") and `Status_PongFormat` ("Pong! {0:F1} ms") are byte-identical to English in several Latin-script locales — but checking what the *already-translated* locales did settles it: French and Polish also keep "Zoom" and "Pong", while Ukrainian and Hindi render them in their own scripts. So identical-to-English is correct behaviour for a Latin-script loanword here, not a gap. `Status_FoundHostFormat` failed that same test in the other direction — every other locale translates "Found PC" — so it was fixed. **Comparing against sibling locales, rather than against English alone, is what separates the two cases**, and a length threshold alone would have got both wrong. The applier again refuses to touch any value that differs from the English source, so it cannot overwrite existing work; 14 values were skipped on that basis. The localization baseline fell 218 → 203. 873 tests green, 0 warnings. (5 locale resx files; RemEx-lo5w.)
- **The onboarding tutorial and the feature glossary are no longer in English for non-English users — 125 values translated across eight languages.** This was the largest residual-English surface left on the PC side, and the worst-placed: the glossary is what explains *what each feature is*, and the tutorial is the first thing the app shows, so a Spanish, Hindi, Portuguese, Turkish or Ukrainian user met RemEx in English at precisely the moment they were trying to learn it. Sixteen glossary entries (title and body for App Launcher, Command Palette, Customization, File Transfer, Quick Settings, Remote Desktop, Sensor Canvas and Task Manager), the QR-pairing page, the HWInfo, launcher and IP-address step lists, and the "don't show again" control. **The bead's inventory needed re-deriving, as usual, and this time in the safer direction:** it listed `Tutorial_P0_Body`, `P2_Steps`, `P3_Steps` and `P9_Steps` among the untranslated, but those are either already translated or were purged as orphans in RemEx-b5kx — measuring found 23 keys still identical to English, not the 28 claimed. **The applier compares against the English source and skips anything that differs**, so it physically cannot overwrite existing translation work; one value was left alone on exactly that basis. Technical tokens stay untranslated where a user must type or recognise them verbatim — `hwinfo.com`, the HWInfo menu path, `ipconfig`, `ip addr`, `hostname -I`, `Ctrl+Shift+P`, `Wake-on-LAN` — while the surrounding instructions and the label `IPv4 Address` are localized, since that one is read rather than typed. Verified from both ends: zero `Tutorial_*` values now match the English byte-for-byte, and the localization baseline fell 270 → 218 as 52 staleness findings resolved themselves. 873 tests green, 0 warnings. (8 locale resx files; RemEx-ew2t.)
- **Four background operations that could fail silently now report when they do.** `_ = SomethingAsync()` is the normal way to start work you cannot await — from a timer callback, a `ct.Register` handler, a UI post — and it also discards the exception, so the task faults, nothing observes it, and **the operation simply did not happen** with no trace anywhere. All three of the cases here lose real state that way: an unsent cancel leaves the peer streaming a transfer the user stopped; an unsent layout update loses a dashboard edit; a failed debounce flush loses the saved layout outright. They now route through a `FireAndForget` helper that observes the fault and reports it. **Cancellation is deliberately not reported**, and that distinction is what makes the helper usable: a cancelled task is cancelled, not faulted, so `OnlyOnFaulted` already excludes it — which matters because these run on paths that are cancelled routinely, and a transfer the user aborted must not log an error. The helper also flattens the exception, so an `AggregateException` from a nested task does not hide the real cause. The fourth item was `ShowFileConsentDialogAsync`, a `private async void` invoked from `Dispatcher.UIThread.Post` — an exception escaping an `async void` is re-raised on the synchronization context and takes the process down rather than being observable, so it is now `async Task` with the post site observing it. **One of the bead's five sites no longer existed**: the `_ = SaveInternalAsync` fire-and-forget it names was the Android-only immediate-save path removed in RemEx-eca6, which is why each site was re-located by content rather than by line. The helper falls back to `Debug.WriteLine` where no `ILogger` is available, which is a floor rather than a choice — it compiles out of Release — and giving those classes real logging remains RemEx-t4tc's job. No `ConfigureAwait(false)` anywhere, per the repo's async guidelines. 873 tests green, 0 warnings. (`FireAndForgetExtensions.cs`, `FileTransferClient.cs`, `CanvasDashboardViewModel.cs`, `DashboardLayoutService.cs`, `App.axaml.cs`; RemEx-ajk3.)
- **Two dialogs stopped clipping their own text in the longer languages, and the settings overlay now actually leaves the screen.** `PairingDialog` was pinned at 400×250 and `FileConsentDialog` at 440×300, both `CanResize="False"`, with wrapping instruction, error and detail text inside. A fixed height plus wrapping text is a bet that no translation is longer than the English — and French, Brazilian Portuguese and Ukrainian routinely run 20–30% longer, so the last line simply vanished below the frame with no scrollbar and no way to resize. Both now use `SizeToContent="Height"` with a `MaxHeight` guard, matching what `ConfirmationDialog`, `RestorePromptWindow` and `SetAlertDialog` already do — the pattern existed, these two just predated it. **The settings overlay was a quieter version of the same class of bug.** It hides by translating 420px, but the panel is `Width="440"` with `MaxWidth="460"`, so up to 40px of it never left the viewport. It looked correct only because `Opacity` is 0 — the element was still laid out, still composited, and still hit-testable in that strip. Aligning the transform to 460px makes the hiding real rather than cosmetic, which is the difference between an invisible panel and an absent one. 873 tests green, 0 warnings, verified with `-t:Rebuild` since all three are XAML. (`PairingDialog.axaml`, `FileConsentDialog.axaml`, `ShellView.axaml`; RemEx-vm0j.)
- **The tray flyout no longer looks broken when nothing is pinned, and the Remote Desktop idle screen stopped showing a giant letter D.** The flyout's sensor list had no empty state at all, so with nothing pinned it rendered blank — which reads as a failure rather than as "you have not set this up yet". **It reuses HomeView's existing wording rather than inventing a fourth variant**, because HomeView already has an empty state for exactly this data: no new strings, no new translation, and the two surfaces cannot drift apart later. Trimmed to the hint alone — the flyout is a small transient popup, not a place for a heading and a call-to-action button. One structural detail worth noting: a `ScrollViewer` takes a single child, so the empty state and the list share a `Panel`; adding it as a sibling compiles in some frameworks and simply fails here, which the rebuild caught. The Remote Desktop placeholder was `Text="D"` at 64pt — a leftover from an icon-font placeholder that started rendering as the bare letter once the app stopped using that font. It is now the real `IconDesktopPC` geometry, which also means it takes the theme accent instead of depending on a glyph existing. **The bead's other two items were split to RemEx-n69m** rather than rushed, because they are a different kind of work: the file-manager and launcher-search empty states are three-term compound conditions across two collections, which XAML cannot express inline, and a `Count` binding silently keeps a stale value if the view-model replaces a collection instead of mutating it — so the state would appear at the wrong moment with nothing failing. That needs view-model properties with real change notification, plus three new strings across nine locales. 873 tests green, 0 warnings, verified with `-t:Rebuild` since both changes are XAML. (`TrayFlyoutWindow.axaml`, `RemoteDesktopView.axaml`; RemEx-po2x, partial.)
- **Two theme-blind colours in the personalization panel now follow the active theme.** The accent-picker hover ring was literal `White`, which is invisible against SolarFlare's near-white surface — so on that theme hovering a colour swatch gave **no feedback at all**, not merely weak feedback. And the font-warning banner used an amber pair (`#22F59E0B` / `#55F59E0B`) mixed for a dark glass background, which washes out on the same theme. Both now resolve from keys verified present in all four theme files: `TextPrimaryBrush` for the ring, and `SystemWarningBackgroundBrush` / `SystemWarningBrush` for the banner. Being XAML rather than C#, these use `DynamicResource`, so live theme switching works natively — none of the per-call lookup machinery the converters in RemEx-8tt2 and RemEx-xw1u needed. **The bead's line numbers were stale and are corrected in its notes:** the banner is at 254, not the 228 claimed, and the `SettingsView:208` cited as the pattern to copy is now an unrelated row — the real pattern is at `RemoteView.axaml:44`. That is the third bead this session whose own coordinates had drifted. RemEx-fy0a stays open: five site groups remain, and everything accent-coloured is still blocked on an accent ramp being designed across all four themes, since no `AccentBrush` key exists anywhere. 873 tests green, 0 warnings, verified with `-t:Rebuild` because a plain build skips Avalonia's XAML compilation entirely. (`PersonalizationPanelView.axaml`; RemEx-fy0a, partial.)
- **Sensor readings now take their warning and danger colours from the active theme, and the rest of the theme-bypass work turned out to be blocked on a key that does not exist.** `SensorColorConverter` held three fixed colours, so a temperature that had crossed a threshold was shown in the same red or amber whatever it sat on — the same failure that made the diagnostic log unreadable on SolarFlare's near-white surface (RemEx-8tt2). It now maps onto the theme's own warning and error brushes, keeping the meaning (amber is warm, red is too hot) while letting each theme choose a contrast that works against its own background, resolved per call so a runtime theme switch is picked up and degrading to the previous literal rather than to null if a key were ever missing. **The more useful outcome was discovering why the remaining sites are not the same job.** The bead listed four files as though they were one mechanical sweep. Two were: converters mapping onto `TextPrimaryBrush`, `SystemWarningBrush` and `SystemErrorBrush`, which all four themes define. The other two are not, and the reason is concrete rather than a matter of effort — **there is no accent brush key in any of the four themes.** `AccentBrush`, `AccentColor` and `SurfaceBrush` return zero matches in all four theme files; only the text ramp, the two system severity brushes and `GlassBaseDark` exist everywhere. So the minimap, the sparkline and the card accent fallbacks cannot be pointed at anything: they need an accent ramp designed and added to four theme files with four *considered* values, because copying one value into four themes is the same bug in a new place. Two further constraints are recorded with them: several of those colours carry an alpha applied at construction, so a key returning an `IBrush` is not a drop-in, and the minimap and sparkline are drawing controls, which must invalidate and redraw on a theme change — something a converter never had to solve. That is RemEx-0k4x. 873 tests green, 0 warnings. (`SensorColorConverter.cs`; RemEx-xw1u.)
- **The diagnostic log list is readable on SolarFlare again — its severity colours were hardcoded, and the comment defending them was wrong.** Five fixed colours were justified in the source by the claim that "the log panel always sits on a dark glass background". It does not: on SolarFlare `GlassBaseDark` is `#F8FAFC`, near-white, so the informational level's `#D1D5DB` rendered light grey on white and the list was barely legible on that theme. **The severity semantics that comment was really protecting are kept** — warnings stay the theme's warning colour and errors its error colour, so amber-means-warning and red-means-error still read identically everywhere; what changes is that each theme now supplies its own version at a contrast that works against its own background. The three non-alerting levels map onto the text ramp (muted, secondary, primary), which is the hierarchy the original greys were imitating. All four themes were checked to define all five keys before relying on them. Two implementation details carry the weight. The lookup happens **per call** rather than in a static field, and that is the live-theme-switch story the bead asked for: a brush captured once at class-initialisation time would freeze whichever theme happened to load first. And a missing key degrades to a named fallback rather than to null, because a converter returning null leaves the text invisible — an unreadable log is worse than an off-palette one — with the previous literals kept as those fallbacks so the degraded path is a known-legible ramp rather than a guess. The four remaining static-brush sites named in the bead (minimap, sparkline, sensor and card-customization fallbacks) are split into RemEx-xw1u with the pattern and the API recorded, including that `TryFindResource` does not exist on `Application` in this Avalonia version and `TryGetResource` with an explicit `ThemeVariant` is the one that compiles — and the caveat that the two drawing controls also need a redraw on theme change, which a converter does not. 873 tests green, 0 warnings. (`LogLevelToBrushConverter.cs`; RemEx-8tt2.)
- **Seven decorative icons stopped speaking over the text beside them, and the "Icon" content descriptions went with them.** TalkBack announced both the icon and its adjacent label — "Play, Start streaming" — and the descriptions themselves contained the word *Icon*, which the screen reader duplicates because it already announces the role: `cd_section_icon` was spoken as "Section Icon, image". The bead framed these as two problems and proposed deciding new wording for seven keys across nine locales each. **Checking each site showed there was nothing to word.** Every one of the seven is an icon sitting beside a `Text` in the same container that already carries the meaning — a section header, a category row, an error row, three empty-state illustrations, and a labelled button — which makes them decorative by Compose's own convention. The right description is not a better sentence; it is `null`. So all seven are nulled, each with the reason inline so a future contributor does not helpfully "fix" them back, and the seven keys, now referenced nowhere, were deleted from all nine locales with their 63 values recorded first. **One of the seven nearly escaped, for a reason this repo has already been bitten by:** ktfmt had wrapped it as `R.string` / newline / `.cd_play_icon`, so a `R\.string\.cd_\w+_icon` pattern did not match it — the same line-wrapping trap that once made a live key look dead and caused a wrong deletion. It was found by re-sweeping with a whitespace-tolerant pattern, which is the only kind that is trustworthy here, and that sweep is what confirmed all seven keys were safe to delete. `assembleRelease` succeeds, unit tests pass, localization check clean. (`RemoteDesktopScreen.kt`, `PersonalizationScreen.kt`, `RemoteControlScreen.kt`, `PairingScreen.kt`, `QrScannerScreen.kt`, `AppLauncherScreen.kt`, 9 `strings.xml`; RemEx-xqli.)
- **The remote-control screen stopped putting raw exception text on screen — and a cross-feature key borrow that had been blocking a cleanup finally disappeared.** Two catch blocks on the screen that shuts the PC down showed `e.message` verbatim, in all nine languages, with no next step. They now log the exception and show a sentence naming what failed and what to do. **The interesting part is what was NOT changed:** `rc_failed_format` keeps its `%1$s`, because its other two uses interpolate the *host's* own reply rather than an exception — the same distinction RemEx-mznc drew on the PC side, where a family of messages may only be collapsed when every member truly shares a cause. Only the one site that fed it an exception moved to the placeholder-free key. **The second half was a key borrow that no prefix search would catch:** the remote-control screen used `file_transfer_unknown_error` as its null fallback, which is why RemEx-ixsk could not retire that key even after removing both of its file-transfer uses — a key named for one feature was load-bearing in another. Dropping the placeholder removed the need for any fallback at all, so the borrow is gone and the key, verified unreferenced across every file type including the ktfmt-wrapped qualified form, was deleted from all nine locales with its values recorded first. That also removes a trap for the orphan purge (RemEx-3jne): `file_transfer_unknown_error` looked like file transfer's and was not. Noted out of scope, pre-existing and unchanged: both catches are `catch (e: Exception)`, which also swallows `CancellationException`. `assembleRelease` succeeds; localization check clean. (`RemoteControlViewModel.kt`, 9 `strings.xml`; RemEx-poj6.)
- **A file operation that times out on the phone no longer borrows another operation's words — and one case was literally showing the wrong verb.** `runManage` is shared by delete, rename, mkdir, copy and move, and its timeout branch returned the DELETE-specific localized string for all five. The visible result was worse than "errors are vague": creating a folder that timed out read **"New folder failed: Delete timed out."** on screen. A rename that timed out was flattened into the same sentence as a rename the host had actively refused, copy and move lost the reason entirely into a tally, and delete was correct only by accident, because the hardcoded string happened to be its own. The cause was the return type: a `String?` cannot say *which way* something failed, so the one function serving five operations had to guess, and guessed delete. It now returns a sealed `ManageOutcome` — `Ok`, `TimedOut`, or `HostRefused` carrying the host's own wording — and the timeout case deliberately carries **no** message at all, because naming the operation is the caller's job and the absence of one is what stops the leak recurring. Each caller picks its own copy, which finally wires up `file_transfer_rename_timeout`: a string that had been written, translated into all nine languages, and referenced nowhere. That stranded key is what RemEx-hgdb refused to delete as dead weight, on the grounds that an unreferenced key can be the fingerprint of a missing branch rather than dead code — this is that branch. One new string was needed, for mkdir, and mkdir alone keeps interpolating the host's own refusal text, because `FileHostHandler` answers it with copy a user can act on and replacing that with something generic would lose the most useful text in the flow. Review caught a debuggability regression in the fix itself: `TimedOut` was a plain `object`, so the log line for the one failure that leaves *no* other trace printed a JVM identity hash instead of its name — `data object` now. `assembleRelease` succeeds; localization check clean. (`FileTransferViewModel.kt`, 9 `strings.xml`; RemEx-201d.)
- **The Linux process listing stopped reading every process's `/proc/<pid>/stat` twice per poll — and the fix removes a repeat of an older bug, not just the cost.** RemEx-on4n added a start time to each row by calling `Process.GetProcessById(pid)` per process, which internally re-reads the very file the listing loop had already read and parsed, and allocates a `Process` object per row on top. The `starttime` field was sitting in the parsed array the whole time. It is now computed there: field 22 of stat, which after the existing split lands at index 19, in clock ticks since boot, plus `btime` from `/proc/stat` read once per poll rather than once per process. **The reason this mattered more than performance is the shape of it.** The kill-time check and the listing were deriving the same fact two different ways — exactly the arrangement that produced this class's last real defect, where a process's name came from `comm` (truncated by the kernel at 15 characters) in one path and `Process.ProcessName` (untruncated) in the other, refusing every kill of a long-named process until review caught it. Both paths now compute from the same fields, so they agree by construction rather than by a tolerance being generous enough to hide the gap. **Verified before the code was written, not after:** a probe run against every process on a live Linux machine put this formula within **508 ms** of what `Process.StartTime` itself reports — the residual being `btime`'s whole-second granularity, comfortably inside the guard's two-second tolerance. That measurement is also the answer to why the tolerance exists at all. `USER_HZ` is a named constant with the assumption stated rather than a bare `100`; reading it properly needs `sysconf(_SC_CLK_TCK)` through a P/Invoke, and it is fixed at 100 for userspace regardless of the kernel's internal `CONFIG_HZ`. Compiled and verified under Linux as well as Windows, per the cross-platform parity rule. 873 tests green, 0 warnings. (`LinuxProcessMonitorService.cs`; RemEx-nchu.)
- **"End process" failure reasons are now shown in the user's language on both clients instead of the host's English.** Every reason a kill can fail — no permission, the program is already gone, the process ID now belongs to something else, or an unspecified failure — was authored in English on the PC host and shown verbatim on both the PC and the phone, at exactly the moment something had gone wrong. The host cannot fix that itself: it does not know which language the window is running in, and the phone does not share the PC's `.resx` files at all. So the host now sends a stable code and each client owns the wording, using the **existing** `code␟arg␟englishFallback` convention that remote-desktop errors have used since RemEx-728 rather than inventing a second one — which also means nothing was added to the wire envelope and no `protocolVersion` bump was involved. Four codes, four keys per platform, translated into all nine languages on each side; the identity-mismatch one carries the name that now owns the PID so the message can say what it is rather than just that something changed. "Could not be found" and "has already exited" deliberately share one code, because the user's next step is identical — refresh the stale list — and splitting them would buy a distinction nobody can act on. **The compatibility direction that matters most is tested rather than assumed:** untagged text from an older host is passed through unchanged and unknown codes fall back to the host's English, so a client always shows the most specific thing it can understand — which is also why the host must keep sending a complete English sentence rather than a stub, and why a test says so. **One skew is knowingly accepted and worth stating plainly:** an un-updated *client* talking to an updated host will show the raw tagged string, code prefix included, where it used to show a plain English sentence. That is the same tradeoff RemEx-728 already shipped for remote desktop, so it is a known property of this convention rather than a new one, but it is real and it resolves as soon as the client updates. The Android side gained the same coverage guard the pairing codes have: a test that parses `ProcessKillErrorCodes.cs` and fails if any declared code has no Kotlin branch, because a missing branch degrades *silently* — the phone falls through to English, which reads plausibly and produces no crash, no log and no build error. It was proved by injecting an unmapped code, and proved to actually run by checking it failed **without** `--rerun-tasks`, which is what the declared Gradle input buys; the JUnit XML confirms one test executed and zero skipped, since the test's `assumeTrue` guards could otherwise hide a vacuous pass. The PC has the equivalent mapping tests but not the equivalent exhaustiveness parse, which review flagged; its `switch` default already falls back to English rather than to something worse, and closing the asymmetry is filed as a follow-up. 860 tests green, 0 warnings, `assembleRelease` succeeds, localization check clean. (`ProcessKillErrorCodes.cs`, both process monitors, `TaskManagerViewModel.cs`/`.kt`, 9 resx, 9 `strings.xml`; RemEx-r37a.)
- **A read-only shared folder on the phone no longer disables upload, new-folder, paste, rename and delete without saying why.** The read-only fact was already known, already correct, and already acted on — `AndroidFileTransferHost` sets it from the real `DocumentFile.canWrite()`, and `FileTransferScreen` computes `canWrite` and passes it down to gate the controls. It just never reached the user. The flag appeared at exactly three lines and labelled nothing, so selecting a read-only folder greyed out five actions with no stated reason, which is indistinguishable from the app being broken. The string that explains it, `file_transfer_read_only_root`, had been sitting translated in all nine locales and referenced nowhere — which is how RemEx-hgdb found this, by refusing to delete it as dead weight. It now shows in two places: the header subtitle, next to the folder it applies to, so the reason is on screen beside the greyed buttons; and on the folder's own chip, whose icon becomes a padlock, so the state is visible *before* selecting rather than only after. **The condition is deliberately not the screen's `canWrite` flag**, and that distinction is the whole reason the rule became a tested function rather than a string template: `canWrite` is false in two different situations — a read-only root is selected, and *nothing* is selected at all — so driving the marker from it would label the empty "/" placeholder "Read-only", which is untrue of anything and shows before the user has picked a folder. `buildLocationSubtitle` takes a nullable `isWritable` where null means no selection, and three JVM tests pin all three states; they were proved by relaxing `== false` to `!= true`, which failed exactly the no-selection case and nothing else. **The accessibility detail is the part worth recording, because the obvious implementation is wrong.** Marking the chip with `stateDescription` reads naturally and would have been a regression: `FilterChip` is a *selectable* component, so Compose already publishes a selected/not-selected state for it, and `stateDescription` **replaces** that rather than adding to it — a read-only chip would have announced "Read-only" and silently stopped telling a screen-reader user which folder was active, trading one gap for another. The fact rides on the padlock icon's `contentDescription` instead, which keeps both. The writable folder icon stays undescribed because there it genuinely is decorative — the chip's label already names the folder. No new strings and no translation work: all nine locales already had the value. `assembleRelease` succeeds. (`FileManagerQuickAccess.kt`, `FileTransferScreen.kt`, `FileManagerLogic.kt`, `FileManagerLogicTest.kt`; RemEx-dc57.)
- **The file manager's last seven error messages stopped showing developer text — without throwing away the best copy in the family.** The bead described seven sites putting "a raw exception" in front of the user, but the code said something more interesting: fifteen of the sixteen throws in `FileTransferClient` are `IOException($"Add root failed: {hostErrorMessage}")`, so what reached the user was **the phone's own sentence wearing a developer prefix**. Some of those sentences are the most useful text in the whole feature — `FileHostHandler.kt` answers a request to pin a folder with "Adding a shared folder must be done on the phone", which tells the user exactly what to do next and which no generic message can replace. That is why this family could not be collapsed the way RemEx-p9fn collapsed browse and search, and why the caveat carried forward from RemEx-udq9 mattered: a family of messages may only be collapsed when every member truly shares a cause. **The missing capability was that the view-model could not tell the two apart.** A host refusal, a `TimeoutException` from the control-request timeout, a dropped socket and a cancellation all arrived as the same `Exception`, so the only options were to show all of them or none — and both are wrong. A new `FileTransferHostException` now carries the promise that its message is the host's own user-grade text with no prefix, and each of the seven sites catches it ahead of the general clause: host replies are shown verbatim, everything else logs the exception and shows localized copy. The seven keys lost their `{0}` and were reworded with a next step, in all 9 languages, reusing each locale's already-established rendering of "Check the connected device is still paired, then try again." rather than inventing new phrasing. Two details are worth recording. **The catch ordering needs no test** — because the type derives from `IOException`, putting the general clause first is compiler error CS0160, so a clean build proves it at all seven sites. And the blank-reply guard is not hypothetical: `AddRemoteRootAsync` and `RemoveRemoteRootAsync` test the host reply with `ErrorMessage is string err`, a pattern that **matches the empty string**, and unlike the listing, metadata and volumes paths neither adds a whitespace guard — so the two sites whose replies are most worth showing were also the two that could blank the status line entirely. `ForHostError` handles that centrally and is covered by five tests, proved by breaking the guard rather than by watching them pass. Reviewed by Opus (PASS), which caught a real self-inflicted defect the build could not: the script that rewrote the values wrote UTF-8 **with** BOM, silently adding one to ten files that had none. 832 tests green, 0 warnings. (`FileTransferHostException.cs`, `FileTransferClient.cs`, `FileTransferViewModel.cs`, 9 resx files; RemEx-mznc.)
- **Typing "wake" in the command palette found nothing, even though the Remote screen is where waking lives.** Removing the broken Wake-on-LAN entry (RemEx-paa7) was right — it had never once worked — but the palette searches labels and categories only, so the term went from matching a dead entry to matching nothing at all. Discoverability got worse even as correctness improved. Palette entries can now carry **search aliases**: extra localized terms they match on but never display. The Remote Control entry carries the locale's own Wake-on-LAN wording, so "wake", "despertar", "réveil" or "пробудження" all land the user on the screen that actually wakes a PC — with the configured MAC, validation, and the local-send path that works precisely when the PC is off and there is no connection to send *through*. **No new translation work**: the alias reuses the nine values verbatim from the key `paa7` removed, which is why those were recorded on the bead rather than left to git archaeology. This also settles the open question that bead left: **Wake-on-LAN is not returning to the palette as an action.** The working command needs state that lives on `RemoteViewModel`, which the shell builds lazily on first navigation while the palette captures its commands once at construction — and even wired, it would report into a status line only the Remote screen renders, i.e. silent from the palette, which is exactly the defect RemEx-diyv fixed everywhere else. The match rule moved from the view model's filter loop onto `CommandPaletteEntry.Matches(query)` so it can be tested without standing up a `ShellViewModel`; six tests cover it, including a **negative control** — an entry with no alias does *not* match "wake" — so the positive case proves the alias is doing the work rather than passing vacuously, plus a non-ASCII case, because an English-only alias would be half a fix in an app shipping nine languages. 817 tests green, 0 warnings. (`CommandPaletteEntry.cs`, `CommandPaletteViewModel.cs`, 9 resx files, `CommandPaletteEntryTests.cs`; RemEx-efse.)
- **The solution now builds with zero warnings.** The last four were `xUnit1031` in `FileConsentDialogViewModelTests`, which read `.Result` off the decision task instead of awaiting it — the deadlock-prone pattern xUnit flags. They were left behind deliberately by RemEx-5c37 to keep that diff scoped to production code, and have appeared in every build since. The four tests are now `async Task` and `await`. Each also gained an explicit assertion that the task has *already* completed before it is awaited, which preserves what the blocking form was implicitly testing — these commands resolve the decision **synchronously**, and a plain `await` would hang until xUnit's timeout rather than fail with a useful message if that ever regressed. So the tests are slightly stronger than before, not merely quieter. `dotnet build Remex.sln -t:Rebuild` now reports 0 warnings and 0 errors, which is the bead's stated acceptance; 811 tests green. (`FileConsentDialogViewModelTests.cs`; RemEx-46q1.)
- **A file upload or download whose peer died hung the transfer forever, and any fixed timeout would have been worse than the bug.** These waits last as long as the file is big, so a wall-clock deadline either aborts a large healthy transfer or never fires — and aborting also reaps the waiter, so the peer's eventual success reply is dropped and the user is told the transfer failed *while the file appears anyway*. Both now use an **idle** watchdog instead: the deadline is recomputed from the last sign of life and slides forward while data moves, so a 40 GB transfer that is still going never trips it and a peer that dies trips it in two minutes. Downloads count arriving chunks; uploads count the progress messages the host emits every ten chunks while receiving, plus each chunk the PC itself sends — which matters because a file under 640 KiB draws no peer progress at all. The 120-second budget was checked against the real constants rather than picked: one progress message per 640 KiB means a healthy transfer only goes silent that long below about 5 KiB/s, and the Android consent prompt — the most plausible legitimate pause — auto-denies at 60 seconds, half the budget. **Two of the bead's premises turned out to be stale and were verified rather than implemented:** it asked for a waiter-leak fix and for the download channel drain to be moved into a `finally`, both of which RemEx-w9lj had already done. **And the review found a leak in the leak fix** — the new activity map was written through the dictionary indexer, which *inserts*, from the receive path, so a chunk arriving after teardown resurrected an entry nothing would ever remove. That is the ordinary cancelled-download path, since the peer keeps streaming until it processes the cancel. It now writes through `TryGetValue` into a `StrongBox`, which cannot insert. Timestamps come from `Stopwatch`, not the wall clock, so an NTP correction or the RTC-in-local-time adjustment a dual-boot machine makes cannot instantly fail a healthy transfer. **Copy and move are deliberately still unbounded**, because an idle watchdog needs something to observe and they have nothing: `FileManageRequest`→`Response` is a single round trip, the peer copies the whole file before replying, and no manage-progress message exists anywhere in the protocol — so a "watchdog" there would be exactly the wall-clock deadline this bead exists to avoid. That needs a new `file_manage_progress` message and a coordinated PC+Android release, filed as RemEx-hl2v. 811 tests green. (`FileTransferClient.cs`; RemEx-l519, partial.)
- **Two desktop tests could never have passed on Linux, and nobody knew because nobody had run them there.** Both were found by actually running the suite under WSL while verifying the new CI workflow, rather than by reading code. `RemexSavefileServiceTests` built launcher entries pointing at `C:\Windows\System32\notepad.exe` and then asserted there were no warnings — but `ImportAsync` correctly warns when a launcher points at a path that no longer exists, so on Linux it failed. **The product was right and the test's premise was wrong**, which is the more useful way round: the fix creates real files in a temp directory instead, which also drops a hidden dependency on the host machine happening to have Notepad. `AboutViewModelChangelogTests` found `docs/CHANGELOG.md` by walking up from the test assembly's location, silently coupling it to build output living inside the repo tree — build with `--artifacts-path` pointing anywhere else and it failed with an error saying nothing about the change that caused it. It is now anchored to its own source file via `[CallerFilePath]`, with the directory walk kept as a fallback for the opposite case (an assembly built on one machine and run on another). Worth recording that the second of these initially *looked* like a Linux failure and was not — it was an artifact of the `--artifacts-path` used to keep the WSL build out of the Windows one, and reporting it as a cross-platform bug would have sent someone chasing nothing. With both fixed, the Linux CI leg now runs the Core and Desktop suites — 361 tests — verified passing under WSL with the exact build-then-`--no-build` sequence CI uses, and with artifacts redirected outside the repo, the condition that used to break it. `remex.agent.tests` stays Windows-only for now on an honest technicality rather than a defect: `remex.agent` carries a `Microsoft.AspNetCore.App` framework reference, so its test host needs the ASP.NET Core shared runtime, and the Arch WSL image used for validation ships only `Microsoft.NETCore.App`. A hosted runner almost certainly has it — but "almost certainly" is not the standard the rest of that workflow was held to, so it is RemEx-a83w with a one-job recipe to confirm it. (`RemexSavefileServiceTests.cs`, `AboutViewModelChangelogTests.cs`, `.github/workflows/dotnet.yml`; RemEx-6i1l.)
- **The Canvas "Reboot to UEFI" button rebooted the PC into firmware settings with no confirmation at all.** One click, no prompt — while the command palette and the Android card both gated the *identical* command behind `Confirm_RebootUefi_*`. It is arguably the least recoverable action in the app: it discards unsaved work and leaves the machine sitting in firmware setup until someone is physically present to leave it. The earlier destructive-action audit (RemEx-6p1f) had covered kill-process, launcher-delete, remove-shared-folder, revoke-trust and clear-logs, and missed this one. The button now confirms, reusing the three `Confirm_RebootUefi_*` strings that already exist in all 9 locales — no new strings, and it inherits the stranded-connection warning RemEx-mkq1 added to that message. The guard sits at the **caller**, not on `ConnectionViewModel.RestartToUefiAsync`, because the palette already confirms before invoking that command and guarding the command itself would prompt twice; confirming at the caller is what every other destructive action here does. It fails closed per `ConfirmationDialogHost`'s contract: an unwired view-model, or a view with no visible parent window, declines the reboot rather than performing it unconfirmed. **The more valuable finding was about verification, not the fix.** `dotnet build` reports a false pass after a `.axaml` edit — Avalonia's XAML compilation is skipped by MSBuild's incremental up-to-date check, and `dotnet test` then runs the stale assembly and passes too. The first version of this change moved the binding up a scope and got "Build succeeded, 0 Errors" from two plain builds; `-t:Rebuild` produced `AVLN2000: Unable to resolve property or method of name 'RestartToUefiCommand' on type 'CanvasCardViewModel'`. An earlier run *had* reported `1 Error(s)` and was dismissed as a transient file lock — it was the only honest run of the three, and an inconsistent error count across identical deterministic commands is the tell, not noise. The binding needed the `$parent[UserControl].((vm:CanvasDashboardViewModel)DataContext)` escape hatch this file already uses twice, because the enclosing `<DataTemplate x:DataType="vm:CanvasCardViewModel">` overrides the root `x:DataType` — which is also why the sibling buttons kept working, since `CanvasCardViewModel` has its own `Connection` property and they were never reaching the dashboard view-model at all. That trap is now persisted in the project's memory store, and the absence of any .NET build/test CI — which would have shared the same blind spot — is filed as RemEx-jx7r. Verified with a full `-t:Rebuild` and 811 tests against fresh assemblies. (`CanvasDashboardViewModel.cs`, `CanvasView.axaml`, `CanvasView.axaml.cs`; RemEx-5vcb.)
- **Nine power actions ran from the command palette in complete silence, whether they worked or not.** `ConnectionViewModel`'s `[RelayCommand]`s discarded the `(ok, message)` tuple `SendCommandAsync` returns, and the palette invokes those commands directly — so Ctrl+Shift+P then Shutdown gave no indication of anything, **including when the command failed with "Not connected"**, which is precisely the case a user needs to be told about. Lock, Sleep, Hibernate, Sign Out, Shutdown, Force Shutdown, Restart, Force Restart and Restart-to-UEFI now report both directions into the shell status line. Fixed at `ConnectionViewModel` rather than in the palette, so it also covers the Canvas lock button, the other caller of these commands. **No new localized strings were needed** — the bead assumed one would be, but every action already had a `Wol_*Sent` key because `RemoteViewModel` uses the same set, so nine languages gained working feedback with zero translation work. **The change also closes a second bug nobody had noticed:** `PingPongHandler` deliberately skips the Home activity feed for loopback commands, on the documented grounds that they are "already recorded desktop-side" — but that was only ever true of the Remote screen's path. Palette- and Canvas-initiated power actions were recorded *nowhere*: the host skipped them as loopback and the view-model discarded the result. Recording on success here makes the host's existing assumption true for every path. Two findings from review are filed rather than folded in: the Canvas "Reboot to UEFI" button has **no confirmation at all** while the palette and Android both gate the same command (RemEx-5vcb), and the connection status *dot* takes its accessible name from `StatusText`, so a screen reader will now announce "✅ Shutdown sent" as the name of the connection indicator (RemEx-x12a). Wake-on-LAN, the tenth palette power entry, is deliberately excluded: it sends no MAC address at all — the code comment concedes it "might use defaults" — so a success message there would have been a confident lie (RemEx-paa7). 811 tests green. (`ConnectionViewModel.cs`; RemEx-diyv.)
- **Restarting or shutting down the PC from your phone strands the connection, and five confirmations never said so.** `remex.agent` is started by a per-user logon task, so a restart returns the machine to the sign-in screen where that task has not fired — the phone cannot reconnect until someone signs in physically. `Confirm_SignOut_Message` already warned about exactly this; the restart family said only "will restart, unsaved work lost". Worse for shutdown, because **RemEx ships Wake-on-LAN** on the Remote page and on the Android widget, so "shut it down now, wake it with RemEx later" is a plan the product actively invites and that cannot work: WoL powers the machine on, it boots to the sign-in screen, the agent never starts. All five now carry the consequence — including `Confirm_ForceShutdown_Message`, which the bead's own inventory of four had missed. **The clause is lifted per locale from each file's existing `Confirm_SignOut_Message` rather than newly translated**, so nine languages get one phrasing for one consequence instead of a second way of saying it; only the Wake-on-LAN lead-in is new content, since nothing existing states it. The premise was re-verified before writing, as the bead demanded, by inspecting the *registered* task rather than the script that creates it — `MSFT_TaskLogonTrigger` scoped to one user with `LogonType=Interactive` — and by ruling out every other start path: no service, no `Run`/`RunOnce` entry, no Startup shortcut. Review then closed the one hole in that check, confirming Linux behaves the same way (`installer/linux/agent-install.sh` writes a per-user XDG autostart entry and actively disables the legacy service unit) and that the installer *deliberately declines* to create a Run key — which generalises better than a machine-local check, since it shows no other start path is ever created rather than merely that this machine lacks one. A `<remarks>` block now guards `WindowsSystemCommandService`: switching the restart flags to `shutdown /g` would arm Windows Automatic Restart Sign-On, silently making all five strings false in nine languages with no test failure. Review also caught the one locale where the lifted clause dragged its article along — pt-BR read `: O RemEx` where Portuguese takes lowercase after a colon — and corrected an inaccurate claim of mine, that French's U+202F "matches the file convention": it is in fact the minority there (23 uses against 54 plain spaces), so it is kept as the typographically correct choice, not as the prevailing one. The identical Android gap is filed as RemEx-nhc8, and the FAQ entry that still implies WoL restores access as RemEx-0j6z. 811 tests green. (9 resx files, `WindowsSystemCommandService.cs`; RemEx-mkq1.)
- **Arming a destructive power command could push Confirm/Cancel off-screen with no hint they existed.** Tapping Select flips a command card to its confirm face and grows it downward — consequence line, timer field, then the buttons — but the `LazyVerticalGrid` never followed. On a card in the last visible row, with Ukrainian or Hindi text at font scale 2.0, the buttons could sit entirely below the fold while a destructive action was already armed. The card now scrolls its Confirm/Cancel row into view, on every confirmable card rather than only the one that made it obvious. Deliberately *not* fixed by capping the consequence line with `maxLines` — truncating a safety warning is worse than making the user scroll. **The obvious implementation of this is a silent no-op, which is worth recording because it compiles, lints, and passes the fatal `lintVitalRelease` gate while scrolling nothing.** `ContentInViewNode.bringChildIntoView` opens with `if (localRect()?.isMaxVisible() != false) return` and is one-shot with no retry path; `LaunchedEffect` bodies drain in the Choreographer animation phase *before* that frame's measure and layout, so a request made when the confirm face enters composition runs against a Row that has never been measured, degenerates to a zero-height rect at the card's top-left, and — because the card's top is on screen by definition in exactly the last-row case this bug is about — is judged already-visible and dropped. It is also a race, so it can appear to work intermittently. The request is therefore now driven from two places that both run after layout: `onSizeChanged`, and `animateContentSize`'s `finishedListener`. The second is the one that must exist, because while the card is still growing the grid's scroll extent is still short and an under-consumed scroll makes `ContentInViewNode` cancel the request outright rather than resume it. A `DisposableEffect` resets the measured size when the confirm face is disposed, so the timing holds on re-arm and not merely on the first arm. The request passes an explicit rect extended below the row by a new shared `FloatingToolbarOcclusion` constant — which now also supplies the grid's bottom `contentPadding`, so the two measurements of the same thing cannot drift — because the default request stops as soon as the trailing edge reaches the viewport bottom, which is exactly where the floating toolbar sits. **This is committed but not verified on a device** (`adb devices` is empty), so RemEx-tgl1 stays open and deferred rather than closed, carrying the test that would close it: a `ComposeTestRule` case at font scale 2.0 that arms the last confirmable card and asserts the Confirm button is displayed — exercising arm → cancel → **re-arm**, since the timing defect above lives only on the re-arm path and a single-arm test would pass while it was broken. (`RemoteControlScreen.kt`; RemEx-tgl1, partial.)
- **The six remaining Personalization sliders read a bare number to TalkBack, with no name and no unit.** RemEx-porq fixed the card-opacity slider; the other six announced a raw float — "210.0" for hue, "3.0" for a card shape — while the human-readable label sat in a separate, unrelated semantics node. Each now carries `contentDescription` (the control's name) and `stateDescription` (its value with meaning): hue as "210°", chroma as "42", contrast as "-0,50", corner radius as "12dp", font scale as "115%", and each shape slider as the shape's actual **name** — "Circle" tells a blind user what they selected; "3.0" does not. One fix covers every visible shape slider, since they are all one composable. The value-bearing labels are cleared with `clearAndSetSemantics` so the value is not announced twice. **The contrast slider turned out to have a second defect nobody had filed:** Compose's own `formatForSemantics` is locale-independent, so French, Polish and Ukrainian users saw a label reading `0,55` while TalkBack said `0.55`; passing one string to both now makes them structurally incapable of disagreeing. The five accessible names were **derived programmatically** from each locale's own existing label — every one has the shape `<name><separator><value>`, so a regex strips the value off, which also handles French's U+202F narrow no-break space. That is deliberate: the bead records that hand-writing these produced three wrong values last time. Two format-only keys were added (`cd_degree_value`, `cd_dp_value`) and parity went 752 → 759 per locale; a third, an identity `%1$d`, was **removed again during review** as a permanent nine-file translation obligation with no translatable content. Review also verified the mechanism rather than trusting the code comment asserting it, decompiling `material3-android` 1.5.0-alpha24 and `compose-ui` 1.12.0-beta02 to confirm that semantics collapse walks tail→head with a plain overwrite, so the outer `stateDescription` genuinely wins — without that, the whole change would have been a silent no-op. `assembleRelease` passes including the fatal `lintVitalRelease` gate. One pre-existing defect the review exposed is filed rather than fixed: the row `Text` does **not** name the reset button beside it, because that `Row` sets no `mergeDescendants`, so all six reset buttons still announce identically (RemEx-pmo4). Note the coupling `cd_dp_value` creates — it mirrors `personalization_corner_base` byte-for-byte, so if that label is ever plain-Englished away from "dp", this must move with it. (`PersonalizationScreen.kt`, 9 `strings.xml`; RemEx-qiz5.)
- **Four Remote Desktop failures showed the user a raw .NET exception message, trimmed mid-word.** Starting a stream, loading the display list, listing windows and running a window action each did `string.Format(…, ex.Message)` into the status bar — and that bar's first column is floored at 140px with `CharacterEllipsis` (RemEx-9a46), so what a user actually got was a technical English fragment cut off partway through. All four now log the exception and show a short localized sentence with a next step ("Could not start the stream. Try reconnecting."), matching what RemEx-p9fn / RemEx-ixsk already did for the other error families. **The exceptions were not being logged at all before**, so this adds diagnostic information at the same time as it removes the unreadable text — the detail moves to somewhere it can actually be read rather than being discarded. `Status_StreamFailedFormat` and `Status_LoadDisplaysFailedFormat` are renamed to drop the `Format` suffix: once the placeholder is gone, that name is actively misleading, and keeping it would have created two fresh instances of the naming trap RemEx-udq9 exists to clear. The rename is exactly the kind of change that silently shows users a raw key name if one reference is missed, which is what the check's axis 3 is for — it passes, as does the placeholder axis that would catch a locale left holding an orphaned `{0}`. The logging shape was settled once and applied to all five sites in the file, including retrofitting the one added by RemEx-ii6a, rather than being decided twice: failures are identified by `{DisplayId}`/`{CaptureMode}` for display operations, `{WindowAction}`/`{WindowId}` for a window action, `{WindowSearchText}` for the window query (which has no window id to name), and `{HostAddress}` for the display-list query. The window id is captured *before* the call rather than read in the `catch`, because `ApplyWindowResult` re-resolves the selection from the refreshed list and can fall back to a different window — logging it afterwards would name a window the action never ran on, which is the same misleading-information defect this bead exists to fix. 811 tests green. (`RemoteDesktopViewModel.cs`, 9 resx files; RemEx-80xg.)
- **The Remote Desktop panel showed three pieces of hardcoded English, one of them with a raw .NET exception message appended.** `RemoteDesktopViewModel` set `StatusText = $"Display switch failed: {ex.Message}"` — English for every user, in the exact TextBlock RemEx-9a46 floored at 140px with `CharacterEllipsis`, so a Polish or Ukrainian user got an untranslated technical sentence *trimmed mid-word*. It now logs the exception via `_logger.LogError` and shows a short localized message; the user strictly gains, because that exception was previously **never logged at all** while the UI text was already being ellipsized. **The bead's own suggested grep was the wrong one, and the broader sweep is the useful part:** it proposed searching for `StatusText = $"`, which structurally cannot match an expression-bodied property — and `WindowControlCapabilityText` (live, bound at `RemoteDesktopView.axaml:177`) had **both** branches hardcoded in English, plus "this host", the pre-rename word. All three sites are now localized via four new keys across all 9 `.resx` files. Review then caught a defect in the fix itself, on the exact point flagged as risky: a single shared `"unknown"` fallback was being substituted into two different sentence frames, and while a bare adverb reads fine inside parentheses — "Window control ready (unknown)" — it is outright ungrammatical after a preposition, because Ukrainian `невідомо` and Turkish `bilinmiyor` are an adverb and a finite verb, and `через`/`ile` require a nominal. The fallback is now two keys: a noun phrase for the `via {0}` frame and the bare word for the parenthetical one. The remaining defect in that file is filed rather than folded in — four sites still interpolate raw `ex.Message` into localized `*Format` keys (RemEx-80xg), a list the review corrected from three, since the original had been assembled from key names instead of from the values that actually matter. Reviewed by Opus (FAIL, then fixed). 811 tests green. (`RemoteDesktopViewModel.cs`, 9 resx files; RemEx-ii6a.)
- **Spanish users saw a literal "{0}" printed on the canvas selection bar.** `Canvas_SelectedLabel` was `"Seleccionado: {0}"` in `Strings.es.resx` where English is just `"selected"` with no placeholder — and the key is bound plainly (`CanvasView.axaml:437`, `Text="{local:Localize …}"`) with no `string.Format` anywhere, so nothing ever substituted it and the two characters `{0}` rendered on screen. The value was wrong in shape as well as content: lines 436–437 put `{Binding SelectionCount}` and this label in a horizontal `StackPanel`, so English composes "3 selected" and the label is a **suffix**, not the standalone sentence with its own colon that the Spanish had been written as. Now `seleccionadas`, matching the single invariant suffix word all eight other locales use. The gender is the part worth recording: review caught that `seleccionados` — the obvious masculine default — was wrong, because the things being counted are `SelectedCards` and Spanish calls them *tarjetas*, feminine.
